story:
Hunter stared at the fractions on the board, three fourths minus one sixth, and felt like his brain had run into a locked door. In the desk next to him, Priya was already scribbling, and that only made it worse, because Priya had once finished a math worksheet before the tardy bell finished ringing.

"You're overthinking it," Priya whispered. "You just need a number both bottoms go into. Twelve works. Three fourths is nine twelfths, and one sixth is two twelfths."

"Ninth twelfths minus two twelfths," Hunter muttered, and the door in his brain swung open so fast he almost laughed. Seven twelfths. It was like the fractions had been standing on mismatched stairs, and someone finally built them a matching step.

Then Mrs. Okafor flipped to the last problem, a bonus worth two points, and everything got strange again. It showed two straight lines crossing like a giant X. One angle was labeled 50 degrees, and the question asked which two triangles in the figure were congruent and how you could justify it. Hunter could see two triangles hiding in the X, and he knew two of their sides matched the sides of the lines, but side-angle-side needed an angle in the middle, and the angle he needed was sitting in a blank, unlabeled corner.

He tried measuring with his pencil, tilting it along the lines, but a pencil is not a protractor, no matter how confident it looks. He chewed his eraser. He drew a tiny mustache on the X out of pure frustration, which made Priya snort so loudly that Mrs. Okafor raised one eyebrow from across the room.

Then he stopped. The labeled 50-degree angle was at the top of the X, and the angle he needed was at the bottom, directly across the crossing point. Same lines, straight across. He checked the top pair too, the two side angles, and squinted until the paper smelled like pencil shavings and his own determination. They looked like twins. All of them looked like twins, in pairs, straight across from each other.

"Vertical angles," Hunter whispered, pointing. "The opposite ones across the crossing point. They're always equal. My angle's been standing right there the whole time, wearing the same fifty degrees."

"You gave the X a mustache and then solved the problem," Priya said. "That's not a legitimate strategy. That's luck."

"It's a prescription for success," Hunter said, and wrote side-angle-side, because the equal vertical angles gave him exactly the angle he needed, and the two triangles clicked together in his mind like an Oreo.

Mrs. Okafor walked past, glanced at his paper, and drew a small check mark shaped like a smile. Hunter added one more tiny detail to the X: a top hat.

Mason stood at the kitchen counter pretending the cereal boxes were an audience. His speech teacher wanted a two-minute speech with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and he had exactly one point so far, which was about his grandfather's beehives. His little sister Poppy crawled under the table with a feather boa and announced, "I'm a famous explorer. You're my guide."

"I'm not a guide," Mason said. "I'm practicing a speech." Poppy's face went flat, and the kitchen went quiet except for the refrigerator hum. He tried again. "Fine. I'm a guide. Watch out for the lava."

"That's better," Poppy said, poking her boa over the edge of the table.

Later, sprawled on the living room carpet, Mason watched a video on Mom's tablet about improv. Two actors pretended to row a boat, and one said, "We're not on a boat." The scene died right there. The audience went quiet, the same silence as the kitchen. Mason sat up. He rewound and watched again, and this time he noticed a pattern: whenever a player rejected the other player's offer, everything stopped, and whenever a player said yes to the offer, the scene zoomed forward like a sled downhill. He tested it out loud with Poppy, saying "no, that's not my dog" to her stuffed puppy, and the game collapsed. Then he said "yes, my dog, and he's invisible," and Poppy shrieked with laughter and generated three new ideas in ten seconds.

"So that's called blocking," Mason told her at dinner, "when you reject somebody's offer." Poppy nodded and kept eating her peas.

In bed, he thought about how the same thing might work in speeches. An opening hook was like accepting the audience's offer, pulling them in instead of leaving them quiet. He wasn't sure yet which of his three points should come first, or whether his grandfather, the most influential beekeeper he knew, belonged in the hook or the closing. He'd have to try it both ways tomorrow.

The next morning he set the cereal boxes in a strict hierarchy, tallest in the back, and took a breath. "Raise your hand if you've ever been stung," he began.

Hazel spread Grandpa's enormous atlas across the kitchen table so fast that it knocked over the salt shaker, and Nutmeg the cat bolted from the room like a gray turbine spinning out of control. On Monday she had to explain to her whole class why the Roman Empire split in two and then fell, and everyone said use the map, but nobody said how. The empire's borders sprawled across the paper like a giant octopus, and she needed to make it make sense.

"Do you want tea while you stare at that thing?" Grandpa asked. "You look like you're trying to digest the whole empire."

"I'm digesting the borders," Hazel said, tapping the squiggly lines. "Rome got too big to guard, so they split it in half, east and west. Then barbarian groups pushed in from outside the borders." She frowned. "But why did the pushes work? Rome had a huge army."

Grandpa just shrugged and went back to his crossword, which was his way of saying figure it out yourself. Hazel leaned close to the map. The paper smelled like dust and old coffee, and the afternoon light through the window made the yellowed page almost luminous. Then she remembered something from the library book she'd read last week.

In her mind she was back in the library's squishy orange chair, reading about March 1936, when Hitler sent German troops into the Rhineland. That broke the Treaty of Versailles, and she had stared at that sentence so long the librarian asked if she was asleep. The book said Britain and France did not use force to stop him. Nobody stopped the first rule-break. Hazel sat bolt upright at the kitchen table. That was it. The first push into Roman land had gone unanswered, so the tribes along the borders pushed harder, again and again, until the whole western half came apart. It was like when Dario swiped one of Ms. Pratt's dry-erase markers in October and nothing happened, so in November he tried to swipe the whole projector.

"Grandpa, I've got it!" she shouted. "Nobody stopped the first push, so there were bigger ones, and Rome broke!" She grabbed a red marker and traced the borders, then drew fat arrows crashing through them from the outside.

"Well," Grandpa said, peering over his glasses, "please don't arrow my atlas to pieces before dinner."

Hazel grinned and held the marker over the western half like a tiny Roman emperor deciding its fate. "Too late. The western empire falls first, right here."

Luke had ten minutes before the coding club demo, and his program still had two problems. The first was the times table. Ms. Ruiz had never shown them how to print a whole table, only single lines, so Luke decided to draft it himself, guessing that a loop might repeat the same line over and over with different numbers. He typed "for n in range(1, 13):" and then a print statement that multiplied n by whatever number the user typed. When he ran it, the screen filled with rows, one through twelve, all correct. He actually punched the air.

The second problem was the big blue heading at the top of his page, which kept sliding back to the left no matter what he did. He had a rule near the top that moved the heading to the center, and it worked for a second, then it snapped left again. Behind him, Priya was snacking on cheese crackers and watching him glare at the screen. "You look like the laptop stole your lunch," she said.

"Watch this," Luke said. He centered the heading, saved, and refreshed. It jumped left. He did it again. Left again. "The computer is messing with me."

"Maybe it's just doing exactly what you told it," Priya said, brushing cracker dust off the keyboard.

Luke scrolled down and found it: another rule, way at the bottom, that put the heading back at the left. He deleted it, and the heading stayed centered. "Two rules were fighting over the same thing, and the one written later won. Every time." He said the word out loud, testing it. "The cascade. That's what it's called."

"So your assumption was that the top rule was in charge?" Priya said.

"Yeah. And I was being gullible about my own code." He saved the file twice, just in case, and raised his hand. "Ms. Ruiz, I'm ready to demo."

Priya held up a cracker like a microphone. "Give 'em the sixes, Luke."

Tristan held his mother's note in one hand and the quarters in the other. The note, folded twice, read: "Tristan, you're ten now. Walk to Duffy's Corner Store alone. Buy one gallon of milk. Count your change before you leave the counter. Then come straight back to Spin Cycle Laundry. Love, Mom." His heart thumped like the dryer on high. He had never gone anywhere alone before, and Duffy's was a whole block and a half away.

He was halfway out the door when Mrs. Okafor, who folded towels every Saturday in the corner seat, dropped a bottle. Tristan lunged to catch it and the edge of a laundry basket gashed his thumb, a thin red line that welled up fast. Mrs. Okafor reached into her bag and held up a brown bottle. "Fizzy stuff," she said. "Want it?"

Tristan stared at the label. Something in his brain lit up, the same feeling he got when a math problem suddenly made sense. He remembered the first-aid pamphlet taped inside the nurse's office door, the one he had read twice while waiting for his hearing test. He had thought the rule was strange at the time, because everybody in movies poured the fizzing bottle on everything. "No thanks," he said. "The nurse's guide says not to clean a cut with hydrogen peroxide. It says the same thing about iodine, too. Both of them can irritate the wound."

Mrs. Okafor raised her eyebrows and put the bottle away. "Then what, smart guy?"

"Running water and a bandage." He rinsed his thumb at the utility sink, and Mrs. Okafor smoothed the bandage on so it made a neat symmetry down his thumb, both ends even. "There," she said. "Modified bandage, modified hero."

He raced to Duffy's, got the milk, and counted his change right at the register, twice, because the first time he was so excited he dropped a nickel. It was all there. Back at the laundromat he slid the receipt across Mrs. Okafor's folding table like a detective presenting evidence. "Not one penny off," he announced.

She laughed and clapped. "See? And you didn't let me poison you with peroxide."

"You weren't going to poison me," Tristan said. "But you were a little biased toward the fizzy stuff." He hoisted the milk onto the counter beside his mother's note and added, in careful letters at the bottom, "Mission complete."

Michael had the whole afternoon, a bag of pretzels for their carbohydrate value according to his sister, and one job: find the theme of Romeo and Juliet and back it up with a quotation. He curled into the reading nook by the window with the book, a sticky note, and a pencil he tapped against his knee. The theme part he could guess. Love, maybe. Or how fast things go wrong when people hate each other. The quotation was the problem.

He flipped to the balcony scene and started copying a line, then stopped. "But soft, what light through yonder window breaks?" Fine. Then Romeo kept saying thou and thee in the same breath, sometimes one, sometimes the other. Why would Shakespeare switch? He read the lines aloud, quietly, hearing the pattern but not catching it. He began to assume the words were interchangeable, like two ways of saying the same thing, but that felt sloppy. Shakespeare was careful about everything else.

A memory surfaced from two summers ago, when his grandmother read him nursery rhymes on her porch swing. She had pointed at a line and asked, "Notice anything?" He had noticed that the rhymes bumped along like a sidewalk crack under a bike wheel. She'd said, "Noticing is the whole game," and let him find the rest himself.

He played the game now, writing thou and thee in columns wherever they appeared. After a minute he saw it. Thou came when Romeo was doing something, "thou art," "dost thou." Thee came when something was done to the person, "I love thee," "with thee." His sister Zoe leaned into the nook, chewing a pretzel. "Still on that?"

"Watch. Say 'I love she.'"

"I love her."

"So her is the object form of she. Thee is the object form of thou, like me is the object form of I."

"Okay, so 'I love thee' means 'I love you.' Duh."

"Not duh. Significant." He underlined the phrase in his book and wrote his theme sentence at the top of the sticky note. Then he read the quotation out loud, both ways, once in Shakespeare's words and once in his own, and grinned at how they matched. "Zoe, listen to this part."

Maeva slid her flashcards across the table and wished, for the third time that morning, that words in Mandarin came with labels you could read. In fifteen minutes each student had to stand up in Mrs. Trent's language class and describe their family and pets in full sentences, and Maeva's sentences kept falling apart on one word. Her hamster, Biscuit, sat in a little cage on the shelf, and she wanted to say that he always turned left before he ran on his wheel, but every time she said the direction word, her partner Priya made a face.

"Zuǒ," Maeva tried again, flat as a pancake.

Priya shook her head so fast her braids bounced. "That's not it. It sounds wrong, like you're saying a different word entirely."

"But which different word?" Maeva said. Priya only shrugged; her whole goal this morning was to earn the sticker for perfect pronunciation, and she was not going to waste her practice time guessing at somebody else's mistakes.

Maeva closed her eyes and thought of last summer, walking to the market with her grandfather in Kunming. He had pointed at every corner and said "zuǒ" when they turned left toward the vegetable stalls, and "yòu" when they cut right at the tea shop. She had repeated them back, and he had laughed and corrected her over and over, the same two words, until her mouth finally found them. What she could not see now was what had changed between then and today. Maybe her memory had stored the sound wrong, like an entry typed into a database with one letter missing. Or maybe the word itself had a shape she was flattening.

She had one idea left, and it felt impulsive, but the clock on the wall said nine minutes. She stood up, held out her left hand, and sang the word the way her grandfather had sung it at the market, letting her voice dip down as she pointed left, then rise as she swung to the right and said "yòu." Her voice going down for one word and up for the other, that was the pattern. Each direction had its own melody, and she had been squashing both of them flat.

"Zuǒ," she said, pointing left, voice falling like a step down. "Yòu," pointing right, voice lifting.

Priya's mouth dropped open. "Say it again." Maeva did, and Priya repeated it back, then laughed. "I've been saying it wrong too. All week. I was going to ask for the pronunciation sticker and I didn't even have it." She pushed her own flashcards aside, gave up on drilling alone, and turned her chair to face Maeva. "Teach me the pointing thing. Both words, the way you just did them."

"Five minutes," Mrs. Trent called from the front.

Maeva held up her left hand and waited for Priya to copy her. "Zuǒ," she said, and her voice stepped down.

Grandpa kept a price notebook, which Jessica thought was the most retired thing a person could do. Every Saturday he wrote down what strawberries cost at the farm stand, and he let her come along to do the writing. In June the berries were two dollars a basket, fat and red and stacked in pyramids. By late July the stand had tables and tables of them, baskets spilling over, and the sign said a dollar fifty. "Write it down exactly," Grandpa said. "The truth doesn't care how we feel about it."

Jessica's cousin Dana was there too, sulking on the porch with a letter from a card company. "I stopped using it in April," Dana said. "How is the balance bigger than it was in May?" Jessica was working on an answer to that, sort of, because Grandpa had offered her a deal: figure out both mysteries, the strawberries and the debt, and he would fund a strawberry shortcake with the summer-cheap berries. A shortcake was a real, edible reason to think.

The strawberry half she got first. More berries at the stand meant the farmer dropped the price to move them all; in winter, when the fields were frozen and basically extinct until spring, a basket cost five dollars because almost nobody had any. Nobody could see the invisible rule doing it. You only saw prices. Grandpa had pointed at the empty winter field last December and said, "There's your teacher," which was typical Grandpa.

Dana's problem was trickier because the letter just showed a bigger number, no reasons. Jessica asked to see the older statements, and Dana dug them out of her backpack in the guest room, where the window was drafty even in July because the old house had single-pane glass and nobody had gotten around to fixing the insulation. Jessica laid the statements in a row like strawberry baskets. May, June, July. The balance grew a little each month even though Dana had bought nothing with it since April.

"So the interest they charge gets added to what you owe," Jessica said slowly, watching the numbers line up, "and then next month they charge interest on that too. On the interest." Dana stared at the row of statements. "That's why it's going up faster than I pay it down." Jessica nodded. It was like the strawberry rule, another invisible thing you could only see by its footprints.

The shortcake happened on Sunday, built from dollar-fifty berries and Grandpa's heavy alloy mixing bowl, the one that had survived three decades of dropping. Dana brought her statements to the table and announced she was paying the whole balance off before August. Grandpa served the berries and said, "Winter prices are coming, one way or another." Jessica took the biggest slice.

Alexia stood at the podium with three minutes left before her turn and zero speeches in her head. Her partner, Ravi, kept sliding his notes toward her like they were treasure maps, but every card said the same thing: "Zoos are bad," "Zoos cost too much," "Zoos make animals sad." Those weren't arguments. They were opinions wearing arguments' coats. The judges at Table Two had already flipped their ballots face down twice during the morning round, which Alexia decided was their way of saying hurry up.

"We need a hook," she whispered. "Something with teeth." Ravi suggested starting with the word "imagine," which everyone in the history of debate tournaments had already done. Alexia scanned the cafeteria instead. A vending machine hummed in the corner, its candy bars lined up like prisoners behind glass, and suddenly she saw it: a zoo was a vending machine for animals. People paid quarters to look. That was her hook. Now she needed three points, and she had exactly one: money.

She flipped through Ravi's cards looking for evidence and found nothing but feelings. She remembered their coach's favorite question, the one she'd written on her hand at the last practice: "What's your claim, and where are your grounds?" The claim was the point being argued, and the grounds were the evidence behind it. Ravi had been stacking claims all day like pancakes with no syrup, and the judges had noticed. So Alexia made a rule for herself: every sentence she spoke would have a shadow, and the shadow had to be a number, a study, or something a zookeeper had actually said. She would monitor herself, catching every naked opinion before it escaped her mouth.

When the moderator called her name, Alexia took a breath and began. "A zoo is a vending machine, and we are paying to watch it hum." She heard a judge's pen stop moving, which felt like a small lightning strike. Point one: money, with the city's budget figures Ravi found on his phone. Point two: space, with the size of a polar bear's exhibit compared to its range in the wild. Point three: the breeding programs, because she had to be fair to the other side and show she knew their best card. She closed with the vending machine again, unplugged.

At the end, the judge at Table Two said, "Finally, some grounds behind those claims." Ravi grinned and whispered that next round he wanted the frugal budget argument, since democracy in debate, like two whole minutes per speech, was only fair if both sides came armed with evidence. Alexia picked up his stack of naked opinion cards, walked to the recycling bin, and dropped them in one at a time, like coins into a machine.

Zoe had been saving for a new bike since September, and today the bank statement finally arrived. She tore it open right there in the lobby, because waiting until she got home seemed like a punishment nobody had ordered. Her grandfather, who had driven her, was busy arguing with a teller about a fee, so Zoe sat down on the granite bench by the window, the one freckled with gray lichen, and spread the statements from the last three years across her knees.

Something was wrong. Or something was weird, which at Zoe's house amounted to nearly the same thing. She had put in one hundred dollars when she opened the account. The first year, the bank added three dollars. She'd expected the second year to be bigger, because now she had one hundred and three dollars earning money. It wasn't. It was three dollars again. Same the third year. Exactly three dollars, every single time, like a bird that refused to learn a new song.

"You look like you're solving a crime," her grandfather said, dropping onto the bench beside her. He was still holding his fee argument like a dog holding a bone, clearly planning to recount it to the teller's manager.

"It added three dollars every year. Exactly three." She showed him the statements. "Why doesn't it grow? Strawberries grow. That's my project for school, explaining strawberries. In June they're two dollars a basket because everybody's got them, and in January they're six because nobody does. More of something, price goes down. Less of something, price goes up. That part makes sense. This doesn't."

Her grandfather tapped the top statement with one finger. "That's simple interest. It's paid only on the original amount you deposited. The original amount is called the principal." He stood up, straightened his jacket, and went back to battle with the teller, leaving Zoe staring at the word on the page.

So it wasn't broken. It wasn't even stubborn, exactly, though "obstinate" was the word she'd put in her vocabulary list last week and this seemed like a fine place to use it. The interest only looked at the hundred dollars, never at the extra three, never at the pile that came after. Zoe did the math on the back of the envelope: one hundred, one hundred three, one hundred six, one hundred nine. A staircase with steps exactly the same height, going up and up at three dollars a year, while her bike sat in the shop window, unimpressed.

She folded the statements, walked to the counter beside her grandfather, and slid her papers toward the teller. "Excuse me," she said. "Is there an account where the interest isn't like this one?"

Nathan held the recipe card in one hand and a bag of walnuts in the other. The card said to chop the walnuts fine, stir them into the batter, and bake the muffins at three hundred seventy-five degrees, but the very first line said something he had never done before: preheat the oven. At home his dad always did that part. Here at the campsite, where his family had set up a little propane oven on the picnic table, the whole recipe was his job from start to finish, because he had promised to make breakfast muffins all by himself tomorrow morning. Tonight was the practice run.

He turned the oven dial and listened to the click and hiss of gas catching. While it heated, he spread his cutting board on the metal table and set a handful of walnuts on it. The first chop sent the board skidding sideways, and the knife clattered down a inch from his thumb. He tried again, pressing more gently, but the board slid again, and a walnut shot off onto the gravel.

Nathan stared at the board. The table was smooth and the board was smooth, and somehow the two smooth things could not hold still together. He noticed a pattern: the board only skidded when he pushed down hard, not when he lifted the knife. It was like the table had a layer of something invisible under the board, letting it glide. He crouched down and looked at the underside of the board, but there was nothing to see, which meant the cause was something he could not look at directly.

He had to test an idea instead. He remembered how his sneakers squeaked on the wet rocks by the lake but gripped the dry ones, and he wondered whether wet might grip here too. He dunked his dish towel in the water jug, wrung it out so it was damp, and spread it flat on the table. Then he set the board on top of the damp towel and chopped.

The board did not move. Not on the first cut, not on the fifteenth. He pressed down as hard as he dared, and the board stayed planted. "A damp cloth under the cutting board stops it from sliding," he said out loud, mostly to the gray lichen creeping over the rock behind the table, because there was nobody else to tell yet. The nuts chopped small and even, and the sound of the knife traveled cleanly through the quiet camp, no clatter, no skid.

His little sister padded out of the tent in her pajamas, following the smell of batter. "Are those almost muffins?" she asked, pointing at the bowl where the walnuts had already disappeared into the batter.

"Almost," Nathan said, and slid the tray into the hot oven. "Give them eighteen minutes."

Addison pressed her sheet music flat on the riser and watched the piano keys instead of the words. The eighth graders were supposed to sing the high part while her row held the low one, and every time the two parts came together, hers wobbled like a rope bridge.

"Don't think about their part," whispered Marisol beside her. "Just count."

Easy for Marisol to say. In the last rehearsal, Addison had followed the high voices straight up like a balloon on a string, and Mrs. Okafor had stopped everything. Today she would hold the low line even if it felt like a rebellion against the whole choir. She decided to test an idea: instead of listening to the singers, she would hang every note on the piano, which never got pulled away.

The accompanist, a lanky tenth grader named Dev, played the tricky passage again. He slowed down beautifully where the page said "rit.," letting the notes stretch like taffy, and the high voices floated with him. Addison gripped her low line and stayed on the piano. It was working.

Then Dev turned the page and kept playing slowly, slow, slow, even though the music on her sheet said "a tempo."

"That means go back to the original speed," Marisol murmured, tapping the marking. "After it slowed down."

Addison's part suddenly felt wrong, and she realized why: it wasn't her. The piano was dragging everyone behind. She raised her hand. "Dev, the a tempo. You're still slow."

He flushed, found the marking, and lifted his hands. "Again from bar twenty."

This time the piano snapped back to the steady first speed, and the two parts landed on top of each other like hands stacking. Addison's low line held firm, and for three whole bars the sound was one wide, braided thing.

Afterward Mrs. Okafor asked Dev to move the music away from the stage lights, since the old backdrop was flammable and the bulbs ran hot. While he stacked the props safely at the back wall, he gave Addison a thumbs-up.

"You saved the whole passage," Marisol said.

Addison looked at the piano, still open to the same page. "Want to integrate our parts at recess and try it once more?"

Blake sat cross-legged on the grass with his sketchbook, a basketball on the picnic table in front of him, and one very strict art assignment: shade a sphere with a highlight, a shadow, and a cast shadow. The assignment was mandatory, due Monday, and his stomach did that hormone thing where it churned just enough to make him lean harder on his pencil. His art teacher had told them a "real artist observes before drawing." Blake had rolled his eyes at that in class. Now he rolled the basketball a few inches and watched how the shadow stretched and slid across the tabletop like it was alive.

The sphere itself went okay. He found the highlight where the late sun hit the ball, built a gray curve around it, and pressed darkest on the far side. The problem was the table. He'd drawn the tabletop's far edge sloping upward, and no matter how he shaded, the whole surface looked like it was floating away from the basketball, like a magic carpet with a ball parked on it. He frowned, erased, and drew the edge tilted up again. Same problem. His little sister Maya wandered over with a popsicle and said, "Your table's flying."

"Thanks. Very helpful." But she was right, and he knew it. He thought about last summer, when he'd tried to draw his bedroom and sloped the ceiling edges the same wrong way. He'd crumpled that drawing and shoved it in the desk drawer, too annoyed to figure out what had gone wrong. He still kind of regretted quitting instead of looking harder. He decided not to quit this time.

He stood up and looked straight at the table's far edge, then lowered himself slowly to a crouch. Something changed as his eyes went down past the level of the tabletop. Below his eye level, the far edge didn't slope up anymore. He straightened, crouched again, accelerated his knees all the way to the grass, and there it was: edges above his eye level sloped down toward their vanishing points, while edges below his eye level sloped up toward them. He'd been standing, so the tabletop was below his eyes, which meant its edges should slope up toward the vanishing point, not tilt off into the sky.

"Maya, come look," he said. She crouched next to him, popsicle dripping. "When you're above the edge, it goes down to the vanishing point. When you're below it, it goes up. That's why my table was flying. I was below the tabletop but I drew it like I was above it." Maya squinted, then said, "So if you drew the ceiling while sitting on the floor, it slopes down toward the vanishing point?" Blake grinned and redrew the table with the edges climbing gently toward the vanishing point, then set the basketball on it, highlight, shadow, cast shadow and all. It sat there. Solid. Maya tapped the page and said, "Okay, that one's not flying. That one's just fat."

Gabrielle stood at the kitchen counter on Monday night with a stack of index cards and a timer that kept beeping at her like a smug little rodent. On Friday she had to give a two-minute speech in English class, and Ms. Petro had been relentless about the rules: an opening hook, three points, a closing. Gabrielle had all of that. Her cards were perfect. The problem was that last week, when she had practiced for her little brother, he fell asleep somewhere around point two, face-down in his cereal.

"Your voice is like a robot reading a menu," Theo had told her, spitting out a Cheerio for emphasis.

At lunch on Tuesday, Gabrielle watched her best friend Priya perform a tiny drama across the table. Priya's lab partner had knocked her volcano project onto the floor, and when the teacher asked if she was okay, Priya said, "I'm fine." But her shoulders had slumped, her voice had gone flat, and she'd paused a long time before saying it. Everyone at the table knew she was not fine. Not one bit.

That afternoon, Gabrielle cornered Priya by the lockers. "How did you do that? You said fine, and I knew you weren't."

Priya grinned. "It's called subtext. It's what you mean under the words. My cousin's in theater, and she says actors show it with pauses, tone, and gesture. Like, watch." Priya straightened her back, smiled brightly, and chirped, "I'm fine!" Then she slouched, dropped her voice, waited a beat, and mumbled, "I'm fine." Same words, two completely different messages.

Gabrielle had a hypothesis: if subtext worked on real people, it would work on a speech too. Her speech was about why the school should keep its garden, and her three points were solid, but on Thursday she tried an experiment in front of Theo. For her hook, instead of starting with "Did you know the garden has forty kinds of plants?", she picked up an empty seed packet, turned it over slowly, and paused before saying anything. Then, quietly, she said, "This packet used to be full." Theo actually looked up from his video game.

"You're trying to trick me with sadness," he said, but he didn't leave the room, so she counted it as a win. She kept testing. A pause before her second point made Theo lean forward. A random hand gesture at the wrong moment, though, exposed her nerves completely, because Theo laughed and said she looked like a confused traffic cop. So she cut that one.

On Friday, Gabrielle walked to the front of the room holding the seed packet. She let the silence sit for two whole seconds, which felt like two hours, and then began. When she finished her closing line and looked up, half the class had their hands raised, and Ms. Petro was writing something in her notebook. Behind her, Priya gave a slow thumbs-up, then slouched, dropped her voice, and mouthed, "I'm fine."

Juliette spread the topographic map of Miller Ridge across the library table and weighted the corners with four books from the return cart. Her plan for Saturday was simple: find the steepest slope on the hill before her family's hike, so she could tell her dad which side to avoid. She had read that close-together contour lines meant steep ground and far-apart lines meant gentle ground, and now she meant to test it.

At the next computer, a boy named Deshawn was watching a flight tracker site. "Flight 482, 40 degrees north, 73 degrees west," he read off the screen. "My grandma's on that one. Which number says she's almost here? This one or that one?" He pointed at the 40, then the 73.

Juliette looked over. The topographic map had numbers along its edges too, and she had been ignoring them. "Those are coordinates," she said, and then she stopped, because she was not actually sure which was which. She pulled the atlas over and found a page marked with a line labeled 0 degrees running top to bottom, with numbers climbing east and west from it. "Okay, so the up-and-down lines are longitude. Longitude measures how far east or west a place is from the prime meridian, from 0 degrees up to 180 degrees east or west." She traced it with her finger. "So 73 degrees west, your grandma is west of the prime meridian."

"Is west where we are?" Deshawn said. "Then she's on our side of the world. Good."

"That's the east-west number," Juliette said. "The 40 is the other one. North-south." She turned back to her map, and now the edge numbers made sense too, and she could see they told her nothing about steepness at all. The contour lines did that job, and she got to work counting them.

The west side of Miller Ridge had lines stacked so tightly they nearly touched, like the stripes on a candy cane. The east side had fat, lazy gaps. She marked the west face with a sticky note: STEEPEST, STAY OFF.

Deshawn leaned over. "Too bad. That's the side with the old fire tower."

Juliette checked the legend. The tower wasn't on the steep face at all. A thin dotted trail switchbacked up the east side, gentle all the way, and met the ridge behind the tower. She laughed. "The easy side gets you there anyway."

"Your dad will be relieved," Deshawn said.

"My dad will not cooperate until I tell him the fire road is closed," Juliette said. "He insists on vigorous uphill hiking. He calls it a vacation."

"Mine calls baggage fees a tariff and refuses to pay them," Deshawn said. "That's why Grandma flies alone."

Juliette peeled the sticky note off the map and moved it to the east face. "Enter from the easy side, end up at the tower anyway," she said, and pressed it down flat.

Hailey had decided to try keeping Shabbat from Friday sundown to Saturday noon, the way her family did, even though her best friends were all at the pool by ten. In the kitchen, the last thing she did before sunset was tape a note over the light switch, because her mother said the rule was no electricity, and Hailey wanted to be systematic about it. No phone, no TV, no turning things on. She set a loaf of challah on the table and waited in the dimming light, wondering what would actually be different.

Saturday morning she sat at the same table with her two cousins, Maya and Dov, who had come for lunch. Bored already, Hailey asked the question she'd been carrying around for weeks: "What happens after you die?"

"Orthodox Jews believe there'll be a resurrection of the dead," Dov said, tearing his bread. "Like, actually, in the future. Bodies rising."

Maya shrugged. "At our synagogue, our rabbi says what matters is how you live now. That's the whole point."

"They can't both be right," Hailey said.

"Why not?" Maya said. "Nobody's seen it. It's not like you can check."

That stopped Hailey. She looked at the covered switch, the silent phone in the drawer, the candles burnt down to stubs. She couldn't see whether resting had changed anything inside her either, but she had a way to test it. She had gone all morning without checking her phone once, which had never happened on a normal Saturday, and she had noticed the smell of the bread and the sound of Dov chewing, small things the screen usually magnified into the only things in the room.

She thought about last winter, when she'd skipped her grandmother's shiva because a swim meet mattered more to her, and how she still couldn't decide if that had been a mistake or just a choice.

"Okay," she said at last. "Different answers to the same question. Maybe that's allowed."

Maya stole a piece of Hailey's challah and grinned. "Maybe that's the most Jewish answer of all."

Dov reached for the butter dish and knocked over the candle stub, and all three of them scrambled to catch it before it rolled off the table.

Arianna's backyard pool was barely nine metres long, and on Saturday she had to swim twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing in front of the whole swim club. Her father would have helped, but last spring he had twisted his knee on the driveway and bruised the cartilage so badly he still limped, so all he could do was stand at the edge and count laps. Arianna pushed off, took three strokes, turned her head, and got a mouthful of water. Again. She coughed, tried again, and choked a second time.

At the far side of the pool, her neighbour Theo was playing one-on-one against his cousin Marco on the driveway hoop. Theo set a screen, planting himself so his body would obstruct Marco's defender, and Marco drove past. But Theo just stood there, hands on his hips, while every passing lane closed. "Nobody's open!" Marco shouted. They ran it again. Same result. Arianna gripped the pool ledge, watching. Something was off, some rule she couldn't see. Theo set the pick, then froze, as if the play ended there.

"Roll!" she called across the fence. Theo stared at her. "After you set the screen, turn and move toward the basket," she said, "so you're ready for a pass from whoever has the ball." Theo ran it once more. He set the pick, rolled to the hoop, and Marco's bounce pass arrived just as he turned. Layup. Marco whooped like it was a buzzer beater.

Watching them, Arianna floated on her back, thinking. Theo had been stuck because he kept doing the same motion and expecting a different ending. So was she. Every time she breathed, she was lifting her head forward, out of the stroke, instead of turning it to the side. She pushed off the wall, counted three strokes, and let her cheek rest on the water as her face rotated sideways. Air, clean air, no coughing. She kept going, one length, then a turnaround, then another, her father's voice counting from the fence. At the far wall she stopped, dripping and grinning, and shouted to Theo, "Run it again. I want to see that pass."

The petition had forty-three signatures when Elena walked into the town hall, and it needed fifty before she could hand it to a single councillor. She wanted the bylaw against skate ramps on residential driveways changed, because her brother's ramp had been confiscated last Tuesday and it sat now in a locked storage room behind the recreation centre. Councillor Marsh sat at the long table near the front, so Elena slid into a chair two rows back and began counting the room for anyone who might sign.

Before the meeting started, a boy about her age leaned over from the next seat. "Are you the one with the ramp petition? I'm Theo. We're here for the same reason, kind of. My class is doing a project on how citizens actually get bylaws changed, and my teacher said we could watch a real petition in action." He nodded at her clipboard. "Can I ask how you got started?"

"I found out the bylaw exists, then I found out which councillors voted for it," Elena said. "Then I wrote one page saying what I want changed and why, and I asked people to sign it. Fifty signatures means the clerk puts it on the agenda and a councillor has to move it. That's the rule." She paused. "I still need seven more."

Theo helped her work the room during the break. A woman in a green coat signed. Two teenagers signed. A man refused and said ramps were "subjective, a matter of taste," which made no sense to Elena until Theo whispered, "I think he means it's an opinion thing, not a fact thing." By the time the mayor called the meeting back to order, they had fifty-one.

During the open floor, Councillor Marsh waved Elena forward. She read her page out loud, her voice steadier than she expected, and handed over the clipboard. Marsh asked one question: why had she gathered signatures instead of just asking him directly? "Because one person can be ignored," Elena said. "Fifty-one people are a pattern." Marsh looked at the list for a long moment. "Petition's accepted. I'll move it at the next meeting."

Afterward, walking out, Theo told her about his mock election at school, where his small party had lost badly for the third year running. "Every year it's just the two big parties that ever win, and our teacher wouldn't say why. We vote the same way adults do, first past the post." Elena thought about that. "So everyone knows small parties lose, so nobody votes for them, so they lose." Theo stared at her. "That's actually a thing. A French political scientist figured it out. It's called Duverger's law." He wrote her inference down in his notebook, then said the names of the two big mock parties out loud, and laughed.

The ramp came home the following Friday. Elena had made one more inference on the walk home from the town hall: Councillor Marsh's name had appeared on the bylaw's original vote, listed with the minority who had opposed it. She had chosen him first, and she planned to persist with the other four councillors next. That night she taped the fifty-one signatures to the garage door beside the ramp.

Samuel stood at the counter with his mother's five dollar bill folded in his fist like a secret. "You can supervise from the porch," she said, "but you're doing it yourself. Milk, and bring me the change." From the porch she watched him march down the walk, and Samuel pretended not to notice, though he stood a little straighter anyway.

At Marta's Corner Market he found the milk, cold and sweating, and carried it to the register with both hands. Marta rang it up, took his five, and handed him a quarter, a dime, and two pennies. Samuel stepped aside, laid the coins on the edge of the counter, and counted. He counted again. If the milk was $4.56, he was owed forty-four cents, and thirty-seven cents was not forty-four cents. Either he was wrong or she was, and he did not think he was wrong, because he had done the subtraction twice in his head while walking past the blue house with the influential yellow mailbox, the one everybody in the neighborhood used when giving directions. "Excuse me," he said, holding up the coins. "I think I'm short seven cents." Marta squinted at the register, said, "The button sticks on the fours," and dropped a nickel and two pennies into his palm.

He was still grinning about that when he got home and found his little cousin Theo on the back steps, knee bleeding in a long red smear, sniffling. "I fell off the wagon," Theo said, which was his whole diagnosis and clearly enough for him. Samuel set the milk on the kitchen table and reached for Theo's knee, then stopped. Last year the school nurse had helped Samuel with a gashed palm, and the first thing she had done, before anything else, was walk to the sink and wash her hands. He had thought it was strange then, but now it clicked into place like the change problem: something you did before the touching, not after. Germs didn't get into the cut if they never got onto the hands that touched the cut.

"Wait right there," Samuel said. "I have to wash my hands first." Theo looked at him like he was crazy. "My knee is the problem, not your hands." "My hands are going to land on your knee," Samuel said, soaping up to the wrists, "so they're part of the problem now." Theo thought about that, frowned, and held still while Samuel rinsed, dried, and pressed a clean paper towel against the scrape.

Samuel carried the milk to his mother along with the exact change, forty-four cents, counted twice. She looked at the coins, then at Theo's bandaged knee, then at Samuel's still-damp hands. "Forty-four cents and one fixed cousin," she said. "Not bad for a first trip." Theo lifted his leg into the light to admire it. "He washed his hands before he even touched me," he announced. "Like a doctor."

Grace ran her monologue for the fourth time on the draft of a stage built from plywood scraps, but every time she reached the line "You never listen to me anyway," her arms hung stiff at her sides and the words came out flat as cardboard. The community theatre was so dilapidated that rain dripped into a bucket near the props table, and the director wanted pauses and gestures that showed real anger before Friday's audition.

Across the stage, Marco was struggling too. His partner hadn't shown up, so he was supposed to improvise a scene with a girl named Priya, but Priya stood frozen near the curtain, saying nothing, staring at her sneakers. Marco tried asking her questions. Nothing. He waved a hand in front of her face. Still nothing.

Then Marco turned, planted his feet, and barked, "Captain, the ship is taking on water! I need orders!" Priya's shoulders snapped back as if someone had pulled a string. "Seal the lower deck," she said at once, pointing toward the wings. "And send two men to the pumps. Move!" Grace watched from her plywood corner, and something clicked. He had made her the captain just by calling her one. Priya hadn't been stuck because she had no ideas; she'd been stuck because she had no part to play yet.

After rehearsal, Grace caught Priya by the costume rack. "That thing Marco did, what was it?"

"Endowing," Priya said. "Giving your partner a role or trait through what you say. Like if I say 'Doctor, my arm hurts,' I've just made you the doctor."

Grace tried it that night with her little brother, who was sprawled on the couch. "Grandfather, tell me again why you never listen to me." He sat up, wheezed in a creaky old voice, and said, "Because you mumble, child." Grace felt her fists find her hips on their own, and the anger line burst out of her with a pause before it that surprised them both.

"Again," her brother said, settling back into the cushions. "And this time, Grandfather, you'd better answer me."

Hudson had a report due Monday on why ancient Egyptians built the pyramids, which would have been fine if the exhibit he needed hadn't been closed for cleaning. A paper sign, unbothered by his opinion, said so.

"Gift shop's open," said his little sister Priya, who had come along for the air conditioning and wanted a replica canopic jar she'd been guarding with her eyes since noon.

The museum guide, sweeping near the barrier, tipped her head toward a corridor. "Pioneer wing's open. There's a river model down there too. Sometimes the river helps with the Egypt questions."

Hudson doubted a covered wagon could explain a pyramid, but he followed the corridor anyway. He found a long table with water and silt, a model of the Nile flooding its banks, and a wall panel about fields turning green every year while the desert stayed brown. He pushed a wooden lever and watched the water rise, leave dark mud, then sink. The river was the signal, he thought, the thing farmers watched to know when to plant. That's why priests studied the flood, and why the pharaoh, whose pyramid sat above the sand like a promise, got credit when the harvest came in. Priya pressed the lever too, twice, just to see the mud decompose into the water like cocoa in milk.

Beyond the river table sat a glass case with a diary from 1837. Hudson read the line out loud because it stopped him. "The bank took the farm in the spring. We hear land out west is cheap and the soil is black as coal, so we will risk the trail."

"So they just left?" Priya asked.

"The Panic of 1837 ruined a lot of farmers," Hudson said slowly, connecting it. "Then they went west for the good land." Ruined farmers, black soil, a dangerous trail. People following a signal of their own.

Priya tugged his sleeve. "You owe me a jar."

He bought her the small one, not the big one. She held it up to the light, decided it was better anyway, and marched out the door ahead of him.

Benjamin stood at the edge of the school auditorium stage, the spotlights making him squint, and tried again. "My brother took my compass. My brother sailed away. My brother was swallowed by the sea." He had marked seven places to pause and seven gestures, one for every sentence, but when he finished, his friend Priya just blinked from the third row.

"I counted your moves," she called up. "It felt like a list, not a story."

"That's the problem!" Benjamin said, flapping his script. "Seven pauses, and they all cancel each other out." He had been sure that more gestures meant more feeling. Now he suspected the opposite, that the audience could only hold a few big things in their heads at once, but he needed proof.

In the library the next day he flipped through a book on Rome and stopped at a page about a battle. "Listen to this," he told Priya. "Julius Caesar reported a quick victory at the Battle of Zela in 47 BC with just three Latin words. 'Veni, vidi, vici.' I came, I saw, I conquered."

"Three words?" Priya said. "For a whole battle?"

"That's the trick. Three beats, not seven." Priya frowned, because she still believed more was more, but she agreed to watch one more rehearsal after school.

The auditorium was notorious for its squeaky third floorboard, so Benjamin avoided it entirely and stood dead center. He decided to use only three gestures, and to conceal his nerves by gripping the edge of his sleeve during the rest, letting his hands be still on purpose. Before he began, he and Priya had a quick negotiation: she would raise a finger at every move he made so he could count them himself.

He let the silence stretch. "My brother took my compass." One step forward. "My brother sailed away." One arm lifted toward the back wall. "My brother was swallowed by the sea." Both hands opened, then slowly closed.

Nobody said anything for a second. Then Priya stood up and clapped.

"Okay," she said, "I take it back. Three wins."

Benjamin grinned and looked out at the empty seats, imagining them full. "Tomorrow we run it for the whole class," he said. "Same three. Don't touch the third floorboard."

Emile had been practicing the jarabe in his cousin Rosa's garage for three days, and his boots still tangled on the zapateado every fourth count. Rosa's quinceañera was on Saturday, and the whole family expected him to dance in the performance at the party. The trouble was that Rosa kept disappearing every Tuesday and Thursday afternoon, right when they were supposed to rehearse together, and he couldn't figure out where she went. "You can't fix a pattern you can't see," his grandfather always said, so Emile decided to test it. If Rosa was hiding from the dancing, she would be anywhere the music wasn't. If it was something else, there would be one consistent place.

He found her in the den, sitting under the attic's pink insulation that showed through a gap in the ceiling tiles, holding a folded piece of paper. She looked up, and her shoulders dropped. "You're going to think it's silly," she said. "Read it," said Emile. She stood and read a passage aloud, slowly, the way you'd read something that mattered. "The party isn't until eight," she said. "But the day starts with the Mass. It's a Mass of thanksgiving." Emile had assumed the quinceañera was just the party, and now the whole day rearranged itself in his head: church first, family giving thanks, and only then the food and the dancing.

He remembered last summer, when his other cousin Marisol had turned fifteen and he'd been bored through the ceremony, squirming in the pew, thinking it was something to get through before the cake. He'd changed his mind about a lot since then. Now he understood why the girls practiced their readings so seriously, why Marisol had carried a small crown that her mother said was meant to symbolize something passing from one generation to the next.

"I'll help you," Emile said. "You read, I'll be the congregation." Rosa smiled and started over, and Emile stamped a soft zapateado under the table to keep her rhythm steady. When she finished without stumbling, he clapped so hard the paper jumped right out of her hands.

Mia stood in front of a painting of an orange with a single lamp shining on it, sketchbook clamped under her arm. She had come to the gallery because her art club's sketching day was mandatory, and because she wanted one thing: to make her drawings stop looking flat. She picked a spot on the bench, opened to a blank page, and drew a circle. Then came the hard part. Where exactly did the light go, and where did the dark?

She shaded one side of the sphere, leaving a bright spot where the lamp would hit it. Behind it she dragged a smudge of graphite for the cast shadow on the table. Then, to make the ball look round, she erased a pale curve along the bottom of the dark side. She held the sketchpad out at arm's length and squinted.

A boy on the next bench leaned over. "Why does yours look like it has two lamps?"

Mia looked again. He was right. The pale curve at the bottom glowed almost white, like a second light hidden under the table. "It's not supposed to be that bright," she muttered. She studied the painting on the wall instead. On the orange's dark side, near the bottom, there was a soft lightness, lighter than the deepest part of the shadow, but never as light as the sunlit side. She tested it: she darkened her pale curve two pencil steps, keeping the core of the shadow darkest of all and the lit side still the brightest.

"Better," the boy said. "It looks like it's sitting on something."

"It's the table bouncing light back up," Mia said. "You just can't let it win."

She decided to isolate that one strip of reflected light and practice it on a second sphere, then a third, building her values in order, brightest to darkest, like a hierarchy. Her eraser was nearly a stub by the time the guard announced closing. Mia packed up slowly, then turned back for one last look at the orange.

"Same model tomorrow," she told it.

Emmett coasted to a stop in front of his grandfather's gate, one foot down on the gravel lane, and stared at the sign he'd never noticed before. "No skateboarding in Harrow Park," it said, in letters too tidy to have been scribbled by anybody who actually skated. The park was two blocks from Grandpa's house, and Emmett had been riding its smooth paths since he was eight.

He remembered last summer, the day he'd finally landed the kickflip on the park's long concrete curve. He'd been so proud that he'd rolled all the way to Grandpa's back garden, where the tomato vines grew lush and green along the fence, and announced it through the screen door. Grandpa had come out wiping his hands on a towel and said, "Do it again, then." Emmett had tried six times and landed it once, and Grandpa had clapped like it was a home run.

Now the sign was up, and Emmett pushed through the gate with the board under his arm, already halfway through the question. "Grandpa, who puts up a sign like that? Can they just decide?"

"They can if the town council decides it," Grandpa said from the porch. He was sorting a crate of tomatoes, turning each one over. "It's a bylaw. A rule made by the local government, and it applies only inside this town. You could ride that thing in the next county over and it wouldn't mean a thing to them."

Emmett sat down on the steps, spinning one of the board's wheels with his thumb. The wheels were a tough polymer, some kind of plastic his cousin had told him about, and they spun a long time on a clean bearing. So the sign wasn't a law of the whole country. It was a town rule, made by town people. Which meant, maybe, town people could change it. "How would somebody get them to change it?"

"Petition," Grandpa said. "You collect signatures, you show up at a council meeting, and you ask. Enough names can generate a fair bit of attention. I did it once, over the garbage pickup schedule." He held up a tomato, ripe and heavy. "Worked, too."

That was the thing Emmett hadn't known: Grandpa had wanted the pickup moved off Tuesdays because it clashed with his market day, and forty signatures had done it. Emmett turned the problem over the way Grandpa turned the tomatoes. If the ban was a bylaw, then the people who signed didn't have to be skaters, just townspeople. If the council made the rule, the council could unmake it.

He spent the afternoon at the kitchen table with a notebook, drafting a page headed "Petition to Allow Skateboarding in Harrow Park." Then he rode to the community center, where Mr. Deloach, who ran it, looked at the page for a long moment. "You know," Mr. Deloach said slowly, "I've wanted a skate afternoon in the gym for years. Nobody ever asked me the right way."

"Then sign here," Emmett said, and slid the notebook across the desk, pen already lying on top of it.

The glass doors of city hall were so translucent that Jaxson walked toward them too fast and nearly bumped his nose on the frame. He straightened his backpack, which held one petition sheet with eleven signatures, all from kids at Riverside Park who wanted the bylaw banning skateboards there changed. His teacher had said a citizen could bring a petition to a councillor, but she had not said how, exactly, and the hallway ahead of him split into three different corridors.

He picked the corridor with a sign that said COUNCIL CHAMBERS and found a display case outside the big double doors. Inside, under old photographs, hung a copy of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. He scanned it while he worked up his courage, and something caught his eye. Most of the document was marked as coming into force in 1982, but section 15, the equality rights, had a different date printed beside it: 1985. He read the little card next to it twice. The equality rights had waited three years, the card said, to give governments time to update their laws. So the whole Charter had started in 1982, and this one part had started later, in 1985, three years after the rest.

Jaxson had a thought, and it made him grin. If even a country's most important rules could need time to be updated, then maybe a small city bylaw could be changed too. Maybe things that seemed permanent were really just waiting for someone to point them out. He tested the idea right there, whispering it to himself: "Rules can catch up."

A woman with a lanyard came out of the chambers carrying a box of agendas. "Can I help you?" she asked.

"I want to give a petition to a councillor," Jaxson said. "About the skateboard bylaw at Riverside Park. I have signatures." He held up his sheet, and his face went hot, because eleven signatures suddenly felt small. The embarrassment made his voice thinner than he wanted.

She looked at the names. "Eleven's a start," she said. "Councillor Amadi handles parks. Third floor, office twelve. She's in until four."

Jaxson rode the elevator with two men in suits who ignored him completely, which he decided was fine. At office twelve the door was open, and a woman was stacking papers behind a desk cluttered with coffee cups. He knocked on the doorframe anyway.

"Are you the councillor for parks?" he asked.

"I am."

"I have a petition. Eleven people signed it. I know that's not a lot, but I can get more, and I can contribute the research too. I already looked some stuff up." He stepped forward and laid the sheet on her desk. "The whole Charter started in 1982, but section 15, the equality rights, didn't come into force until 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws. So rules can be updated. That's what I'm asking for."

Councillor Amadi set down her stack and read every signature, top to bottom, before she looked up. "Tell me exactly what happens at that park on a Saturday," she said, and pulled out a chair.

Kate stood at Mr. Oliver's cheese stall on Saturday morning, a wooden spoon in her hand and a small pot on his portable burner. Last summer, at her grandmother's house, she had watched a pot of macaroni and cheese go from silky to lumpy in about ten seconds, and she had promised herself she would figure out why. Today was her chance, because Mr. Oliver had offered to teach her, and his sauces never had a single lump.

"Flour and butter first," he said. "Equal parts, stir until it smells like toast. Then the milk, a little at a time." Kate stirred the flour and butter together, and it looked like wet sand at the beach, the kind you'd use to build a doomed castle. She added the milk slowly, whisking, and held her breath. "The suspense is killing you," Mr. Oliver said, laughing. "You can let your shoulders down. It's just cheese." The sauce turned smooth, and Kate felt like she had uncovered a secret rule of the universe: add the liquid gradually, whisk hard, and the lumps never get a chance to form.

Two stalls over, her little brother Theo was helping their dad sell jars of jam, and every few minutes he darted back to check the pot of rice simmering on their camp stove. He lifted the lid, peered in, and clapped it back down. He did it again. And again. When he served sample cups of rice and beans to customers, one man chewed thoughtfully and said, "Bit crunchy, isn't it?" Theo's face went pink to the tips of his ears.

Kate carried a taste over and crunched her way through it. She remembered the toast smell of the roux, how the timing had mattered, and she thought about Theo's lid. "Theo," she said, "when you kept peeking, the steam escaped, and that leaves the grains undercooked." Theo stared at the pot as if it had betrayed him. "So the rice needed the lid on the whole time?" "The whole time. No peeking." She handed him a fresh pot to start over. "Want to make the roux with me while it cooks? Fair warning, though. You have to whisk until your arm wants to fall off." Theo grabbed a spoon. "My arm never wants to fall off," he said. "It's that kind of arm."

Luca knelt at the edge of the inflatable pool his dad had set up on the grass, breathing hard. Twenty-five metres of front crawl with side breathing, that was the goal, and so far he had managed about six before his face came up like a startled frog. The pool wasn't even twenty-five metres long, so he had to swim laps, turning at each end, which made everything worse. His younger brother Marco was supposed to count laps but kept getting distracted by the basketball game on the portable TV by the fence, the one Marco had bought with two months of income from mowing Mrs. Petro's lawn.

"Two laps," Marco called, not looking up.

Luca tried again. Kick, pull, breathe, but when he turned his head he always lifted it too far, and his legs sank, and he ended up spluttering. He climbed out, dripping, and stood next to Marco to watch the screen while he caught his breath. On the play, one team's guard dribbled around a big teammate who blocked the defender chasing him, and the defenders swapped who they were guarding.

"Switch," Marco muttered. "They switched on the pick and roll."

Luca squinted. The shortest defender on the court was now guarding the tallest player, who was posting up right under the basket, and the tall defender had been left chasing the quickest guard out top. Both matchups looked wrong. Luca wondered: did the switching team plan that, or did they just get stuck with it? It was like something hidden had shifted underneath the visible play, a rule you couldn't see until you traced each defender's path.

The tall player caught the ball and scored easily over the short defender. On the next possession, the same thing happened in reverse, and the quick guard blew past the lumbering tall defender.

"They keep switching," Luca said, "and every switch makes a mismatch."

Marco nodded. "The point guard spots it. Smallest guy on their tallest player."

Luca looked back at the pool. He'd been thinking about his breathing all wrong, like it was one fixed problem. But maybe it was a chain: something invisible upstream caused the spluttering downstream. If his head position was the "blocker," then maybe his arm pull was the defender getting switched onto the wrong job. When he lifted his head to breathe, his pulling arm stalled, and his legs, unguarded, sank. He had to keep the pull going while he turned, like the offense kept moving through the switch instead of freezing.

He asked Marco to retrieve the orange cones from the garage so they could mark twenty-five metres along the grass first, then measure the pool exactly, so the count would be credible instead of a guess. Four and a half lengths, it turned out.

Back in the water, Luca kicked off, pulled with his right arm, turned his head just enough, and kept the left arm moving through the switch. Breathe. Pull. Breathe. His legs stayed near the surface, almost weightless. He touched the far side, turned, and went again, counting under his breath. On the fourth length he was tired but smooth, and when his hand slapped the vinyl wall at the end, Marco was on his feet.

"That was five," Marco shouted. "You went past it!"

Luca laughed, gasping, and pushed wet hair out of his eyes. "Run it back," he said. "I want to see if it works twice."

Tyler had promised his mom the kitchen table would be clear by six, and it was now 5:15, with the table covered in marbles, peppercorns, toothpicks, and a poster board that still said ATOM in crooked letters. The science fair was tomorrow morning. He had a model to build and, more urgently, a claim to fix, because last week he had told his whole class that burning toast was "basically the same as ice melting, just warmer." Priya had looked at him the way you look at a rodent that has wandered into your lunch bag, and Mr. Okafor had assigned him a demonstration to prove he understood the difference before the fair.

He set up on the counter, since the table was a disaster zone. Two slices of bread went into the toaster: one he would watch melt butter on, and one he would, if necessary, burn. Melting was a physical change, because the stuff was still the same stuff, just softer. Burning was a chemical change, because it turned into something new that smelled terrible and could not be unburned. He remembered his dad's old iron kettle rusting on the porch one whole winter, and how no amount of scrubbing ever brought the shiny metal back. That was the flashback he'd put on the poster, drawn as a sad kettle.

But the model was the real problem. He had used a marble for the proton and a marble for the electron, and something about that had bothered him all afternoon. He found the fact in his science book, in a corner, in small print: a proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron. He read it three times. "Eighteen thirty-six," he said to the toaster. His little sister, Mia, wandered in looking for cheese.

"A proton has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron," he told her, pointing at the page. "So almost all of an atom's mass is in the nucleus."

"So your electron-marble is basically a lie," Mia said, and took her cheese elsewhere.

Tyler dumped the marble electron back in the bag and hunted through the junk drawer until he found a single poppy seed. He glued it to a toothpick, spun it far out from the marble nucleus, and stepped back. The atom looked suddenly enormous and mostly empty, like a robust orange with one tiny gnat orbiting it. Then the toaster screamed up burnt, and the second slice came out black and smoking, definitely a chemical change, definitely not reversible. He cracked the window so the kitchen wouldn't smell like a cave where something had gone to hibernate, opened the butter dish for the good slice, and wrote "DEMONSTRATION COMPLETE" on the poster in his most confident handwriting. At 5:58, he carried the whole thing to his room, and the table was clear by six, give or take a poppy seed.

Raphael sat on the floor of Mateo's kitchen, a paper menu spread between them and a box of cookies pretending to be a restaurant. Mateo's grandmother had come from Lyon in the spring, and she spoke almost no English, which meant Mateo was teaching Raphael enough French to survive a meal at her table. Today they were practicing what Raphael would say when the meal ended.

"Ask me for the bill," Mateo said, folding his arms like a waiter. He had even put a dish towel over his arm.

"La facture, s'il vous plaît," Raphael said, feeling proud. He had looked up "bill" in his notebook the night before, and facture was what the dictionary gave first.

Mateo winced. "Grand-mère will look at you like you asked for a tax invoice. That's for paperwork, not for restaurants."

Raphael's ears went hot. Last month he had tried ordering in French at the bakery near his house, and when he'd asked for something in the wrong words, the man behind the counter had laughed before correcting him. The humiliation had been small, but it stuck to him like gum on a shoe, corrosive enough that he'd almost skipped this whole project. Now he studied the menu again, thinking. If facture was a paperwork word, then French must have a separate word just for restaurant bills, the way English had "check" as well as "bill." Languages liked to hide the right word in a special pocket.

"Wait," he said. "Does the restaurant word sound like anything English?"

Mateo's little sister Camille wandered in and stole a cookie before they could stop her. "It's addition," she said with her mouth full.

"Like math?" Raphael asked. That seemed absurd. He turned it over in his head, testing it the way he tested a rule. "You add up everything you ate, so the bill is the addition?"

"Maybe," Mateo said. "Grand-mère just says it." He never explained things further than he had to.

They dragged Grand-mère in from the garden, her hands smelling of tomatoes and rain-wet soil. Raphael stood as straight as he could, held out the empty cookie plate, and said, "L'addition, s'il vous plaît." The words meant "The bill, please," though nobody translated; he just knew it now.

Grand-mère's whole face lifted. She clapped once, said something fast and delighted, and pressed a euro coin into his hand as if he had truly paid for his cookies.

"Keep it," she said in her slow, careful English. "You earned."

Raphael closed his fist around the coin and grinned at Mateo. "Same time next week?"

The folding tables at Uncle Sam's house were crowded with mango sticky rice, spring rolls, and a whole tray of fried bananas, and nobody was eating any of it. Gavin stood in the kitchen doorway holding a plate, because it was two o'clock in the afternoon and his stomach had been growling since the car ride. His grandmother poured tea for the aunties and handed him a cup. "Tea is fine," she said. "No food today, not after noon."

Gavin looked down the table at his cousins, who were sipping water and playing cards like this was normal. He felt like the only protagonist in a story where everyone else had read the ending. When he asked his older cousin Mali, she shrugged and kept shuffling. "It's an observance day," she said. "Uposatha." That was all she offered, so Gavin had to devise his own way to find out what was going on.

He started with what he could observe. His grandmother had on her white blouse, the stiff one she only wore to the temple. At breakfast that morning, everyone had eaten a huge meal at ten, which had seemed strange at the time. Now it made sense: they had loaded up early because food was stopping at midday. He counted what he knew on his fingers. One, a special day. Two, special clothes. Three, a big early meal and nothing after noon. He tested the idea out loud at the card table. "So it's like a rule? A whole list of rules for today?"

Mali finally looked up. "Eight precepts," she said, laying down a queen. "Grandma took all eight this morning. One of them is not eating after midday."

Gavin put his plate back on the counter, washed his hands, and came back to the table. He picked up his cards and lost three hands in a row. Around four o'clock his stomach gave a loud growl, and Mali laughed so hard she knocked over her tea. "Tomorrow," Gavin said, "we eat the fried bananas first."

Max had claimed the shady end of the picnic table before anyone else was awake, because today the art teacher was going to let them draw with charcoal. "Sphere shading," she had promised, "highlight, shadow, cast shadow," and Max had been thinking about it all night. He pressed his thumb into the black stick and dragged a circle across his paper, then squinted at the orange he'd set on the table as a model. The brightest spot sat up and to the left, where the morning sun caught it, and a dark crescent curled along the bottom right. He smudged gray under the orange and a stretched oval of it on the paper beside it. "That's the cast shadow," said Priya, dropping onto the bench across from him. "It points away from your light."

"It's like the light is a factor you have to account for," Max said, darkening the crescent. "Move the light and everything moves." Priya held up her own orange, turning it slowly, and Max noticed that when she turned it, the highlight slid to a new place, like the orange had its own private sun. He filed that away.

The real test came after lunch, when the teacher set out photos of living rooms for a perspective challenge. Max chose one with a big TV on the back wall and an armchair angled toward it, not lined up with anything. He had drawn the room's walls first, and every set of parallel lines ran off to two points way out at the edges of his paper. He knew those were the vanishing points, and he knew they both sat on the horizon line he'd drawn first. Then he stopped, pencil hovering. The armchair wasn't parallel to the walls. Could it use the same points?

He tried it. The chair's arms swooped toward the wrong places and the whole thing looked like it was melting. Max flipped to a fresh sheet and tried the opposite idea: give the chair its own two points. He lined his pencil along the seat edge, along the armrest, along the back, and each pair of lines met in its own two new spots. His heart jumped. He checked twice, and both new points landed exactly on his horizon line, same as the walls' points. "Priya, look. Its own pair, but on the same horizon line." She leaned over, then checked it with her ruler. "They do. Symmetrical and everything."

At dinner Max was still buzzing, and he decided to petition the teacher for one more photo, a kitchen with a turned stool, so he could test it again tomorrow. She wrote his name at the top of her list and said, "First thing after breakfast." Max grinned and went to sharpen every pencil he owned, lining them up by the lantern light with the sphere drawing clipped above them, highlight, shadow, cast shadow, like a trophy.

Autumn had read the last page of The Scarlet Ibis twice, and she still could not say what the book was about in one sentence. Mrs. Ruiz's book club met in the library on Thursdays, and today each member had to state a theme and back it up with a quotation. Autumn's hand was sweating against her notebook.

She assumed everyone else had figured it out already. Marcus was flipping through his copy with a smug little smile, and Priya had three sticky notes bristling from her pages. Autumn had one sticky note, stuck to a page about a red bird. When the storm blew the scarlet ibis into the family's garden and it died, she had felt something tighten in her throat, though she could not say why.

"It's about guilt," Marcus announced. "The narrator's conscience bothers him, so it's about a guilty conscience." He read his quotation in an eloquent, dramatic voice, wobbling his eyebrows at Priya, who snorted so hard she knocked over the pretzel bowl.

Then it was Autumn's turn. She opened to the red bird. "I think it's about fragility," she said. "When the scarlet ibis dies in the garden, it's like the book is telling you something before it happens." She read her quotation about the fallen bird, and her voice came out steadier than she expected. "Doodle is fragile too. And later, in the storm, when the narrator finds him under the tree with his neck bent, it's like the bird all over again." The room went quiet except for the radiator ticking. Priya leaned over and flipped back to the bird scene, her finger moving down the page.

"That's foreshadowing," Priya whispered, tapping the dead red bird. "You found it before me."

Mrs. Ruiz wrote "storm" on the board and underlined it twice. "Notice," she said, "that a storm brings the bird, and a storm takes Doodle."

Autumn copied the word foreshadowing into her notebook, pressing hard enough to dent the next page, and then tore off the corner and folded it into a tiny paper bird.

Zoey had been building her Scratch game all afternoon, a dodgeball arena where a cat in a top hat dodged flying doughnuts. Every time the cat got hit, the score went up by one, and every time a doughnut sailed past, the cat earned a point instead. She had the loops spinning the doughnuts in circles and if-then blocks checking collisions so often that her brother Marcus, wandering through the kitchen, said the project looked like a census of every possible crash.

"Very funny," Zoey said. "At least my doughnuts don't invade my side of the couch like your socks do."

But now she had a second problem. She wanted a printed score table on the side, a neat row of numbers she could save and show her friend Priya, so she was writing a tiny Python program that printed the round scores one after another.
