Dad says pilots use numbers like that for everything." She wrote "20 S, 70 W, Atacama, zero rain ever" and underlined it twice, then drew a small triumphant camel in the margin, even though camels definitely did not flourish there. She doubted many organisms did, actually, in a place with no rain at all.

Marcus peered at her notebook. "Can I draw the camel a hat? Camels look versatile, they could pull off a hat."

Samantha handed him the pencil just as the gate agent called their row, and the two of them folded the map into a lopsided square and ran.

Julia slid her coordinate grid across the table until it bumped Mr. Okoye's tray of colored pencils, and the smell of sharpened wood drifted up as Marcus grabbed two and tossed her the green one. Math club met in the cafeteria every Tuesday, and today the whiteboard read "Two-Step Equations: y = 2x + 1." Julia's problem was y = 2x + 3, and she needed two points so she could draw the line. She picked x = 1 first, because one was easy, and got y = 5. Then she wanted x = one half, just to see what would happen.

"When x is one half, I get two times one half plus three," she said, talking it through. "So that's one plus three. Four." She plotted (1, 5) and then moved carefully to the halfway point between 0 and 1 on the x-axis, and up four. Marcus leaned over, chewing the eraser end of his pencil, which Julia could perceive was his thinking habit, because he only did it when a problem had him stuck.

"I wanted x = one third," Marcus said. "But then y equals two thirds plus three, and I can't add those." He scribbled, crossed out, scribbled again. "So I multiplied the denominators instead. Three times one is three, and I turned three into three over one, so three times one gives me three over one." He frowned at his paper. "Two thirds plus nine thirds is eleven thirds. It works, but it's ugly."

Julia tried it herself with different numbers, using the flat side of her ruler as a straightedge and making a quick adaptation to her method: instead of guessing, she multiplied the denominators every time. Each answer came out correct, and each time the fraction was bigger than it needed to be, waiting to be simplified. "It always works," she said slowly. "Multiplying the denominators gives you a common denominator. Just not always the smallest one."

"So it's like a shortcut that costs you later," Marcus said. "You get there, then you have to clean up."

Julia drew her line through both points, checked it against Marcus's paper, and pressed the green pencil down hard where the two lines crossed. "Same line," she said. "Different roads."

Rebecca had signed up to speak at the town hall meeting because of the bench. The old stone bench outside the library had been tagged with a bylaw that banned anyone from sitting on the plaza after 6 p.m., and her grandfather, who read the newspaper there every evening, now had nowhere to wait for her after chess club. She stood in the lobby holding her petition form, watching the double doors of the council chamber.

Beside her, a boy named Dhruv was bouncing on his heels. "I'm here about the ice rink schedule," he whispered. "They cut open skate to two hours a week and I want it back. But speaking up there feels like an audition I didn't practice for." He exhaled, then seemed to inhale his nerves right back in. "You go first. Show me how it's done."

When the chair called her name, Rebecca walked to the microphone and pushed her form across the table toward Councillor Okafor. "I'm petitioning to change the plaza bylaw," she said. "I learned how at the courthouse on our class trip. The clerk showed us that a petition has to state the bylaw, say what change you want, and carry signatures from people who live here. I have ninety-one." She paused, because a thought she'd been testing all week had finally lined up. "The clerk also told us that when a federal bill passes, the Governor General gives royal assent, and a deputy, like a Supreme Court justice, can stand in for the monarch. So even the big rules get signed by someone filling the role. Which made me think: somebody must have written our plaza bylaw too, and somebody can change it. That's why I'm here instead of just being mad about it."

The councillor turned the form toward the light and read the signatures slowly, which was tedious for Rebecca, who could feel her heart thudding the whole time. "Ninety-one names," the councillor said at last. "Including, I see, Anton Ferreira, who taught me chess in this very building. I'll move it onto next month's agenda." She slid a blank petition sheet across the table. "You'll want signatures for the change wording. Bring it to my office any Tuesday."

Rebecca carried the blank sheet back down the aisle and pressed it into Dhruv's hands. "Your turn," she whispered. "Say the bylaw, say what you want, and count your people."

Dhruf stood, straightened his jacket, and walked toward the microphone.

Nolan set the recipe card on the counter and read it top to bottom twice, the way his older sister Priya had told him to. Preheat the oven to 375. Grease the muffin pan. Stir the wet ingredients and the dry ones in separate bowls, then fold them together. He twisted the oven dial and waited for the preheat light, feeling like he had finally been trusted with something real, because Priya had promised he could bake these blueberry muffins entirely on his own while she worked on her own project: the pasta sauce simmering on the back burner, which she was determined to make thick enough to cling to a spoon.

While the bowls came together, Nolan measured the flour carefully, level with the back of a knife. Last winter, he remembered, he had tried pancakes without measuring anything, and the batter had rebelled by turning into a gluey lump that refused to flatten even in the pan. Priya had laughed until she couldn't breathe, and then she had shown him how to scoop flour lightly and sweep the cup clean. "That's why recipes exist," she had said. He wasn't going to make that mistake again, and besides, the muffins were his proof that he could feed himself something that wasn't toast.

Priya lifted the lid off her sauce and frowned. "It's still soupy. It's been twenty minutes." She stirred it and sighed toward the window. Nolan glanced over while spooning batter into the pan, and something clicked. The lid had been clamped on the whole time. "Try it with the lid off," he said. She gave him a look. "Steam can't get out with the lid on," he said. "Try it and see."

She propped the lid against the sugar jar and let the sauce bubble uncovered. By the time his muffins had risen into golden domes and he was sliding the pan onto the rack, her sauce had gone from watery to thick enough to coat the wooden spoon. "Hey, it worked," she said, dipping the spoon and tilting it slowly. "Ours both worked." Nolan pulled the oven mitt, the one with the frail thumb worn almost through, onto his hand and opened the door. "Careful," Priya said. "Hot." He lifted the pan out and set it on the rack, and the smell of blueberries filled the whole kitchen.

Emily slid her Spanish workbook across the library table and tried to ignore the fact that her presentation was tomorrow. Sra. Alvarez wanted each student to describe their family and pets in full sentences, spoken out loud, no notes. Emily could say "tengo un perro" in her sleep. The problem was her brother Marcus, and the verb.

"You look like you're defusing a bomb," said Priya, dropping into the chair across from her with a stack of books.

"Close. I wrote 'Mi hermano está alto' on my draft, and I don't know if it's wrong." Emily turned the notebook around. "Marco helped me after class, but he was in a rush, and he changed one of my sentences and didn't say why. I can't read his handwriting." The scribble in the margin looked like "es" or maybe "e's" or possibly "ews." Her flashcards, her textbook index, and the librarian's Spanish dictionary had given her three different vibes and zero answers.

Priya leaned in. "So ask someone who actually speaks it."

"The only person I know is my brother's friend Daniela, and she thinks I'm reckless because I fed the class fish over winter break. Twice." Emily had been trying to diminish that reputation for weeks, mostly by saying hello in a very small voice.

"You have forty minutes until the library closes," Priya said. "I'm going to find a book on deep-sea organisms for my science report. You're going to text Daniela."

Emily texted. Daniela replied fast, which was either a good sign or a trap. Emily typed the sentence, sent it, and turned her phone face down on the table so she couldn't watch the three dots appear and vanish, appear and vanish. She alphabetized Priya's flashcards. She counted ceiling tiles. When she finally flipped the phone over, the message was long.

"OK so," Daniela had written, "you said your brother is tired. Like, permanently tired. Forever."

Emily stared. Marcus had slept until noon on Saturday, but that hardly seemed like a criminal accusation. She scrolled up. There it was: she had written "Mi hermano está alto" when she meant tall, and somewhere between the draft and the final copy she had swapped her verbs. She typed back, "How do I say he IS tall? Like, all the time?"

"Es," Daniela answered. "Mi hermano es alto. Es for how he always is, like tall. Está for how he is right now, like tired. Estás vs es. Not the same."

Emily copied the rule onto a fresh card and held it up to the light. Then she built her sentences one at a time, testing each one before she wrote it down: Marcus es alto. Marcus está cansado. Her dog es pequeño and, after a bath, está mojado. She read the whole paragraph aloud in a whisper while Priya shelved her organism book and gave her a thumbs-up from between the stacks.

The next morning, Sra. Alvarez called her name third. Emily stood, took a breath, and said, "Mi hermano es alto. Mi hermano está cansado." From the back row, Marcus's friend Daniela nodded once, slowly, and mouthed, "¿Y el perro?"

"Mi perro es pequeño," Emily said, "y está mojado."

Isabella slid her notebook across the library table and tapped the page where she had written, in her best cursive, "Dogs are smarter than cats." The writing club had exactly fifty minutes before the librarian kicked everyone out for a chess tournament, and her five-paragraph persuasive essay was due at the next meeting.

"Your thesis looks solid," said Marcus, peeking over. "Mrs. Ruiz called it a working thesis, remember? Because it can change."

"It's not changing," Isabella said. "I have three days of evidence to gather." She opened the library's dog encyclopedia and started copying facts. Dogs guide blind people. Dogs sniff out bombs. That was paragraph two sorted already.

Then she found the cat book someone had left beside the chair, and it ruined everything. Cats solve puzzle boxes. Cats recognize their owners' voices. One study, she read with growing horror, tested both animals on the same puzzle, and the cats finished faster.

"You look like you swallowed a bee," said Priya, sliding into the next seat and handing her a spare pencil without being asked, because Priya always noticed who needed things.

"My evidence says cats are smarter." Isabella turned the book around. "If I ignore this, my essay is a lie. If I use it, my essay argues the opposite of my thesis."

"So argue the opposite," said Marcus, shrugging. "That's why it's a working thesis. If the evidence points somewhere else, you revise it instead of pretending the evidence doesn't exist."

Isabella stared at the page. She crossed out her old thesis with one dramatic stroke, which felt spontaneous and slightly heroic, and wrote, "Intelligence depends on what you measure." Then she paused. "Wait. If my thesis changed, my whole introduction changed too. My first paragraph says dogs are obviously smarter."

"That's why you draft the introduction after the body," Priya said, already delegating jobs around the table with the calm authority of someone with a reputation for finishing essays on time. "Marcus, find her one more cat study. I'll check her conclusion."

Isabella read her new introduction aloud, quietly, testing it like a recipe. The clock above the biography shelf showed ten minutes left. "Cats and dogs can both be brilliant," she whispered, "depending on the test."

Marcus flipped a page and held it up. "Found one. Cats beat dogs again."

"Perfect," said Isabella, and wrote it down.

Logan had exactly one class period to figure out why the Egyptians built the pyramids and what the Nile had to do with their farms, because his poster was due tomorrow and so far it said, in giant letters, PYRAMIDS: BIG. He spread three books across the library table and began to monitor his progress with a sticky note he labeled EVIDENCE. So far the note said "grain?" which was not going to impress anybody.

Priya slid into the seat across from him with her own project, a thin old book wrapped in a paper towel. "My grandma lent me this," she said. "It's a settler's diary from her house. I'm supposed to write about the trail years." She opened it carefully. "This guy writes about crossing a river. He says it was the hardest week of his life. Oxen, mud, everything."

Logan leaned over. The handwriting was cramped and brown at the edges. "He crossed a whole nation's land, though. Doesn't he mention who was already living there?" Priya flipped pages. "No. It's all oxen and mud." She frowned. "One guy's diary, one guy's view." She tapped the page. "I guess a settler's diary rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events. I'd need their side too, or I'm only telling half the trail."

Logan sat back so fast his chair squeaked. Half. He looked down at his stack: every book he had told the pharaohs' story, because the pharaohs were the ones who hired the writers. He grabbed a fresh sheet and started again, this time drawing the Nile first. The river flooded every year, so farms got water and rich mud, so there was grain, so thousands of workers could be fed while they stacked stones for a pharaoh's tomb. Then he added a second column: what the workers themselves might have said about it, if anyone had asked them.

"Ms. Ruiz says we have a silverfish problem," Priya whispered, pointing at a trap near the returns cart. "Little parasites that eat the glue in book spines." Logan packed up his poster paper and grinned. "Then let's get out of here before they eat my evidence."

At Sunday dinner, Jaxon's little sister Zoe and his cousin Marcus started fighting before the rolls even hit the table. Zoe wanted the chair by the window. Marcus wanted the chair by the window. Aunt Rosa kept saying "somebody has to give in," which Jaxon knew from experience would end with somebody crying into the mashed potatoes.

He watched them instead of eating. Zoe kept glancing at the window itself, where a cardinal was hopping along the ledge. Marcus kept shifting his plate so it wouldn't sit on the wobbly spot in the table, which the window chair avoided because it was the one chair on solid floor. That was interesting. They both demanded the same seat, but they weren't actually demanding the same thing.

"Hold on," Jaxon said. "Zoe, why the window chair? Not because it's yours. Why?"

"The bird," Zoe said. "I can see it from there."

"Marcus?"

"My plate tips at the other spots. Gravy slides off."

Grandpa, who was buttering bread like the argument was a TV show, raised an eyebrow at Jaxon. "You figured something out, kid. I can tell by your face."

"A position is what somebody demands," Jaxon said. "An interest is the reason they want it."

Grandpa pointed his butter knife. "Now you're cooking."

Jaxon turned the butter dish toward Zoe so the light caught it. "Zoe, take my chair. It's two seats over, and the window's still right there, you can watch the bird fine. Marcus gets the solid spot." Zoe moved, the cardinal flared red against the glass, and she actually said thank you, which happened maybe twice a year.

After dinner, Marcus pulled out his phone. "Best of three in Street Racer?"

They were tied at one game each when it happened. Both of them grabbed for the last controller, the good one with the sticky-free triggers. "I won the last round, it's mine," Marcus said. "It's my house," Jaxon said, and then he stopped, because he heard himself doing exactly what Zoe and Marcus had done over the chair.

"Wait. My position is I get the controller. My interest is I want fair triggers so the race is even." He looked at Marcus. "What's yours?"

"I don't care about triggers. My battery's at four percent. My interest is I want a controller that won't die mid-race."

"You're immune to the sticky trigger thing?"

"Completely. I barely notice it."

"So we're not actually contradicting each other," Jaxon said. "We only sound like it." He brought the good controller to the charger by the couch, plugged in the weaker one, and handed it to Marcus. "Yours, charged in ten minutes. Race after."

Marcus plugged it in and grinned. "You're weird now, you know that?"

Jaxon shrugged and picked up the good controller for practice laps, listening for the soft click of the triggers under his thumbs.

Aubrey crouched by the fence with her notebook, drawing the chain she had to turn in Monday: sun, then the tropical milkweed in the corner, then the monarch caterpillars that chewed it, then the mockingbird that patrolled the yard, and at the top, the red-tailed hawk that circled every afternoon. She was halfway through the arrow from caterpillar to bird when she counted the milkweed stems and her stomach dropped. The caterpillars were gone. Every one.

Her little brother Theo came out with a snack, celery in one hand and a folded piece of ham in the other. He bit the celery and it snapped so loud the mockingbird flinched. "Why does this crack like that," Theo asked, "and the ham just bends?" Aubrey took a stalk and pressed it. It resisted, then gave way all at once. She remembered the science book open on her bed: plant cells have a stiff cell wall outside the cell membrane, made mostly of cellulose. "Cellulose," she said, mostly to herself. "Animal cells don't have that wall." Theo nodded like this settled something and wandered toward the garden.

That was when she noticed it. The milkweed was brown at the base, the leaves curling, and she saw the green hose coiled beside it, still dripping. Someone had left the sprinkler aimed there for days, or worse, Dad had sprayed something. She knelt and dug her fingers into the soil. It smelled sour, like the compost bin where the fallen apples slowly decompose. Whatever had killed the plant was still working in the ground.

She tested it the only way she could. She picked one healthy stem from a pot by the porch, the one she'd grown from seed, and set it near the fence where the caterpillars used to cross. Then she waited behind the shed, notebook flat on her knees, pencil still. The mockingbird came first, landed, found nothing, left. The hawk circled at four o'clock, higher than usual, and drifted off toward the creek without stopping.

"Monday," Aubrey said to Theo, tapping her drawing. "I'm going to explain what happens when a link disappears, because I just watched it."

Lauren had to negotiate for the lamp, because Marcus was notorious for claiming the best equipment and then fiddling with it for the whole period. "You hold the ball," she said, "I get the lamp. Deal?" Marcus considered this, then agreed, which surprised her so much she almost forgot what she was doing.

The ball was their Moon and the lamp was the Sun. Lauren switched it on and dimmed the classroom lights, and Marcus walked the ball in a slow circle around her. That was the plan. The problem started when Priya, watching from her desk, shouted, "It's full!" and Devon, watching from the other side of the room, shouted, "It's new!" They argued until Ms. Okafor said, calmly, "Both of you are looking at the same ball." Lauren stared. Half the ball was lit and half was dark, always, no matter where it stood. The phase you saw depended on where you stood, and whether the lit side faced you or away from you. She made Marcus walk the circle again while she spun slowly in place, and there it was: full, then gibbous, then half, then a sliver, then dark, and back again. "Ha!" she said. "I'm Earth. I'm doing the phases."

Later, at recess, the sprinkler line by the fence had leaked all week, and a little stream ran across the blacktop and into the retention pond. At the edge of the water, Devon pointed at a fan of wet sand, spread out like a tiny triangle. "What made that? The water just stops there."

"The stream slows down when it hits the pond," Lauren said, "and it drops all the sand it was carrying, so the sand builds up and makes new land. That's called a delta."

"That's it? That's the whole trick?"

"Rivers do it too," Lauren said, "when they reach a lake or the sea." She crouched, poked the wet edge of the fan with a stick, and said, "I made half the Moon phases with a lamp and a tennis ball this morning. I'm basically unstoppable."

Marcus snorted. "You negotiated that lamp from me, is what happened."

"Same thing," said Lauren, and drew a delta in the sand with her stick, one careful line at a time.

At the French booth at the cultural festival, Penelope clutched her practice sheet and inhaled the smell of butter and melted sugar. Her task: by the end of the afternoon, she had to introduce her whole family and her dog Biscuit in French, using complete sentences, no English allowed. She had practiced all week. "J'ai un chien," she whispered. "Il s'appelle Biscuit."

She spotted the perfect practice partner, a boy about her age waiting at the crêpe stand with a handful of coins. His little sister tugged his sleeve and pointed at a chocolate crêpe. The boy frowned at his coins, then at the price sign, which was smudged beyond reading. Penelope realized he needed to ask the cost, and from the banner above the booth she remembered the phrase written in curly letters: "C'est combien ?" She had also heard the vendor say "Combien ça coûte ?" a minute earlier. Both meant "How much is it?" That was a concept worth testing.

She marched over. "C'est combien ?" she asked the vendor, figuring the boy would hear the answer too. The vendor smiled and said, "Trois euros." The boy's face transformed from worry to relief because he had four euros. "Merci," he told her. "Combien ça coûte ?" he then asked, pointing at a second crêpe, using the other phrase he'd just picked up. "Deux euros cinquante," the vendor answered. The boy counted again and bought crêpes for both of them, one for Penelope, since she'd saved him from a smudged-sign disaster.

Between warm, gooey bites they practiced. "J'ai une soeur," the boy said. "J'ai un frère," Penelope answered, then added, "J'ai un chien. Il s'appelle Biscuit." She rattled off her mother, her father, and her terrible cat in full sentences, and the boy clapped. Later, at the festival stage, when the booth leader asked who could introduce their family in French, Penelope's hand shot up first. She stood tall under the lights and began, "J'ai une famille formidable."

Evelyn pressed the last wire into the clip and held her breath. The bulb stayed dark. Somewhere behind her, a boy was shouting at the radar-speed pitching cage, and the noise made her fingers feel clumsy.

"Try jiggling the switch," said the boy, whose name tag read Marcus. He was lanky and loud, and he had been pacing by her table since she sat down at the Build-a-Circuit station. "Mine lit up on the first try."

"I don't want it to light by accident," Evelyn said, turning the switch over in her hand. "I want to know why it lights." She bent the little metal arm and saw it, a gap where the arm touched only air instead of the screw. A circuit was invisible, a loop of something you couldn't watch move, so she had to picture it, like water in a hidden pipe. She slid the screw closer until the arm pressed flat against it. The bulb glowed.

"Your fastball was twenty meters per second," the museum attendant called to Marcus, whose throw had just clocked on the radar screen. "That beats a walker for sure."

"Does it beat a runner?" Marcus asked. "Runners go, like, twenty kilometers per hour. I don't even know how to compare those."

Evelyn had read a placard near the entrance, a small chart half hidden behind a case of glass that refracted the overhead lights into little rainbows on the wall. She hesitated, then said, "To change a speed in meters per second into kilometers per hour, you multiply by 3.6." She did it in the margin of her worksheet. "Twenty times 3.6 is 72 kilometers per hour."

"Seventy-two!" Marcus yelled. "That's faster than cars in a school zone!"

Evelyn smiled and unscrewed her bulb, then screwed it back in, watching the light return. On the far wall, an exhibit about glowing fungus flickered in its dark case, tiny lights like the one in her hand.

"Throw again," she said, picking up a spare ball. "I bet mine's faster."

Joshua's class had come to the courthouse for a mock legislature, and Ms. Ferrante had promised a prize for whoever could explain a bill's journey best. That's what Joshua wanted, the prize and the glory, but first they had twenty minutes to wait in the lobby. He wandered past the security desk and stopped in front of a framed poster. It showed a document with a heading, The Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and below the title, a date: proclaimed April 17, 1982. He read it twice. His little sister was eleven in dog years compared to that document. He'd assumed rights were just always there, like air. If the Charter became part of the Constitution in 1982, what had people had before that?

He found Priya by the water fountain and pointed at the poster. "Look at the year. Nineteen eighty-two. That's after our parents were born."

"So it's like a bill," Priya said. "It had to pass through the legislature too, sort of. It didn't just appear."

That gave Joshua an idea. He decided to decompose the problem, break it into pieces the way Ms. Ferrante taught them for word problems. A bill starts as an idea, gets introduced, gets debated, gets voted on, and then, if it survives, becomes law. If he could trace the Charter's path, he'd understand the whole system, because it followed the same rule.

When the mock session started, the guide handed Joshua's team a bill about bike helmets on municipal paths. Joshua argued against it at first, thinking a fun field trip shouldn't involve rules. Then Priya whispered, "Think about the poster. Rights got written down because people debated them." He changed his mind mid-debate, which surprised him, and stood up to speak in favor.

"An idea has to travel through the legislature," he said. "Like the Charter, proclaimed on April 17, 1982, becoming part of Canada's Constitution. It's the irony of rules, we have to debate them to be free."

"The irony," the guide repeated, smiling, "is that the kid who opposed the bill just made the most influential speech of the day."

The vote passed, six to two, and Ms. Ferrante wrote Joshua's name at the top of the scoreboard.

John stood in the middle of Ms. Reyes's studio between two rubber plants she called "the choir" and tried, for the fourth time, to sing the low part of "Emperor of the Popsicle Kingdom" while Priya sang the high part. Every single time, his voice climbed up to join hers, like a dog escaping a yard to chase a squirrel. Ms. Reyes played along on her old guitar, but halfway through the verse she stopped, let the strings ring out, and frowned at the instrument as if it had betrayed her.

"That low string's gone flat again," she said. "Controversial little thing. Here, John, hold the neck and turn that peg while I pluck. I'll tell you when it matches my pitch pipe." John gripped the peg and scrutinized it, turning it slowly one way, then the other. When he twisted it left, the note sagged lower, all droopy and sad. When he twisted it right, tighter, the note rose back up. The string rang against her pitch pipe and finally matched, and John felt like he'd solved a tiny mystery, even if the mystery was only a stubborn piece of wood and wire.

Then came the twist, because Priya was watching him with her chin in her hand like a detective. "Wait," she said. "That's your whole problem. Your voice is like that string. When you get nervous, you go loose, and loose goes lower, except your low part isn't low enough, so your brain drags you sideways into my part instead." John opened his mouth to argue, then closed it. It actually fit. Every time he lost his part, he'd been sagging flat first, then grabbing the nearest safe sound, which was her.

"Tightening a string raises its pitch," John said slowly, "and loosening it lowers it. So I need to tighten. Not louder. Tighter." Ms. Reyes raised an eyebrow, clearly deciding not to rescue him. John planted his feet, imagined an invisible peg behind his ear, and gave it a firm twist to the right in his imagination. Priya started the high part. John held his line, steady and low, and for the first time the two notes stacked together instead of crashing like shopping carts.

"Emperor of the popsicle kingdom, please grant me a fudgy crown," they sang, and it worked, it actually worked, both parts locking together like zippers. At the end Priya pointed at him and said, "You may address me as the emperor now." John bowed so low he knocked over a rubber plant, caught it mid-topple, and set it back upright while Ms. Reyes strummed a dramatic finish.

Dad had promised to teach her something on this trip, and by the second morning he still hadn't, so Lily took matters into her own hands. She spread the topographic map of the park across the picnic table, weighed its corners down with pinecones, and frowned at it until Marcus, her little brother, leaned over her shoulder.

"What are you doing?"

"Finding us." She traced her finger along the thin curved lines that looped around a brown blob near the middle of the map. She knew from school that the numbered lines running up and down and side to side were latitude and longitude, and that the town of Fairview sat where two of them crossed. If she could read those numbers, she could tell anyone on Earth exactly where Fairview was. But first she wanted to know how tall the hill above their campsite was, because Dad had bet her a marshmallow that she couldn't figure it out. She counted four lines from the bottom of the hill to the top and multiplied. Two hundred feet per line meant eight hundred feet, which seemed too steep for a hill that had taken them only twenty minutes to climb.

Marcus poked the tiny print along the map's bottom edge. "What's this little box say?"

Lily bent closer. The legend, small enough that she'd walked right past it, said the contour interval was forty feet. "The contour interval," she read slowly. That meant the difference in height between one contour line and the next was forty feet. She redid her count, and the hill came out at one hundred sixty feet, which felt about right for their burning calves and one rest stop. Her first answer had implied the hill was five times taller than it was. She thought about last summer, when she'd guessed the lake was a mile across and refused to check, and Dad had rowed her across it in twenty minutes without saying a word.

"So the hill's smaller than you thought," Marcus said.

"It's exactly the right size. I was the wrong size." She found Fairview's crossing lines, copied the numbers onto her hand, and held it up. "Thirty-four point six north, ninety-eight point two west. Now I can find anything."

"Even the bathroom?"

"Especially the bathroom," Lily said, and folded the map into her back pocket.

Oliver dropped his backpack at the top of the stairs and took them two at a time, because today was the day. Today he and Maya were going to finish their Scratch game, the one where a cat dodges falling donuts and every dodge earns a point. "Did you bring the snacks?" Maya called from the basement couch, already clicking blocks together on her laptop.

"I brought pretzels and a plan," Oliver said, flopping down beside her. On the screen, the cat sprite slid back and forth while donuts rained from the top of the stage. "Now we need the score. Watch this." He dragged out a block that said "change score by 1" and tucked it inside the loop that moved the donuts. Then he added an if-then block: if the cat touched a donut, the score would reset to zero. "So every donut that misses adds a point, but one hit and you lose everything."

They tested it. The cat slid, donuts fell, the score climbed to 7, then 12, then 20, and Oliver pumped both fists. It was working, and it was durable, too, because they ran it five times in a row and the score behaved every single time. "We integrate the high score next," Maya said, opening a second variable. "My brother says that's the fancy word for putting two things together so they work as one."

That was when Maya's brother Dev stomped down the stairs, holding his own laptop and frowning at it like it had insulted him. "My times table quiz is broken," he groaned. "It's supposed to go up to twelve, but it mysteriously stops at eleven. Every time. Eleven times twelve, and then nothing." He turned the screen toward them. Oliver leaned in. At the top of the code sat a line that read range(1, 12).

"Wait," Oliver said slowly. He stared at the line, then at the quiz, then at the line again. Something invisible was going on here, a rule he couldn't see, and he wanted to grab it. "Your table goes to twelve, but it stops just before twelve. What if the second number works like the finish line at a race? You stop at the line, you don't step past it." He reached over and changed the 12 to a 13, so the line read range(1, 13). "Try it now."

Dev hit run. The quiz marched through twelve times twelve, clean and complete, and Maya let out a whoop loud enough that they could hear their mom upstairs. "Oliver, you fixed it with one number," Dev said, shaking his head. "One number. And I've been at this for an hour." Oliver grinned and turned back to the Scratch game, where the donut cat waited. "Okay, high score next," he said, and cracked open the pretzels.

Florence stood at the German club's table at the cultural festival, holding a paper map of a pretend town and trying to remember how to say that her family had two cats and a loud dog. She despised feeling stuck, especially in public, so she kept repeating the sentence under her breath until it came out whole.

Then Marco from her class appeared, dragging a folding chair and a red scarf. "We need you," he said. "Priya is blindfolded, and I'm supposed to guide her through the obstacle course, but I have to go help at the food table. You know the direction words, right?"

Florence did not know the direction words, not really, but she said yes anyway. Priya stood near the stacks of plastic crates, the scarf tied over her eyes, waiting. Marco scribbled three words on a scrap of paper and shoved it into Florence's hand before jogging off. On it were links, rechts, geradeaus.

Here was a puzzle she could actually see, in a way. If Priya turned the wrong way, Florence could guess what she had said. She started easy. "Geradeaus." Priya walked straight between two crates. So that one meant straight ahead. Then, quietly, Marco's little brother Tomas whispered near her elbow, "Links means left." That narrowed it down: if links was left, then rechts, the remaining word, had to be right. She tested it. "Rechts." Priya turned right and bumped gently into a cushioned mat. "Correct side!" Florence called. The pattern held every time after that.

When Priya pulled off the scarf, blinking in the sunlight, she grinned. "Say the family sentence now," she said. "You always stop halfway." Florence took a breath and got through the whole thing, cats and loud dog and all, and it felt almost easy. "Zwei Katzen und ein lauter Hund," she finished, and Priya applauded with two plastic cups from the food table.

Noah had one week to build a model that would illustrate the phases of the Moon, and his science table already looked like a disaster. The lamp stood in for the Sun, a styrofoam ball for the Moon, and a basketball for Earth, but every time he walked the ball around the lamp, his best friend Priya frowned.

"That's not right," she said. "The Moon can't have a shadow on it from that angle. Half of it should be lit no matter where it is."

"Then why do we see phases at all?" Noah asked. He stopped the ball, squinted at the lamp, and turned the styrofoam sphere slowly in his fingers. Half of it was bright white. The other half sat in darkness. He walked around the table himself, watching the ball from Earth's position, and suddenly only a sliver of the lit side faced him. A crescent. When he moved to the far side of the table, the whole lit face swung into view. A full Moon.

"The phases are just my point of view," he said. "The light doesn't change. Where I stand changes."

Priya grinned and wrote it on their poster. But the next day, when Mr. Okafor set a globe on the table for their presentation, Noah noticed an anomaly. The globe was leaning, its pole tipped far from straight up, and nobody had bumped it. He tipped it upright and the globe wobbled back into its tilt on its stand.

"It's supposed to lean," said a girl named Marcus's sister, passing by their table. "Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun."

"That's a weirdly exact number," Noah said, but he wrote it down anyway, because their grade depended on getting details right. He checked the classroom globe with a protractor the teacher lent him, and the tilt matched. On the display screen, a diagram of Earth's path around the Sun showed the same lean, steady the whole way around.

Their presentation time was endangered when the lamp's cord came loose and the bulb flickered, but Priya held the plug in the socket while Noah walked the Moon ball around the basketball globe, calling out each phase as the fifth graders in the audience saw it happen. New Moon. First quarter. Full. When he finished, he pointed at the globe.

"And notice it's leaning," he said. "About 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun. That's not a mistake. That's just how Earth is."

A boy in the front row raised his hand. "So if we ever move to Mars, will we lean too?"

Alexandra slid her worksheet toward the middle of the table, where the rest of the math club could see it. Fraction problems covered the page, and she had gotten stuck on the third one: 1/2 plus 1/3. She knew the answer had to be bigger than one half but smaller than one whole, and she said so. "Then test it," said Marcus, tapping her pencil. "Try cutting both fractions into sixths. Two sixths plus three sixths." She wrote it out, added, and got five sixths, which fit between her two bounds, so she grinned and crossed out the wrong answer above it. Mr. Okafor had a reputation for never giving away an answer, and now she saw why.

Across the table, Priya was not grinning. Priya wanted the team's geometry trophy back more than anything, because last spring her older sister had dropped it in the hallway and the club had never won it again. She had spent a week on her proof for the practice meet, and the judge's paper came back with a red circle around one line. "Two sides and an angle," the note read, "but not the included angle."

Alexandra leaned over. "What's that mean?" "I don't know," Priya said. "The angle has to be the one between the two sides. That's the included angle. I used a different one, so it doesn't prove the triangles match." Priya's shoulders sagged.

Alexandra remembered sitting in this same room last fall, when she had glued two paper triangles together because two sides matched, and they had still been different shapes. She had thought she was just bad at geometry. Now she looked at Priya's diagram and noticed the angle Priya had marked sat at the end of both sides, not in the notch between them. "There," Alexandra said, pointing. "Your sides are here and here. The angle between them is that one." She could not see why it worked, only that the judge's rule was explicit about it, so it had to sit in that spot.

Priya erased the mark, drew a new one in the notch, and rewrote the whole line. Then she copied the diagram onto a fresh sheet and slid it across the table to Alexandra. "Check it with me," she said.

Sara stood in the living room on Sunday morning with her arms crossed and her hip stuck out, which was her official arguing pose. "The festival is tomorrow, and I still can't get the timing right. I need the video, just for one hour."

Mom did not even look up from her crossword. "You know the rule. Sunday morning until noon is our rest time. No screens, no rushing around, no frantic practice drills. That's the whole point. We slow down so the day doesn't get away from us, and so we notice each other instead of our phones."

"That's a lovely reason," Sara said. "I will notice everyone tomorrow while I'm dancing completely off beat." She flopped onto the couch beside Uncle Kimo, who was visiting from Hilo and had been quietly watching this whole thing like it was a very good show. He was holding something round and brown with a cord around its neck.

"You're dancing the old style, yeah?" he said. "Hula kahiko." He lifted the round thing and thumped it against the floor, and a deep hollow boom rolled through the room. Sara sat up straight. That was the sound from the video, the one she kept missing. "This is an ipu," Uncle Kimo went on, "a gourd drum. The old hula isn't danced to a song at all. It goes with chanting and drums like this. No melody to follow. That's probably why you can't find the beat, cousin. You've been listening for singing that isn't there."

Sara stared at him, then at the ipu, then at the ceiling, where an invisible lightbulb might as well have switched on. All week she had been trying to catch a tune, waiting for a note to tell her when to step. But the timing wasn't hiding inside a melody. It lived in the chant, in the words themselves. It was like hunting for her missing sock under the bed when it was in her shoe the whole time.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Rest time. No screens. But nothing in the rules says no chanting." Mom's pencil paused over the crossword. Sara planted her feet, took a breath, and began, low and shaky at first, the old words about the sea. Uncle Kimo kept time on the gourd drum, and her feet found the boom, boom, then the quick double beat, exactly where they belonged. Little brother Noah wandered in wearing a random cape made from a beach towel and started chanting along, getting every word hilariously wrong, which broke Sara up laughing so badly she had to start over twice.

At noon Mom declared rest time officially over and went to take her antibiotic that had been waiting in the cupboard since breakfast. Sara, dripping with effort, begged Uncle Kimo to dismantle his plan to head home early. "One more hour," she said, and struck her opening pose. Noah, still caped, picked up the kitchen pot and a wooden spoon, and raised both like drumsticks. "Ready, cousin," he said.

The washing machine at home had died on Tuesday, so on Saturday Mya and her dad carried three baskets of laundry to the Spin Cycle Laundromat, which smelled like warm soap and pennies. Her dad dropped the baskets, fed quarters into two machines, and then handed her a five dollar bill and a short list written on a dryer sheet. "Milk and stamps," he said. "The corner store. You know the way."

She knew the way. She had walked it maybe two hundred times, but always with somebody. The light at Foster Street took forever to change, and the store's bell jangled when the door moved even a centimeter, so you could hear customers coming before you saw them. Still, standing at the laundromat door with the bill folded in her fist, she felt hesitant, like the sidewalk outside had gotten longer since the last time she'd looked at it.

"Your mother walked to that store alone at nine," her dad said, which was supposed to be encouraging but wasn't. Mya thought about her mom at nine, small and fearless, and decided she could manage at twelve. She walked out. At the corner store she found the milk, stood in line, and counted her change twice at the register because the cashier had already turned to the next customer. Two dollars and thirty-one cents. She counted it again on the walk back, lips moving, and it came out the same both times, which felt like passing a secret test nobody had announced.

Back at the laundromat, the first load had finished, and Mya pulled out her white school shirt and winced. It was pink. Not pink like a sunset, pink like a watermelon that had lost an argument. Her dad held it up and said, "Well." In the load there was also one red sock, brand new, that her little brother had insisted needed washing before Monday.

Mya laid the shirt flat on the folding table and stared at it. She hadn't mixed the clothes up; her brother had dropped the sock into the whites basket himself. But something had to have traveled from the sock to the shirt, because the sock had come out barely lighter than it went in, and the shirt had gone in white and come out pink. She thought about the water, how it had sat in the machine with all of it tumbling together for half an hour, and she said, "The new sock let dye go into the wash water, and the water carried it to everything pale in there." Her dad said, "That's why people sort by colour, kid," and she thought, nobody ever tells you why, they just say sort.

She ran a test with the second load, which was her idea. Darks in one machine, whites and pale things alone in another, no new red anything. When that load came out, everything was the color it was supposed to be, and she folded it in stacks, smug, while her dad watched his phone.

Later, walking home with the milk, she turned the pink shirt over in the bag and thought about her brother's sock, which was technically his fault but mostly just a sock doing what new red socks do. She hadn't checked the basket before starting the load, either. She still wasn't sure whose job that was.

"I'm wearing it anyway," her brother announced at dinner. "Pink's my color."

Alexis stood at the zucchini booth at the farmers' market, holding a recipe card her grandmother had written out in loopy blue ink: Zucchini Honey Muffins, makes twelve. "One dollar each," said the farmer, "or three for two." Alexis counted her coins and picked three, choosing the ones that were small and heavy, the way Gran had taught her last summer.

She could still remember that day clearly. Gran had let her measure the flour all by herself, and Alexis had been so proud that she'd declared the kitchen a monarchy with herself as queen. "Then I hereby classify you as the royal taste tester," Gran had said, bowing so low her reading glasses slid off. They had laughed until the muffins almost burned.

Today was different, though, because Alexis was baking alone. Gran was at the dentist, and the kitchen was Alexis's whole responsibility. She grated the zucchini, cracked the eggs, and stirred until her arm ached. The recipe card said, in Gran's handwriting at the bottom: Preheat oven to 375. Don't skip this. Alexis looked at the oven. The oven looked back, cold and blank. The last time she'd baked with Gran, she remembered, the muffins had come out pale and squat, dense as hockey pucks. Gran had frowned at them and said, "Hmm. What did we do differently?" Alexis hadn't known then.

She thought about it now, turning the wooden spoon in the batter. Gran always put the tray in after the oven had beeped. Alexis, that day, had slid the tray in right away to save time, because waiting was boring. The pale, squat muffins had gone in before the oven was hot. She had never connected those two things until this moment, standing alone in the kitchen with the oven still cold. So that was what preheating meant: waiting until the oven reached the temperature you set before the batter went in, so baking started at the right heat. She turned the dial and sat on the counter to wait, swinging her sneakers against the cupboard.

The wait felt endless, so she cut the last zucchini into diagonal slices and arranged them on the counter like a tiny green fence. When the oven finally beeped, she filled the paper liners, slid the tray in, and set the timer for twenty-two minutes exactly.

The muffins rose into golden domes, crackled on top, and smelled like honey and Sunday morning. She carried them, still warm, to the farmers' market in a basket covered with a dish towel. The zucchini farmer took one bite and closed his eyes. "Your gran's recipe?"

"Mine," Alexis said. "Baked by the queen herself."

He bowed so low his cap fell off. "Then I hereby classify myself as the royal taste tester."

"Get in line," Alexis said, and lifted the towel.

Harrison stood in the kitchen holding his speech cards like they might bite. Tomorrow he had to give a two-minute speech in front of the whole class, with an opening hook, three points, and a closing, and every time he practiced, he sped up until the words crashed into each other like dominoes.

"Again," said his sister Priya, munching a granola bar at the table. "You just said your hook and your first point in one breath."

"I know." Harrison dropped into a chair. "I can't figure out where to stop."

Priya shoved her laptop toward him. On the screen was a script from her school play, covered in pencil slashes. "Watch," she said, and pointed at one. "Actors split a script into beats," she said. "A new beat starts wherever a character's thought or tactic changes, and a pause often marks that shift." She tapped a slash between two lines. "My thought changes there, so I stop. New thought, new beat."

Harrison grabbed a pencil. That was the hidden rule he'd been missing. His speech wasn't one long river of words; it was chunks, and each chunk had a job. He spread his cards on the table and hunted for the places where his thinking changed. After the hook, slash. After point one, slash. He marked all of them, then added one more and excluded the part about his uncle's failed business, because it didn't fit any of his three points no matter how much he liked it.

"Ready?" Priya set the kitchen timer for two minutes.

He stood up, took a breath, and started. "What if I told you a lemonade stand could pay for a new bike?" Pause. "That's income, money coming in." Pause. At every slash he stopped, and the stops made the next sentence land harder. Priya grinned so wide her grin looked infectious, and Harrison caught it.

The timer buzzed. One minute fifty-eight.

"You sounded like a person," Priya announced, "not a panicking vacuum cleaner."

Harrison squared his cards. "One more time."

Parker stared at the tray of parts in the Build-an-Atom lab at the science museum: fat red balls for protons, gray ones for neutrons, and blue marbles that were supposed to be electrons, though they kept rolling off the table. His ticket said his atom was oxygen, which meant eight protons, and his little sister Josie had appointed herself the jury. "Wrong," she announced before he had attached anything. "You dropped one under the bench."

"This is why I didn't invite you," Parker said, fishing out the runaway proton. He counted again, touching each ball with one finger like a banker counting coins. Eight. Then he had to figure out the neutrons, which were allowed to vary, and the electrons, which had to go in rings, two in the first ring and six in the second. He built it, took it apart, and built it again, because the second ring kept collapsing whenever Josie bumped the table with her elbow.

The real trouble started at the station next door, where a volunteer handed out strips of litmus paper. You dipped them in a mystery liquid, and they turned pink or blue depending on what the liquid was. Parker dipped his strip in cup number three and it went pink, while Josie's went blue in cup five. "That's suspicious," she said. "The paper must be biased against my cup." Parker laughed and told her the paper didn't have opinions, it just changed color, and the color was the clue. It was like the atom model, he realized. You couldn't see the thing itself, so you read the evidence it left behind and worked backward to what had to be true.

The word litmus snagged in his mind, and a memory surfaced from last summer at Grandpa's house. Parker had been scrubbing the garden wall with a brush, complaining about the crusty gray-green patches stuck to the stone, when Grandpa came out with a mug of tea and told him to leave those alone. "That's lichen," Grandpa had said. "Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark." Parker had thought that was the strangest fact he'd ever heard, a rock-scab turning into science paper, and now here was the paper, sitting in his hand.

He held his strip up next to the window, where the light was strong enough to show the little fibers. "Josie, guess where this comes from." She shrugged. "A paper factory, obviously." "Lichen. Like the stuff on Grandpa's wall. The crusty stuff on rocks and tree bark." Josie squinted at her strip, then at him, deciding whether to believe a brother who couldn't even keep six electrons in one ring.

The lab assistant walked past and said the museum would enforce the five-items-per-tray rule, so Parker gave back his spare neutrons. Then he carried his finished oxygen atom, both rings wobbling, across the room to the testing station. The checker counted the protons, counted the electrons, and stamped his card. Josie leaned over the card and read the stamp out loud: "Certified oxygen. Congratulations, you just made air."

Elena spread her poster board on the picnic table and stared at the blank page. Tomorrow she had to draw a food chain from the sun all the way to a top predator, and then explain what would happen if one link disappeared. Her motivation was simple: Mrs. Okafor had promised the best diagram would hang in the hallway for the whole school year, and Elena wanted that wall more than anything.

She had just drawn a fat yellow sun when her little brother Theo came out carrying their grandfather's old microscope and two mystery slides. "Grandpa said one is leaf and one is cheek cells," Theo said, setting them down beside her crayons. "But he forgot which is which. Can we look?"

Elena cherished afternoons like this, when a problem just appeared out of nowhere. She clipped the first slide under the lens and leaned down. The cells were neat little rectangles, like bricks in a wall, lined up in tidy rows. She switched to the second slide and squinted. These cells were blobby, roundish, scattered every which way like spilled beads.

"Okay," she said slowly. "Plant cells have rigid walls, so they're fixed and boxy, like these bricks. Animal cells only have a flexible membrane, so they come out rounded and irregular." She tapped the first slide. "Leaf. And the blobby ones are from somebody's cheek." Theo made a face. "Grandpa's cheek," Elena said, and they both laughed.

Then she stopped laughing, because something clicked. She pulled the leaf slide out and looked at her poster. "Theo, that's the whole point of my food chain," she said, grabbing a green crayon. "The sun feeds the leaf, and the leaf is made of those boxy little bricks, millions of them. A caterpillar eats the nutritious leaves and gets fat, a robin eats the caterpillar, and a hawk eats the robin. Sun, leaf, caterpillar, robin, hawk." She drew arrows down the page. "Every link is feeding the next one."

"But what if one link disappears?" Theo asked, peeling an orange and handing her half without being asked, because he could see she was on a roll and wouldn't stop to eat.

"Let's find out," Elena said. She drew a second chain, then scribbled the caterpillars out entirely. "No caterpillars means the robins go hungry and leave. Then the hawks lose their food too, and there are way too many leaves with nobody eating them." She sat back. "One missing link, and the whole chain gets weird."

Theo held up the leaf slide to the light. "So these little boxes feed everything?"

"These little boxes feed everything," Elena said, and drew an extra-large leaf right next to the sun.

Oliver's mother had dropped him at Sunrise Travel for the afternoon because the dentist was next door, and because Mr. Adeyemi, the agent, had known him since he was five. The office smelled of old paper and coffee. On the back wall hung a giant world map with faint lines drawn across it, sideways and up and down, like graph paper wrapped around the world.

"You can find any city on Earth if you can read those lines," Mr. Adeyemi said, resting his coffee cup on the counter. "Latitude lines run sideways. Longitude lines run up and down. A city sits where one of each crosses. Nobody memorizes all the cities. You just read the numbers." He tapped a spot in Africa. "Cairo, about 30 degrees north latitude, 31 degrees east longitude." Oliver leaned close and traced the numbers with one finger, the way he had once traced the letters on his grandfather's frail old globe before it cracked in the move and had to be thrown out. He still felt bad about packing it badly. His grandfather had only said, "Maps outlive globes anyway," and Oliver had never been sure whether that was forgiveness or not.

A woman hurried in with a folder of papers, a customer named Mrs. Okafor who wanted to visit her sister in a city Oliver had never heard of. "Sister keeps saying, come before the heat, come before the heat," she told Mr. Adeyemi, "but she can never tell me why the heat comes when it comes." Mr. Adeyemi began flipping through a fat index of cities, muttering that his filing system was a disgrace and that if he could just win the office pool for most trips booked this month, he would finally buy a proper computerized system and retire the shoebox of index cards under his desk.

Oliver, meanwhile, was not looking up cities. He was looking at the tan patches. The Sahara, the Arabian Desert, the Kalahari, the Australian outback, the stretch across Mexico. He had noticed something at home on his wall map, and now, on this bigger one, he counted again, using the latitude lines like a measuring stick. The big hot deserts were not scattered anywhere. They lined up in two belts, one above the equator and one below, and when he read the numbers, the belts sat near 30 degrees north and near 30 degrees south. He checked one desert after another, and they kept landing on those numbers, as if the map had a rule it was following.

"Where sinking air warms up and dries out," Oliver said slowly, reading aloud from the small print under the map's legend. "That's why the deserts sit there, near 30 degrees north or south of the equator. It's a pattern."

"Find me the pattern for a rainforest, then," Mrs. Okafor said, half joking. Oliver ran his finger along the equator itself, where the green blobbiest jungles lived, past a poster of toucans dipping into flowers for nectar, past a caption about orchids that seemed able to colonize every wet branch in sight.

"Hot and wet at the equator, hot and dry at thirty," Oliver said. "So tell your sister the heat comes because her city sits in the dry belt. Thirty-two degrees north." Mrs. Okafor laughed and booked the ticket. Mr. Adeyemi slid the index card into his shoebox and said, "Two more bookings and that computer is mine."

Oliver went back to the map and put his finger on the empty blue Pacific, right at 30 degrees south, and waited to see if the rule would hold even there.

Zoe arrived at her grandmother's house on Saturday morning with a granola bar hidden in her jacket pocket. Her family had agreed she would try keeping Shabbat for part of the day, from sunrise until three o'clock, the way Grandma did. No phone, no money, no snacks between meals. Zoe had said yes mostly to get her mother off her back, and she planned to eat the granola bar in the garden shed the first time Grandma wasn't looking.

At breakfast, she asked Grandma why rest even counted as doing something. "You're not doing anything," Zoe said. "You're just not doing stuff."

Grandma set down her teacup. "You could put it that way. Or you could say it's a principle, one day out of seven, and the point is to stop," she said. She slid a folded letter across the table. "Your grandfather wrote this the year he died. Read it while the light's good."

The letter was written on translucent paper, the kind that showed the newspaper print beneath it, and Zoe tilted it toward the window. Grandpa had written about his own grandmother, who kept the whole day, sunrise to three stars, and how at first he thought it was empty. Then he described sitting with nothing in his hands and noticing, for the first time, the sound of the kettle and the creak of the third stair. He wrote that the day was like a window that had been painted shut and someone finally pushed it open.

Zoe put the granola bar back in her pocket without taking it out. At noon she went with Grandma to Danny's house, where Danny's family was sitting shiva for his grandfather. Danny was in the kitchen, and Zoe asked him what the word meant that people kept saying upstairs.

"Olam ha-ba," Danny said. "That's what they call the afterlife. It means the world to come."

When they got home, Zoe pulled Grandma's big Tanakh off the shelf and searched for the phrase, flipping through Genesis and the prophets. She found nothing. "It's not in here," she said. "Not even once."

"Not in the Hebrew Bible, no," Grandma said, and went back to her tea.

Zoe sat with that. Grandpa hadn't needed it printed anywhere either; he had written his own letter and left it where she would find it, exactly on the day she needed something to fill the quiet. She stayed past three o'clock without checking the clock, and when the shadows stretched across the kitchen floor, she opened the Tanakh again and started at the beginning.

"I'll read until dinner," she said.

The fourth game of the day, and Payton still hadn't beaten Marcus. They were sitting on the porch of the crafts cabin, the chessboard between them, while everyone else was at the lake. Marcus moved his bishop, grinned, and leaned back like he'd already won.

Payton picked up her knight to think, then set it back down without moving it. "Hold on. I want to look at the whole board first."

"No take-backs," Marcus said immediately. "You touched it, you have to move it."

"That's not a rule. I wasn't even going to move it yet."

They argued for a solid minute, getting louder, until Payton held up a hand. "Okay. Naming the problem: you think touching means committing, and I think only moving means committing. Those are different rules."

"Fine," Marcus said, "but which one is the actual rule?"

Payton looked around. The only chess book at camp belonged to Dolores, the craft lady, who was pretending to weave but obviously listening. "Can we borrow that book? Just to check one thing?"

Dolores handed over a worn paperback with a cracked spine. Payton flipped through it until she found the tournament rules, and there it was, in print. In formal chess, the touch-move rule says a player who deliberately touches one of their own pieces must move it, if that piece has a legal move. "Look," she said. "It even has a name. The touch-move rule."

Marcus read it twice. "So you have to move the knight."

"Right. But now we agree on the rule, so it's fair for both of us. Next time you touch your rook, same thing happens to you."

"That's going to be a disaster for me," Marcus said. "I touch everything. I'm like a raccoon."

Payton moved her knight to the only safe square, which, it turned out, forked his rook and queen. "Interesting," she said, and reached for her water bottle very, very carefully, with one finger.

Violet sat at her mother's desk on a Saturday, when the office was almost empty, using the spare computer to hunt for a science project idea. She wanted to build something that would insulate a soda can and keep it cold, and she typed "keep can cold" into the search bar. The first screen full of results was mostly shopping links and a big sponsored box shouting BEST THERMOS. She remembered her mother saying that half of searching was choosing words, so she tried "aluminum can insulation experiment foam." The junk mostly dropped away, and one result from a university engineering page looked real. She noticed the small gray word "Ad" tucked beside the second result and skipped it.

Her friend Marco had come along, and he was supposed to be helping, but he was busy being proud of something else. "Look at my password," he said, turning his phone toward her. "p@ssw0rd. The a is an at sign and the o is a zero. Nobody can guess that." He had changed it that morning so he could log into the project-sharing site they used for science club.

"Ad" or not, Violet couldn't stop wondering about it. She remembered a month ago, when the club's shared account got locked after someone kept guessing at the password, and Mr. Reyes had said guessers work through obvious things fast. She opened a new tab and searched with specific keywords: "password guessing programs dictionary words common substitutions." She skipped the sponsored result and read a short article on a security site.

"Marco," she said. "Guessing programs try dictionary words, names, and common swaps like '@' for 'a' or '0' for 'o' early." She read the line twice to be sure. "So your at signs and zeros add almost nothing."

"No way," Marco said. He looked at his phone. "It looks so tricky."

Violet tested it. She searched "p@ssw0rd common password" and found it on lists of the most guessed passwords in the world. Marco made an abrupt grab for the keyboard, but she was already typing, and she pulled up a page where he could make a longer password out of four random words instead. He typed in "copper foam jar moon" and hit save.

"Fine," he said. "But I'm keeping the can project."

"Then help me search," Violet said. She slid the notepad over and wrote "soda can insulation" at the top of a fresh list of keywords. Marco sighed, pulled his chair closer, and started typing.

Jaxon stood in front of the bilingual booth at the festival, holding his crumpled worksheet about next year's plans. His teacher had circled one word in red: "teneré." Next to it, a single question mark. The booth had a sign that said "Habla con nosotros," and behind the table sat a girl about his age wearing a shirt with a luminous sugar skull glowing under the string lights.

"Tengo un perro y una hermana," Jaxon said, mostly to prove he could. "Mi perro se llama Biscuit. Mi hermana se llama Dana."

The girl laughed. "Biscuit is the dog or the sister?"

"The dog. Dana would retire from being my sister before answering to Biscuit." He flattened the worksheet on the table. "But I wrote this paragraph about next year, and this one word came back circled in red. I figured you just stick an é on any verb. Tener, teneré. Boom."

She shook her head and wrote on a napkin: tendré. "Tener becomes tendré," she said. "It means I will have. Not teneré."

Jaxon stared at the napkin. So the verb wasn't just getting a new ending; it was changing its stem too, and there was no way to see that coming unless somebody showed you or you caught the pattern yourself. He tested it out loud. "El año que viene tendré trece años. Y Biscuit tendrá... um, much older in dog years."

"Better," she said. "Try the whole paragraph."

He worked through it slowly, fixing verbs one by one, while somewhere behind them a drummer started up and a vendor carried a luminous glass vessel of lemonade past the booth, ice cubes rattling like tiny applause. When he finished, the girl clapped anyway, louder than the ice.

"Next year," Jaxon said, pointing at the napkin, "tendré un perro que habla español mejor que yo."

"Keep practicing," she said, and wrote her number for the language exchange club on the corner of the napkin, right beside tendré.

Kaitlyn had exactly one night to figure out an opening hook, because Mrs. Parekh had made it very clear: tomorrow, everyone gives a two-minute speech, three points, a closing, and no starting with "Hi, my name is." Kaitlyn's draft began with "Hi, my name is," which she now regarded as evidence of a desolate imagination. She crumpled it into her pocket and wandered toward the auditorium, where the drama club was rehearsing because Mrs. Parekh refused to retire the old tradition of holding the sixth-grade speech contest on the same stage, one night after the actors.

One boy, Dev, stood alone under a single spotlight, saying strange things to nobody. "To be, or not to be," he told the empty air. Kaitlyn sat down in the dark rows and watched. There was no other actor. No reply. Just Dev, pacing, thinking out loud as if the audience were inside his head.

"You missed your cue partner," she whispered to herself, then frowned. There was no partner. So who was he talking to? She tested the simplest idea she had: maybe nobody, and that was the point. She slipped backstage after the run-through and asked him straight out.

"Who are you talking to up there? The stage is empty."

"Exactly," Dev said, peeling off his pretend crown. "It's a soliloquy. The character's alone on stage, and the audience gets to hear his private thoughts."

Kaitlyn walked home fast, turning it over. A speech that let the audience hear her private thoughts. Her topic was "why the school should fix the drinking fountain by the gym," which was, she admitted, not a natural thriller. But what if she started alone in thought, like the boy in the spotlight? She rewrote the opening at her kitchen table while her little brother banged his spoon. "Every day I walk past that fountain and think, not again," she wrote, and underlined it twice.

The next night she stood on the stage, waited for silence, and began, "Not again. That's what I think, every single day, in the east hallway, and I've never told anyone until now." She heard a kid in the second row sit up. She gave her three points, steered the ending like a boat with a good rudder, and closed with, "So tomorrow, when you pass that fountain, you'll know exactly what I'm thinking." Mrs. Parekh wrote something on her clipboard and did not frown. In the wings, Dev gave her a small bow.

Mathis crouched between the rows of onions with his sketchbook balanced on his knee, and so far the page held exactly one thing: a sun with rays radiating out of it in every direction. His assignment was due Monday. Draw a food chain, his teacher had said, from the sun all the way to a top predator, and explain what happens if one link disappears. The garden was supposed to give him the whole chain for free, but so far it was giving him nothing but dirt under his nails.

"You're staring at an onion," said Priya, dropping down beside him with a bucket of water she was supposed to be carrying somewhere.

"I'm looking for aphids." Tiny green aphids meant the food chain's middle links. Aphids sucked juice from the onions, ladybugs ate the aphids, and the ladybug was his top predator. If he could find the bugs and sketch them, the poster would practically draw itself. He had already tried three plants in vain. Then he spotted them, a whole crowd of green specks clustered on an onion leaf, and right beside them, one round orange ladybug, steady as a stone. He copied the scene fast, before anything hopped away.

Priya leaned over his shoulder. "You made the leaf way too plain. Mrs. Okafor will want the cells. She's got that microscope in the shed, the one the bank donated when the garden almost got sold to pay somebody's mortgage." Mathis had forgotten about the microscope. He picked a thin sliver of onion skin, carried it to the shed, and slid it under the lens. The cells appeared like neat brick walls, each one boxed in. He labeled the cell wall, then the nucleus, easy. Then he reached the label that said cell membrane, and his pencil stopped. There was no line inside the boxes. Nothing. He turned the focus wheel back and forth until his eyes ached. "Maybe onion cells don't even have one," he muttered.

He tried a second slide, then a third. Same thing. The box stayed clean and single-lined, and the missing membrane stayed missing, no matter how he squinted. Then, staring until the brick shapes blurred, he understood. The membrane wasn't gone. It was pressed right up against the inside of the wall, so tight against it that it didn't show as its own line at all. The cell was full, that was all, so full that the membrane had nowhere to be except flat against the wall. He wrote "cell membrane" with an arrow pointing at the very edge of the box, right against the wall line, and drew a small tight second line beside it on his poster version so nobody else would hunt for it the way he had.

On the walk home he thought about the aphids, fat and crowded on that leaf, and the lone ladybug holding the border. Back at the garden, Priya was still watering. "Finished?" she called.

"Almost." He flipped his sketchbook open to the sun. "Watch this." He drew a big X through the ladybug, then over the aphids he wrote, in careful block letters, "100 of them by Friday."

Mathis tapped the recipe against his knee and stared at the little propane oven bolted to the corner of the camper. Breakfast was at seven o'clock sharp, because Marcus and Theo were hiking over from the far campsites at six forty-five and would arrive starving. The muffins needed twenty minutes in the oven, and the oven needed fifteen minutes to preheat, plus ten minutes to mix the batter. The eggs, on the other hand, would take five minutes flat. He had been naive to think, when he'd volunteered last night, that everything could just happen at once. Now, with the clock reading six o'clock, he grabbed his pencil and flipped the recipe card over.

He remembered the time last summer when his cousin Priya had invited him for dinner and everything had come out wrong, the potatoes cold, the chicken still pink, the salad sweating on the counter. Priya had shrugged and said, "You start with the one that takes longest and plan backward from the time you want to eat." At the time Mathis had only cared about the pizza they'd ordered afterward. Now, at the picnic table under the pines, he wrote 7:00 at the bottom of the card and started climbing. Muffins out at 7:00 meant they went in at 6:40. Into a preheated oven meant the oven had to be on by 6:25. Batter mixed by then meant mixing at 6:15. Eggs, the quick thing, could wait until 6:55.

He cranked the oven dial and checked the time. Six oh five. Ahead of schedule, for once. Then a gust off the lake rattled the camper and the pilot light went out with a soft pop. The wind had thwarted him. Mathis crouched down, relit it, and dragged the picnic table's windward side against the camper wall as a shield, checking the little blue flame every few minutes after that.

By 6:22 the oven ticked warmly, the batter stood in paper cups, and Theo's voice came up the trail calling his name. Mathis slid the tray in at 6:40 exactly and cracked the eggs into the skillet at 6:55, watching both timers like a hawk. From Theo's perspective, arriving to the smell of baking, Mathis looked like somebody who had done this a hundred times.

At 7:00 Mathis pulled the muffins out, golden and steaming, and set them beside the eggs just as Marcus reached the table. "You're a wizard," Marcus said, already reaching. Mathis slid the plate closer and said, "First one's yours if you get the butter."

The kitchen smelled like garlic bread, but Payton could barely taste it. Her cousins Dez and Marisol had spent the whole afternoon playing their dinosaur card game, and now nobody was speaking except through her. "Tell her the T. rex beats everything," Dez said, jabbing his fork toward Marisol. "Tell him the volcano card wiped out the whole herd, so my raptors win," Marisol shot back. Payton put down her spoon. "Why do you keep telling me? I wasn't even playing."

"Because you're in the middle," Dez said. "You decide who won." Marisol nodded and slid the whole messy pile of cards across the table, waiting. Payton stared at the cards, at the greasy fingerprints, at the volcano card sitting on top of a herd of plastic-coated raptors. If she named a winner, the loser would carry that resentment around for a week, and next Sunday's dinner would be nothing but cold silence and kicked shins under the table. She had seen it happen before, like a species going extinct one Sunday at a time.

Then she remembered the word from the poster in the school hallway, the one about arguments: mediator. "I'm not a judge," she said slowly. "A judge decides who's right. A mediator is a neutral third person who helps two sides reach their own agreement." Dez squinted. "So who won?" "Nobody yet. You two are going to decide, not me." She held up the volcano card. "First we name the actual problem. Marisol, you say the volcano makes the herd extinct. Dez, you say the T. rex wasn't in the herd."

They argued for a minute, but quieter now. Payton tested an idea: what if the rule depended on whether the T. rex card had been played before the volcano? She asked each of them to show the order the cards had gone down, and Marisol checked the app, which transmitted the game log to her phone. The log showed the T. rex had landed last. "So," Dez said, "new rule. Anything played after the volcano survives." Marisol considered it. "Fine. But the volcano can only be used once per game." Dez stuck out his hand. "Deal." They shook over the mashed potatoes. "Same rule next Sunday?" Marisol asked, already shuffling.

The waiting room of Bright Smiles Dental smelled like mint and rubber gloves, and Landon had already read the poster about molars twice. His problem was bigger than a cavity. Next week he had to give a science report on how bees pollinate flowers, standing in front of the whole class, and ever since Ms. Rivera announced it, his hands got clammy and his brain went fuzzy. His mom said everyone gets nervous, which did not help at all.

In the corner, a girl about his age sat tracing something on the armrest of her chair. Up, across, down, across. Slow and steady, like she was drawing a square over and over. Landon watched her do it four times before his curiosity won.

"Are you drawing a map?" he asked.

She looked up like she'd been caught. "It's box breathing. My sister taught me before her recitals." She traced one side with her finger. "You breathe in for four, hold for four, breathe out for four, then hold for four. Then you do the whole pattern again." She demonstrated, sliding her finger up the invisible left wall while she inhaled, across the top while she held it, down the side while she breathed out, and along the bottom during the last hold.

Landon tried it right there, drawing his own square on the magazine cover in front of him. In four, hold four, out four, hold four. By the time the receptionist called his name, something surprising had happened: the fizzy feeling in his chest had shrunk to almost nothing.

In the chair, Dr. Okafor tilted her light and peered at his back teeth. "You're growing fast, Landon. Growing bodies sweat more, which is why showering every day and using deodorant becomes a significant part of the routine around your age. It's not a punishment, just biology."
