Landon grinned around the suction tube. Growth, sweat, breathing squares: it was a lot of new information, but he felt ready. Monday morning, standing in front of his class, he traced a square on the podium, one side for each count of four, and began: "Bees don't just visit flowers. They pollinate them."

Olivia stood at the garage door with a five-dollar bill folded in her pocket, staring down the sidewalk toward the corner store. Mom had said she was old enough to go alone this time, but the trip felt enormous. First she had to find the milk in the back cooler, then pay Mr. Patel, then count her change without letting the line behind her grow impatient. She recited it like a spell: walk, find, pay, count. On the workbench beside her, a note in Grandpa's shaky handwriting lay next to something lumpy and small. "Ran your red sweater through the wash on hot," it said. "Now it would fit a doll. Sorry. It was the sloshing." The sweater that had reached her knees last winter was now the size of a cat.

She picked it up and squeezed it. It was stiff, like felt, not stretchy anymore. On the drive last summer she remembered Grandpa explaining that wool had tiny scales on every fibre, and that heat made the scales open up and grab the neighbouring fibres, pulling the whole knit tighter and tighter. He had called it felting. She turned the little sweater over in her hands. So that's what happened, she thought. Hot, sloshing water, scales locking on, everything shrinking. She wondered if cold water would have left it alone, and decided to ask Mr. Patel, who knew about everything, including wool and milk prices.

The walk to the store was longer than it looked from the garage, but she distinguished the landmarks as she went: the cracked mailbox, the house with the barking poodle, then the blue awning. Mr. Patel was stacking cartons behind the counter. "Milk's three eighty today," he said. "Going up next week, they tell me. Currency never sits still." She handed him the five and counted her coins slowly, one by one, until she had one dollar and twenty cents, exactly right. She almost smiled.

"One question," she said. "If wool goes in a hot wash, and the water sloshes around, do the fibres really lock together?" Mr. Patel laughed. "My mother ruined a sweater that way once. Shrank it to nothing. Felting, they call it." On the way home, milk jug swinging against her leg, Olivia planned to test a tiny corner of the little red sweater in cold water, just to see, and she called over her shoulder, "I'm doing it alone next time too."

Payton set the popcorn bowl between herself and Dad and waited for movie night to begin, but instead of laughing at the funny parts, Dad snapped at her twice for slurping her drink, and he got up three times to pace in the kitchen. That was the fourth grumpy night in a row, and Payton had started keeping a tally in her notebook. Friday: snapped at Mom. Saturday: couldn't focus on fixing the porch step, kept wandering off. Sunday and Monday: more of the same. Something was wrong, and it had started the exact same week Dad threw his vape in the trash and announced, "That's it, done forever."

"It's like he turned into a different person," Payton whispered to Mom while Dad got water from the fridge. "Not a bad person. Just... rattled." She flipped her notebook open on the counter. "Look, I summarized every day since he quit. Grumpy, jumpy, couldn't concentrate on his crossword, and he kept opening the drawer where he used to keep it, like he wanted something that wasn't there." She tapped the page. "I tested an idea, too. On Tuesday I asked him to play cards, and he couldn't sit still for even one round. Then Wednesday I left a note saying I was proud of him, and he got teary over a note. It all started the day he quit."

Mom pulled up an article on her phone and slid it over. Payton read fast, then read it again. "When a dependent person stops using nicotine, withdrawal can bring irritability, anxiety, trouble concentrating, and strong cravings," she read aloud. "Cravings. That's the word. That's what's happening to Dad." She had almost decided Dad was just mad at her, and now she saw her own bias, blaming herself when the pattern pointed somewhere else the whole time.

"So it's temporary?" Payton asked, bouncing on her toes.

"Temporary," Mom said. "And we can help. More popcorn, more patience."

Payton grabbed the bowl, wrote "Day 5" at the top of a fresh page, and drew a big sticker-worthy star next to it. From the living room Dad called, "Coming! Pause it!"

"Don't worry," Payton shouted back. "We saved you the fluffy part!"

Brayden sat at the corner desk in his mom's office, squinting at her coworker Dev's laptop. Dev had promised him a soda from the break room if he could figure out why the password "brayden123" was, in Dev's words, "about as safe as a screen door on a submarine." Brayden typed it into a little testing program Dev kept on his desk, and a red bar shot across the screen like it was trying to escape the monitor. "That password would take about two seconds to crack," Brayden read out loud. "Two seconds? Even my gym teacher runs slower than that."

He tried again, this time with something longer, mixing letters and numbers and one of those symbols that looked like a spider fell on the keyboard. The bar turned green and crawled along, slow and stubborn. Then Dev dropped the real trap. "Here's the part most people miss. Say you use that same great password for your game account, your email, and the library site. The library site gets broken into, and now the thieves have your password for everything. One site goes down, they all go down." Brayden thought about it like dominoes standing in a row, invisible until the first one tipped. You couldn't see the connection, but it was there. "So it's like giving every teacher the same key to your locker," Brayden said slowly, "and one of the teachers loses their keys in the parking lot."

Dev grinned. "Exactly. Different password for each door." He handed Brayden a sticky note covered in scribbled fragments, and Brayden built four different passwords out of them, testing each one, watching the green bar stretch out like taffy, elastic and slow, every single time.

"Okay, that earns you a soda," Dev said, "but first, one more mystery." He pulled up a spreadsheet of survey results, rows of numbers about how much coffee each department consumed on Mondays. "My analysis keeps coming out looking wrong. The chart looks sideways. Marketing should tower over Accounting, but instead it stretches across like it's lying down for a nap."

Brayden leaned in. The chart did look odd, every category stretched out horizontally instead of standing up. He remembered a project from school in the fall, when his own chart had come out lying flat and his teacher had laughed and said the class had accidentally picked the wrong one. He scrolled through the chart menu and found two side-by-side options, bar and column, and he noticed the tiny pictures next to the words. One showed flat bars, one showed upright ones.

"Wait," Brayden said, tapping the screen. "Bar chart and column chart. That one's a bar chart, that's why it's horizontal. A bar chart has horizontal bars. A column chart has vertical bars, even though both compare amounts across categories." He clicked column, and Marketing shot straight up like a skyscraper while Accounting stayed low and modest. Dev clapped him on the shoulder, then Brayden pointed at the break room door. "So, about that soda."

Rebecca stopped at the third marker on the nature trail, where her worksheet was supposed to correspond with the little numbered post that did not, as far as she could tell, correspond with anything. The assignment said to draw a food chain, sun to top predator, using one real organism she could actually find. Her brother Denny, who was a chronic complainer even on good days, had already found three ticks and no inspiration.

"There's grass," Denny said. "Grass eats the sun. Congratulations, food chain, let's go home."

"Grass doesn't eat. It makes food from the sun." Rebecca crouched and sketched the sun, an arrow, the grass. Then a grasshopper, because one flicked past and landed on Denny's sleeve, which he did not appreciate. She drew arrows from grasshopper to the snake she'd seen warming itself on the rocks by marker two, and from snake to the hawk circling overhead, patient as a substitute teacher.

"Question," she said, chewing her pencil. "What if the grasshoppers all vanished?"

"Then the snake starves, then the hawk starves, then the ticks get me instead. See, I'm learning."

"That's three links gone from one." She frowned at her drawing. Every arrow stood for something she couldn't actually watch happen. She wanted to see a chain work, not just believe in it. From her backpack she took the pocket microscope kit she'd brought for reasons she could no longer defend, and the prepared slide of onion cells. The cells looked like neat little bricks, and she couldn't find the membrane anywhere, which ruined her whole "seeing is believing" plan.

Denny, who poked things when bored, added a drop of water from his salty snack lid to the slide. Under the lens, the membranes pulled inward, shrinking away from each cell wall and suddenly, unmistakably, visible.

"It's called plasmolysis," Rebecca said, reading off the kit card, "when salt water draws the water out like that."

"So when one thing leaves, something else shows up?"

"Basically." She handed him the lens, and the hawk screamed once above them, low and bright.

Zachary had come to the bank only because his mom needed a countersigner for a loan, and the waiting area had exactly one interesting thing in it: a first-aid poster next to the vending machine. He read it twice. Apply pressure. Clean the wound. Cover it with a bandage, wrapping firmly but not so tight that fingers turn purple. He practiced on his own knuckle, tearing a bandage from his lunch bag and wrapping it in slow spirals, then doing it again to see if he could replicate the neat result. His second try was better than his first, which felt like actual progress.

He was on attempt three when the doors slid open and Mrs. Okafor from his street came in holding her grandson Danny's hand, along with the leash of her huge brown dog, Biscuit. Danny was crying and shaking his right hand, and there was a red line across the knuckles. "He grabbed Biscuit's ear when the automatic doors banged," Mrs. Okafor said, mostly to the room, the way people do when they're embarrassed. "He didn't mean anything by it."

Zachary leaned closer, wondering. Was that a scrape, or had the skin actually broken? Danny's hand told him one thing and Danny's crying told him another, and crying wasn't evidence. Then Zachary spotted two tiny dark pinpoints on the knuckle, welling up slow. Not gushing, not deep, but broken. The poster's bottom line came back to him, the part he'd almost skimmed: any animal bite that breaks the skin should be checked by a doctor, because bites can carry germs deep into the wound. A scrape you could bandage. This was something else.

"Mrs. Okafor," he said, "the skin's broken. I think it needs a doctor, not just a bandage." She looked at the pinpoints, then at him, and changed her mind about the walk-in clinic being an overreaction. "You're right," she said. Danny sniffled, "Is Biscuit toxic?" and Zachary laughed. "No, buddy. He's just a dog." Danny wiped his nose. "Can I still keep the bandage?" "You can keep two," Zachary said, and pressed one into his hand as they headed for the door.

Connor's mom had left the recipe card on the counter before her shift started, along with a note that said, "You've got this." The card was from a prestigious baking contest she'd entered years ago, and the muffins were savory cheddar ones with a cheese sauce swirled on top. At the bottom she'd written a reminder in her looping handwriting: "Sunflower seed butter only, for Marcus," because his best friend had a nut allergy and would want one the second he smelled them.

He preheated the oven to three seventy-five, the way the first line told him to, and mixed the dry ingredients in the big yellow bowl. Then he reached the part that said, "Make a roux with butter and flour, cook until pale, whisk in milk until thick." He knew the word roux from watching his mom, but he'd never made one himself. The butter melted and foamed in the pan, and he stirred in the flour. It smelled like warm toast. He kept stirring, thinking that darker probably meant more flavor, the way bread gets better the browner it toasts. When it turned the color of peanut butter, he poured in the milk and whisked.

The sauce stayed thin. He whisked harder. He waited. It still ran off the spoon like plain milk with a tan tint. "Weird," he said out loud to the empty kitchen. He stirred in the cheese and tried again, and the sauce clung a little, but it pooled on the counter when he dripped some off the spatula. Why would it be thin? He hadn't skipped anything. He checked the card twice. The answer kept sliding away from him, evading him like a fish in shallow water.

Then he noticed the one word he'd brushed past: pale. The card had told him exactly what color to stop at, and he'd decided he knew better. What if the color itself was the whole point, like a rule hiding in the recipe? There was only one way to find out. He scooped the thin sauce into a jar for later, wiped out the pan, and started over. This time he pulled the pan off the heat the moment the roux turned pale, barely beige, earlier than his instincts wanted to. He whisked in the milk, and within seconds the sauce grew thick and glossy, thick enough to hold the spoon tracks for a full second before smoothing over.

"Whoa," he whispered. He folded the cheese in until it pulled in slow ribbons, swirled it through the batter, filled the muffin tin, and slid it into the hot oven just as the timer beeped that the preheat was done. His mom would never believe which batch had failed. While the muffins rose, filling the kitchen with a cheddar smell, he found a marker and wrote on the recipe card, right beside the word pale, "SERIOUSLY. Pale means pale." Marcus was going to get the first one.

Alyssa pushed the microphone closer and looked at the rows of folding chairs in the town hall basement. Her sixth-grade class had been given five minutes at the meeting to argue for a new skate park, and Councilwoman Reyes had told them that first they had to explain how a bill becomes a law by passing through the legislature. "No bill, no park," she had said.

Alyssa had practiced the steps all week: a proposal gets drafted, then a committee reviews it, then the whole legislature votes, and if it passes both houses it goes to be signed. But halfway through her speech, a man in the back stood up. "Kids always want rules changed when they lose," he said. "Like voting. You'd complain about the system too, if you understood it."

"My uncle lives in New Zealand," Alyssa said, mostly to buy time while she thought. Then the idea landed. She hadn't known this two weeks ago, but she'd found it while hunting for examples, testing whether any country had really changed its voting system instead of just arguing about it. "They voted in a referendum in 1993 to replace first-past-the-post with a proportional system called MMP. Then they first used it in the 1996 election. So it can be done, through a legal process, by voting."

The man sat down slowly, the way people do when they're changing their minds. Councilwoman Reyes leaned toward her notes. "Could you paraphrase that for our minutes?" she asked. "In one sentence."

Alyssa put it in plain words: New Zealand held a referendum in 1993, switched from first-past-the-post to the proportional system called MMP, and used it for the first time in the 1996 election. The clerk wrote it down under the agenda category marked "Citizen Comments, Youth." The overhead lights made the page luminous under the clerk's pen, bright white and official.

"Motion to draft a bill for a skate park feasibility study," said Councilwoman Reyes. "All in favor?"

"Seconded," said the man from the back, without standing up this time.

Aurora spread her supplies across the kitchen table: a foam ball for the nucleus, a bag of small red beads for protons, gray beads for neutrons, and blue ones for electrons. The project was due first period tomorrow, and her model of a lithium atom still looked like a pile of craft supplies instead of science. She had drawn a diagram in her notebook, seven protons and seven neutrons packed in the middle, seven electrons in two rings around it, but the diagram was flat and the assignment demanded a model you could hold.

While she sorted beads, her little brother Theo leaned over the table with a bright red ice pop. "You're going to incorporate a snack into an atom?" he asked, and before she could answer, his ice pop slipped and landed on the stack of napkins she needed for cleanup. Aurora pushed back from the table. It had already gone soft in the heat of his hand, and now a red puddle was spreading, flattening, turning liquid in front of them.

"Great, now it's ruined," Theo said, watching the puddle grow.

Aurora stared at it. Actually, it wasn't ruined, not exactly. It had changed shape, gone from solid to liquid, but nothing new was there. "It's still the same stuff," she said slowly, thinking out loud. "The shape changed, the state changed, but it didn't turn into something else. It's a physical change, like ice melting into water and it's still water." Theo tilted his head, then dipped a finger in the puddle and licked it. "Tastes the same," he reported. "Verdict: still ice pop." Aurora laughed and slid the napkins out from under the mess.

The idea settled somewhere in her mind while she worked. She needed the electrons to sit in the outer ring without falling, and she'd been planning to glue them, but glue was permanent and she kept second-guessing the placement. Instead she melted a stick of old craft wax in a jar in the microwave, watching the solid chunks go liquid. Nothing new was made; if she let it cool it would harden into wax again. She dipped each blue bead, pressed it onto the wire ring she'd bent from a paperclip, and held it steady for three seconds until the wax set. The bead stayed exactly where she put it, and if she ever needed to move one, she could melt the wax again.

By dinnertime the atom stood on the table, the nucleus dense with red and gray beads and the two electron rings circling it in a slow, careful orbit, the whole thing catching the light from the window where the lush green of the backyard hedge made a backdrop. Theo set down his new ice pop, untouched this time, and leaned in close. "So the red ones are the protons?"

"Seven of them," Aurora said, and gave the ring one last gentle turn.

Emma slid her draft across the library table and counted the paragraphs with her pencil tip. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Seven. The assignment sheet, which she read again under the tall window, said a five-paragraph persuasive essay with an introduction and a conclusion. She had written an introduction, a conclusion, and five paragraphs in between, because she had a lot to say about why the school should keep its recess period.

Across the table, Marcus was hunched over his own draft, frowning at his paper. "How many paragraphs do you have?" Emma asked. He counted silently, mouthing the numbers. "Seven," he admitted. "You?" She turned her paper around so he could see. "Seven." They both stared at the pages as though the extra paragraphs might vanish on their own.

Emma thought about the shape of the assignment. If the essay had an introduction and a conclusion, and the whole thing was five paragraphs, that left three paragraphs in the middle. Three body paragraphs, then. She tested the idea on her own draft: her middle five paragraphs were really only three reasons, stretched long. Paragraphs two and three both argued that recess helped students focus, so they could join into one. Paragraphs five and six both used the same survey from the science teacher, so they could join too. She drew a curved arrow with her pencil, pulling one paragraph into the next, and the draft took shape like light bending cleanly through a prism. Marcus watched her arrows and then studied his own paper. "Mine's just one reason split into pieces," he said, and began circling.

It was probable that Mrs. Okafor would notice if they both turned in seven paragraphs again; she had circled the structure on the board twice last week. Emma worked in steady silence, cutting and stapling, while the afternoon light moved slowly across the shelves of atlases behind them. Marcus read his new third paragraph aloud in a low voice, testing whether his sentences propelled the argument forward or just repeated it.

When the librarian tapped the desk at closing time, Emma counted her paragraphs one last time. One introduction, three body paragraphs, one conclusion. Five. She packed her bag and Marcus held up his paper, grinning. "Five," he said.

Scarlett had wanted canoeing all week, but her friend Priya hadn't touched her breakfast, and now Priya was saying her stomach hurt and she didn't want to go to the lake. That was the third morning in a row. Scarlett counted it on her fingers under the table: no breakfast, no canoe, and last night Priya had stayed in the cabin while everyone else did the campfire. Something was wrong, and Priya wasn't saying what.

At the lake, Scarlett kept watching the dock instead of the water. Her paddle drifted. Maybe Priya was just tired. But Scarlett didn't think so, because tired people complain, and Priya had gone quiet instead, which was worse. Scarlett formed an idea and decided to test it: she would ask a small question and see what Priya's face did.

"You okay?" she asked when they were carrying life jackets.

Priya's shoulders jumped. "Fine. Why does everyone keep asking?" Her hands were shaking as she buckled a strap, then unbuckled it, then buckled it again.

Scarlett found their counselor, Dara, by the boathouse. Dara was a competent paddler who could flip a swamped canoe upright alone, so Scarlett trusted her with this too. "Priya's acting scared but she won't say it," Scarlett said. "She's not eating. She jumps when I talk to her."

Dara nodded slowly. "That was smart, coming to me. I'll sit with her at lunch, no pressure."

Later, Scarlett caught Priya behind the craft shed with a girl from the older cabins who was holding something small and silver. "You don't have to be a baby about it," the older girl was saying.

"I'm not a baby," Priya said. "My brain's still under construction. It keeps going until about age twenty-five, and that makes people my age more likely to get hooked than adults. I read the whole pamphlet."

The older girl rolled her eyes and walked off.

Priya turned around and saw Scarlett. For a second she looked ready to bolt. Then she sat down on the stump beside her. "My brother sent me that vape thing," she said. "I've been scared to say no and scared to say yes."

"Dara's looking for you," Scarlett said, sitting down too. "She's not mad. She just wants to sit with you at lunch."

"Okay," Priya said, and for the first time in three days, she smiled. "Lunch. I'm actually kind of hungry."

Hazel had one shot left at the science demonstration contest, and her entry was falling apart in her hands. Her plan was to show the whole class something nobody could argue with: a physical change, which could go backward, and a chemical change, which could not. She had an ice cube in a dish, already half melted on the radiator, and a charred stick of wood she had burned at her uncle's campfire over the weekend. The ice would refreeze in the cafeteria freezer by fifth period. The stick was the problem. Somehow she had to prove, in front of everyone, that it could never be wood again.

Her friend Marcus wanted the opposite of proving things. He wanted to dismantle last year's winning project, a clunky volcano, and salvage its parts for his own robot arm, which was currently spreading through the science room like a virus. "Take the pump," he begged, unscrewing the base. "You don't need it. You've got a dish of water and a dead stick."

"That's the whole point," Hazel said. "The stick isn't dead. It's changed." But when Marcus lifted the volcano's lid, they found something better than a pump: a sealed glass jar with a candle stub and a long match. Marcus shrugged. It was equivalent to garbage to him. To Hazel it was a dare. Her old stick told the class nothing. They would look at it and say, so what, it's burnt, big deal. But if they watched wood burn in a jar, right there, and she asked them the impossible question afterward, they would have to think.

Fifth period came. The ice cube came back from the freezer solid and whole, and the class murmured approval. Then Hazel lit the match, touched it to the wood in the jar, and let the flame climb until it guttered out. She held up the jar so the back row could see the gray ash inside, the fog of water vapour on the glass. "The wood combined with the oxygen in there," she said. "What's left is ash, carbon dioxide, and water vapour. Now, who can turn it back into wood?" Nobody raised a hand, not even Marcus. He stared at the jar, screwdriver still in his fist, and said quietly, "You can keep the volcano parts."

Gabriella spread the map of South America across the kitchen table and pinned the corners with salt shakers. Her homework sheet asked for the location of one city on another continent, given in latitude and longitude, and she had chosen Manaus, Brazil, because her family was flying there on Friday to visit her grandmother. She ran her finger down from the equator. Three degrees south. Then she traced east from the prime meridian printed at the bottom of the inset, counting the curved lines until her fingertip landed on the dot. Three degrees south, sixty degrees west. She copied it onto the sheet, then texted the numbers to her grandmother: "I can tell anyone in the world where you live now."

Her grandmother wrote back a question mark, then a phone call came. "You sound proud," her grandmother said over the crackling line. "Now pack. Have you looked at the weather there?" Gabriella pulled up the climate chart on her mother's laptop while she balanced the phone against a mug. The chart showed monthly average temperatures for Manaus, and she read them out loud. "August is about eighty. January is about eighty. They're almost the same all year." She had been planning to stuff her suitcase with shorts and nothing else, since the numbers never changed.

She clicked further and found a second chart, one that split each day into daytime and nighttime readings. The daytime column sat near eighty. The nighttime column dropped into the sixties. She frowned, grabbed her sweater from the back of her chair, and draped it over the open suitcase, then checked the two charts side by side to be sure. "Grandma, listen to this. The difference between day and night is bigger than the difference between the warmest and coolest months." Her grandmother laughed. "Now you understand why I keep a blanket on my chair."

Gabriella persisted with her packing even after her mother called her to dinner twice. Outside the window the winter light was already failing, ironic for a girl stuffing summer clothes into a bag. Her grandmother's last email included a photograph of the river behind her house, where the seasonal recession of the floodwater had left a wide strip of cracked mud below the dock. "You will see the water rise again while you are here," the email said. Gabriella printed the photo and slid it between the pages of her atlas, right beside the dot marked three degrees south, sixty degrees west.

Amelia stood on the back porch of Grandma Dot's house, holding a photocopied sheet of "Down in the River to Pray." The alto line ran along the bottom staff, and Grandma Dot had circled the hard part in red pencil. On Sunday, Amelia would sing it with the church choir, and the choir director had been clear: the altos had to hold their part even when the sopranos soared off in a different direction.

"Sing it with me," Grandma Dot said. She was an alto too, and for twenty minutes they worked through the page. On the last phrase, though, the sound coming off the porch wasn't one note. It pulsed, like a wobble, fast and then a little slower and then, when they stopped, gone.

"There it is again," Amelia said on the second try. "That wobbling. Is something wrong with your piano?" The piano was inside and silent, so that couldn't be it. She hummed her note alone, and it sounded clean. Grandma Dot hummed hers alone, and it sounded clean too. Together, the wobble came back.

Amelia tried an experiment. She slid her pitch slightly up, and the wobble got faster. She slid back down, the other way, and it slowed, and when she landed in exactly the right spot, it stopped altogether, and the two voices fused into one wide, steady tone. She did it three more times to be sure. The closer the notes came to matching, the slower the wobble, until it disappeared.

"That's beats," Grandma Dot said. "Sing against them instead of with them and you'll hear them every time." Amelia wrote in the margin of her sheet: listen for the wobble. Then Grandma Dot switched to the soprano line, which sat a whole different distance away, and the wobble vanished from the problem entirely. No pulsing, just two notes stacked on top of each other, neither one giving way. That was the part she actually had to survive on Sunday.

At the rehearsal, the sopranos came in loud, their sound extravagant compared with the four altos in the back row. Amelia gripped her music, found her note, and imagined the wobble as a kind of empathy between voices, each one leaning toward the other until they agreed. When the altos around her drifted, she slid her pitch until the pulsing slowed and died, and her voice helped contribute to a low, locked tone under the melody. The director cut them off, looked at the alto section, and raised her eyebrows.

"Whatever that was," she said, "do it again on Sunday."

Maya sat in the waiting room of the Riverside Veterinary Clinic with her cat carrier on her lap and her little brother Ben squished beside her, holding a worksheet about Galapagos finches. "I have to write whether it's natural selection," Ben said, "but I don't even know how to tell." Maya peered at the paper. Some finches had thick beaks, some had thin ones, and after a drought, the thick-beaked ones were the only ones left. She was still puzzling over it when a vet tech named Rosa called them back.

Their cat Pickles needed a checkup, and while Rosa looked at Pickles' ears, Maya noticed a microscope on the counter. "Is that for dog cells?" she asked. Rosa smiled and slid over a slide. "Cheek cells from a golden retriever. Want to look? I've got a leaf slide too, from the clinic's pothos plant." Maya leaned in. The animal cells looked like soft gray blobs with a dark dot in the middle. Then Rosa swapped slides, and the plant cells snapped into view like bricks in a wall, each one boxed in and speckled with green. "The green parts are chloroplasts," Rosa said. "Only plant cells have those, and the stiff boxes around every cell, cell walls, only plants have those too. Animal cells have neither one." Maya copied both drawings into her notebook, labeling the parts only plants had.

Then she turned back to Ben's worksheet. "Okay," she said slowly. "For natural selection, I think we have to check three things before we can call it that." She counted on her fingers. "First, the finches vary, thick beaks, thin beaks, that's the varying part. Second, beak shape has to be inherited, passed from parents to chicks. Third, one variation has to help its owners survive and reproduce more than the others." Ben frowned. "The drought," Maya went on. "Only the big seeds were left, so the thick beaks got the food and lived to have chicks, and the thin beaks didn't. All three things check out." "So it's natural selection," Ben said, and wrote it at the top of his page.

"I can't justify that without the third part, though," Maya said, tapping the drought sentence. "If the beaks varied and were inherited but neither kind survived better, it wouldn't count." Rosa, still holding Pickles, laughed. "You two did my whole college homework just now."

At home, Maya found a folded note waiting on the kitchen table in her mother's handwriting. "Dear Maya, Pickles' ear medicine is only temporary, so keep giving it until the bottle is empty, even when he fights you. Ben showed me his worksheet and read his answer out loud. He says you taught him better than the textbook did. P.S. Do not let Ben tell you the beak story is propaganda against thin-beaked finches. I already heard that argument at dinner." Maya laughed so hard Pickles wriggled out of her arms and landed on Ben's worksheet, one paw smack on the finch drawings. "Thick paws," Ben announced. "Definitely inherited." Maya chased Pickles toward the kitchen.

Carter sat on the floor of Desh's kitchen with his laptop open, glaring at the sign-up page for the game site they both wanted to try. "It wants a password," he said. "I'll just use the same one as always. Cats123."

"That's your password for everything?" Desh pulled a box of crackers from the pantry. "Even your email?"

"Obviously. It's easier." Carter typed it in and hit enter. The screen flashed a red bar: Password rejected. Too common.

"Cats123 is too common," Desh said, reading over his shoulder. "So now you know a million other people probably had the same idea."

Carter winced. He had never thought of a password as something other people could guess, like a door with a lock that fit a million keys. It was invisible, so he had treated it like it didn't exist. He thought about it while chewing a cracker. If the site leaked passwords, then whoever got the list could try Cats123 on his email, his video account, everything. Same key, every door.

Desh's dad came in for coffee, still wearing his badge from work. "What's the frowning about?"

"Passwords," said Desh.

"Ha. At the office today someone was showing the new hire pivot tables, and I remembered when those were brand new," his dad said. "Pito Salas is credited with inventing the pivot table. He was working on the spreadsheet program Lotus Improv, and it came out in 1991. I felt like a dinosaur."

"That's not that old," Carter said.

"You'd be surprised how fast software feels obsolete," his dad said, and left with his mug.

Carter tried an experiment. He typed Catz!92Blue to test it, and the bar turned green. Then he made up a second one, totally different, for his email, and a third for the video site. He wrote them on a scrap of paper just once, then shredded it into the cracker box. "Each door gets its own key," he said.

Desh dropped a cracker into the shredder pile. "There, now the paper has a crumb sensor on it."

"It's a cracker," Carter said.

"It's security."

Peyton slid into her seat in the computer lab just as the screens flickered on. Her problem was waiting for her at home: Grandma had promised to help her set up an account for the geology game they both liked, but Grandma used the same password for everything, the name of her old cat plus the number seven. Peyton had tried to tell her that was risky, and Grandma had laughed and said, "Who would bother with me?" Peyton wanted proof.

Today's assignment was password practice, so she started typing suggestions. Hers were terrible at first: password123, then peytonrocks. The program rejected each one and asked for something longer, with capitals and symbols. She built a better one, a whole sentence squished together with a star in the middle, and the bar at the top turned green. But the part that really got her thinking was the last question on the worksheet: Why should you never use the same password on two sites?

She wondered about that. A password was invisible, just letters stored somewhere. How could anyone even test whether reusing one was dangerous? Then she remembered something her cousin had mentioned at Thanksgiving, a website that could check whether an email address had shown up in a breach. It was called Have I Been Pwned, and it had been launched by a security researcher named Troy Hunt in December 2013. She typed the address carefully and stared at the single search box.

Here was her test. She could classify people into two groups, she thought: those whose addresses had shown up in a breach and those whose addresses had not. Grandma always said her accounts were safe, so if the website agreed, maybe Grandma was right. Peyton typed Grandma's email address and pressed Enter. The page turned red. Grandma's address had appeared in a known data breach, an old one, from a shopping site she hadn't used in years. Peyton sat back. There was the contradiction, plain on the screen: Grandma believed she was safe, and the evidence said her address was already floating around out there. If she used the same password everywhere, that old breach might hand strangers the key to everything.

On the bus home, Peyton planned her argument the way she planned a rock collection, biggest piece first. She imagined showing Grandma the red screen. She would say, "The password isn't for protecting you, it's for protecting your name, and your name is already out there." She got off at her stop and ran up the driveway, backpack bouncing, calling through the front door before she was even inside. "Grandma! Bring your cat's name and come look at this."

Ariana sat at the kitchen table with her notebook open to a page titled "Mi familia." Her Spanish homework was to write five full sentences about her family and pets, and so far she had two: "Mi mamá es alta" and "Tengo un gato negro." The rest of the page glared back at her, blank. Her cat, Biscuit, walked across the notebook as if to volunteer, and she lifted him off and set him on the floor. "You can't be every sentence," she told him.

The problem was her grandmother, Abuela Rosa, who lived two floors down in the same building. Abuela had sent a letter, an actual paper letter, and Mom had put it on the fridge. In it, Abuela wrote about a new restaurant in her old neighborhood where the food was wonderful but the service was strange. We waited forty minutes at the end, she wrote, sitting with empty plates, and no one ever brought us the bill. Finally another customer said something to the waiter and the bill came right away. I don't know what she said. Ariana read the letter three times. How could a bill arrive only after certain words were spoken? There had to be a hidden rule, some sentence waiters were listening for. She wondered if it was like a secret knock, and if she could find out what it was.

Ariana was skeptical at first that a phrase could matter that much. She tested her idea by calling her cousin Mateo, whose Spanish was better than hers. "If you wanted the waiter to bring the check," she asked, "what would you say?" Mateo answered without hesitating. "La cuenta, por favor." He said it meant "The bill, please." Ariana wrote it down, then said it out loud four times until it felt smooth. So the waiter hadn't been ignoring anyone. Nobody had asked. The words were the whole cause, invisible until you knew them.

She wrote back to Abuela in a letter of her own, which pleased her because Abuela loved mail. At the top, Ariana copied her homework sentences too: "Tengo una abuela que come en restaurantes. Mi abuela es divertida. Tengo un gato negro y juguetón." Then she added, "At the restaurant, you can say 'La cuenta, por favor.' It means 'The bill, please.'" She sealed the envelope and carried it downstairs herself, Biscuit trotting behind her like a small black shadow.

A week later a reply arrived. I used your words at the restaurant, Abuela wrote, and the bill came in two minutes. I thought I was too old to learn from an eleven-year-old, but I changed my mind. Ariana read that line twice, feeling something warm spread through her, and she had already decided her next letter would teach Abuela how to describe Biscuit. "Mi gato es negro," she practiced to the ceiling, "y mi abuela es la mejor."

Owen had a problem, and the problem had a name: the essay contest about school improvements, due Friday, with a trophy that went to the winner's homeroom and got displayed in the front hall all year. Mr. Delgado had written one requirement on the board in tall letters: thesis plus three points, outlined before drafting. Owen had never outlined anything in his life. He usually just started writing and hoped the sentences would find their shape, which they mostly didn't.

At lunch he sat with Marisol, who had won the spelling bee twice and kept her contest notes in a color-coded binder. "You have to say what you want in one sentence," she told him, tearing the corner off her napkin. "Then three reasons under it. That's the whole secret." She drew a little umbrella shape with one line on top and three lines underneath, then distributed pickle slices onto Owen's tray because he was too busy staring at the napkin to eat.

Owen's idea was a covered walkway between the gym and the main building, because every year during monsoon season the sixth graders arrived to class soaked and dripping on their homework. He wrote his thesis: "The school should build a covered walkway." Then his three points: it would keep students dry, protect books and papers, and stop wet floors in the hallway, which were a slipping hazard. It looked small on the page. It sounded small in his head, too, like something a machine would say.

That afternoon, rain came in over the soccer field and the air smelled like wet gravel, and everybody groaned because the storm seemed imminent and nobody had a raincoat. Owen stood under the gym awning watching kids bolt across the open stretch, arms over their heads, and he noticed something. In his mind he wrote: "Kids ran very quickly through the rain." It sounded slow. The scene in front of him was not slow at all. He tried again. "Kids sprinted through the rain." One word, and suddenly the sentence had legs. He said it out loud, quietly, and Priya next to him gave him a strange look and he didn't care.

He found his old draft in his binder, the one about the walkway, and hunted through it. "Students walk very slowly when they are wet." He crossed it out and wrote "trudge." "The rain comes down very hard." He crossed that out too and wrote "pounds." His outline points got sharper as well, because once he started swapping weak verbs for strong ones, he could see which of his three points actually carried weight. The wet floors point was the strongest, so he moved it first.

That night Owen wrote a message to Marisol on a folded page, planning to leave it in her cubby before first period. "The verb thing works. Sprinted instead of ran very quickly. It says more. Also I finished the outline, umbrella shape and everything. If I win, the trophy is partly yours, pickle share included." The next morning he delivered it, and by fourth period she had written back on the same page in green ink: "Deal. But I want extra pickles."

On Friday, Mr. Delgado read a line from Owen's essay out loud to the class: "During monsoon season, sixth graders trudge into Room 12 soaked, their worksheets limp as old lettuce." He set the paper down and looked around the room. "That," he said, "is a sentence." Owen grinned at Marisol, and she slid her tray down the lunch table toward him, one pickle already pushed to his side.

Nathaniel had prepared for the debate tournament for two months, and now his debate partner, Marcus, was in the nurse's office with a fever. But the tournament had a second event, improv duet, and teams could substitute a member if the tab room approved it by nine o'clock.

"You," said Priya, from the rival school's team, whose own partner had also dropped out that morning. She pointed at him across the cafeteria. "You talk fast and you don't panic. Want to team up? Two orphans make a pair."

He wanted to say no. Improv terrified him because you couldn't memorize anything, and memorizing was the only thing he trusted himself to do. But a blank score sheet was worse than a scary one, so he signed the form and walked to the practice room with her.

"Only one rule matters," Priya said. "Whatever I say, you say yes, and, then add something. If I say we're astronauts, you don't say no, we're pirates. You say yes, and the pirates are chasing us. Got it?"

Nathaniel nodded, then decided he should confide the truth while there was still time. "My whole plan was to do my debate case as a speech. I've got it word perfect, eight minutes."

Priya stared at him. "You'd just stand there talking alone? That's a monologue. One long speech by one character, to the other characters or to the audience. It's not even two people." She grabbed two chairs and set them facing each other. "You'd win the debate and lose the improv. Here, watch how it breaks."

She pretended to open a package. "Yes, and it's ticking," he said flatly, just reciting her example back. She shook her head. "You copied me. Try accepting something new." She picked up an invisible object and held it out. "Grandma sent you a birthday present."

Nathaniel took it carefully, the way you hold something that might be alive. "Yes, and it just blinked at me," he said. Priya's face lit up, and she leaned in to peer at his empty hands. "It's a lizard," she declared. "Yes, and it's wearing my debate badge," he shot back, and then they were off, passing an invisible lizard back and forth, building a ridiculous story about a reptile that joined the debate team and doubled their school's ticket revenue by being the mascot. When the lizard "escaped" under the door, they both dove for it, and Priya laughed so hard she had to sit on the floor.

In the round itself, his hands still shook when the judge started the timer. Priya began, "We're the last two students in the school at midnight." His mind went white for one second. Then he thought of the lizard, of how the story had grown only when he'd accepted her offer instead of replacing it, and he heard himself say, "Yes, and the lockers are humming."

"The revenue from the bake sale is inside one of them," Priya added without missing a beat, and Nathaniel ran down the row of chairs, pressing his ear against each metal surface.

"Grandma's lizard is in this one," he said. "I'd know that humming anywhere."

Elizabeth had exactly one hour before her grandfather came back to check the garage, and the note taped to the toolbox was not going to open itself. "Congratulations on turning thirteen," it read. "The combination is three numbers. Find the number of protons in iron, then silver, then potassium. The table knows. P.S. A wrong guess on the padlock sticks for ten minutes."

The padlock was heavy and brass, and the toolbox smelled like machine oil and old pennies. Ten minutes stuck meant she would still be standing there when Grandpa returned, and she refused to ask him for help. She dragged the stepladder over to the far wall, where a giant periodic table hung above the workbench, its squares faded from years of sawdust. Grandpa had hung it there decades ago, back when he repaired radios, and he had told her once that he'd kept working through the recession because people fixed things instead of buying new ones. The poster was the one thing in the garage he never let get dusty.

She climbed up and ran her finger along the top row. The elements were numbered, one through whatever, and she remembered enough from school to know the number was called the atomic number, and that it told you the protons. Fine. She just had to find the symbols. Potassium was probably P. Silver had to be S. And iron, obviously, was I. She scanned the row for the letter I, expecting it to be somewhere near the middle, near the metals.

There was no I.

She checked again, slower, her finger hovering a centimeter from the paper so she wouldn't smudge it. The letters jumped out at her in a jumble: Fe, Au, Ag, K, Sn, Pb. No I at all. Not anywhere. She climbed down, stood in the doorway with the cold draft on her back, and felt a small, acute alarm, the kind you get when a door you locked is standing open. The symbols were wrong on purpose, she decided. That had to imply something, some rule she hadn't been told, some pattern hidden inside the table itself. A rule that couldn't be seen directly could still be tested, and she had an idea for a test.

She climbed back up and looked at potassium, because she was almost sure potassium was K in the book her class used. There it was, number 19, and its symbol really was K. So P wasn't potassium either. She wasn't dealing with English initials at all. Her eyes moved to silver, and there was Ag, number 47, sitting in a square that plainly said silver underneath. Au said gold. Fe said iron, number 26. She tried a different language. Grandpa's old radio manuals on the shelf were full of words like ferrum, aurum, argentum, and she'd flipped through them once and asked why they looked like spell ingredients. Now she understood: some element symbols came from Latin names, like Fe for iron, from the Latin word ferrum.

Iron was 26. Silver was 47. Potassium was 19. She slid off the ladder and knelt in front of the padlock, her palms suddenly cold even though the garage was warm. 26. Click. 47. Click. 19. The lock gave a heavy clack and dropped open, and she lifted the lid with both hands.

Inside, wrapped in a shop rag, was a brass key and a second note. "Toolbox was practice. The key opens the cabinet in the recess behind the water heater. Your real present is in there. And Elizabeth: I told you the table knows. I never said it knew English."

She turned toward the corner of the garage, where the water heater sat in its shallow recess, and gripped the key so hard its teeth pressed into her fingers. "Okay," she said out loud, walking. "What else don't I know?"

Nicolas slid into the chair at the library computer station and pulled his crumpled list out of his backpack. He had spent two weeks counting every kind of creature in Miller's Pond, from bullfrogs to water beetles, because the parks department had offered a fifty-dollar prize for the best pond survey by a kid. The problem was that his data lived on three soggy notebook pages, and to enter the contest, everything had to go into a spreadsheet with totals and a chart.

He opened the spreadsheet program and typed his first column: frog, 14; water beetle, 38; dragonfly, 22; snail, 45; turtle, 3. Then came the part nobody had shown him. He remembered the afternoon last summer when his cousin Rosa had sat at this same table, typing an equals sign and then something called a formula. "Watch," she had said, "the computer does the adding for you." She had clicked a cell below her numbers, typed =SUM(B2:B6), and the answer had appeared like magic. He had forgotten the exact words at the time, but now he found himself wondering: was the rule hiding in the punctuation? He tried typing TOTAL and pressing Enter. Nothing happened. So he typed the equals sign first, then SUM, then his own guess at which cells to grab, and the number 122 blinked onto the screen. He checked it against his notebook. It matched. Rosa's trick had been salvageable from memory after all, even the crumpled parts.

The chart was easier. He highlighted his columns, clicked Insert, chose bar chart, and watched the pond reorganize itself into five rising bars. Snails towered over everyone. Turtles barely showed up at all. Nicolas leaned back. It was strange and wonderful to think that a whole pond's worth of organisms, each one crawling and swimming through the mud, could shrink into rectangles on a screen. Which creature was the tallest bar, and why? He made a note to look up whether snails liked warm weather.

When he clicked Submit on the contest page, the screen asked him to create a password first. He started to type his usual one, then stopped. His old password had already been guessed once by his little brother, who had used it to sign Nicolas up for a clown newsletter. There had to be a better way.

His eyes drifted across the reference shelf beside the computer, where a battered book about webcomics sat next to a dictionary. He flipped it open and landed on a printed page showing an old comic from 2011. In it, a character explained that a passphrase of several random words, like "correct horse battery staple," was long enough to be hard to guess yet easy to remember. Nicolas read it twice. Random words. Just words, stuck together?

He tested the idea, because it felt too simple to be true. He glanced around the room: a poster of a horse, a battery sign on the exit door, a magazine about staples. He laughed out loud, then made up his own version, four ordinary words from things he could actually see from his chair, strung into a sentence so silly he would never forget it. He typed it in, retyped it when the box asked him to confirm, and hit Submit.

The screen flashed: Survey received. Thank you, Nicolas. On the desk beside him, the bar chart glowed, snails on top, turtles barely there, and below it his ridiculous passphrase sat safe in his notebook, four little words that no clown-loving brother would ever guess. "Sorry, Leo," he whispered.

Felix tapped his pencil against the library table and read the assignment sheet again. Mr. Ruiz had allocated each student one primary source, and Felix had drawn a photocopy of an 1852 settler's diary, twenty pages of cramped handwriting by a man named Amos Crane. The task was to use the diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. Felix's problem was simpler and worse: he could not read half of it.

He tried tracing the letters with his finger, in vain, because the ink had faded where the pages had been folded. He was about to raise his hand for a different source when a radiator near the shelf began to clank, and Marcus from the eighth grade knelt beside it with a wrench and shut the valve at the pipe. "Otherwise it floods," Marcus said, standing up. A map of Europe unrolled out of Marcus's bag onto the table, and Felix leaned over it.

"Why is this part colored different?" Felix asked, pointing at western Germany. Marcus looked at where the Rhine River ran along the border with France. "That's the Rhineland," he said. "The Treaty of Versailles banned German troops from it, so it could act as a buffer zone." Felix stared at the map. German land, right next to France, with no German soldiers allowed in it. France would not be safe from an attack coming from Germany if troops could stand right on its doorstep, but with them pushed back behind the Rhineland, there was a stretch in between. He had never thought about space working like that before, like a shield made out of land.

He went back to the diary with the idea. Maybe Crane had moved west for the same kind of reason, a space between him and something. Felix made two columns on his notepad and tested it. He read every entry he could decipher, hunting for danger, but Crane never mentioned fear of anything behind him. What he mentioned, over and over, was the land: forty acres, good soil, a creek, a clear title. In one entry Crane wrote that in Ohio he worked for other men, and in another he counted his own fence posts going in. Felix crossed out his first column. It was not a buffer. It was ownership.

He wrote his paragraph that afternoon at the same table. People moved west because land was cheap and a man could hold a title to it, which the diary showed in Crane's own words about fence posts and acres. Then he read the paragraph once more and added one sentence comparing it to the map, because the Rhineland had taught him something too: look at where the space is before deciding why someone crossed it. Marcus rolled up his map, tapped the Rhineland with two fingers, and said, "You're welcome, by the way."

Mackenzie slid her phone across the food court table so her friend Priya could see the calculator screen. "Okay, so my hundred dollars at five percent simple interest earns five dollars a year, every year, no matter what. That's twenty-five dollars after five years. Boring." She tapped a new number. "But compound interest? The interest earns interest too. After five years I'd have a hundred and twenty-seven dollars and change. It's like the money is sneaking extra money in when nobody's watching."

Priya leaned over a cup of frozen yogurt she was supposed to be sharing with her little brother, Dev, who was guarding his own cup like it was treasure. "You're doing this at the mall?" she said. "We came here for the sneaker release, remember? They drop at two o'clock. I've been waiting a month."

"The line's not even moving yet," Mackenzie said. "And this is actually the fun part. My mom opened my savings account last week and I get to pick what happens with part of it. I couldn't see the interest working, though, so I had to test it. I ran both ways on paper, year by year, and the compound column just pulls away. Simple stays flat like stairs; compound curves." She flipped her notebook around to show the two columns, one ragged with crossing-out, one neat.

Dev set down his spoon. "That's not even the wild part," he said. "Last year our neighbor Mr. Alvarez put all his money in one company's stock, and when that company crashed, poof, almost all of it went. My cousin Ravi did the same amount of money but he bought a fund that holds a bunch of different stocks."

"What's that called?" Mackenzie asked, already writing.

"Diversifying," Dev said. "When one company's collapse happened, Mr. Alvarez got crushed, but Ravi was okay, because spreading it out meant that one collapse hurt way less than if all his money had been in that single stock."

Mackenzie wrote it fast, then sat back. "Hold on. I had it in my head that I'd pick one stock, the winner, and watch it." She looked at her notebook, then out at the crowds moving past the escalators, a whole mall of people with a whole mall of choices. "I'm changing my mind. I don't want to guess a winner. I want the curve plus the fund." She circled both columns. "Compound interest and diversifying together. That's a coherent plan, not just a hope."

Priya stood up so fast her chair squeaked. "Great, you're a financial genius, the line's moving, come on." She grabbed Mackenzie's sleeve, and Dev abandoned his yogurt cup on the table as they ran. Outside the sneaker store, the velvet rope inched forward, and Mackenzie slid her notebook into her backpack with the circled columns still showing. "Five years," she said. "Starting today."

Sebastian stood in the living room holding a spatula like a microphone and waited for his sister Priya to stop laughing at him. She sat on the couch with her arms crossed, still in her soccer cleats, because he had promised her the last slice of pizza if she practiced with him for one whole hour.

"Fine," she said. "What are we doing?"

"Improv," Sebastian said. "Drama club tryouts are Friday. Mrs. Okafor picks partners and you have to make up a scene together, and she said the kids who get in are the ones who accept every offer with yes, and." He raised the spatula. "I start a scene, you say yes, and then you add something. Then I do it back."

Priya rolled her eyes, but she stood up. "Go."

"Welcome aboard the ship," Sebastian said grandly. "We are sailing to Antarctica."

"No," said Priya. "I don't want to sail anywhere. Let's be on a train."

Sebastian dropped the spatula. "That's the whole point! You have to say yes, and. If you block me, the scene just dies." He had tried it alone all week, playing both parts in the bathroom mirror, and every time his imaginary partner argued, the scene collapsed like a wet tent.

Priya picked the spatula up and handed it back to him. "Okay, okay. Again."

"Welcome aboard the ship. We are sailing to Antarctica."

"Yes, and I've nominated you to climb the mast and check for icebergs," Priya said, and Sebastian nearly hugged her. The scene rolled on for five whole minutes, and they discovered that their ship was powered by a giant turbine, which Sebastian had to look up later, and that they were transporting a hold full of impoverished penguins who had lost their fishing grounds and needed new homes.

At dinner, their dad asked what they'd been shouting about upstairs. Sebastian explained the tryouts, and then, because his dad looked confused, he added, "I have to introduce the scene too, right at the start. That's the hard part."

His dad nodded slowly. "When I give presentations at work, they call the opening line a hook. A hook is the opening line that grabs attention, like a question, a surprising fact, or a very short story." He speared a piece of broccoli. "Mine are usually terrible."

Sebastian thought about that. On Thursday, Priya helped him test it. He stood at the end of the hallway and opened the way he'd planned: "Today I will talk about a ship scene." Priya's gaze drifted to the window within four seconds, and she started fiddling with her shoelace.

"Try again," she said.

"Would you sail to Antarctica with forty penguins and no captain?"

Priya's head came up. "Yes, and the penguins are in the kitchen."

Sebastian grinned and pushed open the kitchen door.

Cameron wanted his street to look like it was actually sinking into the paper, the way the avenues in his favorite graphic novels did, buildings leaning toward each other until they vanished somewhere far below the edge. Ms. Ro had shown the class one-point perspective on Monday: a dot on the horizon, then ruler lines running toward it like ropes. Cameron had forgotten the ruler today, so he had to devise a substitute, and he scavenged through the studio's crowded supply shelf until he found a long wooden stirring stick, straight enough to trust.

He drew the vanishing point first, a small dot that he pretended was a doorway to another version of the street. Every roofline and curb had to aim at that doorway. When he leaned close and sighted along the stick, he could almost see the buildings folding inward, tugging each other down the page like the whole street was sliding into the dot. He tested one idea to be sure the trick was real: he drew a line he guessed would hit the dot, then laid the stick on top, and found it missed by a thumb's width. So the eye was a liar. The ruler-stick was the truth. He erased and redrew.

Across the table, Priya, age nine, was painting a portrait of her cat. She had made the cat's nose an unfortunate shade of green yesterday, let it dry overnight, and today she brushed clean water over it to soften the edges. The green moved. It smeared sideways in a slow tide across the cat's cheek, and Priya gasped like the cat itself had twitched.

"It dried," she said. "Dried things aren't supposed to run. Dried glue doesn't run."

Cameron came over and touched the edge of the smear with his fingertip. It came away faintly green. "Ms. Ro said watercolour paint is pigment bound with gum arabic," he said. "That's why it can dissolve again in water even after it's dried." He watched Priya's face do the same thing his had done when the stick proved his guessed line wrong, that flicker of a hidden rule suddenly becoming visible.

"So it's like it's only pretending to be permanent," Priya said. "A hypothetical cat that stays put until water shows up."

"Exactly. Your cat is a spy who dissolves when the rain comes."

Priya turned the smear into a swirl of whiskers, and the accidental green became grass in a reflection, a cat looking into a puddle. Cameron went back to his street and drew the puddle's edge with lines running to the vanishing point, so that even the reflection obeyed the doorway. He held the stick up to check it one last time.

"Bullseye," he said, and drew the dot's tiny doorframe around it.

Nathaniel had a dilemma. His science presentation was due Monday, and he wanted to show how a river could carve a canyon over millions of years, but he couldn't exactly wait millions of years to film it. He stood at the kitchen counter staring at a long plastic tray he'd filled with packed sand and dirt, a jug of water beside it.

"Pour slow at first," his sister Priya said from the doorway. "Rivers don't start out trying to demolish the landscape." She was twelve minutes older than him in twin terms, which she claimed made her an impartial judge of his experiments, though he doubted it.

He tilted the jug and let a thin stream run down the middle of the tray. At first nothing happened. Then a small channel appeared, deepened, and branched. He sped up the water and watched the dirt crumble at the edges of the cut while downstream a little muddy pile grew, spreading out flat like a fan. Erosion there, deposition here. He grabbed his phone and started recording, then poured again, and again, and by the fourth run the channel had widened into something that actually looked like a tiny canyon with a delta at the end. Priya leaned over it. "Okay, that's better than I expected. You should say the river carries the dirt away and drops it where the water slows down."

After she left, he scrolled through his notes and hit a snag. He'd written that summer heat peaked at the summer solstice, the longest day, because that part felt obvious. But when he checked the backyard thermometer log they'd been keeping since June, the highest numbers weren't anywhere near the longest day. The really hot readings, the sweat-through-your-shirt ones, were stacked up weeks later, in the middle of July. He frowned at the notebook, then at the thermometer, then back at the notebook, as if one of them would confess.

He found the answer in one of Dad's old weather books, and it stopped him cold: the hottest weeks usually come several weeks after the summer solstice, because land and oceans take time to warm up. He crossed out his old sentence, feeling his ears go warm too, and rewrote the whole last section. His river worked the same way, he realized. The water needed time, run after run, before the canyon took shape. Nothing big happened all at once.

Monday morning he set the tray on the desk, poured the water, and watched the channel deepen while the class leaned in. "The river did this in four minutes," he said. "A real one takes millions of years, and the hottest part of summer comes weeks after the longest day, because the land and oceans take time to warm up." He pointed at the muddy fan spreading at the end of the tray. "Same idea. You just have to give things time."

Sydney's paper bag of onions slid across the table while the farmer counted her change. "Romanas," he said. "Sweet enough to eat raw, if you're brave."

She wasn't that brave, but she had a plan. Her grandmother was teaching her to make pasta sauce from scratch tonight, and Sydney had exactly one hour to buy onions, garlic, and canned tomatoes before the market closed. She moved through the stalls like a scavenger hunting treasure, sniffing garlic heads, squeezing tomatoes, and wondering why the tropical fruit stall smelled like a vacation even in October.

Then she smelled something else. Butter and cinnamon, drifting from the muffin stand at the end of the row, where a woman pulled a tray of blueberry muffins from a small oven. The timer had dinged, but the woman frowned at the tray. "Tops look pale," she muttered. "They usually brown by now."

Sydney drifted closer, curious. How could anyone know the inside of a muffin without cutting it open? The woman turned the tray, tapped one top, and sighed. Last summer, Sydney remembered, she had bitten into a muffin at camp and hit a pocket of raw batter in the middle, gooey as glue. The cook had shrugged and said the outside had looked done. Looks, apparently, could lie.

"Could you check one?" Sydney asked. "Like, without cutting it?"

The woman tapped her chin. "My grandmother used a trick. Push a toothpick into the centre of a muffin. If it comes out clean, or with a few dry crumbs, it's baked through." She pulled a toothpick from her apron pocket and handed it over. "You try."

Sydney pushed the toothpick straight down into the centre of the biggest muffin, held her breath, and drew it out. Wet batter clung to the wood, glistening. "Not done," she announced, almost triumphantly. The woman slid the tray back into the oven and set the timer again. While they waited, Sydney tested two more muffins; one came out clean, the other showed dry crumbs. "That one's fine too," the woman said. "Crumbly counts." Sydney filed that away, pleased to have a rule that worked. When the timer dinged the second time, she tested the big muffin again and the toothpick came out clean. The woman insisted Sydney take it, still warm.

That evening, in her grandmother's kitchen, Sydney curled her fingers into a claw over the onion she'd bought, knuckles forward like tiny shields, and cut slow, careful slices. "Smart hands," her grandmother said. "You're going to cherish that sauce, and I'm going to cherish not driving you to the emergency room." Sydney laughed so hard she nearly lost her claw grip. The onion sizzled in the pan, going soft and gold, and she took a bite of her muffin on the way past the counter: baked through, every last crumb.

Eve had been washing dishes at her uncle's restaurant for two Saturdays, and today she had been promoted, which meant she was standing over a cutting board with an onion and a very sharp knife. "Claw grip," her uncle Rafi said, curling his fingers so the knuckles stuck out ahead of the fingertips. "The knife rides your knuckles. Your fingertips stay under, where the blade can't find them." Eve bent her fingers the same way, decided it made her hand look like a crab, and started cutting. The first slices were uneven. The fifth ones were not.

The lunch rush wanted pasta sauce, forty portions of it, and Rafi wanted it from scratch, which was how Eve ended up with a pan of oil on high heat and a board full of chopped onion and minced garlic. He was called away to the front when a delivery coincided with a health inspector's surprise visit, and he left her with exactly one instruction: "Cook."

She dumped everything in at once. The onions hissed and softened and smelled wonderful, and she felt extremely professional until she tasted the sauce ten minutes later. It was bitter. Not burnt-on-the-bottom bitter, because she'd stirred, but bitter in a way that coated her whole tongue. She tried a second spoonful in case the first spoonful was a mistake. It was not.

She stood there chewing her lip and staring at the pan like it owed her an answer. If it wasn't the bottom, it was something in the pan. The tomatoes were from a can that Rafi himself had opened, so they were probably fine. The oil was fine, the salt was salt. That left the onions and the garlic. The onions looked soft and golden and innocent. The garlic, she noticed, had gone dark around the edges, and when she fished out a piece and ate it alone, it was the exact bitterness from the sauce. The garlic had burned. It had gone in at the same time as the onions on high heat, but the onions were golden and the garlic was black, which meant the garlic had cooked faster and burnt while the onions were still catching up. She felt like she'd solved a crime with only one suspect.

Rafi came back, tasted it, and made a face. "Bitter."

"The garlic," Eve said. "It burned before the onions were done."

He raised an eyebrow, which for Rafi was applause. "So what's your plan?"

"Onions first, on lower heat. Then when they're soft, the garlic goes in after, just for a minute." She was already chopping the second onion, claw grip and all, knuckles leading, fingertips tucked safely away.

"Good. And next time don't leave the pan alone with the whole garlic at once."

"It wasn't the pan's fault," Eve said. "The garlic's just faster." Rafi laughed at that, a real one, and told her that if she kept this up she'd break the stereotype of dishwashers who only break dishes. She said she'd try, and she slid the onions into the fresh oil, watching them turn soft and sweet while the garlic waited on the board, patient as anything, like it had never ruined anything in its life.

When the second sauce came together, Rafi tasted it, then tasted it again, which he never did. "Get me forty containers," he said. "And don't let the garlic fool you twice."

Mila leaned her bicycle against the railing outside the bank and noticed the front tyre was flat, soft all the way around, with a hiss she could not hear but could imagine. She had ridden there to deposit a birthday cheque from her grandmother, and now the deposit would have to wait, because riding home on a flat would wreck the rim. In her backpack she had a repair kit her uncle had sent with a note, and she had never once used it.

She sat on the wide stone step beside the doors and unfolded the note. "Tyre levers go under the bead, three of them spaced around, then spoon the tyre off," her uncle had written in his careful, diligent handwriting. "Find the puncture, patch it, pump it up. You can interpret a flat two ways: bad luck, or a chance to learn something. Your choice." Mila read it twice, then dug out the levers, three curved plastic strips, and the little hand pump.

A security guard came out on his break and watched her work the first lever under the edge of the tyre. "You want to hook that second one a few inches along," he said, "and clip the third to a spoke." She did it, and when all three were set, the tyre popped loose and she could pull the tube out. As she ran her fingers along the rubber to find the hole, a spoke nicked her knuckle and a bead of blood rose up. She stuck it in her mouth.

"Put a plaster on that and let the air at it," the guard said. "Dries out faster that way."

A woman waiting by the doors shook her head. "My nurse said the opposite. A thin layer of petroleum jelly keeps the surface moist, and that helps it heal and can reduce scarring." The two of them went back and forth while Mila held the tube under the fountain by the wall, watching for bubbles. One small stream rose from a spot the size of a pinhead, near the valve. She marked it with the crayon from the kit, roughed it up with the sandpaper, spread the glue, and pressed the patch on until her thumb ached.

Then she took the small jar from the kit's zip pocket, dabbed petroleum jelly on her knuckle, and covered it with a plaster from her pencil case. "I'm going with the moist version," she said, holding up her finger. She tucked the tube back inside the tyre, seated the bead with her thumbs, and pumped until the tyre was firm enough to bounce a little when she pressed it. Inside the bank, she slid the cheque and the deposit slip through the slot at the counter. On the way out she rang the bell on her handlebars once, for the guard, and pedalled home over the bridge with the front tyre humming on the pavement.

Jeremy slammed his notebook onto the kitchen table so hard the salt shaker rattled. Tonight he was going to write the best short story Mr. Doran had ever graded, one with real dialogue, quotation marks, commas in the right spots, and a climax that actually felt like a climax. He sharpened two pencils even though he was using a pen, because it helped him think, and the smell of cedar and graphite made the whole project feel official.

His sister Maya dropped into the chair across from him with her laptop and a groan. "My essay is broken," she said. "I moved my paragraph about the leaky plumbing to the end because it made more sense there, and now everything feels off, but I can't say why." She spun the screen toward him. The kitchen smelled like the spaghetti sauce simmering on the stove, and somewhere under it Jeremy could hear the faucet dripping, which seemed like a sign.

Jeremy read her first paragraph, then the three body paragraphs, then the first paragraph again. Something clicked. "Your intro says you'll talk about leaks, then bad pipes, then mold. But the paragraphs go bad pipes, mold, leaks." He tapped the screen. "It's like my story problem. My narrator promises trouble in the basement, but the trouble shows up upstairs first."

Maya frowned at her screen. "So the thesis has to name the supporting points in the same order the body paragraphs discuss them?" She highlighted her opening sentence, dragged the list of points around until leaks came last, and read it aloud. It sounded smooth, like fixing a crooked picture frame. "Jeremy, you're a genius," she said, and stole one of his sharpened pencils to circle her revised sentence.

He turned back to his own notebook feeling like he'd found a secret passage. He had been letting his scenes arrive in random order because each one was fun to write, but readers needed the map first. He crossed out his opening line and wrote a new one that promised exactly what would happen, in the order it would happen. Then he fixed his dialogue, comma before the quotation mark, period inside, reading each line out loud in a dramatic voice until Maya threw a folded napkin at him. "The pipe burst at midnight," he wrote, "and water shot across the basement like a fountain."

"Nice climax," Maya said, mouth full of spaghetti.

"Regulate your volume," their dad called from the stove, because Jeremy was now reading the burst-pipe sentence at full volume, both fists in the air.

Evan sat on the crinkly paper of the exam table, rolling up his sleeve for his flu vaccine, when Dr. Okafor paused with the syringe in her hand. "Before I do this, tell me something. Your mom says you've been getting stomachaches. When do they happen?"

"Sunday nights, mostly." Evan watched her give the shot, a quick pinch in his arm. "And Monday mornings. It's weird. I'm not even sick."

"Anything big happening at school on Mondays?" she asked.

That was the question that snagged in his head on the drive home. Mondays meant math, and math meant timed multiplication quizzes. He remembered last Monday: his stomach churning, his palms so sweaty the pencil had slipped, and the Sunday before, lying awake until almost midnight, staring at the ceiling. He'd thought those were three separate things, like three separate bad days. Now he tried to isolate the one thing they had in common. Monday. Every time, Monday.

He dug out a notebook and drew a chart, two parallel columns: one for how his body felt, one for what was coming the next day. Headache, Sunday. Upset stomach, Sunday night. Sweaty palms, Monday morning, right before the quiz. Trouble falling asleep, the night before every single one. When he looked at the two columns lined up side by side, his stomach dropped a little, the way it did in an elevator. The pattern was too neat to be a coincidence. His body was reacting to the quizzes before his brain had even admitted it was worried.

That night was Wednesday, so he decided to test something. No quiz tomorrow, but he practiced anyway, the way Dr. Okafor had shown him in the office: breathe in for four counts, hold it, let it out slow, like he was fogging a window. He also set up a routine, same time every night: pajamas, teeth, ten minutes of a book, lights out. He did it Thursday and Friday and the weekend too, filling in his chart each morning. Sleeping, he wrote. No headache.

Sunday night came, and his stomach tightened at eight o'clock, right on schedule. Evan noticed it, actually noticed it this time, and instead of just lying there waiting for it to get worse, he sat up and breathed. In for four. Hold. Slow fog on an imaginary window.
