His stomach didn't vanish, but it loosened, like a fist uncurling one finger at a time.

Monday morning he walked into math with dry palms. When the timer started, he took one breath before picking up his pencil, and his hand stayed steady all the way through.

"Feeling okay?" his teacher asked as he handed in his paper.

Evan glanced at the clock, then at his hands. "Ask me Sunday night," he said. "That's the real test."

Carson stood behind his science fair table staring at the periodic table taped to the wall, and he could not find sodium. His project, a tray of three cloudy jars labeled "Saltwater Experiment," depended on it, and the judges were already two tables away.

Last spring, his grandmother had narrated her entire garden tour, explaining how an invasive vine had swallowed her tomato plants while she was in the hospital. "The invisible things are the powerful ones," she'd said, pointing at a spot of gray mold on a fence post, "like that microbe eating the wood right now." He hadn't understood what she meant until now, squinting at the tiny numbers crammed into each square. He traced his finger along row three and there it was, Na, with the number 11 sitting on top like a tiny hat. Eleven. He counted the columns and rows again just to be sure he hadn't drifted into magnesium by mistake. Sodium had eleven protons, and the box said so, if a person could learn to read the map.

"Tell me about your project," said the judge, a woman with a clipboard and pen shaped like a thermometer.

Carson picked up the first jar. "Two weeks ago I dissolved salt in water and put it in my bedroom window, the sunny side. I kept a second jar on my desk in the shade, and a third in the fridge." He held up the window jar, which now had white crystals crusty around the bottom and edges. "The water's mostly gone from this one, and look. Salt. The same salt."

"Same salt?" the judge asked.

"That's the twist. I thought dissolving it destroyed the salt and made something new, a chemical change. But when the water evaporated, it left the same salt behind." He touched the jar. "So dissolving salt in water is a physical change. Nothing got destroyed. The salt was just hiding."

The judge smiled and wrote something. Behind her, a small boy in a dinosaur shirt tugged her sleeve and whispered, too loudly, "I thought he was going to show a microbe." A woman at the next table snorted, and Carson's ears went hot, but the judge laughed kindly.

He turned to the periodic table anyway. "See, sodium is number eleven, so every single salt crystal in there has eleven protons in every atom," he said, tapping the square. "I can't see them. Nobody can. But the map tells you where they are, if you know how to read it." The dinosaur boy leaned in, squinting at the tiny numbers. "Whoa," he said. "It's like a treasure chart."

Grayson had one week to turn a primary source into an actual answer, and his grandfather's attic had exactly one box labeled OLD PAPERS. The assignment wanted him to use something written at the time, not a textbook, to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. He had guessed the answer would be gold, because everyone in his class would guess gold, and he wanted something better than the obvious.

Grandpa set the box on the kitchen table beside a rolled-up wall map he'd taken down from the hall. "That map's from my teaching days," he said. "You can spread it out when you need a break." Inside the box, under church programs and a ribbon from a prestigious agricultural fair, Grayson found a small leather book. The handwriting was cramped, and the ink had bled through the thin pages in places, so some words dissolved into pale blue shadows he could only guess at.

The diary belonged to a great-great-something named Elias Ward, and the first entry was dated April 1852. Grayson read slowly, hunting for the word gold. It never came. Instead Elias wrote about a letter from his brother in Iowa, describing soil so dark it "stains the boots," and about a failed mill back east, and about land selling for a dollar and a quarter an acre. Grayson sat back. His easy answer had just collapsed. He decided to test a new one: maybe people moved for cheap land and work, and the gold story was only part of it. He counted the reasons Elias gave across four entries, and land came up in every single one.

When his cousin Marisol arrived to borrow the map for her own homework, the two of them unrolled it on the living room floor. It showed the Roman Empire, not America at all. "You have to trace the biggest border," Marisol said, "for my teacher." Grandpa leaned in the doorway. "Biggest it ever got was around 117 CE, under Emperor Trajan," he said. "Britain in the northwest, all the way to Mesopotamia in the east." Grayson and Marisol ran their fingers along the edge together, from the top corner of Britain across to the far eastern edge, and it took a long time, longer than either of them expected.

Marisol asked whether the empire lasted like that. "No, it got smaller after," Grandpa said, and rolled the map shut, and that single word, smaller, made something click for Grayson. Elias had written that his town back east was shrinking too, mills closing, neighbors leaving. Growing big and then shrinking had a consequence: people went looking for somewhere else. He copied three lines from the diary into his notebook, word for word.

Then he noticed the signature inside the back cover. Not Elias Ward. Ellen Ward, 1852. He flipped to the front again and read the April entry more carefully. "My husband reads this to me and I hold the pen," Ellen had written in the first line, which Grayson had skimmed right past. The settler's diary he needed had been written by the settler's wife, all along. "Grandpa," he called toward the kitchen, "did anyone in the family ever know Ellen wrote this?" Grandpa came back drying his hands on a towel and bent over the page for a long moment. "Well," he said, "they do now."

Sofia pushed the kitchen chairs aside to make a stage in the living room and set her phone on the bookshelf to record. Tomorrow was her first improv workshop, and she wanted to walk in already knowing how it worked. Her older cousin Denise had agreed to practice with her over video call, and now Denise's face filled the screen, waiting.

"Okay," Sofia said. "You start a scene, and we build it together."

Denise rubbed her hands together like a villain. "Welcome to my store. We only sell one thing: shark teeth."

Sofia froze. She had planned to say something clever, but nothing clever came, so she blurted, "No, we're not in a store, we're on a pirate ship."

Denise dropped the villain pose. "Hold on. You just erased my whole scene. In improv that's like slamming a door in someone's face."

"I didn't like the store," Sofia said. "A pirate ship is better."

Denise tilted her head. "Maybe. But think about what just happened. You proposed the change, and you acted like it was my job to show why your pirate ship was bad. It doesn't work that way. The side that proposes a change carries the burden of proof. That means you have to show why the change is needed instead of me proving it isn't."

Sofia rewound the moment in her head. She had assumed the opposite rule, that whatever she threw out must be accepted until Denise knocked it down. No wonder Denise had looked annoyed. "So if I want the pirate ship, I have to earn it," Sofia said slowly. "I have to build from your shark teeth instead of deleting them."

"Try it again," Denise said.

Denise started over. "Welcome to my store. We only sell one thing: shark teeth."

"Yes, and business is booming," Sofia said, "because the local sharks went predatory and everyone needs proof of what happened."

Denise grinned. "Yes, and a merchant just walked in offering to transport the whole inventory across the harbor for a fee."

"Yes, and the fee is ruining our economy, so we'll pay you in shark teeth instead."

They went back and forth for ten more minutes, building a market, a storm, a smuggler with a peg leg. Twice Sofia slipped and denied an offer, and each time she stopped, rewound, and found a way to say yes to it. The second slip turned into her favorite moment, when Denise's "the harbor is frozen" became Sofia's "yes, and that's why we're racing the ice truck across it."

At the end, Sofia flopped onto the couch and scrolled back through the recording. She watched herself stumble, repair, stumble again, and land the scene. Tomorrow she would walk into that workshop and say yes.

Alexandra had exactly one week to finish her science project, and the microscope sitting on her grandfather's kitchen table was the most interesting thing on the whole farm. It belonged to her Uncle Theo, who had won a scholarship to study biology years ago and left the heavy black instrument in the attic with a box of slides. Alexandra's project was supposed to be about the finches of the Galapagos Islands, how their beak shapes had changed on different islands until each kind matched the seeds available there. She could write that down, but she wanted to see something real under the lenses.

She pulled out a slide of an onion and dropped it onto the stage. The microscope had three lenses, and she turned the big knob until the longest one, the strongest one, clicked into place. Surely the strongest was the best place to start. She pressed her eye to the eyepiece and saw nothing but a milky blur. She turned the focus wheel, first one way, then the other, and the blur only swam. After ten minutes her neck ached and there were no onion cells anywhere, only fog.

"You look like you lost a fight with that thing," her grandfather said from the doorway.

"It won't show anything. Maybe it's broken." She said it as an accusation, which implied she believed the microscope, not herself, was at fault.

He shrugged and went back out to the barn, and Alexandra slumped in the chair, ready to quit. Then she sat up. The blur wasn't empty. It moved when she moved the slide, just a little. Maybe the cells were there but she was too far off. She clicked the smallest lens, the lowest power, into place, and suddenly the fog resolved into a pale landscape, orderly rectangles edged in faint lines, like a brick wall. There were the onion cells. She found one sharp, clean group in the center, focused carefully, and only then clicked up to the stronger lens. Now the magnified cells filled the view, and the detail was astonishing. She sketched fast, in case it vanished.

Afterward she carried the notebook to the barn, where her grandfather was stacking hay. She showed him her drawing and then flipped to her finch pages, the tracings she had made from Uncle Theo's old book, the thick crushing beaks on one island and the slender probing beaks on another. "Nobody watched the beaks change," she said. "But the pattern is there, the same way the cells were there under the blur. You just have to start in the right place and look."

Outside, the sun was sinking, and the sky over the silo glowed like molten copper. Her grandfather studied the pages for a long moment, then said, "Help me finish this row, and after supper you can tell me the whole thing, start to finish."

Every August, watering Grandma's tomato beds was a ritual: fill the can at the spigot, haul it down the gravel path, pour, trudge back. Jade had assumed the tomatoes needed her, but by the third trip her arms burned, and she began to think the tomatoes mostly needed somebody with stronger shoulders.

Grandma was at the picnic table with her coffee, reading, while Jade lugged the can again. "My arms are going to fall off," Jade said.

"Farmers along the Nile had the same problem," Grandma said. "They used a shaduf." She pointed her cup at the tool shed. "Your grandfather built one for the pond years ago. It's behind the rakes." That was all she said, and she went back to her book.

Jade found it leaning against the wall: a long pole with a bucket on one end and a heavy stone wired to the other, balanced on a post. She hauled it to the pond, dipped the bucket, and pulled down on the rope. The stone rose, the bucket swung up over the bank, and the water poured out toward the beds. It still took work, but it took half the work, and Jade stood there dripping and grinning, moving bucket after bucket. It was so simple it felt unfair. One heavy thing lifting another, so nobody's arms had to do it all.

Then she remembered Monday. Her history teacher had asked the class to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War, and Jade's rough draft was one flat sentence: the treaty punished Germany after World War I. Mrs. Okafor had written, "But how? Show me." Jade sat down on the gravel, still holding the shaduf rope, and thought about punishment. Germany had been made to carry payments so heavy they never seemed to end, like being handed a watering can that never got lighter. People who feel crushed year after year look for someone to lift the weight, and someone had promised he could. She couldn't see a country or an armistice the way she could see this pole, but the shape was the same, a burden doing something over time. She pulled out her notebook and wrote: imagine carrying the can forever, and imagine the person who says, put it down.

"Did you figure out your homework out here?" Grandma asked, coming down the path with the empty coffee cup.

"I think the treaty is a watering can," Jade said, and hauled up another bucket.

The bus smelled of wet raincoats and pencil shavings, and Rosalie had her boots propped on the metal bar under the seat in front of her when she heard the laughing start. Derek was holding his phone toward the window seats so everyone could see the screen. "Look what Milo wrote in the group chat," he said. "Can you even read this? It's like a baby typed it."

Milo sat two rows up, hunched into his jacket, staring at the back of the seat. Rosalie knew about the group chat. She was in it too, and last night she had watched the mean comments pile up under Milo's question about the agriculture project, comments about his spelling and his old shoes. This morning they had all vanished. Derek had deleted them, or someone had, and now there was nothing to point at. Last month something like this had happened to her friend Tessa, and Rosalie had stayed quiet, telling herself the bus wasn't the place. She had regretted it for weeks.

Derek kept scrolling, hunting for the messages. "Wait, where'd they go?" he muttered, tapping the screen. Rosalie's stomach tightened. The evidence was disappearing while everyone watched, and once it was gone, who would believe Milo? Then she remembered her own phone. She hadn't deleted anything. She never did, because her storage was always too full to bother. Last night, before bed, she had taken screenshots of the worst comments, mostly because reading them twice had felt so unfair she'd wanted proof they were real. They were still in her camera roll, time-stamped, eleven o'clock at night.

She stood up in the rattling aisle, gripping a seat back as the bus swayed. Her plan felt small and maybe useless, but she wanted to test one thing: whether Derek would back off if the proof could not be erased. "Those comments you deleted," she said, keeping her voice even, "I have screenshots." She held up her phone from where she stood, not close enough for him to grab, and let the words land. "So deleting them didn't make them never happen."

The bus went quiet except for the engine. Derek dismissed her with a shrug, "Nobody cares," but his ears turned red and he put his phone away. A girl near the window said, "I saw them too." Milo turned around slowly, and his eyes went from Rosalie's phone to her face.

"I'm going to show my screenshots to Ms. Okafor at first period," Rosalie said. "You can come with me or not, but they're not going anywhere." Milo blinked, then nodded and gathered his backpack onto his lap like he was ready for the bus to hurry up and arrive.

Derek stared out the window the rest of the ride. When the doors hissed open, Rosalie waited for Milo in the aisle and said, "Walk with me."

The floorboards in Grandma Ruth's attic creaked as Levi and his cousin Marisol set up two folding chairs. In two hours, the whole family would gather downstairs for Grandpa Joe's seventieth birthday party, and the two of them had promised to perform a five-minute improv scene, even though Levi had never done improv in his life.

"Rule one," Marisol said, tapping the chair like a game show host. "Whatever I say, you say yes, and then you add something. So if I say, 'We're astronauts landing on a cheese moon,' you don't say, 'No, that's silly.' You say, 'Yes, and the smell is making me hungry.'"

"That sounds easy," Levi said.

It was not easy. Every time Marisol made an offer, Levi's brain revolved around all the things that could go wrong, and out of his mouth came a dodge. "Um, I guess so," he said to the cheese moon. "Uh, okay," he said when she suggested they were being chased by a vacuum cleaner. Marisol pulled a small notepad from her pocket and started making tally marks, one for every um and uh. After ten minutes she turned the page toward him: twenty-three marks.

Levi stared at the tallies like they were evidence at a trial. He had thought his problem was not knowing what to say, but the marks showed a different pattern. The ums appeared exactly when an offer arrived, right at the moment of choice. He decided to run a test. Instead of filling the gap with a sound, he would stay silent for a beat, then say the words "Yes, and" and let them carry him wherever they wanted.

They started the scene again. Marisol said, "Our spaceship runs on pickle juice." Levi paused, silent, letting the pause sit there. "Yes, and we're almost out, so we have to land at the space diner." Marisol's eyebrows shot up. She kept the scene going, and the tally marks slowed, then stopped. By the third run, she put the notepad away entirely and started laughing so hard she fell off her chair.

Downstairs, the smell of Grandpa Joe's lemon cake drifted up the attic stairs. Levi heard chairs scraping, the screen door banging, and Grandma Ruth calling that the show would start in five minutes. Marisol grabbed his arm. "One last treaty," she said. "Whatever happens down there, nobody says no, not even once." Levi shook her hand, and they headed for the stairs, where the first row of relatives, looking cheerful but slightly obstinate about being entertained, was already waiting. Marisol leaned over and whispered, "We're two penguins who opened a lemonade stand in Antarctica." Levi let the pause hang there, took a breath, and said, "Yes, and business is about to pick up."

Ryder stood at the counter with a whole onion in one hand and his mom's sharpest knife in the other, glancing at the clock. His parents would be home at seven, and he had promised them a pasta sauce made entirely from scratch. His little sister Nadia sat on a stool nearby, arms crossed, watching him like a judge.

"I'm not eating anything with onion in it," she announced. "Onion is sharp and mean. It bit me once at Maya's house."

"That was raw onion," Ryder said. "This is going to be different." He hoped he was right. He curled the fingers of his left hand into a claw, fingertips tucked behind his knuckles, and guided the knife with his knuckles leading the blade. The first slices were uneven, but none of his fingertips went with them, which he counted as a win. The raw pieces smelled so sharp that Nadia leaned away, fanning the air with her hand.

He melted butter in the pan and turned the heat down low, because the recipe card his mom had written said low and slow, no rushing. He remembered how the tomatoes in their garden thrived when he stopped overwatering them, and he figured onions might have their own hidden rule too. His motive was simple: get Nadia to eat the sauce without complaining. He decided to test one piece on her before he finished, so he fished out a small strip of cooked onion, blew on it, and held out the fork. "One bite. If you hate it, I'll pick every single one out of your bowl."

Nadia eyed it like it might bite back, then took the tiniest nibble. Her eyebrows went up. She took a bigger bite. "It's soft," she said, chewing slowly. "And sweet. It tastes like it got dipped in honey. Why isn't it mean anymore?"

"That's the trick," Ryder said, stirring the pan, where the onions had turned soft and golden brown, their natural sugars showing themselves as they cooked. "Raw onion stays sharp, but if you cook it slowly over low heat, it turns sweet like this." He poured in the crushed tomatoes, added a pinch of salt, and let the sauce bubble while he boiled the pasta, checking the clock. Six forty. Plenty of time.

At seven the front door opened and his parents came in, sniffing the air. Nadia got to the hallway first. "Ryder made sauce from scratch," she reported, "and there's onion in it, and I'm getting seconds."

"Seconds?" his dad said. "You picked onion out of your chili last Tuesday."

"Not anymore," Nadia said. "Ryder, save me the fertile pieces. The golden ones." Ryder laughed and lifted the pot, steam rising as he carried it to the table.

Stella's pencil hovered over the paper, and the paper was winning. In art cabin three, everyone else had already drawn a street with one-point perspective: two rows of buildings whose edges ran uphill and downhill toward a single dot, the vanishing point, where the whole road disappeared. Hers looked like a street built by a drunk giant. The left side tilted one way, the right side the other, and the road climbed instead of receding.

She wanted this badly, because tomorrow the camp was holding a small gallery night, and the pottery instructor, an artisan from the town who sold glazed bowls at the market, had promised to trade one bowl for any drawing she liked. Stella had her eye on a blue-green one with a wobbly rim. She also wanted to beat Marcus, who kept leaning over and saying, "Mine looks like a photograph, Stella. Yours looks like a melted crayon."

She decided to test an idea instead of guessing. First she retraced the road with her ruler and saw the problem: her building lines weren't parallel with each other before they angled in, so they ran to two different vanishing points instead of one. Two vanishing points meant two roads, and two roads meant melted crayon. She marked a single dot with a pushpin, tied a piece of string to it, and pulled the string tight to guide each line. The string made a faint sound, a small humming like a plucked guitar, and she pretended it was the street singing itself into place. Pin to corner, line. Pin to corner, line. Slowly a real street appeared, a candy shop, a lamppost, a mailbox, all obedient, all sliding toward the dot.

But her street was empty, so she added a boy juggling on the sidewalk and, near him, a ball resting on the pavement. The ball looked wrong. No matter how she shaded the rounded side of it, the ball seemed to hover a little above the ground, like it was floating an inch of air, refusing to land. She erased the shadow, drew it again, shaded the whole shadow evenly. Still hovering. Marcus leaned over. "Nice balloon," he said.

Stella glared at the drawing, then at the actual sunny porch step outside, where a soccer ball sat in the sun. She went out and knelt beside it. The shadow on the step wasn't the same darkness all the way across; the outer edge looked soft and gray, but the part right under the ball, in the narrow space where the ball touched the step, went almost black, the darkest shadow of all. She hadn't shaded that spot at all. Back inside, she pressed her pencil down hard in the tiny area where the ball met the pavement, making it the darkest mark on the whole street, and left the rest of the shadow lighter. The ball dropped onto the ground like it had been waiting for permission.

At gallery night the artisan stood in front of her drawing for a long moment. She tapped the place where the ball touched the street and said, "You saw it. Most people never look at the dark part where the ball touches the ground." Stella retrieved the blue-green bowl from the trade table with both hands, and Marcus, standing behind her with his photograph-perfect street, said, "Okay. Fine. That one's better."

Naomi had exactly one hour before the health expo opened, and her model of the brain's reward pathway still looked like a pile of yarn and buttons. "The nicotine goes in here," she said, threading a blue bead along the yarn from the front of her cardboard brain toward the middle, "and it lands on these cells, and they flood the gap with dopamine." Dopamine was the messenger that made the brain say yes, do that again. Nicotine tricked the pathway into saying it about something harmful.

"Is that the formula for addiction?" asked Priya, crouching beside the picnic table. "Like, chemical in, dopamine out, want more?"

"Sort of a formula," Naomi said. "Want to test it?" She held up a marble, a magnet, and a paper clip. She was trying to show how nicotine made the pathway react faster and harder than ordinary rewards did, so quitting felt like losing something. Priya flicked the marble down the yarn track. It bumped past the magnet without stopping. Then Naomi taped the magnet to stand for nicotine, and the paper clip snapped sideways toward it before the marble even arrived. "See? The pull starts before the reward shows up. That's the craving part."

Priya went quiet. She turned a button over and over in her fingers. "Can I tell you something? I've been so anxious this whole session. Like, chest-tight, can't-sleep anxious. I thought I was the only weird one here."

Naomi remembered the binder from the camp office that she'd flipped through while waiting for glue. "You're not. There was this big U.S. survey of teens aged thirteen to eighteen, and about a third of them had had an anxiety disorder at some point. It said anxiety was the most common kind of mental disorder among them." She stacked a third of the buttons from the table into one pile and left the rest scattered. "Look. If this table were the survey, this pile is you."

"One third," Priya said slowly. "That's, like, two other girls in our cabin, probably." She almost smiled. "Where's the binder? I want to see it with my own eyes."

They ran through the lodge together, and Naomi felt oddly competent, like her brain had its own reward pathway lighting up. The binder was on the shelf where she'd left it, but when she opened it, a folded note slid out, addressed to the camp director. Priya grabbed her arm. "That's my handwriting," she whispered. "I wrote that note two weeks ago about my anxiety and never sent it."

"So send it now," Naomi said, holding out a pen.

The driving school shared a parking lot with a laundromat, and Aubrey's mother taught behind the wheel all afternoon, so the basket of family laundry came with them every Tuesday. Aubrey had resigned herself to spending those hours in the back room of Hometown Driving Academy, sorting darks from lights beside the humming dryers, while her mother's voice drifted in through the propped door. "Check your mirror, Mr. Delgado. Mirror, signal, shoulder." Her mother wanted her to have the whole laundry system mastered by summer, and Aubrey wanted the opposite: to be out in the training car, learning something that actually moved.

Today she was determined to get it right anyway. She pulled Aubrey's dad's work shirts from the pile, felt a wet patch, and discovered a red sock hiding inside a white pillowcase, the culprit behind months of pink undershirts. "That's the contradiction," she muttered. "Dad says hot water cleans everything, but hot water is exactly what sets the pink." She wrote it in her notebook: cold rinse, darks, always. Then she reached deep into the basket and something sharp caught the pad of her thumb.

At first it looked like nothing. Then the blood came, bright and steady, and Aubrey's mother hurried in from the parking lot, still holding her clipboard. She grabbed a clean towel from the folded stack and pressed it firmly over the cut. "Keep this on," she said. "Firm, like you mean it." The clock on the wall read 3:12.

Aubrey held the pressure and counted the dryer cycles. Her mother went to the office phone and called for medical help, then came back and crouched beside her. "Ten minutes is the rule," her mother said quietly. "If it's still bleeding after ten minutes of firm pressure, it needs real medical help." Aubrey watched the second hand sweep. At 3:22 she peeled the towel's edge back just enough to see, and the blood was still coming. "It's still going," she reported, and pressed down again, harder, the way she'd been told. Her mother stayed on the line with the dispatcher, one hand resting on Aubrey's shoulder.

The ambulance took eleven minutes to arrive. Aubrey kept the towel pressed the entire time, her other hand steady on top of it, while her mother gave the address twice. When the medics finally knelt down and took over, one of them nodded at the towel and said, "Good, you didn't let up." Aubrey looked at her notebook on the folding table, open to the page about cold rinses and hidden red socks. "Next Tuesday," she said, "I'm finishing that load."

The lemonade stand had been Victor's idea, but the notebook on the counter was his sister's idea, and that was the problem. Dana was leaving for college in the fall, and she had put two hundred dollars of her birthday money into something she called an investment account. She wanted Victor to understand it before she went. "Stock or bond," she had said that morning, tapping the notebook. "Pick one, and be able to tell me which is riskier and why. I'll stop by at noon and quiz you."

Victor poured lemonade for a man in a red cap and thought about what he had read the night before. A stock was a tiny piece of a company. A bond was more like lending the company money, and the company promising to pay it back with a little extra. He could recite that. But which was riskier, and why, kept sliding around in his head like ice in a glass.

By ten thirty he had sold nine cups at fifty cents each, and there was a line of four kids from the soccer field. Then his friend Marcus arrived with a wild plan. "Double the price," Marcus said. "A dollar a cup. They're hot out there. You'll make twice the money."

Victor hesitated. He remembered last summer, when he had tried to sell friendship bracelets at three dollars each and nobody bought a single one. He had blamed the bracelets. Now he wondered if he should have blamed the price. "Let's test it," he said. They taped a new sign to the jug: ONE DOLLAR.

The line did something strange. The next kid looked at the sign, dug in his pocket, and walked away. The three behind him turned and drifted back toward the field. For twenty minutes not one person stopped. "It's like they vanished," Marcus said. "Nothing else changed. Same lemonade, same sun." Victor wrote it down in the margin of Dana's notebook: when the price goes up, people buy less, as long as nothing else changes. It wasn't the bracelets last summer. It never had been.

He changed the sign back to fifty cents, and by eleven fifteen, the customers had returned, laughing and spontaneous, splashing quarters on the counter and arguing about who had the driest soccer sock. Victor watched them and turned the stock-and-bond question over again. A company that did badly could skip the extra payment on a bond, but the company usually still had to pay the bondholder back eventually, because the bond was a contract. A stock, though, was just a claim on whatever was left. If the company fell apart, the stock could be worth nothing at all.

At noon, Dana pedaled up the driveway on her old bike, kicked the stand down, and sat on the curb with a cup sweating in her hand. "Okay," she said. "Quiz time. Stock or bond. Which is riskier?"

"Stock," Victor said. "A bond is a contract, so the company owes you. A stock is only worth what the company turns out to be. No promise, no payback order, just the risk." He slid the notebook across the counter, open to his scribbled margin note. "And I figured out something else today. Price up, buyers down. I proved it with lemonade."

Dana read the page, then grinned at him over the rim of her cup. "Okay, one more question, and this one's for double. If you had two hundred dollars, what would you do with it?"

Victor looked at the line of quarters, then at her, and said, "First, I'd buy another bag of lemons."

The graph paper sat between Aubrey and her partner, Marcus, with two climate charts pinned at the corners. One showed a hot desert: a thin scrub of rainfall bars, barely a few centimeters a year, with a temperature line that climbed high and stayed there. The other showed a rainforest, where the rainfall bars towered so tall that Marcus had needed a second sheet of graph paper to fit them all. Their science teacher had written one instruction on the board: compare the two climates before the bell, because the packets were due at the end of the period.

"Easy," Marcus said, tapping the desert chart. "Desert wins on temperature. Rainforest wins on rain. Can we turn it in?"

Aubrey frowned at the desert's rainfall bars. They looked almost like a mistake, so small she could cover all twelve months with her thumb. "But that can't be the whole answer," she said. "If it rains at all, why is the ground always dry in pictures of deserts? Where does the water go?" Marcus shrugged and started doodling a cactus on the margin, which meant he was done thinking.

Then she remembered something. Last fall, before the unit on decomposers, her cousin Elena in Arizona had sent her a video. Elena had dumped a bucket of water on her backyard patio just to see what would happen, and by lunch the whole puddle had vanished, even though it had only been a drizzle-free morning. At the time Aubrey had assumed someone wiped it up. Now she looked at the temperature line again, flat and burning across the whole year, and a different idea felt plausible. The water had gone up. The sun and the dry air could take far more water in a year than the rain put down.

"I think I've got it," she said. She grabbed a sticky note and wrote across the desert chart: the sun and dry air could evaporate far more water in a year than falls as rain, so the ground stays dry. "So even when it does rain, the desert loses it. The ground can't hold on."

Marcus stopped doodling. "Wait. So the rainforest is the opposite?" He flipped to the second chart, where the rainfall bars looked like a skyline. "The rain comes faster than anything can take it away." He wrote that on a sticky note too and pressed it beside the tall bars. Then he looked at Aubrey. "So for our answer, the desert isn't just hotter. It's a place where the water leaves."

"There's ten minutes," said Priya from the next table, glancing over at them. Aubrey noticed Priya's own packet was still blank except for a title, and Priya's pencil was hovering without moving. "We're stuck on the same question," Priya admitted.

"Take this." Aubrey slid the desert chart across so Priya could see the sticky note, and Priya copied the comparison onto her own sheet while Marcus flipped their rainforest chart around. They each wrote a sentence about which months preceded the heavy rain in the rainforest and how the desert's heat held steady no matter what.

When the bell rang, Marcus handed in the packet with both charts and three sticky notes flapping off the sides. Priya slid hers in right behind his. On the way out, Marcus pointed at the thermometer by the door. "Eleven degrees. If I dumped a bucket outside right now, it would still be there tomorrow." Aubrey grinned and said, "Then let's be glad we don't live in a desert," and pushed the door open into the cold.

Naomi had until Sunday night to finish her biology sheet, and the only microscope within forty miles sat in the back room of her grandmother's farmhouse, under a dust cloth. The sheet asked for a drawing of onion skin cells with three labels: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She had peeled a paper-thin layer from an onion that morning, carried it in a jar, and now she waited for her grandmother to finish the milking so she could ask for the key to the back room.

"Third drawer down," her grandmother said, wiping her boots. "Mind the scope, it was your grandfather's." The room smelled of old paper and machine oil. Naomi found the key, unlocked the cabinet, and set the microscope on the table by the window, where the light was best. Then she discovered the problem. Through the eyepiece she could see the cells clearly, little brick-shaped boxes in neat rows, and the thick outer lines had to be the cell walls. But everything inside was pale and blank. The sheet demanded a nucleus, and there was nothing to label.

She sat back and drummed her fingers. Somewhere in this room her grandfather had kept his science notebooks. She pulled a box from the shelf, and that was when she found the loose page folded inside a notebook from his marine course. It described a stretch of Washington State shore where an ecologist named Robert Paine removed a starfish that ate mussels. After that, the mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other species. "You couldn't watch the starfish matter," her grandfather had written in the margin, "you could only see the shore change and work backwards."

Naomi read the page twice. The important thing had been invisible while it was there; you noticed it only when it was gone. So maybe the nucleus was like that. Maybe it was in her slide, just faint, and she needed to change something, not find something. She remembered the little brown bottle in the kitchen her grandmother used for tinctures, and she fetched it and added one drop to the onion skin.

The suspense while she refocused was almost unbearable. She turned the fine knob a hair at a time, the image swimming, blurring, sharpening. Then it snapped into view: a small dark sphere inside each cell, plain as a stone in shallow water. The nucleus had been there the whole time, waiting for the stain to let her see it. She traced the thin line just inside the wall and labeled the membrane too, then finished her drawing while the afternoon light held.

Outside, a raccoon, one of the nocturnal visitors her grandmother swore about, had already begun prodding at the compost bin, and the chickens would not cease their squawking until someone chased it off. "All right, all right," her grandmother called from the yard. "Naomi, grab the broom."

Naomi spread her graph paper across the kitchen table and wrote "SIMPLE" at the top of one column and "COMPOUND" at the top of the other. She was saving her birthday money, forty dollars a year, and her mother had said, "Five years. Figure out which account pays more." The simple account added three dollars for every hundred, every year, straight across. The compound one added three dollars on whatever was already there, including the interest from before. She worked the simple column fast. The compound column made her stop and squint, because the numbers climbed a tiny bit faster each year, like something growing quietly underground.

Her cousins burst in before she finished. Marcus waved a crumpled certificate. "Toytown stock. Uncle Rick gave it to me last summer." Priya held up a fancy printed sheet. "I got a Toytown bond. Same company." Toytown had gone bankrupt in the spring, and every kid on the block had heard about it.

"Mine's a stock," Marcus said. "Stocks sound bigger."

"I don't even know what a bond is," Priya admitted.

Naomi tapped her pencil. The word bankruptcy had shown up in her mother's newspaper pile, and one afternoon she had read enough of an article to provoke a question she'd been chewing on ever since: when a company died, who got paid first? She had made an inference from the article's grumbling quotes, and now she wanted to test it. "Trade me," she said suddenly. "Straight across. My next two weeks of allowance for your bond."

Priya stared. Marcus laughed so hard he knocked over the lemonade. "You'd trade real money for paper from a dead company?"

"Twenty minutes," Naomi said. "Then decide." She flipped her graph paper over and wrote fast, then handed Priya a note:

"Priya. If we're right about the order they pay people, your sheet is ahead of his in line. Stocks are last in line, and often get nothing at all. I'll still buy it from you either way, but only for a dollar. That way you can't lose much. Your choice. Naomi."

While Priya read, Marcus kept gloating, which provoked nothing but Naomi's patience. Priya looked up. "Last in line? So Marcus's stock is behind mine?"

"Only if my inference is right," Naomi said. "Grandma's neighbor worked at a bank. Let's ask her, but I'm asking, and nobody talks but me."

Mrs. Okafor, three doors down, was watering her tomatoes. She listened, wiped her hands, and said, "When a company goes bankrupt, bondholders get paid back before stockholders. Stockholders are last in line, and often they get nothing."

The walk home was quiet except for Marcus's sneakers. He stopped at the driveway. "Okay. I changed my mind. Your compound interest thing, the one you were drawing? Teach it to me and I'll trade you my stock for Priya's bond. She said yes already." He pointed at Priya, who was grinning and holding out the crumpled certificate.

"Deal," Naomi said, and she cleared a space at the table between her two columns. "Now watch what happens in year three."

Marcus pulled up a chair.

Carter sat on his grandfather's porch with a battered paperback open on his knees. He was supposed to be rehearsing. On Monday, his drama teacher had paired him with Priya for the improv unit, and their rule was simple: whatever your partner offers, you accept it and add to it. "Yes, and," the teacher kept saying. But every time Carter tried it at school, he froze, and Priya was left hanging like a climber whose rope had gone slack.

The paperback was a play he'd pulled off his grandfather's shelf, mostly to have something in his hands. It was by a playwright named Harold Pinter, and at first Carter thought the pages were misprinted. Whole lines were taken up by single words. Pause. Silence. They sat there in the middle of the dialogue like stage directions that had wandered into the wrong job. "Grandpa," Carter called, "did somebody write in this book?" His grandfather squinted at the page from his rocking chair. "Nope. That's how Pinter wrote it. The pauses and the silences are printed in like lines. Part of what the characters say."

Carter turned back to the page and read a scene again, slowly. Two characters were talking about almost nothing, the weather, a cup of tea, and yet the silences between them seemed to fluctuate, swelling and shrinking, sometimes a beat long, sometimes a whole breath and a half. It was strange. Nobody had ever told him that nothing could be written down and performed. He wondered: if a pause could be a line, then was his own freezing in improv really nothing? Or was it something he could use, something he could offer Priya on purpose?

He had an idea, and he wanted to test it. That afternoon Priya came over to practice in the living room, because the Monday performance was two days away and she refused to carry the whole scene by herself again. "Same rules," she said, pushing the coffee table aside. "Yes, and. You take whatever I give you and build on it. Your protagonist can be anyone. Ready?" Carter nodded, but he had a secret plan.

Priya started. "We're two astronauts and the oxygen is running out." Instead of scrambling for a joke, Carter said, "Yes, and there's a light blinking on the console." Then he stopped. He let the silence sit, counting one breath, the way Pinter's pages had taught him, eyes on the imaginary light. Priya blinked, then leaned in and matched him, quiet too, her hand hovering over the pretend controls. The pause wasn't dead air. It was the two of them trapped in a ship, deciding whether to touch that button. When Carter finally spoke, the words felt spontaneous, like they'd risen out of the quiet on their own. "Yes, and," he said softly, "I think it's blinking faster."

They ran the scene three more times, and each time the silences did different work. Once the quiet felt like fear, once like grief for a planet they'd left behind. Priya kept sneaking glances at him like he'd swapped bodies with somebody braver. "Where did that come from?" she asked afterward, flopping onto the couch. "You used to just stand there."

Carter held up the Pinter paperback. "Turns out you can write down nothing," he said. "Pause. Silence. Right there in the script, like lines." Priya grabbed the book and flipped through it, hunting for the single words on the page. "Show me the longest one," she said. "The performance is Monday, and I want a silence in our scene so big the audience forgets to breathe."

Grandpa had dumped a bag of wrapped caramels on the kitchen table and told Nevaeh to count them into piles. "Forty votes," he said. "Green party, sixteen. Gold party, fourteen. Blue party, ten. Now, we've got five seats on this town council. First-past-the-post, you split the town into five districts." He slid the caramels into clumps. "Eight caramels per district."

Nevaeh leaned over the table. In the first district, Green got five votes and Gold got three, so Green won the seat. Same thing happened in the second and third. But in the fourth and fifth, Grandpa shuffled the piles so Gold squeaked ahead each time. "Wait," Nevaeh said. "Green has the most votes in the whole town, but Gold got two seats and Green got three. That's barely fair." She grabbed a napkin and drew it out, wondering what would happen if she stopped dividing the town at all.

"Try it the other way," Grandpa said. "Proportional representation. No districts. Five seats, forty votes, so eight votes per seat." Nevaeh divided each pile by eight. Green got sixteen, which was exactly two seats. Gold's fourteen votes gave it one seat with six left over. Blue's ten gave it one with two left over. She counted on her fingers, then pushed the last caramel back and forth between Gold and Blue. "It doesn't come out even," she said. "Somebody has to get the leftover seat."

"Every system has to decide that somehow," Grandpa said. "The question is which one feels fair to the most people, and which one lasts."

That made Nevaeh pause. "Which one is more durable?" she asked. Grandpa shrugged. "Proportional ones usually match how people actually voted. But a system can be fair and still fall apart if nobody trusts it." Nevaeh tapped the napkin. "So you can't just assume the one with the neatest math wins. People have to believe in the counting." Grandpa grinned and ate one of the caramels, which she pointed out was voter suppression.

Just then her cousin Marcus came in from the porch, still arguing with his friend Deon over the speakerphone. "I'm telling you, freedom of expression means anyone can say anything," Marcus said. Nevaeh opened her mouth, but Deon's voice came through first, steady as a kid reciting something he'd looked up an hour ago. "Section 1 of the Canadian Charter says its rights are subject to reasonable limits that can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society." Marcus stood there with his hand still raised, like the sentence had taken the wind out of it. "So they're limits," he said at last. "Reasonable ones."

Nevaeh looked from her cousin to the caramels, and a question formed slowly, the way the seat math had. "So even rules about talking have to be fair to everybody, like a vote." She slid the leftover caramel across the table to Marcus. "Sit down. You're the tiebreaker."

The screen door banged behind Evelyn, and the smell of Grandma's lemon cake followed her into the kitchen, where Grandma was on the phone with a pencil tucked behind her ear. "Hold on, Ruth," Grandma said, then covered the receiver. "Two of my garden club friends are having a spat. Want to watch? It's better than television." Evelyn flopped onto the stool. Garden club spats, it turned out, were serious business, involving a borrowed trellis and a lot of hurt feelings.

Ruth's voice came through the line like a wasp. "Marjorie said I'm so selfish, keeping all the prize dahlias to myself." Evelyn braced for Grandma to yell back, or to take sides, which is what happened every single time in the cafeteria at school. Instead Grandma said, "So what I'm hearing is, you want a fairer share of the dahlias this year." There was a pause, long enough for Evelyn to hear the clock tick and smell the cake starting to burn at the edges. Then Ruth said, in a much smaller voice, "Well. Yes. That's all I want."

After Ruth hung up, Evelyn slid off the stool. "You changed what she said. She called Marjorie selfish and you turned it into something about sharing." Grandma pulled the cake out, waving away the smoke with a dish towel shaped like a rooster. "That's called reframing," she said. "Now go call your mother back, she's been waiting an hour." Evelyn noticed Grandma hadn't explained anything more than that, so she carried the idea to the porch swing like a warm slice of cake, turning it over. The insult hadn't been repeated to Marjorie at all. It had been caught in midair, the way Dad caught flies with his bare hands, and set down as something harmless.

That was exactly what she needed, because on Monday, Marcus Teague had told half the sixth grade that Priya's synthetic fur jacket looked like a dead raccoon, and Priya hadn't come to lunch since. Evelyn had been trying to figure out a negotiation between them all week, and failing. Maybe the problem wasn't the jacket at all. Maybe it was the word "raccoon," which had traveled from mouth to mouth like a cold germ, getting worse each time. She wondered: what if she could catch it before the next person repeated it?

On Monday she found Tara repeating the raccoon joke near the gym, everybody laughing. Evelyn's stomach did a somersault, but she kept her voice level. "So basically, you think her jacket is too fuzzy for your taste. Noted." The laughter wobbled and died out, like a radio losing signal. Tara blinked. "I guess," she said. The group drifted off, and Evelyn spotted Priya at her locker, watching. Priya walked over and held out half a granola bar. "You want to delegate someone to sit with us at lunch, or should we just go claim the good table ourselves?" Evelyn grinned. "Let's go claim it."

"Nobody in the Rockhound Guild is going to believe a seasons video filmed in a quarry," said Priya, hoisting her backpack onto a flat slab of granite.

Matteo set down the flashlight he'd carried all the way from the parking lot. "That's the point. Mr. Ferreira says if you can explain something in a weird place, you really understand it. I got a C minus on my seasons essay. He wrote that I sounded like I was reciting." He pulled out the round mirror his mother used for canning jars and propped it against a shard of stone. "Earth's axis tilts, so the same sunbeam spreads over more ground or less ground. Watch."

He tilted the mirror and moved the flashlight in a slow arc. The light on the granite stretched into a long, pale oval, then tightened into a small bright circle. Priya crouched and put her hand in the beam. "When it's spread out, my fingers are barely warm. When it's small, it's hot." She looked up. "Okay, that part's good. But you said tilt, and your mirror isn't spinning."

Matteo held the mirror steady against his knee so the angle stayed stable while he swept the flashlight again. "Tilt first, spin later. One thing at a time, or everyone gets confused." He was so focused on the light that he almost put his hand down on the dark pebble Priya had been examining. "What's that?"

"Basalt, I think. It's from the piles over by the crusher." She held it beside the granite slab. The slab glittered with fat, sparkly crystals you could see from a step away. The basalt was plain and dark, its surface almost smooth. "Same quarry, and they look nothing alike."

Matteo turned the pebble in the light, and the flashlight beam refracted off a tiny crystal face, throwing a thin gold thread across the stone. He stared at the granite, then at the pebble, then back. "The granite's crystals are huge. This thing's are so small I can barely see them." He thought about the quarry walls, all that rock sitting deep underground for who knows how long before anyone cut it open. "Granite cools slowly, way down under the surface, so the crystals get big. Basalt cools fast at the surface, so they stay tiny."

"So it's like your seasons thing," Priya said. "The thing you can't see is what makes the difference."

Matteo had been sure the quarry was a dumb location. He looked at the glittering slab, at the small hot circle of light on it, and changed his mind completely. "Start the camera. I'll explain the tilt first, then the crystals."

Priya pressed record. "Go," she said.

Aria set up her easel on the grass beside the shed, where the afternoon light fell evenly across her cousin Marcus's face. He sat on an overturned bucket, holding still the way she had asked, because today she was going to paint his portrait in watercolour. Her art book said to build the picture in thin washes, starting with the palest colour and letting each layer dry before adding a darker one. That meant the shadows around his eyes would come last, and the whole first hour would look like almost nothing. Aria decided she could allocate one whole hour to the light layers and another to the dark ones, and she wrote the plan on her wrist in pen.

Marcus wanted to be useful while he sat, so he was drawing his own bedroom on a clipboard. "I'm going to enter it in the county fair," he said. "My room, from the doorway, so you can see two walls." He worked in silence for a while, tongue between his teeth.

By the time Aria's second wash was dry, Marcus held up his clipboard and frowned. "Something's wrong with it," he said. "It looks like the room is tipping over. Like the whole bedroom is sliding off the page sideways." He tilted the clipboard one way, then the other, but it looked wrong in every direction.

Aria came over, still holding her brush. She looked at the two walls slanting away from the doorway, their edges marching toward faraway points, which was right. Then she looked at the door frame, and there was the problem. He had angled its upright edges too, leaning them toward the same faraway points, as if the door itself were about to fall flat. She held her brush up straight against the drawing, then against the real back door of the house. "Look at the actual door," she said. "The corners go straight up and down." She took his pencil and drew the frame again with its edges parallel to her brush handle, straight and vertical, while only the horizontal lines kept slanting toward their points. When Marcus held the page up, the room stood solidly on the paper.

"That's kind of aggressive shading," Aria said, pointing at his heavy scribbled carpet, and Marcus laughed and softened it. The irony was that her own portrait had a tipping problem too. While she had been fixing his door, her light wash had dried with a hard dark edge across Marcus's forehead where the paint had pooled. She had been so aggressive with the water that it had made a tide mark. She dampened the whole forehead area with clean water and touched in a pale wash over it, and the line softened into skin.

Then she layered the middle tones, his hair, the shadow under his jaw, waiting and waiting for each wash to dry, which was the hardest part of all. When she finally added the darkest darks around his eyes, Marcus leaned in and grinned. "That's me," he said. "That's actually me."

"Fair entry number two?" Aria asked, and Marcus went inside to get the entry forms.

Rose counted bars under her breath, her fingers resting on the keys of the old upright piano backstage at the Hartwell Concert Hall. In fifteen minutes her small jazz combo would open for the visiting trumpeter, and she had one job in the tune: keep the form. Twelve bars, then around again, chorus after chorus. The trouble was that Dexter, the sax player, had a habit of wandering off somewhere in the middle and never finding his way back.

Last month at the school gym it had been a disaster. Dexter had soloed straight past the end of a chorus, landed his phrases in the wrong place, and finally stopped playing altogether, his face pink under the fluorescent lights. Rose had ended the tune early just to rescue him. On the bus home she had stared at her sheet music, running a quiet analysis of where things fell apart, and she had noticed something she'd never seen before. Near the end of each twelve bars, the bass walked up and the piano hit a chord that felt like a door swinging open. Her teacher never explained it, but the chart labeled it in small print: turnaround.

"They call that part the turnaround," Rose had said to Dexter on the bus, pointing at the page. He had only shrugged.

Now, side stage, Dexter was pacing. "I still get lost," he admitted. "Twelve bars is twelve bars until it isn't."

"Listen for the turnaround," Rose said, adjusting the bench. "It's the end of the twelve-bar form. It usually lands on the V chord, and that chord pulls the music back to the start of the next chorus. When you hear it, you're home."

"What if I miss it?"

"Then you wait twelve more bars. It comes around again. That's the whole trick."

When the lights came up, the tune rolled out smooth for the first chorus. Then Dexter stood to solo. Rose watched him close his eyes, and she knew from his loosening shoulders that he was drifting. But she kept her left hand steady, and when bar ten arrived she leaned into the V chord, letting it ring a half beat longer, pushing the sound toward the top of the form. Dexter's eyes snapped open. His next phrase landed square on bar one, and he built it upward like he had never been lost at all.

Afterward, the trumpeter with the visiting band came over. "Nice mediating," he told Rose, nodding between her and Dexter. "You held the form together without playing over him." The others crowded in to hear the story, and Rose realized the evening felt full instead of thin, nothing impoverished about it. Dexter raised his sax case like a trophy.

"Bar ten," he said. "I heard it. I heard the door open."

Lucy dumped the duffel bag onto the folding table and stared at the pile of clothes like it was a math test. Mom was at work until six, the soccer jersey had to be clean for tomorrow's game, and Lucy had exactly one hour to figure out laundry on her own.

"Separate the colours," she told herself, sorting into dark, light, and a hopeful little heap of pink things that she finally tucked into the dark pile as a compromise. Whites with whites, she reasoned, or the red sock would turn everything the colour of a sunburn. She fed quarters into the machine, poured in detergent, and watched the drum start to tumble.

Outside the window, a boy about her age was crouched beside his bike, pumping the tire pump like he was trying to inflate a bowling ball. He pumped, checked, frowned, and pumped again. Nothing was happening, and he was getting that red-faced, about-to-kick-something look. Lucy's washer would take forty minutes anyway, so she pushed out the door.

"Your pump is broken?" she asked.

"It's my little brother's bike, and he has a race at five, and I have to get the tire up." He pumped furiously. "It won't take air. I've been at it forever. My arms are getting cumulative tiredness."

"That's not what cumulative means," Lucy said, "but I get you." She crouched down and looked at the valve. It was skinny, nothing like the fat ones on her own bike, and on top of it was a tiny nut. She had read something about these once, in a bike magazine at the dentist's office. She turned the little nut counterclockwise until it wobbled loose, then pressed the pump on. This time when the boy pushed the handle, the tire began to firm up under his hand. He laughed out loud.

"The nut has to be unscrewed before any air can go in or come out," Lucy said. "That kind of valve is a Presta valve. You have to loosen it first."

"You are a genius and I will buy you a snack forever," the boy said, and pumped until the tire rang firm when he thumbed it. "My brother burns through carbs before races anyway. He'd eat your whole snack shelf."

"Carbohydrates," Lucy agreed. "He'll need them."

Her washer's spin cycle was shrieking by the time she got back inside. She moved everything to the dryer, and when the clothes came out warm she folded the jersey first, sleeves tucked in, just the way Mom did it, and laid it on top of the stack like a trophy. At 5:40 the boy pedalled past the window, his brother clinging to the back, both of them waving.

"Good luck tomorrow!" the brother shouted through the glass, holding up a granola bar in salute.

The stream table in the back of Mr. Okafor's room was just a long plastic tray, a hose, and a bucket of sand, but to Henry it looked like the Grand Canyon waiting to happen. The class had spent two days arguing about how rivers cut canyons, and a small controversy had broken out: Marcus insisted a river could only dig down, while Priya said it also carried the sand away and dropped it somewhere else, which she called deposition. Henry wanted to settle it, and more than that, he wanted to watch a canyon actually form under his own hands.

"Ten minutes of water equals millions of years," Mr. Okafor said, turning the hose on low. "Fast time."

But nothing much happened. The water slid over the sand in a thin sheet, barely leaving a scratch, and Henry began to resign himself to a boring tray of wet sand. Marcus smirked. "See? Rivers can't do it."

That weekend Henry visited his grandpa, who kept a wall calendar in the kitchen and made a small mark on it every evening he spotted the Moon. Henry noticed something odd: on one page there was a dark circle with the word new written beside it, and no mark at all that night, and then the marks began again, a sliver, a half, a full round circle, shrinking back down. He counted the days from that first dark circle to the next one, half expecting it to be a tidy number like thirty.

He counted twice. "Grandpa, is it twenty-nine and a half days?" he asked. "From one new moon to the next?"

"Every time," Grandpa said. "About twenty-nine and a half days. The sky doesn't hurry."

Henry stared at the little marks marching across the calendar. Half a day. The Moon couldn't even be bothered to finish on a whole number. Nothing dramatic had happened on any single night, yet the Moon had gone from dark to full to dark again, one tiny sliver at a time. He thought about his stream table, ten minutes of water that had barely wrinkled the sand. Maybe he had expected a canyon in fast time when he should have expected a sliver.

Monday after school, Henry barricaded the end of the tray with a dam of pebbles and let the hose drip, low and patient, into one narrow channel he had dug with his finger. Priya stayed to watch. "It's going to take forever," she said.

"That's the point," Henry said, defiant against the clock on the wall.

They checked every fifteen minutes. First the channel deepened, a real groove now. Then a curve formed where the water slowed, and sand began to settle there in a tiny, fan-shaped delta. Priya leaned down until her nose almost touched the tray. "It's dropping the sand," she whispered. "It carried it and dropped it."

By the time the custodian knocked on the door, the groove was a canyon, deep enough that its walls cast shadows, and at its mouth a small smooth beach had grown where nothing had been an hour before. Henry turned off the hose and looked at the little delta, then out the window at the pale daytime Moon hanging over the gymnasium roof.

"Twenty-nine and a half days," he said, "and I only needed an hour and a half."

Ava slid the short story across the library table like it might bite. "Mr. Okafor wants two paragraphs on foreshadowing and symbolism by Friday," she told her friend Dev, "and I don't even know what I'm looking for."

"You're looking for clues," Dev said, popping a cheese puff into his mouth despite the NO FOOD sign looming above them like a threat. "Like when the narrator says the ice on the pond looked thin, and then later somebody falls through. That's foreshadowing. The ice is telling you the future, but quietly, like a gossipy snowman."

"That is the most bizarre description of foreshadowing I have ever heard," Ava said, but she picked up her pencil anyway. The story was called "The Kite," and sure enough, on page one, the kite string was described as frayed. On page three, the kite was red, "the color of the flag on Grandfather's old letter." Ava sat up straight. The frayed string might correspond to something breaking later, and the red flag might connect to something Grandfather had lost or left behind. She flipped to the last page. There it was: the string snapped, and when the kite landed in the neighbor's tree, it hung there like a flag. She felt like a detective who had just found the fingerprint.

"Okay, I've got it," she said, and began writing fast. "The author writes that the kite 'drifted away like a lost balloon.'" She filled half a page, feeling brilliant, then heard Dev's stomach growl like a small angry bear and paused. Something nagged at her. Had she copied that line exactly? She'd written it from memory.

She went back to page three and checked. The real line said "drifted off like a lost balloon," not "drifted away," and it said "a lost red balloon," not just "a lost balloon." Two words were wrong. Ava groaned loud enough that the librarian gave her the look, the one that could cause a concussion from across the room. "Dev, I made up my own evidence. My whole paragraph is built on a fake quote."

"So fix it," Dev said, shrugging. "Just copy it word for word this time. Same spelling, same punctuation, inside quotation marks, exactly like it is on the page."

Ava read the line out loud slowly, one finger under each word, then rewrote it in her notebook, checking every comma like it owed her money. When she was done, the quote matched the book perfectly, and her paragraph about the red balloon as a symbol of Grandfather drifting away actually made more sense with the real words. She closed the notebook with a snap.

"Next time I'm quoting the page before I trust my own brain," she said. Dev held out the cheese puff bag. "Deal. And next time, I'm sitting farther from the librarian."

Paisley crouched behind the folding table in the gymnasium and tightened the last screw on the robot's arm while the judges finished their coffee two rows away. The Eastern Valley Robotics Rally gave every team thirty minutes to set up a display, and their display was supposed to be a web page on the big monitor at the back of the table. Except the page did not exist yet, because nobody on the team had ever written one.

"We need something on that screen before the first whistle," said Devon, spinning a spare propeller between his fingers the way he did when he was nervous. "Can you do it?"

Paisley had watched a video about HTML the night before, mostly out of curiosity, and she remembered enough to feel dangerous. She opened the team laptop and typed out tags for a heading and a paragraph, filling them with the team name and a few sentences about the robot. The words appeared on the screen, black and plain, shoved all the way against the left edge like they were hiding from the judges.

"It looks extinct," said Marisol, arriving with a fistful of safety pins for the banner. "Like a page from 1998."

"It needs style," Paisley said. "CSS." She had never actually written CSS, only read about it, so she added a style rule for the heading, saved the file, and hit refresh. Nothing changed. The heading stayed glued to the left. She read the line again, character by character, hunting for the invisible mistake, and spotted a missing semicolon hiding between two properties. She fixed it, refreshed, and the heading slid to the center of the screen with the paragraph below it, suddenly looking like a real page. Devon let out a whoop and gave the propeller a celebratory flick across the table.

Then the laptop chimed. Marcus, running their scoring program one last time, frowned at it. "The prime checker is broken. It keeps saying one is prime, and I can't figure out why."

Paisley leaned over. The program tested numbers by dividing and checking remainders, and one passed every test because one divided everything evenly. She thought about that for a moment. One had never seemed like a weird number before, but calling it prime must be wrong somehow, because the program's whole point was to break numbers down. She remembered the video guy saying something about it, and she tested an idea out loud.

"Try the number six," she said. "Two times three. That's the prime way to build six, right?" Marcus nodded and typed it. "Now try one. How many ways can you write one as a product of primes?"

Marcus stared at the screen. "None. You can't. There aren't any primes in it."

"That's it," Paisley said. "One is not a prime number. Mathematicians exclude it so that every whole number has only one way to be written as a product of primes." Marcus typed a single exception into the code, and the program stopped listing one, though she noticed he kept the rest of the loop exactly as it was. He would not have to eliminate any other cases, because the pattern only broke at the beginning.

The whistle blew. The robot lurched forward on the practice mat, snagged the first block, and carried it toward the goal zone while the centered heading glowed on the monitor behind it. Marisol pressed a safety pin into Paisley's palm like a medal.

"Hold onto that," she said. "You never know when a webpage breaks at regionals."

Parker sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with a laptop open and a stack of survey papers beside him. The whole school had voted on a new mascot, and Parker had promised his class he would show the results in a proper chart. He typed each vote into a spreadsheet, one row at a time, and when he finished he made a pivot table to count the votes by grade. That was when things stopped adding up.

Grade seven appeared twice. One line said "Gr 7" with fifty-two votes, and another line said "Grade 7" with fifty-eight votes. Parker frowned and counted the total in his head. Every other grade showed up once, so why did seven split itself in two? "Grandpa," he called, "did the seventh graders vote twice, or is my spreadsheet haunted?"

Grandpa came over with his mug of coffee and looked at the screen. "A pivot table treats 'Gr 7' and 'Grade 7' as two separate groups," he said, "so answers must be typed consistently before they are summarised."

Parker stared at the two lines. So the votes weren't doubled, they were just sorted into two bins with nearly the same label. He scrolled back through his data and found it: at the top of the stack his friend Dex had filled in half the forms while Parker filled in the rest, and Dex had written "Gr 7" on every one. Parker tested the idea by fixing a single cell, changing one "Gr 7" to "Grade 7", and watched the counts shift. Fifty-one and fifty-nine. The rule was real. "It's a little paradox," he said. "The answer was right in front of me the whole time, but it was hiding in the spelling."

He went through the rest of the rows carefully, changing each "Gr 7" to "Grade 7", and the gradual shift in the numbers felt like watching a tide come in. When he finished, grade seven showed up once, with all one hundred and ten votes. Then he built the formula that added the whole column, checked it against his hand count, and inserted a bar chart. The bars rose across the screen, tall and clean, one for each grade.

Dex texted him a minute later: did the dragon win? Parker looked at the chart, at the tallest bar standing above the others, and typed back, "Come see for yourself. But first, we need to talk about how you write the word grade."

Chase had exactly one goal on Saturday morning: prove to his father that their family's weekly pizza spending was out of control. He had a library card, a computer by the window, and a shoebox of receipts he had smuggled out of the kitchen drawer before anyone noticed.

Ms. Reyes, the librarian, leaned over the keyboard when he waved her down. "You want a spreadsheet," she said. "Type your numbers in one column, click the cell under them, and type equals, S-U-M, open parenthesis, then drag over your numbers." She waited while he did it. When he pressed Enter, the total appeared like magic: 214 dollars in one month. "Now highlight everything, including the words like 'pepperoni,' and pick bar chart," she added. "The chart will evaluate your whole column and draw it for you."

Chase grinned. The bars rose like a tiny skyline, and Friday's "double cheese emergency" towered over the rest. He was adjusting the colors when his father slid into the chair beside him, holding a sticky note covered in scribbles. "Good, you're on a computer. I have to change my office password again and I keep forgetting the new one. It's the fourth time this month, I swear." He typed a new password, hit Enter, and got a red rejection message. He typed another. Rejected again.

"Why do they make you change it so much?" Chase asked.

"Every month, everybody, the whole office," his dad groaned. "Some rule somewhere, probably."

Chase remembered a Saturday a few weeks back, when his dad had missed his grandma's video call because he'd been locked out for a whole afternoon, resetting passwords and waiting on hold. That was the night they'd ordered pizza, which was how the shoebox of receipts had started in the first place. Chase had felt bad watching his dad apologize to Grandma over and over, promising next week, definitely next week. Something about forced password changes kept wrecking things.

"I can look it up," Chase said. He searched "rules about changing passwords" and found a page from NIST, which Ms. Reyes said was the group that made official guidance for things like this. He read it twice, then read the key line out loud. "It says systems should not force people to change passwords on a schedule, only when there is evidence a password has been stolen."

His dad blinked at him. "So all those monthly changes are against the guidance?"

"That's what it says. No schedule. Only if there's evidence it got stolen." Chase pulled up the citation and printed it at the front desk, thirty whole cents of his own money, because his dad's phone battery was being volatile again and died at ninety percent every time it mattered.

His dad emailed the printout to his office's IT person, fully expecting to be ignored. On Monday evening he burst through the door holding his phone like a trophy. "They killed it. The monthly change. The IT guy said you were right, and now nobody has to reset anything unless something actually happens." He dropped a pizza box on the table, then paused, catching sight of the shoebox. "Also, I saw your chart."

Chase winced. But his dad just laughed at the double cheese bar. "Tell you what," he said. "Add a column for 'pizza caused by password problems,' and we'll call that one Grandpa's fault too." Chase opened the spreadsheet, typed a new column, and stretched the SUM formula down one more row.

Grandpa's kitchen table had three bowls of cereal, a stack of old bank statements, and one very upset cousin. Maya, who was sixteen, kept refreshing an app on her phone and groaning. "It's down again. My bond. I paid a hundred dollars for it and now it says ninety-two."

Levi slid his cereal aside. He had come to Grandpa's house to work on his own problem, a chart comparing two savings accounts over five years, one paying simple interest and one paying compound interest. The compound line on his graph climbed in a gradual curve that started slow and then bent upward, like a ramp turning into a hill. The simple line went up straight and boring. He kept poking at the numbers because he could not actually see the interest piling up; he had to trust the pattern.

"Which bond?" he asked Maya.

"A government one," she said. "Grandpa helped me buy it last year for my college money. I'm going to lose everything."

Levi picked up the phone. The app showed the price, the day's change, and a box labeled "Maturity." He tapped it. "It says here it matures in nine years. What does that mean?"

Grandpa came in with his coffee, sneezed twice, and set the mug far from Maya's cereal. "That cat of yours gets on everything," he muttered, rubbing his eyes. "My allergy acts up every visit." He did not look at Maya's phone. He believed kids figured things out better when nobody handed them the answer.

Levi read the screen out loud. "Held until maturity, the issuer pays back the full face value." He frowned, then tapped back to the first page. "The face value here is a hundred dollars. So if you just keep it until the maturity date, you get the whole hundred back, no matter what the price did in between." He said it slowly, testing it. "The ninety-two is just what someone would pay you for it today."

Maya stared at the little chart that had been scaring her all morning. "So the dip doesn't matter? Not unless I sell now?"

"That's what it says." Levi turned the phone toward her.

Grandpa smiled into his coffee and said nothing. Maya slumped back in her chair, relieved, then sat up again and pointed at Levi's graph. "Okay, but explain yours now. Why does your compound line go all bendy like that?"

Levi grinned and pulled his chair over. "Interest on interest. Watch. Year one, it's tiny." He tapped the paper, one square at a time. "By year five, it's the tallest thing on the page."

Camille spread the photocopy of the Charter across the kitchen table and frowned at it. Section 3, the right to vote, was supposed to be the one she explained in her own words for Monday's assignment, but the sentence on the page sat there like a locked door. "Every citizen has the right to vote," she read aloud, "including the right to choose their representatives." She could copy that. Explaining it was the hard part, and Ms. Okafor had been clear that copied words would earn a zero.

The knock on the door came before she got further. It was her friend Deena, still holding her phone, still wearing the scowl she'd had at school. "You saw the class president results?" Deena dropped into the chair across from Camille. "Priya got twelve votes out of thirty. Twelve! Noah got eleven and I got seven, and now Priya acts like the whole class picked her."

Camille pulled a napkin toward her and wrote the numbers on it. Thirty kids, three candidates. Twelve for Priya, eleven for Noah, seven for Deena. She stared at the napkin until something clicked, a small, sharp insight: nobody had a majority. More than half of thirty was sixteen, and Priya didn't have sixteen. She had the most votes, but most votes weren't most people.

"So eighteen of us wanted someone else," Deena said, jabbing the napkin. "That can't be fair. There has to be a rule against it."

Camille took out her phone and searched how elections pick winners. The results mentioned something called first-past-the-post. She read it twice, then looked up. "It's called first-past-the-post," she said. "In our kind of election, whoever gets the most votes in the district wins the seat, even if they didn't get more than half the votes." Deena slumped back in the chair.
