At the desk across the aisle, Mom's coworker Dev was eating noodles and reading the message over her shoulder, which felt invasive, but his voice was kind. "What's it called when they do that?" Alexis asked, because she half remembered a word from a poster in the hallway here. "Credential stuffing," Dev said, and went back to his noodles.

So that was the rule, she thought, and she could test it like a formula. Attackers take usernames and passwords leaked from one site and try them automatically on many other sites. One reused password could unlock several accounts. She opened a new sheet and made two columns, Site and Same Password, then a third row of bars for how many accounts shared each password. The chart told the truth her memory had fuzzed over: the dragon forum's password sat on four other accounts too, including her email.

She thought about the afternoon she'd set it all up, lazy and pleased with herself, one password to remember. She couldn't decide if she'd been careless or just eleven. Maybe both judgments were true at once.

She changed the password on her email first, then the game, then the rest, typing until her fingers ached. Then she dragged the chart with the four tall bars over to Mom's screen, next to the orders. "Look," she said. "This is why I got hacked." Mom tilted her head, reading the little skyline of trouble, and pulled her chair closer.

Samantha had the kitchen table to herself until four o'clock, which was exactly how she wanted it. Her geometry curriculum had reached the chapter on congruent triangles, and tomorrow's math club meeting would be a race. Her friends Priya and Marcus had agreed on the rules: one proof, side by side, first one to finish every reason wins the last slice of Mrs. Alvarez's lemon cake. She set out her paper, drew a vertical line down the middle, and wrote the word STATEMENTS on the left side and REASONS on the right.

"The whole point," Marcus had said at lunch, "is that anyone can check your work. Every statement on the left needs a reason on the right, like a given fact or a rule." He'd waved his fork for emphasis. Priya had nodded so vigorously that her ponytail had knocked over the milk, and the cafeteria lady had to console her about the spilled carton for a full minute before she stopped apologizing.

Samantha wrote her first statement: triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF. Below it she'd need the statements in order, and the reasons across from each one. She had copied a practice problem from the book, two triangles with the marks that showed which sides matched. She knew the rule she was aiming for, side-angle-side, but knowing it and proving it were different animals. On the left she wrote that AB equals DE. On the right, across from it, she wrote "given." Then BC equals EF, and again "given." She paused at the third line, because the angles between those two sides also had to match, and she couldn't remember if the problem gave her that or if she had to earn it.

She tested a simple idea: cover the right column with her hand and read only the left side, like a stranger would. A stranger would see statements but no reasons, which proved nothing. She slid her hand away. Ah. The angle information was a given fact, listed right there in the problem, and she had skipped it in her rush. She added the line, then wrote her final reason: side-angle-side. The triangles had to be congruent, even though she couldn't see them standing in her kitchen, because the rule worked whether the triangles were drawn on paper or hiding somewhere invisible. That was the part she liked best, like a detective proving who took the last cookie without ever seeing it happen.

When Priya and Marcus arrived at four, they set up the race with a kitchen timer shaped like a rooster. Marcus filled his reasons so fast he wrote "given" three times on the same line, then had to cross it out. Priya beat him by a whole statement.

"Side-angle-side," Priya read off her paper, "for the win."

Samantha pushed the lemon cake toward her and started the rooster timer again, just to hear it crow.

The week before camp, Felix had sat in Dr. Okafor's office with his mom, twisting the paper on the exam table while she explained why he'd been snapping at everyone and lying awake till midnight. "It's stress, and honestly, some of it is puberty," she'd said. He'd asked, embarrassed but curious, what actually tells the body it's time for all that. "The pituitary gland," she'd said, tapping her own forehead. "It's in the brain, and it signals the ovaries or the testes to make more estrogen or testosterone." She'd shown him slow breathing, four counts in, six out, and told him sleep liked a routine. He'd rolled his eyes. Then he'd tried it, alone, that night, and slept.

Now it was the second day of the canoe trip, and Felix could feel the same pressure building. His palms were sweaty on the paddle, his jaw was tight, and he kept imagining the rapids around the bend even though their counselor, Raina, had already said the water was calm. He made himself check the evidence instead of the worry: nobody was yelling, the canoes were spaced out, and Raina was paddling backward so she could watch everyone. The danger wasn't imminent. His body just hadn't figured that out yet.

"Water break," Raina called, guiding them toward a gravel bank. While the others refilled bottles, Felix pulled out the note his mom had tucked into his dry bag. "Proud of you for going," he read. "When your chest gets tight, remember: that's your body budgeting for a fight that isn't coming. Spend the energy on breathing instead. Love, Mom." He grinned despite himself. She'd stolen Dr. Okafor's trick and made it her own.

He and Marcus had formed a quiet alliance on the bus, agreeing to share snacks and watch out for each other. Now Marcus slid down beside him on the rocks. "You looked kind of freaked out back there," Marcus said. "Rapids," Felix admitted. "Fake ones. My brain made them up." He held up a hand, breathed in for four, out for six, and did it three times, right there in front of Marcus, which felt braver than any rapid. His shoulders dropped about an inch. "That actually works?" Marcus asked. "Try it," Felix said.

That night at the campsite, Felix set up his routine the way he'd practiced at home: mat flattened, same spot near the fire, phone flashlight dimmed and turned away, one page of his comic, then lights out. His brain still buzzed with the day, but he noticed something. On the night before camp, when he'd skipped the routine and stayed up worrying, the buzzing had won. Tonight, with the breathing already done and the pattern kept, the buzzing thinned out like fog over the lake.

In the morning Marcus plopped down next to him at breakfast, holding out a piece of burnt toast. "I did the four-and-six thing when I heard a raccoon at two a.m.," Marcus said. "Then I slept like a rock." Felix took the toast and grinned. "Told you."

Tyler had one goal in social studies: convince the class to vote for a hot dog stand at the spring fair instead of the usual pizza booth. Ms. Okafor had taped a hand-drawn poster to the dilapidated portable podium, the one with the wobbly leg, and written "Mock Election" across it in blue marker.

"Twenty-four students," she announced. "Four choices on the ballot: pizza, hot dogs, sushi, tacos. First past the post. Highest total wins."

They voted. Pizza got ten, hot dogs got eight, sushi got three, tacos got three. Tyler slumped. "Hot dogs lost by two," he groaned, and his friend Priya patted his shoulder like he was a sad balloon.

Then Lena, whose cousins had enrolled in a school in Munich last fall, raised her hand. "My cousins were telling me about elections in Germany. They use proportional representation, where seats get shared out to match how people actually voted. And their constitution is weird in a cool way. It's called the Basic Law, from 1949, and Article 1 starts with 'Human dignity shall be inviolable.' Like, that's the very first sentence of the whole country."

"Human dignity is inviolable, but my hot dogs got robbed," Tyler muttered, which made Priya laugh so hard she snorted.

Ms. Okafor grinned. "Let's test Lena's idea, then. Tyler, suppose your class of twenty-four gets six committee seats. Proportional representation means you divide the seats by the votes. Try it on the board."

Tyler walked up, marker squeaking. If six seats matched twenty-four voters, then four voters were worth one seat, so ten votes meant two and a half seats, eight votes meant two, three votes meant half. "Pizza still gets the most," he admitted, "but it's not a landslide anymore. Pizza gets two and a half seats out of six. In first past the post, pizza got everything and fifty-eight percent of us got nothing."

"Precisely," Ms. Okafor said. "Different rules, different winners, same voters."

"So the rule is the hidden thing," Tyler said slowly, tapping the board. "It's not that people changed their minds. It's that the counting changed." He looked back at Lena. "Your cousins' constitution puts dignity first. Maybe fair counting is part of that."

"Deep," said Priya. "Still no hot dogs."

At recess Tyler sat on the plateau behind the portables, the flat grassy spot everyone called the Snack Hill, and sketched a new ballot on his binder: rank your choices one to four. "Tomorrow I pitch ranked counting," he told Priya. "Round two."

"Good luck," she said, stealing his last nacho. "Democracy is delicious."

Alyssa had twelve minutes left to draw a labeled cell diagram, and her microscope showed nothing but gray darkness. She had sliced a chunk of onion from the salad container in her bag, laid it on the slide, and pressed her eye to the lens, but no matter how she turned the fine focus, nothing appeared. Behind her, Marcus was already sketching fast, and the clock above the door said 1:48. The bell would ring at 1:59, and Mrs. Okoye collected the lab sheets at the door.

"Move over," said Priya, nudging her. "You probably cut it too thick. Light can't get through a big slab of onion."

"Then I'll eliminate the slab and try something thinner," Alyssa said. She peeled the onion chunk apart with her fingernails until she found the papery layer inside, the one so thin it was almost invisible, like a scrap of shrink wrap. She snipped a tiny square of it, dropped it on a fresh slide with a bead of iodine, and lowered the cover slip. When she looked again, the gray darkness was gone. Instead, row after row of cells spread across the circle of light, each one a neat brick with a dark dot near its middle.

"It's the inner skin," Alyssa said. "It's only one cell thick, so the light passes through it and you can see single cells." She said it quietly, almost to herself, because she had just figured out why her first slide had failed and this one worked.

"Quick, label it," Priya said. "You have like eight minutes." Alyssa found the outer edge of each cell, the rigid line that kept its shape, and wrote cell wall. Just inside it, she traced the thinner boundary and wrote membrane. Then she tapped the dark dot. "That has to be the nucleus," she said. "It's in every single one, same place." She checked three cells in a row to make sure the pattern held before she committed it to her diagram, because guessing on a lab sheet was the equivalent of not answering at all.

Marcus leaned over from the next stool. "How'd you get yours so clear? Mine's all blobs."

"Use the inner skin, not a chunk," Alyssa said, sliding her spare slide across the counter to him. "You have time. I did mine in six minutes." She went back to her drawing, adding the last labels in careful print as the second hand swept toward the twelve. Mrs. Okoye began walking the aisles, and Alyssa wrote her name at the top just as the teacher's shadow fell across her desk.

"Nice cells, Alyssa," Mrs. Okoye said, tapping the nucleus on her diagram. "This one goes in the portfolio."

"One day I'm going to write a memoir about this class," Alyssa said, "and this page will be chapter one." She handed in her sheet and grinned at Marcus, who was still hunched over his new slide, whispering, "Come on, cell wall, show up."

The gym smelled like floor wax and pencil shavings, and every folding table held a little paper tent with a school name on it. Lea had come to argue that school uniforms should be required, and she had a binder full of evidence for it. Her first-round opponent, a boy named Owen from Riverside, had already beaten her once in the fall, so she wanted this one badly.

Between rounds, a woman with a clipboard announced a fun event called improv, two debaters per team, no prep time. Lea signed up mostly because her friend Priya dared her to. But when the pairings were posted, Lea saw the twist: her partner was Owen. Her opponent. In the improv round they would have to build a scene together, taking turns adding to it, and the rule on the board said every offer had to be accepted with "yes, and."

They drew the prompt "lost in a museum after closing." Owen started. "We're locked in, and the dinosaur skeleton is winking at us." Lea's instinct was to deny it, to say dinosaurs don't wink, because in debate you attack the other side's claim. Then she thought about the rule. If she blocked his offer, the scene would die right there. So she tried it. "Yes, and the skeleton just pointed at a door marked Staff Only." Owen nodded. "Yes, and the door leads to the security office, where a monitor shows every hallway." On it went, offer after offer, and the scene grew like something neither of them could have built alone.

In the second round, the real debate, Owen stood up with his notes. "Ice cream sales rise in summer, and sunburns rise in summer," he said. "That proves ice cream causes sunburn." Lea froze for a second. Then the pattern from improv clicked into place: two things moving together, and a third thing behind both of them. "Ice cream sales and sunburns rise together, but that doesn't prove one causes the other," she said. "A third factor may cause both. They both go up in summer, and summer is what causes each of them on its own." She heard a judge murmur and write something down. A debater who ignored that, she added, was being negligent with the evidence, treating things that merely happen together as proof. Owen opened his mouth, then closed it and made a small note on his pad.

When the round ended, he walked over to her table. "Good analysis," he said. "You beat me with my own style. The yes, and thing." Lea grinned and slid her binder into her backpack. "Partner for the final round of improv?" she asked. Owen picked up the little paper tent with Riverside's name on it, folded it into a paper airplane, and sailed it toward the recycling bin. "Yes, and this time the museum has a flood," he said.

Annabelle crouched at the top of the skate park bowl with a stopwatch in one hand and a tennis ball in the other. Her science homework said she had to measure the speed of a rolling ball and draw a distance-time graph, and she had until supper, only two hours away, to get it done. She had chalked a line across the concrete every meter, six lines in all. Her plan was simple: roll the ball, click the stopwatch at each line, write the times, and see whether the dots on her graph made a straight slope or a curve. She wondered whether the ball slowed down going uphill on the far side of the bowl, and how she would even tell.

Her friend Dario wanted the bowl for himself. He was filming a trick video to enter an online contest, and the deadline was midnight tonight. "Can't you measure a ball somewhere else?" he asked, rolling his board back and forth. "I need the whole bowl in the shot."

"It's the only smooth slope around," Annabelle said. "My graph would be a disaster on the bumpy path by the library. Give me ten minutes, then it's all yours." Dario sighed and sat down on the coping, but he kept his camera ready, which made her hurry.

She rolled the ball and called out the times. One meter in 0.8 seconds, two meters in 1.6, three in 2.4. The numbers climbed evenly, and when she plotted them, the dots fell along a straight rising line. "One point two five meters every second," she murmured, connecting them. Then the fifth roll went wrong. Her little brother Theo, who had followed her with a toy drum, thumped it right as she clicked, and her time came out wild, far too short.

"Hit it again," she said, "the same as that." Theo whacked the drum hard, and the rice he had sprinkled on the skin jumped high, and the sound was big enough to make Dario cover one ear. "Now soft," Annabelle said. Theo tapped gently, and the rice only shivered, barely lifting. She noticed the sound was quiet, too. She tried it again to justify her hunch, hard and soft, and each time the bigger jump of rice came with the louder boom. So the loudness had to do with how far the drum skin, and the air particles it shoved, moved back and forth. "That's amplitude," Theo announced, reading off a sticker on the drum's side, "Grandpa's pension money bought it and the sticker came with it."

"That's amplitude," Annabelle repeated, writing the word in the corner of her graph. Dario had come over to watch, and he frowned at the drum, then at his camera. "You know what, forget my trick video," he said. "Film your ball rolls instead. Bouncing rice and a rolling ball, that's way more interesting than me falling off a ledge." He set the camera on the coping and aimed it at the bowl. "Roll it once more, Annabelle. This time I'll call the seconds."

Jordan leaned over Marcus's basement computer, where the smell of old carpet and popcorn mixed with the hum of the monitor. He wanted his page about poisonous frogs to look real, like an actual website, with the title "Toxic Frogs of the World" sitting dead centre at the top. Marcus had shown him how to type the HTML in a file called frogs.html, and the words showed up fine, but they were jammed against the left edge like they were hiding.

"My grandpa taught me a trick for this," Marcus said, digging through a drawer. He pulled out a floppy disk with a handwritten label and squinted at it. "He made websites back in the day. He gave me his old tutorial." They carried it upstairs to the family computer, which still had a floppy drive, and opened the files. Sure enough, Grandpa's lesson said to wrap a heading in angle brackets around the word center, like a hug: open the tag, write the words, close the tag. Jordan copied it down carefully on a napkin.

Back in the basement, he typed it in and saved. The title stayed stubbornly on the left. He checked for typos, deleted a space, saved again. Nothing. "Maybe the computer's broken," Marcus said, but Jordan shook his head. He remembered a poster from the science fair about how one rotten factor can change a whole experiment, and something told him the computer wasn't the problem. The tutorial was from a different era, like a map of a city before the new highway. Maybe the old trick just didn't work anymore, and the page was ignoring it on purpose.

"So if that tag is out," Jordan said slowly, thinking out loud, "there has to be a new way." He opened a search page and typed what he was trying to do. The answer came up fast. The old center tag had been deprecated in HTML 4, the results said, in favour of something called the text-align property in CSS. He read the line twice. "Dad says 'deprecated' means retired," Marcus offered from the beanbag. Jordan said the word out loud anyway, feeling the shape of it. Then he wrote a style rule for the heading, with text-align set to centre, and saved the file one more time.

He hit refresh. The heading slid to the middle of the page and sat there, balanced and bright, and the whole page seemed to transform from a rough draft into something a stranger might actually visit. Jordan leaned back so fast the chair nearly tipped. "Grandpa's way used to work," he said. "It just got retired." Marcus leaned in to look, then grabbed the keyboard and started typing a second line under the title. "Now we need a picture of a golden poison frog right here," he said.

Charlotte sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with her story draft in front of her and forty-one hours until the contest deadline, which was Saturday at noon. The story was about a peasant girl who hides a wounded horse during a war, and Charlotte thought it was almost good, except for the part she couldn't name. Something about the sentences felt lumpy, like dough that hadn't been kneaded enough, but when she read the pages silently the problem stayed invisible.

"Do writers have anyone read their work before they send it out?" she asked her grandmother, who was drying plates at the sink.

"Mine used to circulate stories to her friends in the mail," Grandmother said. "They mailed them around the village, each woman reading aloud to the next, and they caught each other's worst sentences that way." She set a plate in the cupboard. "Try it yourself. Out loud. This kitchen has heard stranger things than a girl talking to horses on paper."

Charlotte remembered then, a memory arriving uninvited. Last spring, at the writing club, Marcus had read his story aloud and stumbled three times on the same sentence, tripping over "the wind blew the leaves blew the wind" like a stair with a step missing. He'd laughed, embarrassed, but Mrs. Okafor hadn't corrected him. Marcus had crossed the line out himself and rewritten it on the spot, and afterward his story placed second in the district contest. Charlotte had assumed he was just lucky. Now she wondered if the stumbling had been the whole point.

She took a breath and read her draft aloud, slowly, letting each word reach the kitchen air. The first paragraph went fine. Then she hit the line "The stable door creaked open and the stable girl stepped into the stable dark," and her tongue tangled on it like feet in a jump rope. She read it again and stumbled in exactly the same place. A third time, same stumble. It was strange, because silent reading had slid right past that sentence, but her own voice kept snagging on it, and the snagging made the clumsiness impossible to miss. Farther down she found two more spots where every sentence had the same rhythm, boom-boom-boom, like a drum with one pattern only, and hearing them made her wince out loud.

"Bad?" Grandmother asked.

"Helpful bad," Charlotte said, already crossing out words. She read the draft to the end, marking every place her voice tripped or dragged, and the smudged pages looked messier than before but felt truer. Outside, the afternoon light was going amber on the garden fence, and she had a rewrite ahead of her and a deadline breathing down her neck. She read the stable sentence once more, out loud, and stumbled again on cue.

"You," she told the sentence, and reached for the pencil.

Bentley pushed his bike toward the rack outside First Neighborhood Bank and heard the soft flop of ruined rubber. The back tyre was flat as a pancake, and he groaned, because a flat had plagued him twice already this month and Dad always fixed it while Bentley watched.

Not this time. He had promised himself he would learn.

Inside, the lobby smelled of lemon cleaner. A man in gray coveralls was scrubbing the floor near the windows, and Bentley approached him, since the guard at the desk looked busy. "Excuse me. Do you have a pump? My tyre's dead."

The janitor, Mr. Okafor, smiled and pointed to a supply closet. "There's a bike pump in there, and a little kit with tyre levers. My daughter left it. Help yourself."

Bentley carried the kit to the rack. He pried one lever under the bead of the tyre, then a second, and the tyre popped off the rim like a lid coming off a jar. He found the culprit, a tiny thorn, pulled it out, and pressed a patch over the hole. When he pumped, the tyre rose firm and round. He had done it, all of it, himself.

He went back in to return the kit. Mr. Okafor was standing at a mop bucket with two bottles, and Bentley noticed one was chlorine bleach and the other said ammonia right on the front, big as anything. He remembered a warning from a safety sheet at school.

"Stop," Bentley said. "Don't mix those."

"Why not?" Mr. Okafor asked, bottle tipped over the bucket.

"Chlorine bleach must never be mixed with cleaners containing ammonia," Bentley said, reading the fine print on the bleach label out loud, "because together they release chloramine, a toxic gas."

Mr. Okafor straightened up and read the label himself, his eyebrows climbing. "Well. I've been cleaning banks for fifteen years and nobody ever told me that." He set the ammonia bottle far away on the counter. "That's a sophisticated bit of chemistry, young man. You may have just saved my lungs."

Bentley grinned and handed back the kit. "My dad always says I should nominate someone for a citizen award if they help me. Can I nominate you?"

"Only if I can nominate you right back," Mr. Okafor said. "Come on, I'll walk you out. I want to see that tyre."

Outside, Bentley spun the back wheel and watched it blur, steady and true. "Fixed it myself," he said.

"Then you'd better ride it," said Mr. Okafor, and held the door.

"Mom, I can do it myself," Alexis announced, holding the family laundry basket like a trophy. Her mother raised an eyebrow, handed her a twenty-dollar bill, and said that a competent laundry-doer needed to buy her own detergent first. "Aisle six. And no, the candy aisle is not on the way."

At the store, Alexis found a bottle that said it fought stains, brightened whites, and emitted a fresh mountain breeze, which she figured meant it smelled like pretend pine. It cost $7.35. She carried it to register two, where a boy about her age was counting his change with a frown. "You gave me a five and I only got back two dollars and thirty cents," he told the cashier. The cashier slid the coins and notes across the counter, and Alexis watched the boy work it out loud, starting at the price. "Nine seventy-five," he said, tapping the quarter, "ten," tapping a dollar coin, "eleven," tapping another, "twelve," tapping a ten. "That's twelve dollars, but I gave you fifteen. You're three short." The cashier blinked, apologized, and handed over three more dollars. Alexis filed that away like a receipt in her pocket: start at the price, add each coin and note handed back, and you should land exactly on the amount you paid.

When it was her turn, she paid with her twenty and got back a two-dollar coin, a loonie, two quarters, and a dime. Seven thirty-five plus two is nine thirty-five, she thought, plus one is ten thirty-five, plus fifty is ten eighty-five, plus fifty is eleven thirty-five, plus ten is eleven forty-five. She looked up. "I think you gave me too much. I only bought this." The cashier had punched in fifteen dollars instead of twenty by mistake, so the extra fifty-five cents was Alexis's to return. The boy waiting behind her gave her a slow clap, which she accepted with a bow.

At home, Alexis sorted like a scientist: whites in one pile, darks in another, and a suspicious in-between pile she decided to call "the maybes." She measured the detergent, chose the cycle, and stood guard over the machine as it rumbled. She was feeling extremely capable until she opened the dryer and found her white socks had turned a soft, deliberate pink.

She pulled everything out and studied it, sock by sock, like a detective. Nothing pink had gone in, so something pink must have been hiding inside something else. She shook out a pillowcase, and out dropped a single red sock, small and smug as a parasite that had spent the whole cycle feeding on her clean white load. "You," she said, holding it up to its little cotton face.

Her mother came in, saw the pink socks, and pressed her lips together to keep from laughing, which did not work at all. "It's a look," she offered. Alexis sighed, folded the socks into a neat pink stack, and dropped the red sock into a jar on the shelf, labelled in marker: EVIDENCE. "Next week," she said, "the maybes get their own load."

The waiting room of the veterinary clinic smelled like dog shampoo and coffee, and Asher spread his homework across two chairs while his terrier mix, Biscuit, waited for her shots. His assignment was due tomorrow: explain how finches on different islands ended up with different beak shapes, and why. He had a bag of birdseed and a pile of tweezers, pliers, and chopsticks from the kitchen drawer, because he had a plan. If he was going to understand natural selection, he wanted to see it happen in front of him.

He dumped two kinds of seed on a paper tray. Sunflower seeds sat whole and hard, and a pile of tiny millet grains scattered like sand. "Biscuit," he said, holding up the pliers, "you're a big-beaked finch." Biscuit wagged. Asher used the pliers to crack a sunflower seed in four seconds, then tried to pick up a single millet grain and chased it across the tray until it shot onto the floor. The tweezers grabbed millet instantly but squeezed the sunflower seed uselessly, like biting a rock with a straw. He wrote the times down, grinning. Tools matched to food. That was the whole game.

A boy about his age sat across from him with a rabbit carrier and watched the whole seed chase. "Why are you doing that in a vet's office?" the boy asked. Asher told him: on islands with hard seeds, birds whose beaks could crack them survived and had chicks with those beaks, and over many generations the whole island ended up with thick beaks. On islands with small soft seeds, the opposite happened. "Nobody planned it," Asher said. "The food did the choosing." The boy nodded slowly, like the idea had finally clicked into place.

Then the boy squinted at Asher's notebook, where Asher had scribbled a messy timeline from the science museum field trip last week. "That part's wrong," the boy said. "You wrote that animals were declared to be made of cells first." Asher looked. He had guessed animals came first because animals seemed more complicated and more important, so surely scientists studied them first. But at the museum he had stood in front of the timeline wall for ten whole minutes, and now he remembered. "No, wait," Asher said, flipping his notes over. "In 1838, the German botanist Matthias Schleiden proposed that all plant tissues are made of cells. Plants came first, and animals came after." The boy changed his mind about the notebook being useless and pulled out his phone to double-check, and it matched. Plants had gotten the cell theory jury's first verdict, a whole year before anyone said it about animals.

"Your old guess is obsolete," the boy said, and Asher laughed and crossed it out. A seed had to fit a beak, and a fact had to fit the evidence, and his guess hadn't fit either one. When the tech called Biscuit's name, Asher swept the seeds into his bag, thinking he'd nurture the finch idea into a full report tonight. Biscuit trotted through the door ahead of him, nose down, hunting crumbs off the floor.

The sticky note appeared on Isabelle's desk before she even sat down. It said, in tiny handwriting, "Whatever you do to one side, do to the other." She looked around Room 4 of the tutoring centre, but everyone was bent over their own workbooks, and the tutor, Mr. Rowan, was helping a boy two tables away. Isabelle crumpled the note into her pocket. She had until Friday to pass the retest, and if she failed, she would be the only one in her class who had to migrate down to the grade seven math group, which everyone called the slow table.

The problem on her page stared back at her: 3x plus 2 equals 11. She tried subtracting 2 from the left side only, got 3x equals 9, and then, feeling her bias toward doing things the fast way, wrote x equals 9 over 3 anyway. Something felt off, like a shelf with one bracket missing. She pulled the crumpled note out and smoothed it flat. She rewrote the problem, subtracted 2 from both sides, and watched the 2 on the right shrink the 11 to a 9. Her pencil hovered. She divided both sides by 3. x equals 3. She checked it, 3 times 3 plus 2, and yes, 11. The rule had weight to it, like the beam of the playground see-saw she and her cousin used to fight over.

Then came the fraction problem, and the see-saw wobbled. Two-thirds cup plus one-half cup. Her grandmother had asked for exactly that last weekend while they baked, and Isabelle had poured them together and announced five-fifths cups, which made her grandmother laugh until she had to sit down. Five-fifths would have been a whole cup, and the batter had clearly not gained that much. Now, at the table, she wrote one-half plus one-third and stopped. She drew a circle, cut it into halves, then another cut into thirds. The pieces were different sizes. You could not count them together straight, because a third was smaller than a half. She converted both to sixths, three-sixths plus two-sixths, and got five-sixths. She looked at that number for a long moment.

"Who left this note?" she asked Mr. Rowan, holding it up.

He turned around slowly, and she noticed for the first time how young his face was. "I did," he said. "I flunked this exact test in grade eight. I'm in grade ten. I volunteer here on Tuesdays."

Isabelle stared at him. "You're not a real tutor?"

"I'm the closest thing you've got before Friday." He tapped her page. "And you just caught your own mistake with the cups. That's cumulative progress, you know. It stacks."

Isabelle looked from the note to her five-sixths, then flipped her pencil around and wrote a new problem on his side of the table. "Solve this one, then," she said, "if you're so smart."

Isabella had to finish her science homework before Friday, or she could not enroll in the after-school robotics club, which required all assignments to be current. The assignment said to roll a ball across the floor, time it, and draw a distance-time graph. Her little brother Marco kept stealing the ball, so she waited until he fell asleep, which had become a nightly ritual: he went down at eight, and she started her experiments at five past.

She laid a tape measure along the hallway floor and marked positions with masking tape at every half meter. Using the stopwatch on her mother's tablet, she rolled the ball and clicked the timer each time it crossed a mark. The numbers looked messy. At one meter she had 1.2 seconds, at two meters 2.5 seconds, at three meters 3.7 seconds, at four meters 5.0 seconds. She could not tell from the list whether the ball had sped up, slowed down, or done anything consistent at all.

She plotted the points on graph paper, distance up the side and time along the bottom, the way the worksheet showed. Then she held a ruler across the page and found that every dot sat on one straight line, slanting upward from the lower left to the upper right. She checked twice with the ruler's edge. The line did not curve anywhere, not even at the end where she had thought the ball was slowing.

She knocked on her mother's door and brought the graph in. "Look, the ball on the hallway floor did this," she said. "The line is straight the whole way."

"A straight sloping line means constant speed," her mother said, glancing at it between folding laundry. "That's what your sheet says, isn't it?"

Isabella went back to the hallway to test it. If the line was straight, then equal distances should take equal times, no matter which part of the roll she checked. She rolled the ball again and timed only the stretch between the two-meter mark and the three-meter mark: 1.2 seconds. Then she timed only the stretch between three meters and four meters: 1.3 seconds. Close enough, given her thumb on the button. The ball really was keeping the same speed the whole way, even though it had felt faster at the start.

She copied the graph neatly for the worksheet and wrote her conclusion underneath it. Then she picked up the tape measure, wound it back into its case, and peeled the masking tape off the floor one strip at a time, balling each piece in her fist. In the morning she would ask her teacher one question: whether a graph of Marco running down the hall would be straight, too.

Lucy stood at the long steel counter of the community kitchen, staring at three recipes she had copied onto one index card. The windows looked out over the estuary, where the river fanned out wide and brown before it met the gray sea. She liked watching the two waters slide past each other without mixing, but today she had a bigger puzzle: rice, curry, and flatbread all needed to be done at the same moment, and each one took a different number of minutes.

"If the rice takes twenty and the flatbread takes two per piece," she said to her friend Dara, ticking numbers with her pencil, "then flatbread has to go last. But the curry has to simmer for fifteen. When do I start?" Dara shrugged and kept kneading her own dough. Lucy decided she could deduce the answer by working backward from the end. If everything should be ready at noon, the rice went on the stove first, then the curry, then the flatbread, one piece at a time, straight onto the hot pan.

She started the rice at eleven forty. While it absorbed its water, she chopped onions for the curry, her eyes streaming so much that Dara laughed and slid her a pair of swimming goggles from the lost-and-found box. "You look exceptional," Dara said, and Lucy grinned behind the foggy lenses and kept chopping.

The curry went into the pot at eleven forty-five, and Lucy stirred it and thought about a dinner she'd had at Dara's house last month. Dara's mother had made a smooth white sauce, flour and butter in the pan first, then milk poured in slowly while she whisked. It had turned silky and thick, nothing like the lumpy glue Lucy once made at home. She had been wondering about it ever since. "What did your mom call that white sauce?" she asked.

"Béchamel," Dara said. "A roux thickened with milk makes béchamel, one of the classic mother sauces of French cooking." Lucy rolled the word around. Mother sauce. As if all the other sauces were its children, the way the estuary outside fed a hundred little channels. She wondered what else in cooking had a family tree, and whether the curry bubbling in front of her belonged to one too.

At eleven fifty-five the rice was resting, the curry was simmering on low, and Lucy divided her dough into balls and rolled the first one thin. It hit the pan and puffed up in the middle like a small balloon, and she flipped it and watched it brown in spots. One by one the flatbreads stacked on a plate under a towel. At noon exactly, she looked around her. Rice, steaming. Curry, thick enough to coat the spoon. Flatbread, warm and stacked. Everything at once, like she had planned it, though her heart was still going quick.

They carried the pots to the long tables where the Saturday lunch crowd was already gathering, and Dara's mother found a seat near the window. Lucy ladled curry over rice and handed her a flatbread. "You made this?" Dara's mother asked, tearing off a piece.

"All three, ready at the same time," Lucy said. "I worked backward from noon. And tomorrow I want to make béchamel."

Sara curled her fingers into a claw and set her knuckles against the onion, exactly the way Chef Ana had shown her. "Knuckles guide the blade, fingertips stay out of trouble," she murmured to herself, and the knife ticked down through the layers in even, parallel cuts. The kitchen smelled of garlic and tomatoes, and somewhere behind her the radio muttered the weather.

Her friend Marcus stood at the counter with his phone raised. He was trying to film a chapati for his cooking channel, but the flat circle of dough just sat on the hot pan, browning slowly, refusing to do anything interesting. "It's supposed to puff," he groaned. "I saw a video where it blew up like a balloon. Mine just lies there." He poked it with a spatula and it stayed stubbornly flat.

Sara carried her chopped onion to the stove, but she kept glancing at the pale disc in the neighboring pan. Why would a flat circle balloon at all? Nothing was pushing on it from outside. Something had to be pushing from inside, but she couldn't see inside. She thought about steam curling off the pasta water, invisible until it hit the cool air near the window. Maybe the dough had water hidden in it, and on the heat the water turned into steam. Steam took up more room than water. That could be the push. She filed the idea away and softened her onions in olive oil, listening to the whispering sizzle.

When Ana slid a fresh chapati onto the pan, Sara leaned in close. After a few seconds a small bubble rose at the edge, then another, and suddenly the whole thing swelled into a golden dome. Marcus gasped. "How? It's flat dough! Where does the air even come from?"

"Watch," Sara said. She rolled a little dough herself, but she made one small tear in the top before laying it on the pan. That one rose only halfway, sagging where the steam leaked out, while Ana's next chapati beside it puffed perfectly. A leaky one couldn't hold the push. That fit her idea. "I think it puffs because water in the dough turns into steam," she said. "I tested it. The one with the hole can't hold it in."

Marcus lowered his phone. "You tested it. On a stove. While making sauce." He looked at her bubbling pan of tomatoes and onions, then at the two chapatis. "Okay, I have to confess something. My channel has four subscribers and two of them are my mom." He turned the camera toward Sara's experiment, chapati still domed and steaming beside its flat, torn twin. "Tell them again what the steam does, but slower this time."

Grandma's piano sat in the front room under a window full of ferns, and Jade had been dying to play it all summer. On Monday morning she found a piece of sheet music on the stand with markings everywhere: piano, forte, crescendo, ritardando, like the notes were being shouted at. "That's Grandma's old solo," said Cousin Marcus, who was staying there too. "It has dynamics and tempo changes. I want to learn it for the talent show Friday, but I only know keyboard from school." Jade wanted the same thing, and there was only one piano, so they made a deal. "I'll practice in the morning, you take afternoons," she said. "And we can delegate the lunch dishes to whoever doesn't practice." Marcus agreed fast, because he hated dishes even more than he wanted the solo.

That evening a letter came from Mrs. Okafor, who directed the church choir Grandma sang in. "Friday's show will open with a round," Jade read aloud. "Tell your grandmother the choir needs every voice. Row, Row, Row Your Boat, first group, second group, third group." Marcus frowned. "If everyone sings the same song at the same time, how is that interesting?" Jade shrugged, but the question stuck in her head all through dinner, which was frugal but good, rice and beans and greens from the garden out back.

Tuesday morning she tried the solo and got the loud parts and the speeding up, but the music felt flat, like something was missing under the melody. Then she remembered the letter. At the piano she played Row, Row, Row Your Boat with her right hand. When she reached the second line, her left hand came in on the same melody at the very beginning. She held her breath. Where the two lines crossed, they made harmony. Same melody, different starting times. That was it. She grabbed her phone and called Marcus in from the porch, where he was reading a comic about a giant herbivore dinosaur. "Come listen. Every group sings the same melody but starts at a different time, and that's what makes the harmony." He dropped the comic and ran.

They tried it with voices in the kitchen, Jade going first, Marcus jumping in on "gently down the stream," and Grandma arriving home from the store right in the middle. Instead of hushing them she set down her bags and held up one finger, waiting for her spot, then slid in as the third group. The three lines braided together so well that Marcus whooped and knocked over the cereal box.

On Friday the choir opened the show with the round, three groups stacked like stairs, and then Jade played Grandma's solo with every crescendo and ritardando in place, Marcus turning pages beside her. When the last chord faded, Grandma stood up in the second row and cupped her hands around her mouth. "Again," she called. "From the top."

Jaxon stood at the kitchen table with a poster board, a bag of marbles, and his older cousin's phone number written on a sticky note. His health teacher had assigned him the hardest topic in the class: explain how nicotine hooks people, right down to the brain. He could not see a brain working, and that was the problem. He had to narrate something invisible to a room full of seventh graders, and he wanted it to be good.

"Got a minute?" he said when his cousin Dre picked up. Dre had quit vaping last spring, and Jaxon had been meaning to ask him about it for a week. Dre talked while Jaxon spread the marbles across the table like a handful of random pebbles. "It wasn't one big decision," Dre said. "It crept in. Good feeling first, then needing it just to feel normal." Jaxon pushed a marble along a track he had drawn on the poster, a curve labeled REWARD PATHWAY, and watched where it rolled.

Later that afternoon his little sister Riya came in from her checkup and dropped her jacket on a chair. She was quiet in a way Jaxon recognized, because two years ago he had sat in that same beige exam room, in that same squeaky chair, and asked Dr. Okafor why every other boy in gym class seemed to be changing and he wasn't. He remembered staring at the paper on the wall while the doctor talked, too embarrassed to look up. He remembered exactly what it said, too, because he had read it four times.

"Everything okay?" he asked Riya now. She shrugged. "I asked the doctor if something was wrong with me because I haven't started yet, and Ava already has." Jaxon told her what the wall chart had told him, the thing he had tested in his own head that day in the exam room. "Puberty usually starts between ages eight and thirteen for girls and between nine and fourteen for boys," he said, laying out the marbles into two rows, one shorter, one longer, the way he had pictured it back then. "So girls can start as early as eight, boys as early as nine, and starting anywhere in those ranges is normal. You and me, we're both inside the lines." Riya picked up a marble from the girls' row and held it to the light. "So Ava just started early," she said, "and I'm not late at all."

Jaxon looked at his rows of marbles, then at the curving track on his poster, and smiled. Ranges and pathways, both invisible, both working quietly whether anyone saw them or not. For his presentation he would roll one marble down the track for the first cigarette, then a handful for the tenth, showing how nicotine kept hitting the reward pathway until the brain expected it, the way Dre had described. Riya set her marble back in its row. "Can I watch you practice after dinner?" she asked. Jaxon picked up the bag and shook it, listening to the click inside. "Sure," he said. "You can be the audience."

The microscope had come from her uncle, secondhand, in a box labeled FRAGILE in three languages, and Nevaeh's science worksheet was due tomorrow morning. The instructions were simple. Look at onion skin under the microscope, then label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus on the diagram. She had a single onion from the crisper drawer and a plan, which was more than she'd had an hour ago.

The hard part was the skin. She cut the onion in half, peeled off a papery layer, and dropped it into a splash of water on the slide, but through the lens she saw nothing except a gray blur, like weather. She tried the thin skin from between two layers instead, pressing the cover slip down until bubbles skated sideways. That, at least, was something.

Her little brother Desmond appeared at her elbow, breathing near her ear. "I want a turn. I've been waiting my whole life."

"You've been alive seven years."

"That's my whole life." He held up a spoon. "I'll trade you my lucky spoon."

Nevaeh decided to assume he would go away if she gave him a job. "Fine. You're my assistant. Hold this flashlight." Desmond held the flashlight with enormous seriousness, steady as a soldier, which surprised them both.

At forty times magnification, shapes appeared. At one hundred, the shapes sharpened into rows and rows of pale rectangles, neatly stacked, one against the next, a wall going on and on across the whole field. Nevaeh sat back. Her heart sank a little. She had peeled the wrong thing. Somehow she was looking at the onion's actual wall, the structure itself, like bricks in a garden fence. She had no onion wall. She had onion skin. This was a disaster, and it was almost bedtime.

Desmond leaned in anyway. "Whoa. It's like a brick wall in there."

"It IS a brick wall," Nevaeh said. "Except." She stopped. Except onions didn't have brick walls, and even if they did, a brick wall wouldn't be on the thin skin from between the layers. She looked again, closer. Each rectangle had a dark, thick edge, the same border on every single one, and inside each rectangle sat a small dense dot, slightly off center, like a stamp on every brick. Every brick had one. A wall wouldn't do that. She counted five rectangles, then five dots, then five thick borders. The pattern held.

"It's not a wall," she said slowly. "The cell wall is the thick outer border around each onion cell. Each brick is one whole cell. That's why they look like rows of bricks." She grabbed her pencil. The thick border on her diagram, done. The dot was the nucleus, which meant the faint line just inside the border had to be the membrane. She labeled all three, then wrote her name at the top before anything could go wrong.

Desmond took his turn at the eyepiece, still clutching the flashlight, and did not move for a full minute. "Nevaeh," he said finally, "your onion has tiny rooms."

"Cells," she said. "You can keep the spoon."

Alexandre stood at the white line on the track behind the school, breathing into his cupped hands, because Coach Reyes had posted the sign-up sheet for Friday's eight-hundred-metre race and his name was on it, in ink, where anyone could see it. Last year he had gone out like a rocket in this same race and then spent the second half of it jogging with his hands on his knees while other kids streamed past him. He still remembered the exact sound of his own footsteps slowing, slap, slap, slap, like his shoes had given up before he had.

"Track's four hundred metres," said Priya, walking the curve beside him with a stopwatch. "So the eight hundred is exactly two laps. You plan it as a first lap and a second lap, not one long sprint." She was only repeating what the whole team knew, the way she repeated the lunch menu, but Alexandre heard it differently this time, because Friday was coming and his legs already felt tired.

That afternoon he found a folded note taped inside his locker, from his friend Dev, who was home with a broken wrist and apparently too much free time. "Dear Future Champion," it began. "Break a leg. Not like me. Also, I watched your race last year. You ran the first lap like the track was on fire and the second lap like the fire won. P.S. I have started a currency system in math class. One Skittle equals one pencil. The economy is lush and I am rich." Alexandre laughed so hard a sixth-grader turned to stare.

On Friday he made a rule for himself and refused to modify it, even in his head. First lap: fast but not furious. Second lap: everything he had left. At the gun he held back while Marcus from Mr. Okafor's class exploded ahead, arms pumping, and by the backstretch of the first lap Marcus had ten metres on everyone. Coming around into the second lap, Marcus suddenly surged again, threw his head back, and drove across the line, arms wide, shouting before he slowed to a walk.

Alexandre counted the laps on his fingers the whole way. He passed Marcus, who was walking with his hands on his hips near the infield, and heard him mutter, "Wait. That was only one?" Alexandre kept his eyes on Priya at the fence, where she held up one finger, then, a lap later, zero. He emptied everything he had into the last hundred metres, crossed the actual finish line second, and bent over gasping while Dev's crumpled note fell out of his pocket onto the lush green grass. Priya jogged over, looked down at it, and said, "Tell Dev the Skittle economy is doomed."

The community pool at nine in the morning was almost empty, which was exactly why Beatrice had claimed lane two for her secret project: learning to pace an eight-hundred-metre race even though she was standing in three feet of chlorinated water. Her plan, hatched last night with a notebook and two markers, was to walk one pool length fast, then walk a second length immediately, and feel the difference between starting too fast and starting right.

"Move over, you're invading my coaching zone," said a voice from the fence. It was Dominic from her grade, dragging five plastic hurdles onto the grass beside the pool. He wanted to make the county hurdles team more than he wanted lunch, probably, because he'd been out there every morning all week, crashing into the same hurdle and swearing in a way he thought nobody could hear.

"Why don't you just ask Coach to move them?" Beatrice called through the fence.

"He'd say I'm not ready for race spacing." Dominic wiped sweat off his forehead. "But I asked him yesterday anyway, and guess what. He said yes, backwards." He yanked the first hurdle closer to the second and clicked it down to its lowest notch. "We learn the three-step rhythm with hurdles lower and closer together than race spacing. Then we move them apart as we get faster. So today they're short and squished and I only have to survive."

Beatrice stood in the water with her mouth open. Shorter and closer first. Start with the small version of the thing, then grow it. She thought of last Tuesday's time trial, when she'd exploded off the line, led the whole first lap, and then her legs had turned to something molten, like her muscles had melted inside her skin, and three girls had passed her before the final curve. Her coach had said "save something," which had meant nothing to her at the time, like being told to save money when you couldn't see the money.

But pacing was a thing you couldn't see, and that was the problem. Speed you could see. Energy left in your legs, you could not. So maybe, like Dominic's hurdles, she needed the squished-together version. She set her goggles, pushed off, and swam one length flat-out, then tried to immediately swim a second. Halfway down the return lap her arms felt like wet noodles and she had to grab the lane rope, gasping, while a lifeguard gave her the look you give a drowning hamster. Okay. That was the "too fast first lap," demonstrated in a place where she could stop and think about it instead of collapsing on a track in front of everyone.

Second attempt. She counted her strokes on the first length, deliberately holding back, and it felt almost boring, like walking when you wanted to run. Then the second length, and her arms still worked, still pulled, and she touched the wall breathing hard but whole. Through the fence, Dominic cleared all five low hurdles in a row without touching one, and threw his arms up like he'd won the Olympics.

"Did you see that?" he shouted.

"I saw it," Beatrice called back, grinning into her goggles. "Now move them apart."

Rosalie slid her binder onto the desk just as Madame Perrin wrote the assignment on the board: a paragraph about your family and pets, then your summer plans, all in French. The room smelled like whiteboard marker and the dusty radiator by the window. Rosalie had seven sentences already, but the last two were the problem.

"You have to use 'voyagerai,'" said Dominic, leaning across the aisle. "Future tense. It sounds way more official."

"It sounds like a robot," said Priya from the next row. "Nobody talks like that."

Dominic flipped through his textbook, hunting for proof. Priya rolled her pen across her desk. Rosalie stared at her own draft, where she had written "Je vais voyager en juillet." She had copied that shape from a poster near the pencil sharpener, one of a boy loading a suitcase, but she had never asked herself why it looked like that. "Vais" was a form of aller, the going verb, and the second word sat there untouched, like an English verb after "to." So the whole thing must mean "I am going to travel," built out of going plus the plain verb. If that was true, she could say almost anything about summer with it.

She tested the idea on the poster sentence, then on her own. She tried "Je vais nager," pointing at Priya. "I am going to swim?" Priya nodded slowly, and Dominic stopped mid-page. Rosalie tried one more, "Je vais adopter un chat," and it held together the same way. Going, then the verb, nothing changing at the end. Dominic read her paragraph over her shoulder and sighed.

"Fine," he said. "Yours sounds like a person. Mine sounds like a narrator reading the news."

"It's still plausible," Priya said generously. "Just stiff."

Rosalie finished her paragraph while the radiator ticked. Her last line was "Nous allons donner le vieux lit du chien au refuge," because her family had agreed to donate the dog's old bed to the shelter once they got the new puppy in June. She read the whole thing once through, quiet under her breath, and liked the sound of it.

When Madame Perrin walked the rows, she paused at Rosalie's desk, tapped the final sentence twice with her finger, and drew a small sun in the margin. Rosalie looked at Dominic and raised one eyebrow. He slid his paper toward her and crossed out "voyagerai."

Wyatt jogged to the fence line of the outdoor court, where Coach Reyes had chalked a wobbly oval that looped the blacktop. Eight times around made eight hundred metres, and next Saturday was his first real race. His best friend Dez was already there, spinning a basketball on one finger.

"Eight laps, remember," Dez called. "Not a sprint war."

Wyatt ignored him and took off like the race started today. His sneakers slapped the asphalt, arms pumping, and the wind pushed cool against his sweaty neck. He finished the first lap in what felt like record time. By lap three his legs were full of wet sand. By lap five he was walking, hands on his knees, lungs burning like somebody had lit a match inside them.

"That went great," Dez said, grinning.

"It did not." Wyatt gulped air. But something nagged at him, something he couldn't see. He hadn't slowed down because he was tired all at once. The tiredness had been building quietly the whole time, hiding behind his fast first lap like a trick. If spending everything early created the wall later, maybe the opposite was true too. He had to test it. "One more. Timer on."

This time he ran the first lap deliberately neutral, not slow, not fast, just steady as a metronome. It felt almost too easy. He held the same rhythm through lap two, lap three. When lap five arrived, the wall didn't. His legs still had juice, so he pushed harder, and the steady rhythm propelled him through the final two laps faster than his old sprint pace. He leaned against the fence, laughing and gasping at the same time.

While he caught his breath, Dez and two other boys, Marcus and Theo, started a two-on-two game. Marcus had the ball at the top, and Theo ran toward Wyatt's fence side, planting his body like a wall in Marcus's defender's path. The defender bumped off Theo and stumbled, and Marcus darted around them toward the hoop. But a different defender, Theo's man, was suddenly waiting for him under the basket.

"Hey, that's not fair!" Marcus complained, whirling around.

"It's a switch," Dez said, tossing him the ball back. "The two defenders trade the players they're guarding."

Marcus frowned at Theo's screen, then at the two defenders, and Wyatt watched the whole thing click together in his friend's face. It was like his race, Wyatt thought. The move you could see was only half of it; the real play was the hidden exchange happening behind it.

"Again," Marcus said, pounding the ball hard into the asphalt. "This time I'll read the switch and slip the other way."

Wyatt checked his watch and bounced on his toes at the chalk line. "You guys figure out your trick plays. I've got four more laps to run."

"Race you to the fence," Dez said.

The trail climbed through pines that smelled like warm resin, and Kayla stopped every few steps to shove the folded papers deeper into her backpack before they could escape. She had printed two climate graphs, one for a desert and one for a rainforest, because Monday's assignment demanded a real comparison, and she was tired of guessing.

"Are you hiking or doing homework out here?" her friend Priya asked, hopping over a root.

"Both. My teacher said learn it however we want." Kayla pulled out the desert graph and held it up so Priya could see. The rainfall bars were so short they looked like a row of fallen eyelashes. Then she flipped to the rainforest graph, where the bars shot up like a fence. "Look at this. Same planet, and one place gets this," she tapped the eyelashes, "while the other gets a wall of rain every single month."

"That wall one looks familiar," Priya said.

"It should. It's Kerala, where my Ammachi lives." Kayla smoothed the paper against a boulder and squinted at the tall June bar. Something tickled the back of her brain. Every June, without fail, her grandmother sent a photo of the first rain hitting the courtyard, and every June, Kayla's mom would say, right on time. But how could rain have a time?

She called Ammachi right there, because the trail had one bar of signal and Kayla was not the kind of person to waste a miracle. "Ammachi, quick question. Does the rain actually have a schedule?"

Her grandmother laughed so loudly that Priya heard it from a foot away. "Of course. The India Meteorological Department gives June 1 as the normal date for the southwest monsoon to reach Kerala." Down the line came the sound of a calendar page being tapped. "I mark it every year, like a birthday."

Kayla scribbled the date on the edge of her graph. "The monsoon," she repeated, tasting the word. "Okay, that clarifies everything, actually." Because there it was, hiding in plain sight: the June bar wasn't tall by accident. The rainforest graph was a picture of something you could set a calendar by, and the desert graph was a picture of a place where nothing ever arrived on schedule, or at all.

"Wait, say that as a poem," Priya demanded, taking a drink from her water bottle. "One stanza. 'In Kerala, the rain keeps appointments.'"

"In the desert," Kayla countered, "the rain ghosts you for the whole year."

They both cracked up, and a startled jay scolded them from a branch overhead. Kayla folded the graphs with the care of someone holding treasure, shouldered her pack, and marched up the trail. "I'm putting the calendar thing right in my conclusion," she announced. "And Monday, I'm asking my teacher if she knew that rain could be punctual."

Lea's grandmother lived at the end of Ash Street, a street so long and straight that on hazy afternoons it seemed to fold into the sky. Lea sat on the porch with a sketchbook, a pencil, and one burning ambition: by Sunday, she would draw Ash Street so real that her cousin Marco would swear it was a photograph. The trouble was that whenever she drew it, the houses tipped sideways like drunk dominoes, and the road refused to narrow into the distance the way real roads did.

In the kitchen, Grandma was humming over a sheet of watercolour paper. "You look defeated," she said, without turning around.

"My street looks like it got hit by an earthquake," Lea admitted. "Marco says perspective is mandatory if you want anything to look real. He says artists have a secret trick with lines."

Grandma tapped her own drawing, a row of cottages marching toward a pencil dot she had planted in the middle of the sky. "I learned a trick like that from your great-grandfather. He called it a vanishing point. Everything runs toward it." She would say no more; she claimed mysteries were bad luck if explained, and went back to her paint.

Lea stole the idea and tried it herself. One dot on the horizon. Then she drew lines from the dot outward, like sunrays, and let the edges of roofs and fences lie along them. When she stepped back, the street lay flat and deep, the houses shrinking politely toward the dot as though bowing to it. It felt like a magic spell disguised as homework. Marco was going to lose his mind.

To console him in advance, she decided to make the drawing even crueler: a watercolour, painted at her grandmother's elbow. She wet her brush and painted the dark shadowed roofs first, planning to add the pale sunlight on the walls afterward as a final flourish. But when she swept the light yellow wash over a dark patch, the dark stayed dark, staring up through the yellow like a cat through a window. She tried white. The dark still glared through. "It won't cover," she muttered.

Grandma glanced over and gave a low whistle. "Watercolour is transparent," she said. "Every wash lets the ones underneath show through. That's why we work light to dark. A dark wash can't be covered by a lighter one."

Lea stared at her ruined rooftops, then at her grandmother's painting, which was pale as morning and would grow darker layer by layer, never the reverse. She turned to a fresh sheet, painted the whole sky the lightest water-thin yellow first, then added the shadows after, and watched them sink into place like night following day. "Ash Street, take two," she announced, and set the vanishing point down in the middle of the pale gold sky.

Livia wanted her street drawing to look real, not flat like a map. Every time she drew the bakery on the corner, it stood straight at the viewer like a poster, and the road beside it refused to slide back into the distance. Today, at the community art studio on Delancey Street, she had promised herself she would fix that.

The studio smelled like pencil shavings and turpentine. Livia claimed the table by the window and taped down a fresh sheet. Her friend Marcus slid into the seat across from her, holding a print he had taken from the studio's pile of art posters. "Look at this one," he said. "It's old. Like, really old."

The print showed a painted archway with a man standing beneath it, columns rising on both sides. Marcus read the label at the bottom. "Masaccio's Holy Trinity, a fresco in Florence, painted around 1427." He tilted the paper toward the light, and for a second the surface caught the window glare and went transparent, the image washing out to pale gray.

Livia took the print and stared. The ceiling of the painted arch was made of square panels, and something about them pulled her eyes backward, deeper into the picture. She held her pencil above the print, hesitating, then laid the pencil flat along one edge of a ceiling panel. "I have an idea," she said. "Watch." She dragged her fingertip along the panel's line, then along the next one, and the next. All the lines leaned the same way, like they were sliding down an invisible hill. "They're all going somewhere," she murmured. "Somewhere specific."

She borrowed Marcus's ruler and kept tracing, extending each ceiling line with light pencil marks, then the lines along the floor. At first the marks crossed each other like scattered spaghetti. But when she extended the lines far enough, they all crashed together at one single point, right at the level of the painted figures' feet. "There," she said, tapping it. "One point. Everything aims at it." Marcus leaned in and frowned. "So that's how the road works. The edges have to run to the same spot, or the street looks like the sidewalk is eroding away on one side."

Livia went back to her own paper. She drew a small dot in the middle of the page, then let both edges of her street run toward it, the bakery shrinking as it went. When she held the drawing up, the road actually went somewhere. She grinned and slid the Masaccio print across the table to Marcus. "Trace the ceiling yourself," she said. "I want to see if you land on the same dot."

Chloe had one afternoon to figure out the onion cells, because on Monday her science teacher would collect lab notebooks, and Chloe's page was still blank except for the title she'd copied off the board: "Cell wall, membrane, nucleus." She was staying at her aunt's farm for the weekend, which meant no school microscopes, only the dusty old one her cousin Ruth had left in the barn loft next to a crate of empty jars.

"Good luck with that thing," Aunt Delia said when Chloe carried it down to the kitchen table. "Ruth used it to look at pond scum. Maybe pond scum is all it's good for."

The letter from her lab partner, Marcus, was folded in Chloe's back pocket, and she read it again while she peeled a papery skin off one of the onions hanging in the pantry. Marcus wrote: "You left before the teacher explained the stain, so here it is. Put a drop of iodine on your slide. It makes parts of the cell show up. Also, the nucleus isn't always where you expect. Don't give up." He had drawn a tiny onion cell in the corner with the wall, the membrane, and the nucleus labeled, but his drawing was so smudged it could have been anything.

Chloe made her first slide with plain water, clipped a thin purple sliver of skin onto it, and pressed her eye to the lens. She saw boxes, rows and rows of boxes, like a brick wall. She could label the cell wall, the outside edge of every box. But the inside was pale and empty. No nucleus anywhere. Her first thought was that the microscope was broken, and for a minute she sat back and felt like giving up, because a broken microscope was a legitimate reason to have a blank page.

Then she remembered the science museum in the city, the table where you could line up model finch beaks next to model foods. She had spent an hour there once, matching a thin, pointed beak to insects and a deep, heavy beak to hard seeds, getting it wrong, trying again until every beak sat beside its food. The trick was that you couldn't see the answer on the beak itself; you had to test what it could actually do. So the nucleus might be in her cells, just invisible, the way a beak's job was invisible until you tried it on the right seed.

She set up two slides to be sure: one plain, one with a drop of iodine from Aunt Delia's medicine cabinet. That way she had only one variable changed between them, which Marcus would appreciate. On the plain slide, still nothing. On the iodine slide, small dark dots appeared inside the boxes, one dot per cell, and a thin dark line tracing the inner edge of each wall. The nucleus and the membrane, suddenly plain as seeds in a bird's claw.

Chloe drew both slides side by side in her notebook, labeling the wall, the membrane, and the nucleus, and wrote the date and the words "iodine stain" so anyone reading it could see what she had documented. Aunt Delia leaned over her shoulder, sniffing the iodine bottle.

"You changed your mind about my microscope," Aunt Delia said.

"I changed my mind about the cells," Chloe said, and slid the notebook across the table so her aunt could see the little dark dots, each one sitting in its place.

The bus rattled over the pothole by the mailboxes, and Brooklyn slid an inch toward the window. Three rows back, Devon Wright was telling Felix Ochoa that his backpack looked like something a kindergartner would carry, and half the bus was grinning along. Felix stared at the seat in front of him and pulled the straps tighter, like he could make the bag disappear. Brooklyn watched him, and her stomach did the thing it always did, a slow molten drop, hot and heavy.

Last week she had said nothing. The week before that too. Every time someone got picked on, the whole bus went quiet in a weird, comfortable way, and she had started to wonder why. It was not that nobody cared. Priya bit her lip. Marcus stopped his joke mid-sentence. Even Devon's friend Theo looked away. So why did forty kids sit still like furniture?

She had tested one small idea on Thursday. When Dev had grabbed Felix's hat, she had waited to see who would speak first. She counted, in her head, all the way to thirty. Nothing. When she finally opened her mouth, the words came out too loud and too sharp, and Devon had turned it around on her, calling her the bus police for the rest of the ride. That had made things worse, and Felix had told her later, quietly, that she didn't have to fight his battles. But he said it like he was glad somebody had.

Brooklyn turned the puzzle over all weekend. What she noticed was this: when it was just her and Felix at the science fair, nobody teased him. When it was her and two other kids at the lunch table, still nothing. It only happened in the crowd. And in the crowd, nobody moved. It was almost a rule, like the pattern in her math homework. The bigger the audience, the smaller the chance anybody acted, because each person back there was probably thinking exactly what she used to think: someone else will say something.

Monday morning, Devon started in again before the bus even left the lot. "Nice dinosaur bag, Ochoa. Did it come with the museum?" Laughter rolled down the aisle, thin and nervous. Brooklyn felt the old heat in her stomach, but this time she didn't stand up and shout. She picked up her water bottle, walked back two rows like she had a reason, and sat down right next to Felix.

"Hey," she said, to Felix only, ignoring Devon completely. "Did you finish the inflation math? I got stuck on question four." Felix blinked, then dug out his binder. She asked him to explain how he'd set up the percent change, and he did, in that soft, careful voice that got steadier as he went. Devon said something else about the backpack, but the joke landed in empty air, because Brooklyn and Felix were both looking at the page, and the kids around them suddenly had somewhere else to look too.

By the time the bus pulled into school, Priya had leaned over the seat to ask about the homework, and Marcus was complaining that the vending machine prices had gone up again. Devon was telling Theo about the game last night. The aisle filled up with ordinary noise, and Felix zipped his backpack like it was any other bag, because now it was.

In the hallway, Felix caught up with her. "Thanks for not making it a whole thing," he said.

"I read about it," Brooklyn said. "It's called the bystander effect. That's why nobody moved. I figured if I moved first, kind of sideways, then..." She shrugged.

"Then it's not a thing anymore," Felix said. He held the door for her, and they walked in together.

Jayden tapped the stopwatch on the museum's ramp exhibit and glared at it like it owed him money. His best friend Priya had already measured the speed of the rolling ball, drawn her distance-time graph, and written "7.2 seconds, champion" on the whiteboard beside the ramp, with a smiley face wearing a crown. Jayden refused to resign himself to second place. He was going to time that ball properly, mark where it was at every second, and draw a graph so clean it would make Priya's crown fall off.

The trouble was that speed was invisible. Nobody could see the ball moving 40 centimeters per second; they could only see where it was, and when. So Jayden crouched beside the ramp with a meter stick, ready to drop a penny next to the ball's position each time Priya called out a second. That was his foundation: positions at known times, then connect the dots and let the graph show the speed hiding inside them. "Ready?" Priya asked. "Born ready," said Jayden, which was a naive thing to say, because the ball promptly rolled off the ramp and under a bench.

While he fished it out, he noticed the exhibit next door, a wall of wires and bulbs with a big circuit diagram painted on it. Thick arrows marched along the wires from the positive terminal to the negative one. But a kid standing there was frowning at her book, and she read aloud, sounding annoyed: "Conventional current is drawn from positive to negative, but the electrons actually move the other way, from negative to positive." She looked at the arrows. "Then the arrows point the wrong way?"

Jayden stared at the diagram. The wires sat there doing nothing visible at all, and yet something was flowing through them, backward from the painted arrows, and nobody could watch it happen. It was exactly like his ball problem. You could not see the speed or the electrons; you could only catch the clues they left behind and work out the hidden truth. "The arrows show one thing," he told the girl, "and the real stuff goes the other way, negative to positive. Sneaky." She grinned and wrote it down.

He raced back to the ramp. "Drop the ball, mark every second, no mercy," he said, and Priya held the stopwatch while he slid pennies along the meter stick. At one second the ball was at 15 centimeters, at two seconds 40, at three seconds 66. He plotted the points, drew the line, and watched it climb in a neat, steady slope. The invisible speed had finally shown its face on paper.

"Six point four centimeters per second per second," Jayden announced. "It's speeding up. Your crown is in danger." Priya leaned over his graph, checked his dots twice, and sighed. "Fine. Best of three. And you're fetching the ball when it rolls under the bench again." She hit the release lever, and the ball rolled, and Jayden dove.

Blake spread his notebook across the kitchen table and clicked his pencil three times, which was his habit when a problem refused to behave. He had forty dollars from mowing lawns, and he wanted it to grow into enough money for a used skateboard by next summer. The trouble was figuring out where the forty dollars should live.

"Simple interest," his sister Priya said, leaning over his shoulder, "is like a dog that sits. Compound interest is a dog that fetches more dogs." She stole a grape from his bowl and chewed it loudly.

Blake wrote out both cases. At simple interest, the same amount landed in the account every year, flat and boring, like identical pancakes stacked on a plate. With compound interest, the interest itself earned interest, so the pile grew faster each year. Over five years the difference was small, but it was real. He ran the numbers twice and drew a little arrow where the two totals split apart, and Priya traced the widening gap with her finger and said, "There. That's where the magic happens. It's not magic, but that's where it happens."

Then came the harder question. Blake had read a forum post where someone bragged about doubling money in a risky app, and he wanted that speed. He carried his notebook to the porch, where Grandma Ruth was shelling peas into a blue bowl, the pods snapping like tiny green knuckles.

"I could put my money somewhere risky and get more," he confessed, sitting on the step below her.

She shook one pea loose and studied it. "My emergency savings sit in Treasury bonds," she said. "They're backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government. They're considered among the safest investments in the world. I keep them there instead of stocks." She flicked the pea into the bowl. "Risky places can vanish overnight. Safe places just sit there being safe."
