Blake thought about the skateboard. If he lost the forty dollars, there would be no skateboard, no second chance, and a long summer of watching Priya roll past on hers. He felt a stab of empathy for his future self, broke and skateboardless, and decided that guy deserved better.

"So the plan is," he said later at the bank counter, sliding his forty dollars and his notebook under the glass, "compound interest in a savings account for five years, and when I have real savings someday, Grandma's bond trick." The teller read his arrow diagram, smiled, and stamped the deposit slip. Blake pocketed the receipt and, outside, ran his finger over the number like it was already the skateboard's grip tape.

Kaitlyn stood at the front of the empty auditorium with her note cards fanned out like a poker hand, and for the third time that afternoon she forgot her own argument. Marcus sat in the third row, drumming his pencil on the armrest. "Your warrant," he said. "You gave the claim and the evidence, but you never explained why the evidence proves the claim."

"I had it right here." She flipped a card. She was building her first real debate case for Saturday's tournament, three points about the school switching to a later start time, each one needing a claim, evidence and a warrant. The trouble was that only her middle point was any good. It had a study about sleep and grades, a clean piece of evidence, everything. Her first point was weak and her third was mostly a hypothetical about buses that she'd made up on the bus herself. "I'll just put the sleep one second," she said. "It's the middle of my case, so it holds everything together."

Marcus frowned. "Wait. Try it once and let me listen like a judge." She ran the whole case, and afterward he closed his eyes and tried to list her points back to her. "You said something about attendance first, and your bus thing last, because I'm still laughing at that. The sleep one, the one with the actual study? Gone. I lost it completely." He opened his eyes. "Yesterday you made me memorize a grocery list for practice, and I remembered eggs and apples because they were first and last. Same thing just happened."

Kaitlyn sat down hard on the edge of the stage. "The first and last items in a list. That's the ones people remember best." She grabbed her phone and typed it in, and the search gave it a name, which she read out loud. "The serial position effect. It's why openings and closings matter." She looked at her cards, then spread them across the stage floor and moved the sleep point from the middle to the front, where it would hit the judges before their attention drifted. "Okay. New order. Don't presume I know what I'm doing, either. Tell me if it falls apart."

She ran the case twice more, and the second time Marcus listed everything back without a single gap. "That was a real case," he said, standing up and applauding once, like a judge who'd made up his mind. "You might even build a reputation at this tournament." Kaitlyn gathered her cards, squared the edges, and grinned at the empty seats that would be full on Saturday. "First and last," she said, and tapped the top card. "The judge remembers this one, or nothing."

The science quiz was fourth period, which gave Rosalie exactly one lunch break to figure out the giant poster of the periodic table that Mr. Okafor had hung above the chalkboard. "The atomic number tells you the number of protons," her notebook said, in her own handwriting, copied off the board yesterday. That part seemed almost too easy. Carbon was number 6, so carbon had six protons. But then why did the table have all those weird gaps, and why did some squares sit lower than others, like the whole thing had been built by someone who ran out of room?

She stood in front of the poster with her sandwich in one hand, tracing columns with her eyes. "They're called groups," said Dev, appearing beside her with a juice box. He pointed at the tall rows running up and down. "My cousin says elements in the same group tend to have similar chemical properties." Rosalie chewed on that along with her sandwich. Similar properties. She scanned the far right column and noticed helium, neon, and argon stacked one above another like beads on a string. What could a super light gas and a heavier one possibly have in common? She had a sudden, wild idea: maybe it was the protons. Maybe columns were secretly proton patterns.

She tested it right there. Helium was 2, neon was 10, argon was 18. She wrote the numbers on her napkin and stared at them until her eyes crossed. Two, ten, eighteen. It was like a secret code, and for one glorious moment she felt like a spy cracking it. Then she checked a different column, lithium and sodium, numbers 3 and 11, and the pattern faltered. If protons alone made the columns, the numbers should march in tidy steps everywhere, and they didn't. Her whole theory was less credible by the second. She glared at the napkin as though it had personally set out to hinder her, which, in a way, it had.

"Time check," Dev announced. "Eight minutes till the bell." Rosalie flipped her notebook to the study sheet. Question one: How many protons does oxygen have? She found oxygen, atomic number 8, and wrote 8, fast. Question two: Name two elements in the same group. She wrote neon and argon, then hesitated. Mr. Okafor's voice drifted back to her from some Monday long ago: the periodic table is organized by patterns, not by accident. Maybe the principle wasn't that each column shared proton numbers, but that sharing a column meant something else, something about how the elements behaved. She added a note: "similar properties," and underlined it twice.

The bell rang as she was writing question three. Then came the twist: Mr. Okafor walked in carrying a stack of papers and announced, "Change of plan. Open notebook quiz today." Rosalie looked down at her napkin, covered in numbers and arrows, sitting beside her notebook like a treasure map. She slid it under the notebook's cover, and Dev whispered, "Best sandwich investigation ever."

Hudson wheeled his bike through the door of the Spin Cycle Laundromat because it was the only place on Marsh Street with a roof and a bench, and his back tyre had gone flat two blocks ago. He had a patch kit, two tyre levers, and a small pump in his backpack, all of it bought with his own money, none of it ever used. His mother was three washers down, feeding quarters into a machine, so he set the bike against the folding table and got to work.

First came the levers. He slid one under the edge of the tyre, then the second, and the rubber fought him until he learned to pin the first lever under a spoke. The tube came out pale and wrinkled, like a long balloon after a week. He could not see any hole. He knew one had to be there, though, because air had leaked out and air could only leave through an opening, so he decided to test it. He carried the tube to the utility sink in the corner, held it underwater, and pumped a little air in with the hand pump. Somewhere near the valve, a thin thread of bubbles rose up through the water like a silver string.

He was marking the spot with chalk when the man at the change machine called out. "Kid, come here a second." The man had sold Hudson a bottle of milk from the little shelf by the dryers, part of the laundromat's strange side commerce in snacks and soap. "I gave you the wrong change before, I think." He counted coins into Hudson's palm. "One fifty-five."

Hudson looked at the coins. He had paid with a five dollar bill, and he had done the subtraction in his head while the washers hummed. "That's too little," he said. "The milk was two sixty-five. Five minus two sixty-five is two thirty-five."

The man counted again on the counter, slowly, lips moving. "Two sixty-five from five." He opened the register and added coins until the pile came right. "Eighty cents more. You're not as gullible as my nephew." He laughed at that, and Hudson pocketed the coins, which would prolong his afternoon by exactly one ice cream.

Back at the folding table he roughed the chalked spot with the sandpaper from the kit, spread the glue, waited until it went tacky, and pressed the patch down hard with his thumb. Then he worked the tube back inside the tyre, tucking the last stretch over the rim with his thumbs, and connected the pump. The stroke that seemed useless at first gradually stiffened. The tyre rose round and firm against his palm.

Hudson spun the wheel and watched it turn, steady and true, in the fluorescent light.

"Ready?" his mother asked, closing the dryer door.

"Ready," he said, and lifted the bike toward the street.

Clara spread the two flowcharts across her grandfather's kitchen table, weighting the corners with jars of homemade pickles. The assignment was due Monday: pick one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, put it in her own words, and explain it to the class. But her teacher had also promised bonus marks for describing how a bill becomes a law, and Clara had never gotten that far before.

"Still working on the homework?" her grandfather asked, setting down two mugs of tea. He was a veteran who had served overseas decades ago, and he kept a framed photograph of his old regiment in the hallway. "You've been at that table all afternoon."

"I picked section two," Clara said. "Freedom of thought, belief, opinion and expression. My own words for it are: you're allowed to think what you think and say what you think, without the government stopping you." She frowned at the flowcharts. "But I'm stuck on the bill part. The federal chart says a bill goes through the House of Commons and then the Senate, and then the Governor General gives royal assent. The provincial chart just stops after one box."

Last weekend, she remembered, she had complained that the assignment was pointless. She had wanted to quit and write about her weekend instead, and her grandfather had said, "People obstruct laws they've never read, Clara. Read this one." Then he had slid a worn booklet across this same table, and she had opened it just to be polite. The first line had caught her before she could pretend to be bored.

Now she traced the provincial chart with her finger. "That can't be right. Every law should have to pass both houses. Otherwise it's too easy to pass something bad."

"Draw it again," her grandfather said. "Count the boxes yourself. Don't trust the chart."

Clara counted. The federal chart showed two chambers, first one and then the other, before the Governor General. The provincial chart showed one chamber only, and after that single chamber the bill went straight to the lieutenant governor, who gave royal assent. She checked the provincial government website on her laptop, then checked a second site because she was skeptical of anything she found only once. Both said the same thing.

"Grandpa, look. All Canadian provinces have one-chamber legislatures. So a provincial bill passes only one house before the lieutenant governor gives royal assent." She said it slowly, testing each word. "That's why the chart isn't missing anything. It's just shorter."

"So will you change your mind about the shorter chart?" he asked.

"It's not wrong, it's just different," Clara said. She was thinking of the boy in her class, Daniel, who had insisted last week that provincial laws took twice as long to pass as federal ones because there were more provinces. She had believed him then. Now she had a page of counted boxes that said otherwise, and she intended to wave it at him on Monday.

She copied the two flowcharts side by side onto a fresh sheet, wrote "one house, not two" beside the provincial one, and underlined it twice.

"There," she said. "Now for section two."

Zack flattened the big sketchbook on the kitchen table and sharpened his pencil until the shavings curled like tiny scrolls. He was going to draw Draper Street, the whole thing, with the buildings leaning toward each other and every edge sliding back to one dot. His art book called it one-point perspective, and the dot was the vanishing point. Last week his drawing of the street had looked like cardboard boxes glued in a row, and he was not doing that again.

He remembered Saturday morning, standing at the corner with his friend Marcus. The smell of the bakery's cinnamon rolls had drifted down the block, and a bus had rumbled past so close the sidewalk buzzed under Zack's sneakers. "Just draw what you see," Marcus had said, and they had both tried, sitting on the curb with their knees bumping the curbstone. Today Zack wanted to get it right, so he drew a straight line across the middle of his page first, laid out the street, and let every roofline and curb run toward his vanishing point on that line. He leaned back. It looked like a street. He actually shouted, "Yes!"

Then Marcus knocked on the door, holding up his own drawing. "Trade check," Marcus said, which was their rule: you had to find one thing wrong with the other person's art, because otherwise the checking would be Zack's monopoly, since he found mistakes faster than anybody.

Marcus stared at Zack's street. "Where's the sun? Where's the sky? Mine has half a page of sky." He spread his drawing next to Zack's. His horizon line sat way up near the top of his page, and his buildings rose from the bottom edge like towers. Zack's horizon sat low, near the bottom, with walls rising above it on both sides.

"Where did you draw from?" Zack asked.

"My bedroom window. Upstairs." Marcus tapped his page. "You?"

"Curb. Saturday, with you." Zack's mouth went dry with excitement, because he was starting to see it. "So the horizon is low when you're down low, and high when you're up high." He flipped to a new page fast. "Draw mine again but pretend you're on the roof."

They knelt side by side, pencils scratching, the kitchen smelling of pencil wood and the leftover cinnamon toast Zack had eaten. Zack put his new horizon even lower than before, almost at the bottom edge, and suddenly his street felt the way it had felt sitting on that curb: small and huge at once, buildings looming, sky pressing down. "Look," he said, holding it up next to the first one. "A low horizon makes it feel like a kid's view."

"And mine implies you're floating above the bakery," Marcus said, grinning at his tall, towering street.

Zack ran for the stairs, sketchbook under his arm, intricate ideas crowding his head. "Come on, we're doing the roof next!"

"Race you," Marcus said, already two steps up.

Austin stood in the bathroom at Grandpa's house, leaning close to the mirror and studying the red bump on his chin. Tomorrow he had to give a science talk on how nicotine hooks people through the brain's reward pathway, and his face had picked this exact week to rebel. He raised two fingers toward the pimple, ready to squeeze it flat before anyone had to see it.

His older cousin Marisol banged on the door. "Don't do that. Squeezing or popping pimples can push bacteria deeper into the skin, and it can leave scars." Austin lowered his hand and opened the door. "Then what am I supposed to do, submerge my whole face in ice water?" Marisel grinned. "No. You wash it and leave it alone, and it fades. Patience, remember?" She flicked his shoulder and went back downstairs.

Patience. That was the word that had been missing from his notes all afternoon. Austin sat at Grandpa's kitchen table surrounded index cards, a rubber band stretched between his thumbs, and a bowl of peanuts Grandpa had set down without comment. His problem was simple and frustrating: nicotine was invisible. He couldn't show the class a molecule or a brain pathway, so his talk kept sounding like a dictionary reading aloud.

He tried his speech on Grandpa, who was fixing a leaky faucet under the sink. "Nicotine gets into the brain and trips the reward pathway, the system that normally reacts to food and stuff that keeps you alive. So the brain learns nicotine is important, and it starts to want it, and wanting it gets stronger every time." Grandpa's voice echoed up from the pipes. "Like me and these peanuts," he said, rattling the empty bowl. "One handful yesterday, two today. Tomorrow I'll want the whole jar." Austin sat up straight. That was it. Not a definition. A person, wanting something more and more, without seeing why.

He grabbed his rubber band and stretched it, feeling it pull against his thumbs. Every dose of nicotine was like a stretch, and an elastic band that got stretched again and again stopped bouncing back the same way. He wrote that on a card, then hesitated. It wasn't perfect, and he was pretty sure a rubber band didn't really work like a brain. But it was something a class could see with their own eyes.

He looked back at the mirror on his way to bed. The pimple was still there, small and stubborn, and he left it alone. Some things got worse when you forced them, and some things only faded with time and patience. He set his index cards on the nightstand, put the rubber band on top of them, and turned off the light. "Tomorrow," he told the ceiling, "we stretch."

The synagogue smelled of old wood and honey from the year before, when someone had spilled candy behind the radiators. Noemie sat in the back row with her prayer book open, though her eyes kept drifting to her cousin Ari, three seats ahead. Ari had diabetes, and today was Yom Kippur, the day everyone fasted. He had his water bottle tucked under his jacket like something illegal.

Noemie was supposed to be thinking about the service, which talked a great deal about being written into the Book of Life. Instead she was thinking about her friend Priya, who went to the Hindu temple across town. Last week Priya had explained reincarnation over pizza, drawing little circles on her napkin. "Your soul comes back," she had said, "again and again, until it doesn't need to anymore." Noemie had drawn arrows. She wanted to compare it with what her own tradition said, and she had promised to bring an answer by Saturday.

The problem was Ari. He looked pale, and halfway through the morning service he swayed and grabbed the pew in front of him. Noemie's mother hurried over. So did Rabbi Wolk, an eccentric old man who wore two different socks and carried a clock that didn't run. Noemie expected him to tell Ari to be brave and push through. Instead he leaned close and said, "You need to eat something now."

Ari blinked at him. "But it's Yom Kippur."

"Jewish law waives the fast when health is in danger," the rabbi said. "In that case you're actually required to eat or drink. So drink, please. It's the religious thing to do." He said it quietly, without ceremony, the way you'd tell someone to buckle a seatbelt.

Ari drank his juice, and the color came back into his face within minutes. Noemie watched him negotiate a deal with their grandmother, who kept insisting he take a second granola bar, and who won. Meanwhile Noemie turned the rabbi's words over in her mind like a stone. She had thought fasting was simply what you did, no exceptions, the way you don't talk during the silent prayer. But the rules had hidden doors in them. She tested the idea against Priya's tradition, where exceptions and levels and second chances seemed to be everywhere too. Maybe, she thought, every system for describing things nobody can see has to make room for real people, in real bodies, on real days.

At the break, she found Ari eating crackers behind the social hall, his fatigue already gone. "Does it feel strange?" she asked. "Eating when everyone else isn't?"

He shrugged and brushed crumbs off his lap. "A little. But the rabbi said it counts as observing the holiday."

"I'm telling Priya that," Noemie said, pulling out her phone to type a note. "She's going to love it. Her tradition has exceptions for sickness too." Ari held out the cracker box, and she took one.

Evelyn did not cherish Tuesdays, and she especially did not cherish Tuesdays that began with a lab sheet titled Resistance of a Wire. The instructions seemed simple enough: connect the wire to the power pack, measure the voltage across it, measure the current through it, then divide. R equals V divided by I. Her partner, Marcus, read it out loud twice, as if saying it again might make the numbers behave.

The thick copper wire went first. The voltmeter said 1.5 volts and the ammeter said 0.30 amps. Evelyn wrote both down and did the division on the corner of the sheet. Five ohms. She checked it twice, because a number that neat felt suspicious, like it was trying to win her trust.

Then they swapped in the thin wire, the same copper, the same length, and the ammeter barely twitched. 0.10 amps. Marcus tapped the meter with one finger, the universal cure for instruments. "It's not broken," Evelyn said. She wrote the current down anyway and divided. Fifteen ohms. She looked at the two answers sitting side by side on her page, five and fifteen, and frowned at them.

"Same wire stuff, same length," Marcus said. "How can it be three times as much?"

Evelyn laid the two wires on the table next to each other. The thick one was like a piece of spaghetti; the thin one was more like a thread from her mom's sewing kit. She thought about the hallway outside, the one everybody jammed into at the bell, and how the wide stairwell never backed up. "More room to flow," she said slowly, mostly to herself, and Marcus grinned at her with the infectious delight of someone who has just watched an idea arrive.

For their last trial she chose a thick wire again, from a different spool, and got four ohms, which was close enough to five to feel like testimony: the thickness was the thing, not the spool. When Mr. Reyes walked past, he glanced at her data table and raised an eyebrow at the last column, where she had written thick, thin, thick beside each trial like evidence tags.

"Nice control," he said, and moved on before she could decide whether to be proud or to wonder how teachers always knew which student had actually figured something out.

At the bell, Marcus stacked the wires in the bin by thickness. "So the skinny ones are the stubborn ones," he said, holding up the thread-thin copper.

"Exactly," said Evelyn, and clipped the meter leads together one last time, just to see the needle jump.

Megan sat at her grandmother's kitchen table with the laptop open and a deadline hanging over her: the student council meeting was at four o'clock, and she had promised to bring a summary of the field trip survey. Grandpa hovered behind her with his own want, which was to get the kitchen back for his bread baking before the dough overproofed.

"Five minutes," she negotiated, tilting the screen away from his flour-dusted elbow.

The spreadsheet held 212 rows, one for each student who had answered the survey. There was a column for grade, a column for the activity they chose, and a column where everyone rated the trip from one to five. Megan had figured out pivot tables the night before, mostly by clicking things at random until a gray panel appeared and dragged fields into boxes. She put Grade in Rows, and the count of students appeared neatly for each grade. Sixth grade, 74. Seventh, 68. Eighth, 70.

But the count told her nothing about whether anyone had actually liked the trip. She scrolled through the ratings and saw a wall of threes, fours, ones, and fives with no order she could detect. There had to be a pattern in there somewhere, a rule hiding inside the numbers, but it was invisible while the ratings sat scattered down the column.

She clicked into the values area of the pivot table and found a dropdown. Sum was selected, which made no sense; summing ratings would just give giant useless numbers. She changed it to Count, which she already had. Then she saw Average. That had to be it. The whole column of one-to-five ratings would turn into the mean rating for each grade. She clicked it and the table rebuilt itself. Sixth grade, 4.2. Seventh, 3.1. Eighth, 4.6. She sat back. The eighth graders had loved the trip, the seventh graders had barely tolerated it, and now she could say so with actual numbers instead of a shrug.

Megan tested it once to be sure, dragging the Activity field into Columns so the average rating showed for each activity within each grade. The pattern held: seventh graders who chose the museum averaged 4.4, while the ones stuck with the walking tour averaged 2.3. The tour was the problem. That was worth saying at the meeting, and she could even propose fixing it for next year.

"Done," she said, and slid the laptop aside as Grandpa slid the loaf pan in. "Grandpa, you're my spreadsheet mentor now, by default."

"Only if mentoring means standing here eating bread," he said, and set a warm slice in front of her.

Gabriella crouched at the edge of the halfpipe with a battery, a coil of wire, and her older brother's multimeter, while her best friend Devi rolled back and forth on her board above her.

"Are you seriously doing homework at a skate park?" Devi called down.

"It's not homework, it's a mission." Gabriella held up the little black box. "Coach Reyes says the wiring in our float for the parade keeps failing, and nobody knows why. I'm going to find out. Today I learn to measure resistance." She clipped one probe to each end of the wire and read the screen. "Voltage is six. Now the current." She switched the dial, and the numbers crawled into place. "Zero point five amps. So resistance equals voltage divided by current. Six divided by zero point five. That's twelve ohms."

"Twelve what?"

"Ohms. That's how much the wire fights the current." Gabriella jumped up, thrilled with herself. "I can't see resistance, but I can calculate it from things I can see. That's the logic of it. Measure voltage, measure current, divide."

Devi rolled down the ramp and stopped in a spray of gravel. "Show me on the float."

They dragged the float, a decorated trailer with three lights strung along one side, into the shade of the bleachers. Gabriella assessed the problem bulb by bulb, pressing each one and checking her numbers. Then she traced the wire with her finger and stopped.

"Wait. There's only one path. All three bulbs share one loop through the battery." She tugged a bulb loose, and all three lights went dark. She stared at it, then at Devi, then grabbed her notebook. "That's the whole problem! One bulb breaks at the parade, everything goes black. Every time."

"So add more batteries?"

"No. Rewire it." Her hands were already moving, unplugging and reconnecting the synthetic insulation she'd stripped back, looping each bulb to the battery on its own. When she finished, she pulled out the middle bulb. The other two stayed lit. She pulled a second one. The last one still glowed.

"Whoa," Devi said. "They don't care."

"Because each bulb has its own path to the battery now, so the others stay lit if one breaks." Gabriella screwed the bulbs back in and all three blazed against the bleachers, bright enough that a kid on the ramps turned to look.

"Test it again," Devi said, grinning.

Gabriella unplugged, replugged, unplugged, replugged, faster each time, the lights stubbornly staying on. Then she measured the voltage and current on the new wire, did the division in her head, and wrote the resistance in her notebook in big letters.

"Twelve ohms," she announced to the whole park, "and unbreakable lights. Parade's on Saturday. Be there."

The bell over the door had barely stopped jingling when Jeremy started alphabetizing the antacids. He helped out at Reyes Pharmacy every Saturday because his mother worked the register, and because Dr. Reyes herself, an eccentric woman who wore a different vintage hat for every holiday, had told him that a shelf in perfect order could signify a mind in perfect order. Jeremy wasn't sure his mind was in order. For two weeks he'd been snapping at his mom, staring at his ceiling until one in the morning, and getting stomachaches before school, and he didn't know why.

He found a pamphlet in the rack beside the register, the one about stress. It said to watch for tight shoulders, short tempers, and wrecked sleep. Then it gave him an idea he could actually test: breathe in slowly for four counts, hold for four, let it out for four. Three rounds. He stood between the cough syrup and the foot powder and tried it, feeling like an idiot, but by the second round his shoulders had dropped an inch. He tested it again that night, and instead of lying awake he was asleep before his phone's second reminder. So the pattern was real. Something he couldn't see, tension he couldn't point at, could still be measured and loosened.

Then Tyler's message arrived on Sunday, and Jeremy read it three times before answering. "Can I crash at your place soon? Home is bad right now. Don't ask why." Tyler, who always joked in class, who never typed anything shorter than a paragraph, had sent eleven words. Jeremy remembered the pamphlet's list, and now the signs weren't his. They were Tyler's, and Jeremy hadn't spotted them sooner because he'd been too busy cataloguing his own.

He tried the breathing at the pharmacy counter while his mom rang up a customer, because his chest had gone tight the way the pamphlet described. While he breathed, he thought. He couldn't fix whatever "bad" meant at Tyler's house. He didn't even know what it was, and Tyler had said not to ask. But the pamphlet's back page had one more line he'd skipped, about worried friends, and it listed who could be told: a parent, a teacher, a school counselor, the school nurse, or a doctor. Jeremy looked up. Dr. Reyes was standing right there, counting pills, and the plaque on the wall behind her said Doctor of Pharmacy.

"I have a friend who seems scared all the time," Jeremy said. "I don't know what's going on, but I don't want to just sit on it."

Dr. Reyes set down her tray and studied him over her hat brim. "You're not sitting on it. You're telling somebody, and telling somebody is the whole job."

"I'm telling you first because you're here," Jeremy said. "Monday I'll tell my homeroom teacher too. Maybe the counselor."

"Then you've already done the hard part." She pulled a stool over beside the counter and patted it. "Sit down and breathe, kid. In for four."

Jeremy sat, and he breathed.

The letter was waiting on Grandpa's kitchen table when Noah arrived, and he tore it open before he even unpacked his bag. "Noah," Grandma had written from her sister's place, "take care of Grandpa. Count the cigarette packs in the bin for me. I'll be home Sunday. P.S. Try the breathing trick I taught you when your head gets loud." Noah read it twice. Grandma never asked him to count anything unless she was worried, and his stomach did a small flip.

By Wednesday evening he had counted four empty packs, when last summer there had been only one a week. That night he lay awake in the guest room, heart drumming, thinking about it. This was the same jittery feeling he'd had after his concussion in the fall, when the doctor had told him to isolate himself in a quiet room until his head healed. Grandma had shown him back then how slow breaths could settle a racing body, in for four counts, out for six. He tried it now, ten slow breaths, and his thoughts stopped sprinting. Sleep came easier than he expected.

Thursday morning he rode his bike to the pharmacy in the affluent neighborhood across the highway, the one with the fountain out front, because Grandpa needed his blood pressure pills anyway. While the pharmacist, a woman named Dana, filled the order, Noah blurted out his question. "My grandpa smokes way more than he used to. Does smoking change how much you need?"

Dana looked at him carefully. "With regular use, the brain adapts to nicotine, so a person needs more of it to feel the same effect," she said. "It's called tolerance." She handed him a pamphlet about quitting support. Noah gripped it like treasure. So the packs weren't just Grandpa being careless. The habit itself was growing, like a plant nobody pruned.

He tested his idea that evening. "Grandpa," he said at dinner, "how many did you smoke when you started?" Grandpa thought, fork halfway to his mouth. "Two a day, maybe. Navy days." "And now?" A pause. "Don't count, kid." But his ears went red, and Noah had his answer.

Later, on the porch, Grandpa lit another one and Noah sat beside him. "Grandma's home Sunday," Noah said. "Want to talk to her about the pamphlet? I'll do the breathing stuff with you if it gets hard." Grandpa stared at him for a long moment, then laughed and stubbed the cigarette out after only three puffs. "You count my packs," he said, "I'll count your slow breaths. Deal?"

Hazel stood on the back porch of Marisol's birthday party holding a paper with six numbered lines on it, because tomorrow she had to run the first Nature Club meeting of the year and she had never run anything except a lemonade stand that failed. Marisol had offered her party as a practice audience. "Pretend we're the club," Marisol said, waving a forkful of cake at the six kids scattered around the porch. "You be the conductor."

"Conductor of what?" asked Theo.

"Of the meeting," Hazel said. "Like an orchestra, except with people who all want to talk about salamanders at once." She read the first line of her agenda. "Item one: does anyone actually want to sell candy at the fall fair, or was that just Mr. Ruiz's idea?" It went surprisingly well for two items. Priya argued, Dev made a joke about the treasurer's report, but everyone got a turn, and Hazel started to believe she could do this.

Then item three fell apart because of the laughing.

A boy named Quinn was standing near the snack table, and two kids from another school, Rex and some kid Hazel didn't know, were circling him. "Nice shoes," Rex kept saying. "No, really. Nice shoes." They said it in that voice that meant the opposite, and Quinn's ears went red, and every time Rex spoke, the second kid laughed like a drum machine.

Hazel's first idea was to say something sharp to Rex. She even opened her mouth. But then she noticed something she couldn't see directly, only its shadow: Rex kept glancing sideways before each joke, checking whether the porch was still watching. It was like watching a performer count his audience. The laughing kid was the audience. Take away the audience, she thought, and what's left?

She revised her plan mid-breath. "Quinn!" she called, loud and casual. "Come on, let's go. I need help with the snacks in the kitchen." Quinn blinked, then pushed off the table and followed her through the screen door. Rex opened his mouth for another "nice shoes," but there was nobody left to hear it except his one friend, and somehow that wasn't enough. When Hazel peeked back through the window thirty seconds later, Rex was standing there looking bizarre, like a magician whose trick had ended early, and then he wandered off toward the bounce house.

In the kitchen, Quinn dumped chips into a bowl without being asked. "Thanks," he said. "That was getting old."

"That's the whole trick, I think," Hazel said. "They need people watching. No watchers, no show." She looked at her agenda, all six items, and realized item three had taught her more than items one and two put together. Tomorrow she would write the meeting plan differently, with room for whatever actually happened. "Okay, back to the porch," she said. "We never settled the candy question, and I still have three items left. Bring the chips."

Matteo sat cross-legged on the living room rug with his laptop balanced on the coffee table, glaring at a spreadsheet with four hundred rows of survey answers. His class had asked the whole school, "What's your favorite school lunch?", and somehow he had volunteered to summarize the results by grade. His sister Priya, home from college, was doing something on her phone nearby, occasionally flourishing a pretzel at the screen as if celebrating herself.

"I can't do this," he said. "There are too many rows. I'd have to count forever."

"That's why you use a pivot table," Priya said without looking up. "Drag grade into rows, lunch into columns, and it counts for you."

He tried it, and the numbers snapped into place like magic. Sixth grade loved pizza; eighth grade, weirdly, loved the salad bar. He was about to email the file to his teacher when a box popped up on his laptop: someone was trying to log in to his account, and the attempt came from another country. A second later, Priya's phone buzzed. She held it up. "This is your account asking for a code. Why is your account texting me?"

"That's not me," Matteo said, his stomach dropping. "Someone has my password."

Last summer flashed into his mind: he had used the same password for a game site that later got hacked, and he'd never bothered to change it anywhere else. He'd thought, at the time, that nothing important was attached. He was wrong now, and he knew it, watching the login box glow on his screen.

Then he noticed something. The login attempt hadn't gone through. Instead of letting the stranger in, his account had asked for a code sent to a phone, and the code had gone to Priya's phone, not the stranger's. Priya read the message aloud. "Two-factor authentication," she said. "It wants a second proof, a code sent to a phone, so a stolen password on its own is not enough to log in."

"So they can't get in," Matteo said slowly. "Even with my password."

"Correct. Now change your password before they try anything else, and this time make it a legitimate one, not your dog's name."

He changed it, and while he was at it, he checked the login history. The attempt had come from a country he'd never visited, at an hour when he'd been asleep. He copied the details into an email for the survey file instead, then paused, because something about the timing itched at him. He pulled up the survey spreadsheet and made a new pivot table, this time summarizing who had answered the survey and when. The suspicious login had happened three minutes after he'd emailed the file link to his group chat, which included a kid named Devon, whose family had just moved from Portugal. Matteo built a quick filter, then another, testing his idea, and the pattern held: the only person who could have seen the link and had any reason to guess Matteo's password was someone who'd watched him type it during agriculture club, where they shared the greenhouse signup computer.

"It was Devon," Matteo announced. "He saw me log in at the greenhouse. He probably just wanted to read the lunch results early, so he'd know whether pizza won before anyone else."

Priya lowered her pretzel. "So your grand mystery was a nosy kid and a salad bar?"

"And I still have to finish the report," Matteo said, and dragged one more field into the pivot table.

Zack spread his blank essay packet across the library table and stared at the prompt: Should the town build a skate plaza in Milliken Park? The trouble wasn't the topic. It was line one, where his teacher had written in red, "Thesis first. Three points. Outline before drafting." Zack had never done it that way, and his first draft had come back looking like a ransom note of half-ideas.

Priya dropped into the chair across from him, hugging her own folder. She wanted the history essay prize so badly she'd been carrying her research everywhere for two weeks, even to lunch. "You look like your brain hurts," she said.

"It does. I wrote the whole essay, and Mr. Okafor circled the first paragraph and wrote 'flat.'" Zack turned the draft so she could see. "Flat. Like a deflated basketball." He flipped to his favorite part, where he described a skater named Dario sailing over a nine-stair set on opening day. "This part is the best thing in it, and it's at the beginning. I don't get why that's wrong."

Priya tapped the page. "Maybe because it's like telling the punchline first." She was already opening her own folder, hungry to get back to her gold-rush sources, but she paused. "In my book club book, everything terrible happens before the big scene at the end. My sister said that's called rising action." She said it like she was tossing him a key she'd found on the ground. "The problems pile up so the big scene matters."

Zack sat back. Complications, stacking like quarters, before the climax. So what if he saved Dario's flight for the end of the essay and put the buildup first: the cracked sidewalks that made skaters dodge walkers, the tickets, the petitions with their frail, curling edges? Each one was a complication that raised the stakes. He grabbed a fresh sheet and wrote "Thesis:" at the top, then "Point 1, Point 2, Point 3" down the margin. It felt strange, building the frame before the walls, but his intuition said the bones mattered. "So point one is the safety argument," he muttered, "point two is cost, and point three keeps the park busy instead of empty after dark."

He remembered fourth grade then, when Danny Ruiz had ridiculed his book report in front of the whole class, calling it "one big spoiler," and Zack hadn't understood until this moment what Danny meant. He'd opened with the last scene of the book and read it aloud first. No wonder everyone had glazed over.

"Hey Priya," Zack whispered, already filling in point three. She looked up from her folder. "The outline's working. It's like scaffolding." He slid his pen down to the final line and wrote, fast, before the idea could escape him: Save Dario for last.

The counselor's poster said Know Your Stress Signs, and Zoey had copied the list into her notebook on Monday: tight shoulders, snapping at people, trouble sleeping. By Thursday she had checked off all three, because the science fair was in six days and her model of an estuary, where the river met the sea, still looked like a puddle of glue. At lunch she stared at it and realized her hands were shaking. She excused herself to the hallway, sat against the lockers, and breathed the way the poster showed, in for four counts, out for four, until the hallway stopped buzzing.

That was where Marcus found her. He plunked down beside her with his gym bag, and Zoey noticed something right away: two sixth graders walking past turned their heads and drifted to the far side of the hall, the way you'd steer around a spill. Marcus had come straight from basketball practice, hair still damp with sweat, and he had that slumped look Zoey recognized from her own bad days.

"Nobody's sitting with me in the caf," he said. "Third day in a row. I keep thinking it's something I said."

Zoey breathed out slowly, thinking. It wasn't something he said, because he'd said plenty on Monday and people had laughed. It had started after practice resumed this week, and only around Marcus, only in the afternoons. A pattern like that pointed to one hidden cause, and she tested her idea out loud. "Did you change anything this week? Like, are you showering after practice?" Marcus admitted the new coach didn't enforce it, so he'd been skipping and just changing shirts, figuring a quick rinse at home would cover it.

"Showering with soap after exercise washes away the sweat and bacteria that cause body odor," Zoey said, quoting her health teacher's handout, which she'd stuffed in her notebook on Tuesday. "A dry shirt doesn't." Marcus groaned but looked almost relieved, because a shower was a fixable problem, unlike everybody hating you.

That night Zoey wrote him a note and slipped it through the vent of his locker the next morning, since his phone was confiscated until his math grade improved. "Report: I slept eight hours last night because I put my estuary model away at nine and did my breathing thing. You? Shower with soap after practice, then tell me if people stop edging away. Meet me at lunch, either way. Signed, a fellow work in progress. P.S. My stress shoulders are 50 percent less tight."

At lunch Marcus dropped his tray across from her, hair curling and clean, smelling of soap instead of gym. Two sixth graders sat down at the end of the table without steering around anyone, and Marcus grinned and held up a folded reply note. "Eight and a half hours," he read, "and nobody moved away. Testing continues tomorrow."

Bentley unfolded the agenda he had written on the bus that morning, smoothing the crease with his palm. The robotics club met in the art room after last bell, and today, for the first time, he was in charge. Ms. Okafor had left a note on the whiteboard: "Bentley runs it. I'm at a district meeting." He read it twice, then pinned his paper to the easel.

"First item," he said. "Fundraising. The hardware store sponsor pulled out because of the recession, so we need two hundred dollars for parts before the regional meet." He looked around the circle of chairs. "Priya, you had an idea?"

Before Priya could answer, Dex snickered. "Two hundred dollars? Maybe Priya can sell some of her thirty-seven pencils." A few kids laughed. Priya stared at the floor, and Bentley noticed something he had noticed for weeks without really seeing it: after every joke, Dex glanced over at whoever had laughed, quick as a reflex, checking his audience like a satellite checking its orbit.

Bentley had laughed along last week. He remembered it now, the way the sound had come out of him easy and warm, not because the joke was funny but because sitting in the laughing group felt safer than sitting outside it. Dex had grinned right at him afterward and doubled down on Priya's pencil case.

"Fundraising ideas," Bentley said again, keeping his voice level. This time, when Dex cracked a joke about Marcus's laces, Bentley kept his face still. He caught Priya's eye and gave a small shake of his head, and she pressed her lips together and didn't laugh either. Marcus rubbed his sneaker and stayed quiet too. Dex's next joke came out quieter. The one after that trailed off halfway through, and Dex pulled his phone from his pocket and scrolled instead, glancing up once at a circle of faces that gave him nothing.

Priya cleared her throat. "Car wash," she said. "Two Saturdays from now, in the faculty lot. My uncle has hoses."

They voted, and the car wash won by a margin significant enough that they moved straight to item two, assigning jobs. Priya took posters, Marcus took towels, and Dex, without being asked, said he'd handle sponges.

That night Bentley lay on his bed and texted Priya: "Did you see that? He stopped when nobody laughed." Her reply came fast: "I saw. Last year I laughed too. Every time. I keep thinking about that." Bentley typed and deleted three different answers, trying to decide whether to tell her he was thinking about it too. The cursor blinked. Downstairs, the dishwasher hummed into its rinse cycle.

Priya, as it turned out, made the first move. A folded note landed on his desk the next morning in science class. He opened it under the desk. "Next meeting," it read, "I'll hold the agenda sheet while you talk. Then you can watch the room instead of the paper. P.S. Nobody's laughed at Dex since Tuesday. He sat with Marcus at lunch."

Bentley read the last line twice. He looked across the room to where Dex was leaning over Marcus's notebook, pointing at something and asking a question in a low voice. Bentley slipped the note into his binder, between the pages of his lab report where it wouldn't get crushed, and raised his hand to answer the question on the board.

Lincoln stood at the edge of the school auditorium stage, holding a stack of note cards so tightly that the corners bent. In three weeks he would debate the meatless Mondays plan in front of the whole sixth grade, and his partner, Priya, had just flipped her cards facedown on the folding table. "We have a problem," she said. "Read our first point out loud."

Lincoln read it. His cousin Marco had gone vegetarian last spring, and by June he was tired all the time and quit. Our claim is that meatless Mondays make kids unhealthy, and this proves it. He looked up at the empty seats, then at the banner from last year's debate finals still hanging crooked over the stage. "It sounded good when we wrote it," he said. Priya tapped the card with two fingers. "Every point needs a claim, evidence and a warrant. The claim is fine. But watch what happens when I argue back." She cleared her throat like a lawyer on TV. "My cousin went vegetarian and felt great, so vegetarian eating is healthy. Now what?"

Lincoln paced across the boards, his sneakers squeaking. Both cousins could be real, and they pointed in opposite directions, so a single story could not settle anything. That had to be a rule, a pattern he could not see directly but could infer from the way the arguments crashed into each other. "So one person's story, whichever person it is, can't prove a general trend," he said slowly. "Marco might just be Marco." Priya nodded. "It's called anecdotal evidence. Our whole case is anecdotal evidence, one cousin tall."

They went to work. Priya pulled up the lunch counts on the library tablet while Lincoln searched for a real study of school menus, and they rebuilt each point the right way: claim first, evidence that covered many students, then the warrant explaining why the evidence supported the claim. When Lincoln got stuck on his second point, he tested the warrant out loud like a hinge. "Kids need protein to focus, and the study shows focus dropped at schools that cut protein. That connects." It did connect. His shoulders came down an inch.

At rehearsal the next day, Ms. Okafor sat in the third row eating carrot sticks and played the opposing team. She fired the cousin argument at them, the same trap that had eaten their old case, and Lincoln answered without reading a card. "One story cannot prove a trend, because a single case may not be typical. Our study looks at thousands of students." Ms. Okafor raised her carrot like a gavel and called the round for them. Walking offstage, Lincoln straightened the old banner so it hung level, then turned to Priya and said, "Same time Thursday? I want to work on the rebuttals."

Lillian's grandmother had always made dinner look easy, but tonight Lillian was alone in the kitchen with three recipes and one oven, and nothing about it felt easy. Her brother Devan sat at the counter doing homework, which mostly meant watching her.

"You're going to burn something," he said.

"I'm not. I'm going to prioritize." She tapped the printed recipe she'd found on an American website. "Rice takes twenty minutes, the curry simmers for thirty, and the flatbread bakes at 350 degrees Fahrenheit for twelve. The problem is our oven only shows Celsius. It doesn't say Fahrenheit anywhere."

Devan leaned over the recipe anyway, because what he really wanted was for dinner to include the flatbread. He'd been asking for it since Tuesday, and he didn't care about temperatures, only that the bread came out warm and puffed instead of flat and sad. "So what's 350 in Celsius?"

"That's what I have to figure out." Lillian had a candidate answer from a conversion chart printed in tiny letters at the bottom of another recipe page: 350 degrees Fahrenheit was about 175 to 180 degrees Celsius. But she didn't fully trust a chart she'd found by accident, so she decided to test it before the bread went in.

She set the oven to 175 Celsius and put in a spoonful of butter on a scrap of foil. In her grandmother's oven, at the right heat, butter melted and browned gently in about two minutes; too hot and it hissed and scorched almost at once. She watched through the glass. The butter slid into a golden pool, quiet and slow, no smoke. She tried 180 and watched again. Same gentle melt. Somewhere between those two numbers, she decided, the American recipe lived. "One-seven-five," she said, setting the dial back. "Maybe one-eighty. It's a range, not one exact number."

Then she worked backward through the timing, because everything had to land on the table at the same moment. She started the curry first, since it needed the longest, then rinsed the rice and set it bubbling, and only when the rice had ten minutes left did she roll the dough and slide the flatbread into the warm oven. Devan abandoned his homework entirely and stood beside her at the oven door.

"Is it supposed to puff like that?" he asked.

"That's exactly what it's supposed to do." She pulled the bread out, checked that the dish towel she'd left near the burner was nowhere near the flame, since cloth was flammable and she'd nearly learned that lesson the hard way last month, and carried everything to the table in one careful parade.

Devan tore the flatbread in half before she'd even sat down. Steam curled out of it. "Okay," he said, mouth already full. "You can prioritize dinner every night from now on."

Claire kept a systematic list in her notebook titled "What Makes a Story Work," and so far it had three items: dialogue goes in quotation marks, each new speaker gets a new paragraph, and something big has to happen near the end. Today was the read-aloud in Mr. Reyes's room, and she had signed up first.

Her story was about a dog named Biscuit who slipped his leash and ran into the woods behind the school. In her favorite part, the narrator waded through brush and found Biscuit hiding under a log covered with a shelf-like fungus, trembling but safe. She had checked every line of dialogue twice. "Come here, boy," the narrator called. "It's okay." Commas, quotation marks, new paragraphs, all correct. She raised her hand when Mr. Reyes called her name.

She read slowly, saving the best part. When she reached the log, the room got quiet. Marcus, who sat in front and usually drew monsters during read-alouds, had actually put down his pencil. Claire's voice sped up. "The branches snapped back as she knelt. 'Come here, boy,' she called. 'It's okay.' Biscuit crept out and pressed against her legs." She stopped. That was the last line on the page, and it felt like landing a jump off a high wall.

Marcus's hand shot up. "What happened to the dog after that? Did she take him home? Did her mom find out she skipped piano to look for him?" Three other kids nodded. Marcus said, "You can't just stop. I'll boycott sharing day if people keep doing endings like that." A few kids laughed, but Claire's stomach dropped. She had spent all her time on the dialogue and the rescue, and she hadn't noticed that the story quit exactly when the exciting part was over.

She sat down and pulled out her notebook. Mr. Reyes was walking around checking drafts, so she tapped Marcus's shoulder. "You said what happened after. Is there a name for that part?" Marcus shrugged, but Priya behind them held up a checklist from the writing folder and pointed to the last two lines. Claire read them, then read them again. "Falling action and resolution," she said under her breath.

At lunch she added to her list, working through it line by line. After the climax, the falling action and resolution show the consequences of what happened and tie up the story's loose ends. Priya's question was still ringing in her ears, so Claire flipped to a clean page and started writing. "They walked home in the dark, Biscuit's leash wound twice around her wrist. Her mom was on the porch, and she was not smiling." Marcus leaned over from the next seat. "Now I want to know what the mom says."

Joshua had been saving for a new bike all summer, and the lemonade stand was supposed to be his ticket there, but by two o'clock on Saturday he had earned only four dollars and a quarter. He was stirring the last pitcher with a long spoon when Marcus, the teenager from three houses down, pedaled up the street and stopped at the curb, looking bothered.

"You got customers?" Marcus asked, mopping sweat off his forehead with his sleeve. "I need cash today. I'm trying to sell a bond my grandpa gave me. Ten dollars for a ten-dollar bond. It's worth ten, so that's fair, right?"

Joshua poured him a cup. "What's a bond?"

"It's like a loan," Marcus said. "The government pays you interest for lending it money. Mine pays a tiny bit. Grandpa bought it years ago. But I've asked six people and nobody will give me ten dollars for it. Not even nine. Best offer was eight." He looked down the street as if another buyer might appear out of the heat shimmer rising off the pavement.

Joshua frowned. Something about that didn't add up, and he wanted to figure it out, because Marcus was promising five dollars to whoever helped him sell the thing, and five dollars plus four twenty-five was almost half the bike. He thought about the lemonade. Yesterday he had charged a dollar a cup, and today Mrs. Delgado had told him the store brand was on sale for fifty cents, so she would only buy his at half price. His lemonade hadn't changed. The other lemonade had gotten cheaper. So the price of his old lemonade had fallen because something new had appeared that was a better deal.

"Wait," Joshua said slowly. "Did interest rates go up lately? Like, did you hear that somewhere?"

Marcus shrugged. "Yeah, my mom was complaining about it. New bonds pay more interest than they used to. Everybody keeps saying that."

"Then that's it," Joshua said. "People can get new bonds that pay more interest, so nobody's going to pay you full price for your old one. When interest rates rise, the prices of bonds that already exist fall." He set down the spoon. "It's like my lemonade. It's the same lemonade, but the competition changed, so my price had to change."

Marcus stared at the cup in his hands. "So my bond isn't broken? It's just... out of date?"

"Right. It's still worth something, just not ten dollars." Joshua wiped his hands on his shorts. "Take the eight. And then come help me run this stand, because my whole network of customers is two families and a mail carrier, and I've been negligent about putting up signs on Elm Street. With two of us, we can sell the rest of this pitcher and regulate the price so we both make money."

Marcus drained his lemonade, slapped eight dollars of future earnings on the counter as a promise, and dragged the folding table into the shade where more people could see it.

The smell of whiteboard marker hung in the air of Room 12 as Noemie stared at the board. 3x + 4 = 19. She was supposed to do the same thing to both sides, like a scale that had to stay balanced, but the x kept hiding behind the numbers, refusing to show what it was worth.

"How do you know it balances if you can't see inside?" she asked her lab partner, Deshawn.

"You just trust it," he said, tapping his pencil. Deshawn wanted to beat his older brother, who had finished this worksheet in ten minutes flat. He was racing, and racing made him messy.

Noemie tried it anyway. Take 4 from both sides. 3x = 15. Divide both sides by 3. She whispered it aloud, feeling the balance of it, and wrote x = 5. She checked by putting 5 back in, and both sides came out 19, like two doors opening onto the same room. Something she couldn't see had been there the whole time, and she had dug it out.

Then came the next problem, and the trouble. Deshawn grabbed the marker and wrote 2x + 3x + 3 = 23. Under it, fast and confident, he scribbled 5x + 3 = 23, then kept going, but before that he had crossed something out. Noemie leaned over. His first line had said 2x + 3 = 5x, treating the lonely 3 as if it belonged with the x's.

"You combined the 3 with the 2x," she said.

"So? They're all smushed together on the same side."

"But they're not the same kind of thing." She picked up a handful of counters from the bin. Two red counters, then three more red counters. "Two x's plus three x's, that's five x's." She set down a single blue counter. "But this 3 is just a 3. You can't squish it in with the x ones. It's like adding apples to a mystery box."

Deshawn frowned at the counters. "The 2x and the 3x are like terms," he said slowly, as if remembering something. He tried combining the 2x and 3x first, leaving the plain 3 alone, then subtracted 3 from both sides and got 5x = 20. "So x is 4." He checked it, and his face split into a grin. He was still going to tell his brother he'd won.

At lunch, Deshawn pushed his tray across the table toward Noemie, offering half a cookie, a small payment that symbolized more than it looked. "My grandma," he said, "she's a retired teacher. I told her about the apples and the mystery box, and she asked me one thing. She asked, 'What does the x stand for?'"

"What did you say?"

"I said, I have no idea, but it's definitely not a 3."

Noemie laughed so abruptly that milk nearly came out of her nose. "Okay, but seriously. What does it stand for?"

Deshawn shrugged and bit into the cookie. "Grandma says that's the whole game. Find out what's hiding."

Natalie had one day left before her grandmother flew in from Monterrey, and so far she could say exactly one full sentence in Spanish: "Tengo un perro pequeño que se llama Biscuit." She said it to the mirror, to the toaster, and to Biscuit himself, who wagged at anything with her voice attached to it. Her mother, who advocated loudly for family bonds whenever Natalie wanted to skip a call, had made her a deal: describe every person and pet in the house in full sentences by tonight, and she could pick the movie on Friday.

She was working on "Mi hermano Marcus tiene quince años y toca la guitarra mal" when Marcus wandered in eating cereal from the box. "You know what's weird," he said. "In French class we just learned you're supposed to say vous to strangers. Like, always. Madame Perrin made us practice it on the janitor and he looked so confused."

Natalie wrote that down, mostly to make him go away. Then she texted her friend Priya, who took German on weekends, and Priya sent back a single message: "Sie. Same thing. My teacher says you'd sound like a toddler without it." So French had vous, German had Sie, and Natalie had a suspicion her Spanish book was hiding the same rule somewhere. The book only said usted meant "you," which was spectacularly unhelpful, since tú also meant "you." Two words, one meaning, no explanation. There had to be a pattern, and nobody was going to hand it to her.

The doorbell rang before she could stew on it. On the porch stood a small older woman in a raincoat, holding a handwritten address that had clearly survived a washing machine. "Busco Maple Street," she said. "Perdón, ¿dónde queda?"

Here it was: a stranger, a real one, asking directions, and Natalie's mouth was already loading the familiar tú she used with Marcus and Biscuit. She caught it mid-launch. Testing time. "Queda a dos cuadras, señora," Natalie said. "¿Usted busca la casa azul?" The woman's whole face did something warm and unhurried, like a cat settling into sun. She talked for a full minute about her granddaughter, the weather in Guadalajara, and the terrible numbering on Maple Street, and Natalie understood maybe half of it and nodded at all the right gaps. When she left, the woman squeezed her arm and said, "Qué niña tan educada."

Natalie closed the door and stood there feeling extremely spontaneous, in a planned and rehearsed sort of way. Then she went back to the kitchen, erased half her sentence list, and rewrote every line for her grandmother in the usted form, out loud, while Biscuit supervised from the warm spot by the fridge. "Mi abuela llega mañana," she told him. "Ella es la persona más terca que yo conozco." Biscuit yawned. From the hallway, Marcus called, "Was that Spanish or did you hurt yourself?"

"Usted no entiende nada," she called back.

The paper was creased into eighths from living in Eleanor's back pocket, and the blessing on it had gone soft at the folds. Her bat mitzvah was in three weeks, and she still stumbled in the same spot every time, right where the melody jumped. She sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor, cat at her knee, and sang it again. "V'ein keil," she began, and then the jump came and she lost her place, and the cat flattened her ears like she'd been struck.

Her mother called up that Rabbi Solomon wanted the blessing memorized before Friday, because after Friday there would be no time to rehearse. Eleanor didn't understand that. Sunday had always been her slow day, the day for sprawl and practice. She went downstairs to argue the schedule, but her mother was on the porch with her calendar, so Eleanor folded her paper smaller and put it away.

Then she remembered she was spending Friday night at Zoe's house. She'd been looking forward to it all week, mostly because Zoe had a new phone and a trampoline. She packed pajamas and her toothbrush, and she slid the creased paper in her bag too, in case there was a quiet moment.

At six o'clock, just as the sky over the hills went orange, Zoe's mother stood in the kitchen doorway and held out a basket. "Phones in here, please, girls. It's Shabbat now." Zoe dropped hers in without complaining, which surprised Eleanor more than the basket did. Eleanor handed hers over slowly. "It starts at sunset," Zoe said, "Friday sunset. It goes until tomorrow night, after it's dark out. Then we do Havdalah and everything comes back on." Eleanor had known the word Shabbat her whole life but she had never watched it arrive before, like weather you could time by a clock.

That night, after pizza and cards by candlelight, Eleanor sat on Zoe's bedroom floor while Zoe braided and unbraided a length of yarn. She took out her paper and tried the blessing under her breath. Away from her own house, away from the piano where she always got lost, the jump in the melody came easier. "V'ein keil," she sang, and this time she sailed right over the gap, and Zoe said, "Do that part again, it's pretty."

The next evening they stood on the porch waiting for three stars to show, because nightfall, Zoe explained, meant dark, really dark, not just sunset. When the sky finally went black, Zoe's father lit a twisted candle and they passed spices around and said the goodbyes to Shabbat, and then the phones came back and everyone's screens glowed blue all at once. Eleanor checked hers and found nothing waiting that mattered. She walked home through the cold carrying the tune in her head, whole and unbroken, and she sang it all the way up her own front steps.

The auditorium smelled like dust and old curtains, which Connor decided was the smell of drama class in general. Mr. Ruiz had them up on the stage in pairs, and the assignment was simple and terrifying: improvise a scene where you accept every offer with "yes, and." No denying, no changing the subject. Connor's partner, Maya, held an invisible object and said, "I found this compass on the floor of the spaceship."

"Yes, and it's pointing toward the equator instead of north," Connor said, taking it carefully, like it might be fragile. "Yes, and that means we're flying upside down." Maya's eyebrows went up, which he chose to read as approval.

Between turns they sat on the edge of the stage, feet dangling, while other pairs performed. Down in the third row, Connor's grandfather was practicing a speech he was giving at the community center on Saturday, about his old plumbing business. He'd started strong, but halfway through he frowned at his notes and said, "Now, where was I," and then just stopped, staring at the page like it had personally betrayed him. He'd done the same thing twice before, always around the middle, and always with that same lost look.

Connor watched him try again, lose the thread again in the same spot, and started thinking. A speech wasn't a book. Grandpa couldn't flip back a page the way a reader could, so once a listener was lost, they stayed lost. Unless something in the words themselves told you where you were. He glanced at the notes. Grandpa said "next" twice and then just wandered off into a story about a water heater. What if the problem was the wandering, the lack of anything that announced a new part?

Connor slid off the stage, walked down the aisle, and suggested Grandpa mark each part before it started. "First, second, finally," Connor said. "Say them out loud." Grandpa grumbled that he wasn't in kindergarten, but he tried it, and this time when he reached the middle he said, "Second," and his eyes stopped drifting, and the audience of two empty seats and one grandson could follow him all the way to "finally."

Back onstage, Maya was already setting up their next scene. "Okay, new rule," she said. "You keep saying where we are, and I'll keep saying yes."

"So you want signposting words in an improv about a doomed spaceship."

"Obviously," said Maya, and held out the invisible compass again.

Alexandra lay on her bedroom floor with a notebook, a pencil, and a grudge against her own science project. The assignment was to study something you couldn't see directly, and for three days she had been trying to observe her own stress, which was like trying to photograph wind. What she did have was data: every time she felt wound up, she wrote down the time. Wednesday, 4:15, felt like screaming. Wednesday, 9:40, stomach in knots. Thursday, 3:50, snapped at the dog. Thursday, 9:55, couldn't fall asleep until after eleven.

Her cousin Marcus, who was seventeen and living in their spare room while he "figured things out," leaned against her doorframe. "You're tracking your freak-outs? That's adorable."

"It's a science project," Alexandra said. "And they're not freak-outs, they're stress responses." The school nurse had shown her class a breathing trick last week, slow breath in for four counts, out for six, and Alexandra had been testing it like a hypothesis. It worked, mostly, but the knot kept coming back, and that was the part she couldn't explain. She was starting to suspect she was biased toward blaming her little brother for everything, since blaming him was easy and he rarely defended himself.

Marcus, meanwhile, was being weird. Alexandra noticed it because her notebook made her notice things now. On Friday he was fine at lunch, cracking jokes, helping Grandma dismantle the broken ceiling fan and put it back together so it actually worked better than before. Then around four he got twitchy. He jingled the coins in his pocket, paced the hallway, and snapped at the dog too. By seven he was calm again, back to jokes. Saturday, same thing. Calm at two, restless and snappish at four, calm again by seven thirty. She flipped back through her pages. Two days, two cycles, roughly two hours between calm and jumpy.

"Marcus," she said Saturday night, cornering him by the fridge, "do you vape?"

He got very interested in the inside of the refrigerator. "Why."

"Because you get restless every two hours, like clockwork. I charted it." She held up the notebook, where she'd drawn his pattern right under hers. "I read that the body clears about half the nicotine in roughly two hours. So a couple hours after you vape, half of it's gone, and you feel the urge for another dose. That's why you keep getting jumpy." She tapped the chart. "The pattern fits."

Marcus stared at the page for a long moment. "You're a menace," he said, but he didn't sound mad. "Coach thought I just had bad nerves. Grandma thinks it's my heritage, her side of the family, all high-strung. I thought I was broken."

"You're not broken, you're on a timer," Alexandra said. "Want to see the breathing thing? It won't fix the, you know, timer. But it might help the jumpy part. It works on my stomach knots about seventy percent of the time, which my teacher says is honestly pretty good science."

So they sat on the kitchen floor, because Alexandra insisted the floor made it more official, and breathed in for four and out for six while the dog watched them like they'd both lost their minds. On the third round Marcus laughed so hard he broke the count, and Alexandra made him start over, which made him laugh again. But after ten rounds he rolled his shoulders and said, "Huh. The jittery feeling's still there, but it's quieter. Like somebody turned it down two notches."

Sunday night, Alexandra added a line to her sleep routine, lights out at nine thirty, no screens, notebook by the bed. Monday after school, Marcus appeared in her doorway holding two mugs of peppermint tea and his phone, which he handed over with a grimace. "Delete the vape shop app," he said. "And chart me again next weekend, science girl. I want proof I'm getting boring."

Alexandra grinned and hit delete. "Boring is the whole goal," she said, and opened her notebook to a fresh page.

Max stood in front of a painting of a narrow street at the city gallery, his sketchbook clamped under one arm, scowling. His homework was to draw a street using one-point perspective, where every line ran toward a single vanishing point, and his version at home looked like a street designed by a dizzy giant. He had a letter from his art teacher folded in his pocket, and he pulled it out and read it again. "Max," it said, "go find the museum's oldest street painting. Find the point where the buildings' edges would meet if you extended them with a ruler. Then look at the round things. The lamp, the fruit cart, the boy's ball. If a sphere is shaded, the highlight is the brightest spot, and it sits on the side facing the light. Its position shows you where the light is coming from. Copy that, and your street will stop looking flat."

The painting, he discovered, was in a room with a skylight, and it did have a fruit cart with an orange on it. Max found the vanishing point first, tracing the building edges with his pencil in the air until they all aimed at a spot on the far door of the street, like the whole town was sliding toward it. Then he looked at the orange. It had one bright dab of paint on its upper left side, brighter than anything else on it. He held up his pencil as a pretend lamp, imagining the light arriving from exactly there, and checked a marble on the cobblestones nearby. Brightest spot, upper left. The cart wheel's rim caught its shine on the upper left too. It was a rule hiding under the paint, invisible until you hunted for it, and now Max saw little spotlight dots everywhere, like the street was secretly lit by a guild of tiny invisible lamplighters, all standing in the same corner of the sky.

"Excuse me," said a girl beside him, maybe ten, holding her own sketchbook open to a gray circle that looked like a flat gray cookie. "Mine's supposed to be a sphere but it looks like a blob. The docent said I should shade it, but I don't know where."

"Which side is the lamp on?" Max asked. He had decided to pretend he was a gallery wizard, since the skylight made everything glow anyway. "A sphere's highlight is the brightest spot, and it's on the side facing the light. So pick where your lamp is, and put your brightest spot there."

The girl bit her lip, jabbed a finger at the upper right of her circle, and drew one small brilliant dot. The blob popped into a ball so suddenly that she laughed out loud, and a guard three rooms away said "Shh" with impressive authority for someone so far away.

Max sat down on the gallery bench and started a fresh street. This time he drew the vanishing point first, aimed every roofline at it like roads to a castle, and gave each round thing, a lamp, a barrel, a bicycle bell, its brightest spot on the upper left, so that his whole imaginary street was lit by the same invisible sun. He was halfway through when the girl leaned over and said, "Your street looks nutritious enough to eat," and Max, who had been thinking of it as a place, had to admit that a street you could eat was even better, so he added a bakery with round golden loaves in the window, each with one bright spot, upper left, shining.

Charlotte wanted the green record card, the one Mr. Dover awarded for a perfect graph, and she had been close twice. Today her plan was simple: roll the steel ball down the long ramp, time it with the electronic timer box, mark distance and time, and draw the graph. Speed was just distance divided by time, and a straight line on the graph would prove the ball kept the same pace. She could already picture the card taped above her desk.

Her friend Dev spread the paper tape along the ramp and pinned it at each end. "One meter, two meters, three," he said, tapping each mark. "You release, I read the timer." The timer box had a thin metal wire stretched across the ramp at each mark, and when the ball bent a wire, the box printed the elapsed seconds on its little screen. Dev blew on his cold fingers and joked that the lab was cold enough to submerge them all in hot chocolate.

Their first run was beautiful. Charlotte smoothed the tape, wrote the numbers, and rolled again. By the fourth run she frowned. The times were creeping. At the one-meter wire the ball that had taken 0.80 seconds was now showing 0.86, then 0.91, though she released it from exactly the same spot, the same angle, the same careful push. "The ball isn't slowing down," she said. "Watch it. It looks identical." Dev agreed, and they rolled a marker pen down the ramp as a test and saw it behave the same every time.

She opened the back of the timer box, because Mr. Dover let careful students look inside, and found the wires ran to a coiled component inside the case. Each wire felt warm, and the coil felt warmer still, almost like a mug of tea gone lukewarm. Charlotte thought about the cooling-beaker demo from last term, where a hot thing changes while it settles. She had an idea, and she decided to test it the way you test anything, by changing one thing only. She took a damp sponge from the sink, the porous kind that drank up water when you pressed it, laid the coil gently against it, and waited for the wires to cool. Then she rolled the ball once more.

0.79 seconds. Exactly where they started.

"Try it again," Dev said, bouncing on his toes. She ran the ball three more times, quick ones, before the box could warm up, and the numbers held steady. Then she left the timer running idle for five minutes, felt the wire warm against her wrist, and watched the times drift upward again. When she pressed the sponge to the coil one more time, the readings came back down.

"It's the wire," she said. "The resistance rises as it heats up, so it only stays steady while the temperature stays the same." Dev repeated the sentence slowly, as if tasting it, then wrote it in the margin of their results table. They took all their measurements in fast bursts with sponge breaks between them, and Charlotte laughed so hard at Dev ceremonially announcing "cooling the component, my lady" that she nearly dropped the pen.

Her graph came out a clean straight line, every dot sitting on it like beads on a string. Mr. Dover pinned it to the board and said the class would copy the method. Then he held out the green card. "One question first. Why the sponge?" Charlotte grinned, picked up the timer box, and held the back of it against his hand.

Sofia set out the last four jars of honey on the folding table, wiped the dust off the sign, and counted her cash box for the third time. Fifty-eight dollars. The bike at Reba's resale shop cost two hundred, and it might be gone by August. "You could put your money in the credit union," her mother had said that morning, but the whole idea felt as dry and arid as the August air blowing across the market lot, stirring grit between the stalls.

The vendor across the aisle, a teenager named Marisol who sold goat cheese, leaned over. "Slow day?"

"Somebody haggled me down on the honey and I said yes too fast," Sofia said. "I need to categorize my customers better. People who want a deal, people who just want honey." She said it like a joke, but the mistake still stung. She had studied percentages in math all spring, and knowing six percent of eight dollars should have taken her two seconds. The humiliation of freezing up in front of a stranger had kept her awake half the night.
