"Six percent," Marisol repeated, fanning herself with a paper bag. "That's what my account pays. I put my cheese money in every summer."

Sofia pulled her notebook from under the table. She had been saving one hundred dollars of birthday money, and now she wrote it out right there among the jars. If the account paid six percent simple interest, that was six dollars every year, and after five years she would have one hundred thirty dollars. That she could see plainly, like rows in a garden. But her mother had said to pick the compound kind, and compound was the strange one, where the interest earned its own interest. Sofia tried to picture money growing on money and got nowhere. It was invisible, a rule hiding under the numbers.

"Twelve years," Marisol said, reading over her shoulder. "That's when mine doubles. It's called the rule of 72. Divide 72 by the yearly percentage rate, and that's about how many years it takes to double."

Sofia had guessed doubling would take maybe ten years, because ten times six felt close to a hundred. Now she tested Marisol's rule against her own paper, scribbling year by year, letting each year's interest pile onto the last. After five years the compound account crept past one hundred thirty dollars, only a few dollars ahead of the simple one, which surprised her. But the gap kept widening, and somewhere near year twelve, her pencil crossed two hundred. She checked it twice.

"Seventy-two divided by six," she said slowly. "Twelve. You'd be what, twenty-nine?"

"Twenty-nine and rich in goat cheese," Marisol said.

The honey customer from that morning came back down the aisle, and Sofia straightened her sign, decided to hold her price this time. "Six dollars a jar," she said, "and every dollar goes in the compound account on Monday."

"Make it five and I'll take two."

"Five fifty," Sofia said, and held out her hand.

Kate had one hour before the planetarium's Junior Explainer tryout, and her ball still did not work right. She stood under the dome with a lamp, an orange painted like Earth, and a golf ball on a stick for the Moon, while Marcus from her science class leaned against the console eating pretzels.

"Remind me why I'm here," Marcus said, "instead of at the arcade winning a giant banana."

"Because you owe me for the volcano incident," Kate said. "And I need an audience." Her tryout talk was about the tilt of Earth's axis, how summer and winter come from which way the planet leans as it travels around the Sun. She could say it fine. The problem was the question afterward, the one Dr. Okafor always asked the candidates, the one nobody ever seemed ready for. Last year a boy had walked out mid-answer. Kate refused to be that kid.

She spun the golf ball around the orange to warm up, tilting the orange toward the lamp to show summer. Then she stopped, because something looked wrong. From where she stood, the golf ball showed only a sliver of light, a thin crescent. She moved her head sideways, and the crescent grew into a half, then a bulging globe. She frowned and turned the ball slowly again, watching.

"Move," Marcus said through a mouthful of pretzel. "You're blocking my view of your imminent failure."

"Look at the ball," Kate said. "Not the lit sliver. The whole ball." Marcus squinted and came closer, pretending he hadn't. Kate held the ball still between the lamp and herself. Half of it was bright. She rotated the stick without moving it out of that line, and the bright half stayed bright, exactly half, always. The crescent was just the part of that lit half facing them. "Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun," she said slowly. "The phases show how much of that lit half faces Earth. It's never actually a dark ball with a light stuck on it."

"So all those crescent drawings," Marcus said, "are just the moon being shy."

"Basically." Kate felt something click into place, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. If Dr. Okafor asked about phases, she could infer the answer from what she was seeing, not from a memorized line. For a moment she had felt real despair standing under that dome with a broken model and one hour. Now she had a working one and forty minutes.

Dr. Okafor came out early, arms crossed, and pointed at the golf ball. "Suppose, hypothetically, I asked you why the Moon looks full tonight. What would you tell me?"

Kate lifted the ball into the light and turned until the whole lit half faced her.

"Oops," said Marcus. "I dropped my pretzel."

Alexis pressed the sustain pedal too hard, and the last chord of "Sunrise on the River" clanged instead of fading. He lifted his hands off the keys and stared at the sheet music, where the composer had written a mysterious instruction: hold the final chord for eight full beats, growing softer until it disappears.

The problem was that the chord kept dying at beat five. He had tried pedaling differently, holding his hands flatter, even leaning his whole weight into the keys, but nothing worked. He needed to diagnose the trouble before Friday, when he and Priya would play the duet for the whole sixth grade.

Priya arrived with her flute case and flopped onto the bench beside him. "Still dying at five?" she asked.

"Every time. Maybe the piano just can't do it."

Priya hummed the note, then stopped to breathe, then hummed again. "You know what reminds me of this? Last year in choir, when we held one note for a whole phrase. Remember?"

Alexis did remember. He had been standing in the back row, sure they were about to run out of air, when he noticed something odd. The kid next to him turned his head and snatched a quick breath, but the note never wavered, because Alexis himself was still singing. Then Alexis needed air, and by the time he turned, someone two rows up had already refilled. The sound stayed strong the whole way through even though nobody could have held it alone.

"Staggered breathing," Priya said. "That's what we called it."

Alexis looked at the duet part again. Priya's flute line held the same chord while his piano part faded. "So if I get quieter a beat before you do, and then you fade after me, the sound never fully..."

He set the metronome, counted them in, and played. At beat four he let his volume drop to almost nothing, and Priya's flute carried the chord alone, thin and clear like light through water. At beat six she tapered off just as he pressed the pedal deeper, letting the strings shimmer underneath. Eight beats. The chord dissolved exactly as the composer wanted, into silence.

"That was significant," Priya whispered. "Like, actually significant."

They played it three more times to make sure it wasn't luck. It wasn't. On Friday, when the last chord faded into the hushed gymnasium, nobody clapped for a full second, and Alexis grinned at Priya across the keyboard.

"Same time tomorrow," she said. "I want to try it even slower."

Payton had one job: record a ninety-second video for the museum's junior docenct contest, explaining how a river carves a canyon over millions of years. The prize was a real badge and a backstage tour of the bat cave exhibit. Her little brother Dewey had one job too, which was to stand there holding the phone and not touch the giant erosion table in the Discovery Lab. Dewey's own plan, as far as she could tell, was to touch the erosion table as much as possible.

The table was a long slope of layered sand and clay with a hose dripping at the top, and it drained toward a bin marked DEPOSITION ZONE. "Okay, rolling," Dewey said, aiming the phone at her. Payton launched into her speech about water carrying sediment away, grain by grain, over millions of years. Then the drips found a channel and the whole slope began to slump, and her speech collapsed with it.

"Stop the water," she said. Dewey turned the valve the wrong way and the drip became a small flood. The top layer of clay melted back into a gentle slope, but beneath it a slab of packed wet sand stood out over the cut like a shelf. Payton crouched down and stared at it. The wall of the little canyon wasn't smooth. It was stepped. Some layers jutted out in steep little cliffs, and the softer layers had worn back into gentler slopes beneath them, like a staircase built by accident.

"That's it," she said. "That's why the Grand Canyon looks like that." She rebuilt the slope, pressing the clay layers hard so they'd hold firm and leaving the sand loose between them. "Dewey, water on. Slow this time." She pointed the camera at the model instead of herself. "The river keeps cutting, millions of years, and the hard layers make the steep cliffs, while the soft ones wear back into slopes. That's what gives the walls their steps." She turned the model toward the poster of the canyon on the plateau above the table, where the real stepped walls ran down to the river. If the judges were going to exclude anything, it wouldn't be because she hadn't shown them something true.

They ran it three more times, and the steps appeared every time, which made her explanation seem probable even to Dewey, who had opinions about nothing. On the last run he whispered, "Do the flood again," and she let him open the valve wide just once, after the phone was safely in her pocket. The whole plateau collapsed into the bin at the bottom.

"Deposition," Payton said, pointing at the heap of sand where the river had dropped everything it carried.

"Can we keep it?" Dewey asked, already reaching in.

The rain moved in after lunch on Wednesday, so Cabin 6's whole afternoon revolved around the battered Monopoly box that黛黛 the craft closet. Leah sat cross-legged on the floor between Priya and Marcus, whose family hosted the camp's exchange weekend last spring, so she knew the Rendell house rules. Those rules did not include money on Free Parking.

Priya threw the dice, landed on Free Parking, and reached for the center of the board with a grin. "Payday." When her hand found nothing but dust, she frowned. "Where's the pot?"

"There isn't one," Marcus said, not looking up from his railroads. "Free Parking is just free. It doesn't do anything."

"Everybody plays it with the taxes in the middle," Priya insisted. She sounded certain, the way people sound about things that revolve quietly through every game night at their own house.

"Maybe at your house," Marcus said. "It's a house rule, not one of the official rules." He shrugged. "That's why people from different homes fight about it."

Across the circle, Jake laughed. "Priya's never read the rules. Priya thinks the money just appears, like magic. Maybe she thinks a memoir about Monopoly would explain it." A couple of kids chuckled. Priya's ears went pink and she stared at the board.

Leah wanted to say something, but she'd learned in fourth grade that shouting "be nice" at Jake mostly made things louder. So she tried a smaller door. "Priya's right that most people play it that way," she said, keeping her voice level. "My family does the pot too. It's like half the fun." Then she turned to the box lid. "Hey, the rules are printed on the inside. We could just look."

They did. Marcus read the Free Parking entry out loud, and it was exactly as short and boring as he'd claimed: nothing happened, no money, no pot. Priya read it herself, twice, and Leah watched the pink fade from her ears. "Okay," Priya said. "But next game we vote on house rules before we start. Write them down."

"Deal," said Marcus. "As long as we also vote on whether Jake has to stop being obstinate about the banker job."

"I'm the best banker," Jake said, clutching the box of money to his chest like a rescued kitten.

Leah slid a pencil and the back of the camp schedule across the floor to Priya. "You write. Rule one: pot on Free Parking, taxes and everything, all cash in the middle."

Priya printed it in big careful letters while Marcus pretended to faint and Jake pretended to catch him. Then Priya rolled, landed on Free Parking again, and held out her hand. "That one's free," she announced. "I'm keeping track."

Laurence set her easel on the grass beside her cousin Dev, who had decided that anyone could paint a portrait in one afternoon. She had her grandmother's old box of watercolours, the pan nearly gone in the yellow corner, and a photograph of her grandmother propped against the fence. "You don't just draw it once," she said. "You start with the palest wash and let it dry, then add darker ones. Light to dark. You can't go backwards."

Dev frowned at his paper. He was more interested in the fence behind his drawing of the shed, and he had pressed so hard with his pencil that every guide line had carved a groove. "I'll just erase these later," he said.

Laurence remembered last winter, sitting at the kitchen table while her mother winced over a drawing of the living room. Her mother had pressed hard too, back when she was learning, and no eraser had lifted the lines. The finished room had stayed covered in them, faint rails running across the ceiling and floor, because the guide lines for perspective are drawn lightly with a hard pencil so they can be erased once the room's real edges are darkened in. Her mother had said, "You have to trust that the lines are there even when you can barely see them." Laurence had thought that was strange advice for drawing, and stranger still for everything else.

She laid her first wash, the palest peach, over the whole face and let the sun do the drying. While she waited she watched Dev scrub at his paper with the eraser until it pilled and tore. The grooves stayed. He flipped his board over, and she noticed the lines showed through the back, like bones under skin. "Try drawing the fence again on a fresh sheet," she said, "but press like you're drawing on a soap bubble."

Dev gave her the look he saved for advice from girls, the stereotype that art was her side of the family, some hereditary thing that had skipped him. But he picked up the hard 4H pencil she handed him and drew so lightly he had to tilt the sheet to see his own lines. "That's not drawing," he complained. "That's whispering."

"That's how it's supposed to look," Laurence said. She touched her brush to the second wash, a deeper rose along the jaw, and watched the first layer glow up through it. Dev leaned over her shoulder, holding his whispery fence up beside it.

"Okay," he said. "Teach me the faces next."

Mila slid the onion skin onto the stage and clamped it down, her heart doing a little drumroll. Today was the day she would actually see a cell, a real one, and she had already promised herself she would get the focus perfect on the first try. Ms. Reyes had written three words on the board: cell wall, membrane, nucleus. "Your job," she had said, "is to find all three and label them in your drawing."

She leaned into the eyepiece. Gray nothing. She turned the coarse knob one way, then the other, and still nothing but a pale fog. Behind her, Devon shouted that he could see his cells already, which felt unfair, since his onion sample was so thick it could have been a slice of pizza crust.

"Mine's too thick," Mila muttered. She pulled the razor blade from the tray, peeled a paper-thin layer from the inside curve of a fresh onion ring, and laid it flat in one drop of iodine. The new sample looked almost invisible, like a ghost of an onion, and that gave her a sudden idea. If the fog was just layers and layers of cells stacked on top of each other, then one thin layer should let the light through. It was like the difference between one window and ten windows glued together.

She focused slowly this time, saving the fine knob for last, and the image bloomed all at once. Bricks. Dozens of them, each one a tidy rectangle with a dark dot near the edge. "Look, the wall goes all the way around each one," she said, pulling Devon over by his sleeve. She traced the dark outline of a cell, then the thinner line just inside it. "That thinner one's the membrane, and the dot's the nucleus." She was so excited she nearly knocked the microscope sideways drawing it.

"The nucleus is the part that gets passed down," Devon said, squinting at his own slide. "My cousin has my grandpa's exact nose. My mom emphasizes it every Thanksgiving, like it's the climax of the whole year." He drew a nose in the margin of his lab sheet, a big one with a bump.

Mila laughed, then stopped, because the nose reminded her of something from a documentary she had watched with her dad about birds on islands. "Hey, the finches," she said. "There was a drought in 1977, and only some birds survived, and the ones that made it had big beaks. Then their babies had bigger beaks on average than the birds before the drought. Because the beaks got passed down, like your grandpa's nose." She tapped her drawing, right on the nucleus of cell number three, and labeled it with a hard push of her pencil.

"Exactly like the nose," Devon said solemnly, and drew a beak next to it.

Ms. Reyes stopped at their table, looked at the two labeled drawings, and pointed at the extra beak. "Nice," she said. "Now find me a cell that's vulnerable, one with a broken wall, and draw what's inside spilling out." Mila bent back over the eyepiece, hunting.

Jaxon pressed down on the tomato, and the knife skated sideways off the slick skin and landed on the cutting board with a clatter. Chef Marisol looked over from the stove, where a pot of curry was already bubbling. "Let me see that blade," she said, running her thumb along the edge. She pulled a different knife from the magnetic strip, handed it over, and went back to stirring.

Jaxon set the tomato on the board again, expecting the same fight. Instead the sharp blade slid through the skin with almost no pressure at all, and the slices fell open in neat red half-moons. He tried the next one, barely pushing, and it cut clean too. So that was the trick. The dull knife had needed all that force, and the force was what made it slip. He lined up the rest of the tomatoes and worked through them slowly, letting the edge do the work.

"Rice, curry, flatbread, all on the table at six o'clock," said Priya, the other student, reading the order ticket. "How is that even possible?" Jaxon glanced at the clock, then at the three stations. The rice would take twenty minutes in the pot, the curry needed fifteen to simmer, and the flatbread cooked in ninety seconds a piece. It wasn't arbitrary, he realized; the timing had a pattern to it, like a schedule hiding inside the recipe. If he started the rice first, then the curry ten minutes later, then rolled the dough while everything simmered, the flatbread could come off the pan last, hot, right as the rice rested.

"Twenty minutes for rice, fifteen for curry," he said out loud, checking his math. "That works if I start now." Priya nodded and lit the burner under the curry pot while Jaxon measured rice and water. The two pots refused to cooperate at first; the curry threatened to boil over while the rice sat stubbornly hard. Jaxon slid the curry to a cooler corner of the burner and lowered the flame under the rice until both settled into a steady simmer.

By ten to six he was rolling dough, dusting it with flour, watching Priya lay the first flatbread in the dry pan. It puffed and blistered, and she flipped it with a confident snap of the wrist. "You're the defendant in this kitchen now," she told the flatbread, "and the jury finds you guilty of being delicious." Jaxon laughed and rolled the next round, glancing at the clock, then at the rice, which had finally absorbed all the water.

At six exactly they carried everything to the serving window: a pot of fluffy rice, a pot of curry, and a stack of warm flatbread. Chef Marisol sampled a bite, then a second one, then said, "Same time next week. You're on onions."

"With the sharp knife," Jaxon said, already washing the blade.

Isabelle spread the photocopied page of Arabic across her grandmother's kitchen table, weighted the corners with teacups, and glared at it as if it might surrender. In two weeks, at the gathering her parents were calling her coming-of-age ceremony, she would recite Surah Al-Mulk from memory, all thirty verses, in front of forty relatives. So far she had four.

"You look like your grandfather watching the kettle," Grandma said, sliding a plate of dates toward her. "It boils when it boils."

"That's the problem, it doesn't boil at all." Isabelle tapped the page. "I keep starting at the beginning, and by verse five my brain is tired, so I never get to the end. Maybe I should build it backward, like a countdown." She grabbed her notebook and began sketching boxes and arrows, verses feeding into verses, testing order like a pattern she couldn't see directly. "Grandma, what if I memorize the last verse first? If a pattern works, it should work from any direction, right?"

Grandma laughed and said something in Farsi about stubbornness skipping a generation, which Isabelle took as a yes.

She tried it that afternoon on the porch steps, recording each verse on her phone and playing it while she hung laundry. Last verse, then second-to-last, then snapping the two together. By evening she could chain six verses from the back, and when she recited them for Grandma, word perfect, they both shrieked so loudly the neighbor's cat bolted off the wall.

That night her phone buzzed with a message from Priya: working on my project, need your help. Priya's world religions assignment was on reincarnation, the idea that a soul returns in many lives, life after life. Isabelle sat cross-legged on Grandma's guest bed texting back and forth, and suddenly she noticed something that made her sit up straight. The verses she was memorizing kept returning to a Day when everything hidden would be laid open, when people rise again to be judged, and then paradise or hell. One life, then one judgment. Priya's project had many lives, cycling on and on.

"Grandma!" Isabelle called, padding into the hall in her socks. "The surah I'm memorizing, it talks about the Day of Judgment, Yawm al-Qiyamah. Everybody gets raised up and judged, then sent to paradise or hell. Priya's project has souls coming back over and over instead. Isn't that the biggest difference you could imagine?"

Grandma leaned out of her bedroom doorway, hairnet crooked, eyes bright. "So tell me, then. Which one is the assignment?"

"Yours isn't an assignment. Yours is mine." Isabelle was already turning back toward the guest room, phone in one hand, photocopied page in the other. "I'm going to finish the last third before breakfast."

Grandpa's laptop smelled faintly of coffee and old paperbacks, which was odd, because Grandpa drank tea. Christopher sat at the kitchen table with his own notebook open, copying lines of Python while Grandpa hovered behind him like a large, hopeful shadow.

"So the program asks for a number," Christopher said, typing, "and then it tells you if it's prime." Grandpa had tried to recruit him for this project all summer, promising unlimited snacks, and Christopher had finally given in because prime numbers were actually kind of fun. You couldn't see primeness. A number just sat there, looking innocent, and you had to hunt for hidden factors like a detective checking an alibi. "Seven," Grandpa guessed immediately. Christopher ran the program, typed 7, and the screen said prime. Grandpa cheered as if his team had scored.

While Grandpa tested every number he could think of, including his age and his old street address, Christopher glanced at Grandpa's other project, a homepage for his beekeeping club. The heading, BEE HAPPY, ran along the left edge of the page like it was trying to escape through the margin. "Grandpa, your title's squashed against the side."

"It's been like that for days," Grandpa admitted. "I thought the internet was punishing me for something."

Christopher leaned over and paged through the file. Somewhere in the jumble of styles he found a rule that matched the heading, and he tested a simple idea: he added one short line. "h1, curly brace, text-align colon center, curly brace," he murmured, saving the file. He refreshed the page, and BEE HAPPY slid to the middle of the screen like it had been waiting for permission. Grandpa gasped so loudly that Grandma called from the garden to ask whether somebody had won the lottery.

"That line centers the top-level heading," Christopher said, feeling a little smug. "The big h1 one. Every one on the page, actually."

"Every one?" Grandpa said. "Then watch this." He added a second top-level heading, NECTAR FOR SALE, HONEST, beneath the first, and refreshed again. Sure enough, it sat dead center too, right beside the picture of Grandpa in his bee suit holding a jar. "Although," Grandma said, coming in with dirt on her hands and reading over their shoulders, "that honey you bought from the county fair was counterfeit. It was corn syrup with a bee sticker on it."

"Then we'll sell the sticker," Grandpa said, and clicked publish.

Ellie had been to Fairhaven Cemetery twice before, both times for her grandfather's funeral, when she was too small to remember anything but the cold. Today she came with her grandmother Nani, who carried a small brass pot of water and a bag of marigolds, and with her mother, who carried nothing and kept looking at the ground. They found the flat gray stone with DAVID OKAFOR carved into it, and Nani set the marigolds in a neat ring around the edges.

"His family was Christian," Nani said, arranging the flowers. "The minister said he is in heaven now, resting."

"That's it? He just stays there?" Ellie asked. She was working on a comparison for her world cultures class, and heaven was one half of her notes. The other half she was supposed to get from Nani, who had grown up in Varanasi.

"For them, yes. Forever, in peace." Nani touched the stone the way she touched Ellie's head when checking for a fever. "In what I was taught, a soul is born again. And again. Many times."

Ellie wrote reborn? in her notebook, then thought about it. "Wait. Is being reborn good? Should you hope for it?" She tested the idea out loud, the way she tested answers in math: pick one, see if it breaks. "Because if Grandpa gets to come back, that seems better than lying here."

Nani laughed, a short sound in the quiet. The recession had cut the cemetery's grounds crew to two men, and their negligent mowing had left tall grass between the rows, so the laugh carried farther than it would have otherwise. A man in a suit, two graves over, glanced over at them.

"No, beta. You hope to escape it." Nani sat down on the dry grass beside the stone, careless of her sari. "The wheel goes around and around, birth after birth. The highest thing a life can do is get off the wheel."

"It has a name?"

"Moksha."

Ellie wrote the word carefully. Liberation from the whole cycle of rebirth, she added, and underlined it, and then sat back on her heels. So the two faiths pointed in opposite directions, as far as she could tell. One wanted a soul kept safe forever in one place, and the other wanted it free of the road entirely. She looked at the marigold ring, then at the tall grass bending in the wind past the edge of the mowing, out toward the fence and the fields beyond it.

"Can I try the water?" she asked.

Nani handed her the brass pot. Ellie poured a slow line of it along the top of the stone, watching the water run into the carved letters and gather in the O of OKAFOR, filling it until it shone.

Eli had been a tenant of Birch Cabin for exactly six days, long enough to learn which bunks squeaked and which counselor snored, and long enough to notice something odd. Every afternoon, Owen from Fox Cabin got teased at the boathouse, always at the boathouse, and never anywhere else. Dex would mimic the way Owen's words caught and stuck, and the other boys would laugh, and Owen would pretend to search the water for his paddle as if he'd lost it. Eli wondered about that. Why the boathouse? He watched, and the answer slowly formed: no adult ever came down the dock after lunch. The teasing had a hidden rule, a time and a place where it was safe, and once Eli saw the pattern, he couldn't stop turning it over.

He tested his idea the next day. At lunch, when a counselor stood two feet away, Dex was all grins, passing Owen the ketchup like they were friends. An hour later, at the boathouse, Dex was doing the stuttering voice again. The pattern held. So the problem wasn't Dex exactly, Eli thought, chewing his lip; it was the empty dock. If the teasing needed a hidden spot, then maybe he didn't have to fight Dex at all. He just had to take the hidden spot away.

That evening Owen sat alone by the fire pit, and Eli went over. "I keep reporting it and then deleting it," Owen said, poking a stick at nothing. "Marcus said I'm a snitch."

"It's not tattling if you're trying to keep someone safe, not trying to get him in trouble," Eli said. He'd been chewing on that distinction all through dinner, and saying it out loud made it feel solid. "Tattling is when you want Dex to get busted. This is different. The goal is to protect you."

"So what do we do?"

Eli told him the pattern, the boathouse, the hour when no adult walked the dock. Then he went to find Renata, the waterfront counselor, retrieving his sandals from under the bench as he went. He didn't say Dex's name first. He said, "Nobody watches the dock between one and two, and stuff happens down there that kids are afraid to report." He waited, curious whether the pattern alone would be enough, the way a fishing line works even when you can't see the fish take the hook.

Renata looked at him for a moment, then nodded and pulled a whistle from around her neck. The next day she scheduled paddle practice for one o'clock sharp, right at the boathouse, with eleven boats on the water and her standing on the dock. Dex opened his mouth once, glanced up, and closed it. Owen capsized his kayak on purpose and came up laughing, and from the water he looked at Eli and raised his paddle like a flag.

Owen set his pencil down and glared at the paper. His street looked like a street that had been through a landslide. The buildings on the left leaned one way, the buildings on the right leaned the other, and the road between them wandered off the page like a snake that had lost its glasses. He wanted to draw the view from his grandmother's front porch, the one she said she might have to sell, so he could give her the picture before the moving truck came. He had one week.

"You're frowning at that paper like it insulted you," his mom said, setting a lemon on the counter. She turned it over, squinted, and muttered, "Is that fungus? I think that's fungus." She dropped the whole thing in the trash and came to stand behind him.

"Perspective," Owen said. "You're supposed to make lines go to a vanishing point, and I get that, but my street won't cooperate."

His mom pulled out the chair across from him. "Did I ever tell you about the nail hole? In the Last Supper?" She waited while he shook his head. "The single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there."

Owen looked up. "A nail hole? In one of the most famous paintings in the world? You can still see it?"

"Still there."

He sat with that for a second. Strings, from a nail. Strings that stretched out from one spot to guide the lines. So Leonardo hadn't just eyeballed it, and he hadn't started with the walls or the ceiling either. He had started with the one point, the point at Christ's head, and let every line grow outward from there like spokes on a wheel.

Owen flipped to a fresh page. This time he drew nothing but a small dot first, halfway up the paper, right where the street should disappear. He pressed the pencil tip so hard it nearly poked through, then found a thumbtack in the junk drawer, set it exactly on the dot, and looped a piece of sewing thread around it. He pulled the thread taut and drew along its edge, then moved it and drew again, line after line radiating out from the tack like rays from a tiny sun.

"Why the actual thread?" his mom asked.

"Because my hand curves. The thread doesn't."

When the lines were done he took the tack away and built the street on top of them, storefronts, windows, a mailbox. The buildings stood up straight and tall. The road ran true and narrow and went exactly where it was supposed to go, shrinking toward the dot until it vanished. In the middle of the road, far down where everything converged, the paper held one small, dark pinprick where the tack had been.

Owen leaned close to it. "I'm leaving it," he said. "Grandma can find it."

Aiden carried two paper cups of punch across the community hall, scanning the folding tables for his grandmother's church group. The hall had been split in half for the interfaith evening, with hymnbooks on one side and a cloth-covered table on the other, where a Sikh family was arranging a small stand wrapped in saffron fabric. Aiden's assignment for school was due Monday: compare how two faiths explain what happens after death. He had planned to just look things up online, but his grandmother had said the community hall evening would demonstrate more than any website could.

At the Sikh table, a boy about his own age sat copying something into a notebook in careful Punjabi letters. His name tag read Vikram. When Aiden set a cup of punch down beside him, Vikram grinned and covered his page. "You can look. It's not secret." The page was covered with lines of Gurmukhi script, the same lines over and over.

"That's a lot of copying," Aiden said.

"It's Japji Sahib. The morning prayer." Vikram tapped the notebook. "I have to know it well, because I'm getting ready for my initiation."

Aiden frowned. "Like a ceremony?"

"It's called Amrit Sanchar," Vikram said, and then his little sister tugged his sleeve and he went to help her with her shoes, leaving Aiden staring at the notebook.

Aiden wandered back to the church side, where his grandmother was stacking chairs. She had retired from the post office last spring, and now that she drew a pension, she volunteered at events like this almost every weekend. Aiden asked her what she thought happened after death, and she said what she always said, about heaven and being with God. Then she asked what the family across the hall believed.

"I don't know yet," Aiden admitted. "They said something about the soul merging with God, like a drop going back into the ocean. But I got interrupted."

He remembered then, suddenly, a funeral he had attended two years before, for his grandfather. After the service, in the church basement, a man had stood up and described reincarnation so vividly that several of the mourners had leaned forward, listening to something completely different from the minister's sermon. Aiden had been eleven and had thought the man was simply wrong. Now he wondered whether he had been biased that day, hearing only what he already expected to hear.

He marched back across the hall, punch sloshing. "Vikram. For my project. Does Japji Sahib say anything about what happens after you die?"

Vikram's mother looked up from the cloth-covered table and smiled. "Ask him what he's reciting it for," she said, and went back to smoothing the fabric.

"I'm reciting it because it's part of the ceremony," Vikram said slowly, working it out as he spoke. "And the prayer talks about the soul's journey. So I guess learning it is like practicing for the whole thing, the life after this one too." He looked surprised at his own sentence, then pleased.

Aiden wrote fast, filling half a page. "Can I ask you one more thing on Monday? After you've thought about it more?"

"Bring two cups of punch," Vikram said, and turned back to his notebook, pencil moving through the letters one more careful line at a time.

Florence had one lunch period to build a three-point argument about why the school should restrict phone use in hallways, and her notebook page still held nothing but the word "phones" circled three times. She sat at the back table of the library, where the writing club met on Tuesdays, and stared at the assignment sheet. Thesis statement first, then the outline, then the draft. The draft was supposed to come last, which felt backward to her, like decorating a cake before baking it.

Across the table, Marcus was taping a strip of paper above his laptop. Florence leaned over to read it. "Omit needless words," the strip said, in Marcus's careful block letters.

"Whose rule is that?" she asked.

"It's from William Strunk Jr.'s writing guide, The Elements of Style, written in 1918," Marcus said, smoothing the tape. "Mrs. Pell keeps a copy in the reference section. I copied it out this morning."

Florence got up, found the slim little book on the shelf, and carried it back. Nineteen eighteen. People were writing rules about cutting words before her grandmother was born. She flipped it open anyway, half hoping for a secret chapter on thesis statements, and found rule after rule about sentences, all of them blunt and short, like the book was following its own advice.

Then she looked down at her circled word and tried an experiment. She wrote her first attempt at a thesis: "I think that maybe phones in the hallways are kind of a problem that could possibly be solved." Twenty words, and most of them were hiding the actual point. She crossed out "I think that maybe," then "kind of," then "could possibly be." What remained was "Phones in the hallways are a problem that can be solved." Twelve words, and the sentence stood up straighter, like it had a spine now.

"Marcus, listen." She read it aloud, then read her original. He pointed at the taped strip without saying anything, which in Marcus language meant she had gotten it right.

The outline came faster after that. Point one, phones slow foot traffic in narrow halls. Point two, they make collisions more likely at the stairwell doors. Point three, a hallway phone rule would not restrict phone use at lunch, so students would keep most of their freedom. She numbered the three points, and under each one she jotted two pieces of evidence she could hunt down in the encyclopedia shelf before the bell.

At 12:45 the library lights blinked, the signal for five minutes left. Florence copied her thesis onto a clean page in her buoyant, looping handwriting and slid the notebook into her backpack. The blank page had been her adversary all lunch, and now it wasn't.

"Same table Thursday?" Marcus asked, packing up his laptop.

"Same table," Florence said, and zipped the bag shut.

Lea had exactly one job at the polling station: hold the "Vote Here" sign without whacking anyone with it. She was failing. The sign was nearly as tall as she was, and every time a voter walked past, the cardboard corner lunged at somebody's hat.

"I saw that," said Marcus, her best friend, who was supposed to be handing out sample ballots. "Your sign is attacking Mrs. Okafor. Again."

"The sign has a mind of its own. I'm just the camouflage, hiding its sinister plans." Lea wrestled the cardboard into a corner and propped it against the wall like a sleeping dragon.

Their civics class had sent them here to participate in Election Day, which mostly meant standing in the hallway of the community center for two hours. Their teacher, Ms. Reyes, had assigned a worksheet that Lea had stuffed in her back pocket: Read a right listed in the Constitution, then explain it in your own words. She'd been avoiding it all morning.

"Did you do the worksheet?" she asked Marcus.

"I wrote that the Constitution is a big paper that tells the government what it can't do. Very inspiring. Ten out of ten."

Before Lea could argue, a man with a clipboard hurried over. He was from the local newspaper, and he was upset. "They moved me to the parking lot," he said to the poll manager. "I need to photograph inside."

"Rules are rules," the manager said. "No cameras past this line."

Lea watched the man retreat, muttering. Something nagged at her, a pattern she couldn't quite see yet. Marcus had said the Constitution tells the government what it can't do. So what stopped the government from shutting down a newspaper entirely?

She pulled out her phone and searched. The First Amendment. She read it twice, lips moving. It protected freedom of religion, speech, the press, peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. Five things, all in one amendment. The press. There it was, printed plain as a cereal box label.

"Marcus," she said, yanking his sleeve. "The First Amendment protects the press. And speech. And religion. And peaceful assembly, and petitioning the government. That's why that reporter gets to be annoying at all."

"So the government can't just squish newspapers?"

"Apparently not." Lea flipped her worksheet over and wrote fast, in her own words: The First Amendment means the government can't tell people what to believe, what to say, or what to print, and it can't stop us from gathering peacefully or complaining to its face.

Marcus read over her shoulder. "Complaining to its face. Truly your finest work."

The reporter came back through the doors, camera bouncing on his chest, having negotiated a spot near the door. He raised the camera toward the check-in table, and Lea, without thinking, yanked her sign out of the corner to hold it high and proud.

The cardboard corner clipped his clipboard, and his pen flew across the floor.

"You're attacking the press now," Marcus said. "The exact press we just learned is protected."

Lea chased the pen, held it out to the reporter, and grinned. "Freedom of the press," she said. "And freedom of my sign. Somebody should write an amendment about that one."

At the first turn of the track, Madison bent to retie her shoe even though it didn't need it, because bending gave her an excuse not to look at the girl stretching beside her. That girl was Priya, the fastest eighth grader in the county, and in twenty minutes they would both toe the line for the eight hundred metres, the race Madison had bombed at twice already.

"You went out too fast last time," Priya said, not unkindly. "I watched. First lap like a rocket, second lap like a walk."

"I know," Madison said. The embarrassment still stung from the meet where she'd led at four hundred metres and then been passed by six people, one by one, her legs turning to wet cardboard. The trouble was she couldn't feel it happening. Everything seemed fine until suddenly it wasn't, which meant the problem was hidden somewhere she couldn't see, in the way she spent her energy, like a bank account draining without receipts.

Her brother Dev, who swam, had run into a version of the same puzzle last summer. "Freestyle," he'd told her, frowning at the television. "You'd think everyone would pick something different, right? Like, it's free. Any stroke you want."

"So why doesn't anyone?"

"I asked my coach. Almost all swimmers choose front crawl in freestyle races, because it's the fastest of the competitive swimming strokes. It's just faster. That's the whole answer." Dev had shrugged. "But you still have to swim it smart, because if you go out too hard, even front crawl won't save you."

Madison had rolled her eyes at the time. Now, standing at the line under an ominous gray sky, the idea came back to her from a new angle. The swimmers didn't win by choosing the fastest stroke alone; they won by managing the fastest stroke. Maybe pace worked the same way. The first lap of an eight hundred wasn't the race at all. It was an investment, and if she poured everything into it, there'd be nothing left when the actual race began.

So she made a plan she could test: on the first lap she would stay three steps behind Priya, no closer, no matter how easy it felt. If the plan was wrong, she'd lose again and know it. If it was right, the second lap would tell her.

The gun cracked. Priya swept to the front, and Madison sat three steps back, her legs begging to go, the whole field stringing out behind them. Four hundred metres. The bell. Then, coming off the final turn, the gap ahead of her began to shrink, one step at a time, like the second half of a race she'd never actually run before. She surged. Twenty metres out she was even with Priya's shoulder, hearing her own breath like a drum.

"Where did you come from?" Priya gasped.

Madison didn't waste the air to answer. She just leaned forward and ran through the line.

Carter stood at the counter with the recipe spread out between a bag of onions and a can of tomatoes, and the clock on the microwave said 5:12. His mom would be home at 6:30, and he had promised, actually promised, that dinner would be on the table when she walked in. He wanted to prove he could do this without her hovering, without the word "careful" repeated eleven times.

The onion intimidated him more than the sauce did. He remembered her hand over his once, knuckles curled under, fingertips tucked back like a bear's paw. "The claw grip," she'd said. "Fingertips down, so the blade rides your knuckles." He set his hand on the onion like that, took a breath, and cut. The first slice was crooked, but nothing bled. He went slower, and by the time the onion was diced, his eyes were streaming and his knuckles were whole.

His little sister Maya banged through the back door at 5:40 with a bag of blueberries and an announcement. "Bake sale tomorrow at seven a.m. I have to make muffins tonight, and you have to share the oven." She was meticulous about her recipe, leveling each cup of flour with a knife, cracking eggs into a separate bowl to check for shells. Carter made room, his sauce simmering behind them, and watched her stir.

She stirred forever. Carter watched her go around and around until every last lump vanished and the batter was perfectly smooth and glossy. "It looks like cake batter now," she said, proud.

They slid the muffins in alongside a covered pot, waited, pulled them out golden at 6:15. Maya split one open and her face fell. It was chewy, almost rubbery, and inside, instead of a soft crumb, there were long tunnels running through it like wormholes. "They're ruined," she said. "The bake sale is in thirteen hours."

Carter turned the muffin in his hand and thought about the batter. Hers had been overworked. His sauce had gotten thicker the longer it simmered, but flour wasn't tomatoes; maybe stirring did something different, something you couldn't see until it baked. "Make another batch," he said. "Stir it maybe fifteen seconds. Leave it lumpy. Lumpy is fine." Maya scowled at him. "Lumpy looks wrong." "Your smooth ones came out wrong," he said. "Try it my way once."

At 6:28 the second batch was in the oven and the sauce was done, deep red, onions melted into it completely. Their mom's key scraped the lock at 6:31, and while she hung up her coat, the timer buzzed. Maya yanked the pan out, split a warm muffin, and held it up: tender, no tunnels. "Carter," she shouted toward the door, "dinner smells amazing and I take back everything I said about lumpy batter."

Arianna sat at the kitchen table with two printed graphs spread in front of her: monthly rainfall and temperature for the Sonoran Desert and for a patch of Amazon rainforest in Brazil. Her science tutor had promised that by Thursday she had to be able to compare them without looking, and Thursday was two days away. The rainfall bars for the rainforest towered over the desert's flat little stubs, month after month, and she kept losing her place.

Her little brother Marco leaned over her shoulder, chewing a granola bar. "Why is there a lake in that picture?" He pointed at her open textbook, where a photo showed bright green rice plants rising out of a sheet of standing water.

"That's not a lake, it's a field," Arianna said. She turned back to her graphs.

"It's a lake with plants in it." Marco was obstinate about it. "Look, there's water between every row."

Arianna looked again. He was right that it looked like a shallow lake. Rice growing in flooded fields seemed strange to her, since her graphs said nothing about rice anyway. She flipped to the caption and read it aloud: "Rice is usually grown in flooded fields called paddies." That was the whole caption, no reason given.

"See, paddies," Marco said. "Told you it had a name."

"But why would anyone flood it on purpose?" Arianna asked. "Water that just sits there, everywhere, all season." She stared at the photo, then at her rainfall graph for the rainforest. The Amazon bars showed heavy rain nearly every month, a hundred and fifty to three hundred millimeters, and warm temperatures that barely moved between 25 and 28 degrees Celsius. The desert graph was the opposite: almost no rain most months, and temperatures that swung from baking days to cold nights, 40 degrees down to 5. Then it clicked for her, a slow turn like a key. Rice came from places like the rainforest side of the graph, places where water arrived constantly. The standing water in the paddy wasn't a problem for the rice, and the caption's last line gave her the rest: the standing water helps keep many weeds from growing. So the flood was doing a job.

"So the water is like a weed barrier?" Marco asked when she said it out loud.

"That's what the caption says. The water keeps the weeds down." Arianna had thought the flooded field was a mistake or a waste, and now she thought it was clever. She copied both graphs onto one sheet of paper, desert bars in orange and rainforest bars in green, because drawing them herself was the only thing that ever propelled the patterns into her memory.

Marco tapped the desert bars. "Nothing could grow rice here."

"Not outdoors," Arianna said, and slid the pencil across the table to him. "Here, color the cold nights blue."

Amelia slid her copy of To Kill a Mockingbird across the library table so the worn cover faced the circle of folding chairs. It was her turn to lead book club, and she had drafted her notes on three index cards, which now stuck together in her nervous hands. She peeled them apart and cleared her throat.

"Okay, so, symbolism," she began. "My cards say a symbol is when an object stands for a bigger idea, but I want to try something instead of just reading that. Everybody, think about the title. Why mockingbirds?"

Dev, who had eaten half a cookie already, raised his hand even though nobody needed to. "Because they're in the book? Atticus says something about them."

"That's the thing," Amelia said, flipping to the page she had dog-eared the night before. She read aloud: Miss Maudie explains that it is a sin to kill a mockingbird because mockingbirds do nothing but sing their hearts out for us. She looked up. "So they don't hurt anybody. They just give you music. And they're innocent."

Priya leaned forward, bouncing her chair onto its back legs. "So which characters are the mockingbirds? That's like a scavenger hunt."

"Exactly," Amelia said, her acute attention locking onto the circle of faces. "That's what I did last night. I made a list." She turned over the third index card. "Tom Robinson, first. He never hurt anyone, and they destroyed him anyway. And Boo Radley. He leaves presents in the tree, he saves the kids, and people made up scary stories about him for years."

"Him too?" Dev said. "I only thought of Tom."

"Try it yourself," Amelia said, grinning. "Who else just gives and gives and gets nothing back?"

The room went quiet except for the radiator clicking, which somebody had set by twisting the thermostat until the librarian came over and turned it back down. Then Marisol, who almost never spoke first, said slowly, "What about the kids themselves? Scout just... exists. She gets attacked for something her dad did."

The whole circle erupted at once, everyone talking over each other, and Amelia held up her hands. "Wait, wait, test it like a scientist. Does the person do harm? No. Does somebody try to punish them anyway? If yes, mockingbird."

Dev counted on his fingers. "Tom, yes. Boo, yes. Scout, yes. Man, this whole book is a nest of mockingbirds."

"That's the pattern," Amelia said. "The title isn't just a bird. It's telling you from page one who to watch and who's going to get hurt." She wrote the three names on the whiteboard and underlined them twice.

Priya jabbed a finger at the board. "Next meeting, can we do foreshadowing? I want to find every warning we missed."

"Bring sticky notes," Amelia said, and passed the cookies.

John had until Sunday night to finish his math project, and he had promised his grandfather he would do it at the kitchen table where the light was good. The assignment said to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years, and John had brought his notebook, two sharpened pencils, and a bad mood, because the numbers refused to feel like anything real.

"I don't get why I should care," he said, sliding the notebook aside. "It's just money sitting there."

Grandpa set down his coffee and pulled a folded paper from the drawer beside the fridge. It was a credit card statement, and the interest rate printed at the top was 24 percent. "Care about it now," he said. "I let a balance ride on this thing once, back when I was buying lumber for the porch. Never again."

John stared at the number. Something about it bothered him, an invisible rule he couldn't see. "How fast would it grow? Like, if you just left it?"

"Couldn't tell you," Grandpa said. "That's your department. Mine's the porch."

John flipped through the banking book Grandpa kept on the shelf, a fat one with a cracked spine, and found a page with a tiny headline: The Rule of 72. He read it twice, then grabbed his pencil. He narrated his steps out loud, the way his teacher liked, because saying them helped him check himself. "Seventy-two divided by the rate. At 24 percent, that's three years to double." He checked it against the compound table on the next page and it matched, close enough to make him grin. Three years, and the debt would be twice as big. That he could picture.

"You look like you found buried treasure," Grandma said, coming in with a plate of peanut butter cookies still warm.

"Sort of the opposite." John showed her the arithmetic, and she leaned over his shoulder, one hand resting light on the back of his chair.

For the next hour the kitchen was quiet except for pencil scratches. John built two five-year tables, one where interest stacked on interest and one where it didn't, and the gap between them widened every year like a slow door opening. The compound row pulled ahead by the third year, and he thought of Grandpa's lumber bill doubling in exactly that time. When he finished, he slid the notebook across the table. "Objective proof," he said. "Compound wins. That's my whole conclusion."

Grandpa read it, nodding slowly. Then he stood, went to the hall, and came back with a small green passbook with John's name on it. "Been putting twenty dollars a month in this since you were eight. The rate's 24 percent on the statement you were reading, and I made every payment, so no doubling trick works against us." He tapped the balance at the bottom of the page, which was almost exactly twice what John would have counted in deposits.

"Five years," Grandma said softly, taking John's empty mug before he could ask for more cocoa.

"Your bike money," Grandpa said, and set the passbook down beside the cookies.

The flyer on the community centre door said Free Math Help, Tuesdays Until 4:30, and Nicolas had twelve minutes of Tuesday left. He had missed the placement test twice already, and tomorrow morning was the last sitting before the school authorized him into the advanced stream. No pass, no advanced stream, and everybody knew Mr. Ellis's retest was notorious for being harder than the original.

"You're late," said Priya, the student volunteer at the corner table. She was already packing her calculator into a canvas bag printed with sailboats. "I can give you ten minutes. Sit."

Nicolas sat. He slid his practice sheet across the table. The last problem was 2x + 3 = 11, and beside it, half erased, his answer of x = 5.

"Show me how you got five," Priya said, but she didn't wait. She pulled the sheet back and drew a quick set of axes in the margin. "Do the algebra first. Whatever you do to one side, do to the other."

Nicolas took the pencil. He subtracted 3 from both sides and got 2x = 8, then divided both sides by 2. x = 4. He stared at it. Five minutes ago he had simply moved numbers around until something looked right, and now the steps had carried him somewhere he hadn't chosen.

"Okay," he said. "But why does that work? Where does the four come from?"

Priya glanced at the clock. 4:21. Instead of answering, she drew a line rising steeply through the axes and labelled it y = 2x + 3. "Look at your equation again," she said. "You're finding where the line y = 2x + 3 reaches a height of 11."

Nicolas bent over the graph. He traced the line with his finger, slow, because the clock was ticking and he could hear the caretaker unlocking the storage closet down the hall. The line climbed through the grid. He followed it up and up until it crossed the height of 11, then dropped straight down to the axis below.

"It lands on four," he said quietly. "The same four. Both roads get there."

"Both roads," Priya agreed, zipping her bag.

"But that's not just this problem," Nicolas said, flipping to a fresh page. "It's a rule. Any equation like this, there's a line, and the answer is where it hits the height." He started sketching another set of axes without waiting for permission, plotting, checking, and the pencil kept moving even as the lights in the far half of the hall flicked off.

The caretaker leaned in the doorway. "Centre's closing, kids."

"One second," Nicolas said, still drawing. He followed his new line up to where it crossed, dropped his finger to the axis, and grinned. "Priya. It works. It works every single time, doesn't it?"

She smiled from the doorway and pulled it shut behind her. "Find me Thursday and tell me how the test went."

The community hall smelled of incense and burned milk, and Arthur had forty pages of Sanskrit to get into his head before Sunday. His grandmother had promised him that if he recited the prayer without stumbling at his thread ceremony, she would finally let him carry the brass lamp, the one his older brother had carried. He wanted that lamp. So he sat at the back table under the noisy ceiling fan and whispered the verses to himself, line by line, covering the page with his hand and trying to pull the words up from memory alone.

The hall was busy that evening, which made it worse. Two families had booked the space, one at each end. Near the stage, an old man's family arranged marigolds around a photograph. Near the kitchen, a smaller group stood around a tiny cot with white cloth draped over something no bigger than a bundle of firewood. Arthur stopped mid-verse. He watched the old man's sons carry a bamboo stretcher out toward the river path, where the smoke always rose in the evenings, and he knew what happened there. The body was burned, and the ashes went into the water.

But the small group at the kitchen end began digging. Actually digging, in the corner of the courtyard where the neem tree grew. Arthur frowned. Same hall, same evening, same prayers floating over both parties, and yet one family was heading for fire and the other for earth. He wondered if the two families were angry at each other, or if one had made a mistake. He leaned toward the man handing out tea and asked, "Why are they burying? I thought everyone burns."

The man lowered his voice. "The little one was only four." That answered nothing, so Arthur turned it over while he mouthed the next verse. He thought of the sadhu who used to sit outside the temple, the one everyone called holy, and remembered the mound of earth that had appeared behind the wall after he died. No fire, no smoke. So it was not one rule for everyone. It was a pattern: the old man went to the flames and back to the five elements, while the child and the holy man went into the ground. Fire was for the ones in between. He tested it against everything he had ever seen at the river, every plume of smoke, every mound of earth, and the pattern held.

"Water, earth, fire, air, sky," he murmured, and the verse he had been fighting all week suddenly dissolved into something he could feel rather than memorize, like a door swinging open. His cousin bumped his shoulder. "You've got that look again," she said. "What now?"

"Nothing," Arthur said. "I just figured out who gets the fire."

"Who?"

He nodded toward the neem tree. "Not them." Then he picked up the brass lamp waiting on the shelf, polished it with his sleeve, and set it back down where he could see it from his chair.

"Read it again," Marcus said, leaning over the glass case outside the visitor center at the war memorial. "The part about the mill."

Arianna held the photocopied page of the settler's diary steady. Her history assignment was due Monday, and she needed one primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. The diary belonged to a man named Elias Crane, who had marched past this very hill in 1849. She had expected a story about farmland. Instead, the third line stopped her cold: "Left the farm to Samuel. Gold will do what corn never could."

"He left his farm," Marcus said. "He wasn't going west for land at all. He wanted money."

"That's just one guy," Arianna said. "One anecdote doesn't prove anything." She flipped to the back of the packet, where the park ranger had stapled a timeline. Her finger moved down the dates. Elias Crane had packed his wagon in the spring of 1849, months after something had happened in California. She found the line in the timeline: gold discovered at Sutter's Mill in January 1848.

"That's it," she said. "He read the news, then he left. The diary, the timeline, they fit together." A suspicion began to germinate in her mind, small but persistent. If Crane had left because of gold, how many others had done the same?

"Okay," Marcus said, "but you can't see gold fever in a diary. It's not like he wrote I have a disease."

Arianna pulled her notebook from her backpack and wrote two columns. LEFT FOR GOLD and LEFT FOR LAND. Then she walked along the memorial wall, where plaques listed the names of travelers who had passed through. Beside each name was a destination. Nearly every one said California. She counted eleven out of fourteen.

"They're all going the same direction," she said. "Same year, same place. Crane's diary says gold, and everyone else is headed to the same territory." She tapped the wall. "That's the pattern. That's my evidence."

Marcus squinted at the notebook. "So your whole report is, they weren't farmers, they were dreamers?"

"It's a primary source plus data." She copied the last name from the wall, then reread Crane's line about gold doing what corn never could. "He walked away from a farm he already owned. That tells you something."

The sun dropped behind the hill and the wall went cold and gray. Arianna zipped her notebook into her backpack and stood a moment longer at the plaque for Elias Crane. Somewhere past this hill, he had kept walking.

Naomi had to give her science presentation on Tuesday, and by Monday her body was already acting strange. Her hands were cold, her stomach hurt, and she kept snapping at her little brother over nothing. She wanted the weirdness gone before she had to stand up in front of everyone.

That afternoon, her class did a lab on solvent safety, and Mr. Ruiz held up a bottle marked flammable. "Keep this away from the hot plate," he said. Naomi copied the warning into her notebook, and next to it she doodled a little flame. Then she wrote, in smaller letters, stress feels like that. One spark and everything catches. It was a strange thing to notice, but it made her think that maybe her racing heart had rules too, the way the solvent did.

At the dentist's office that evening, waiting for her checkup, she watched a boy about eight years old sit across from her. He was gripping the armrests and breathing fast. His mother leaned over. "Count your breaths out, nice and long," she said. "Watch what your heart does." The boy breathed out slowly, counting, and then said, "It slows down when I breathe out." His mother nodded. "And it speeds up a little when you breathe in. That's just what hearts do." Naomi sat very still. She put two fingers on her own wrist, breathed in, and felt her pulse tick quicker. She breathed out long and slow, and it settled.

On the bus home she kept testing it. In, faster. Out, slower. Long out-breaths made the settling last longer. She figured the pattern was real, not luck, because it worked every single time she tried.

Tuesday morning she woke at five and could not get back to sleep, which she knew was a factor in how bad she felt. So she made a plan instead of lying there. She did ten slow breaths with the long outs, the way the boy had counted, and her heart stopped hammering. Then she set her alarm fifteen minutes earlier for the rest of the week, put her phone across the room so she would not mess with it after lights out, and kept the same bedtime three nights running. By Thursday she was falling asleep faster and waking less.

When her turn came, she stood at the front with her poster, the one she'd used to illustrate the solvent data with a bar graph. Her heart started to race. She breathed in, felt it climb, then let the air out slowly through her mouth, counting to six, and felt it drop. She did it twice more while Priya was setting up the laptop, and nobody even noticed.

Her voice came out steady. She pointed at the graph, said her first line, and moved on to the flame warning at the bottom of the poster.

Juliette had until fourth period to explain, out loud, the difference between a stock and a bond and which one was riskier, and so far her notecard said only "stock = part of a company, bond = loan, help." Her friend Priya slid into the seat across from her at lunch and read the card upside down.

"That's it? Mr. Okafor said we lose points if we just read definitions."

"I'm not going to read them. I'm going to explain why a stock is riskier. I just don't have a why yet." Juliette looked past Priya at the cafeteria fruit line, where a handwritten sign had appeared that morning: STRAWBERRIES $7. "Wait. Wasn't that sign $3 last week?"

Priya turned to look. "My mom would call that robbery."

Juliette got up, walked over, and asked the lunch lady why the price had jumped. The lunch lady shrugged and said the grower had lost half the crop in that late frost two weekends ago, so what was left cost more. Juliette stood there holding her tray, not moving, until the boy behind her cleared his throat.

On the way back she talked it through with Priya. "The frost ruined part of the crop. Less supply. So the berries that survived are worth more. Nobody had to decide that, it just happened." She set her tray down hard enough to slosh the milk. "That's the part I was missing. A stock's value moves around like that because of things nobody controls. Weather. Or whatever the company equivalent of weather is. A bond just pays you back fixed amounts. It doesn't ride up and down."

"So you'd verify that how?" Priya asked, spearing a fry. "You can't exactly ask a stock about its frost."

"I can ask my brother. He bought one bond and one stock last year with his birthday money." Juliette had meant to text him days ago and kept forgetting. She did it now: did ur stock and bond act different this year? His answer came back before she finished her juice: bond same every month, stock down then up then down. She turned the phone so Priya could see.

"That's your whole presentation," Priya said. "The frost is the show part."

Fourth period arrived faster than felt fair. Juliette stood up with her one sad notecard and told the class about the strawberry sign, the frost, the surviving berries costing more, and how a stock moved like that, sometimes badly, for reasons nobody controlled, while a bond mostly sat still. "So the stock is the riskier one," she said. "It can drop because of something like weather. The bond just keeps paying."

Mr. Okafor wrote something in his book without looking up. "Nice use of the berry stand."

After class, Marcus from the second row caught her at the door. "My dad's company stock just fell," he said. "Is it, like, endangered?"

"Ask the weather," Juliette said, and walked on.

The living history museum smelled like wood smoke and wet wool, and Colton had exactly forty minutes before the bus left. His assignment was due Monday: use a primary source, an actual document from the time, to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. He had tried the library, but the books just said "economic opportunity," which told him nothing he could picture. Here, in the museum's archive room, there was a glass case holding a settler's diary with pages a volunteer had copied so kids could handle them.

"Careful with those," said the volunteer at the desk. She pointed to a cast-iron pump in the corner. "If you want water, that pump still works, but you have to open the valve at the bottom first." Colton nodded and sat down with the copied pages. The handwriting slanted and crowded, and the ink had faded to brown, but he could read it. He was looking for one thing: a reason.

He found it on the third page. The settler wrote that the fields back home had grown poorer every year, and that a neighbor had written from the west describing soil so dark it stained his hands. The settler wrote, "We are not restless people. We are hungry people." Colton copied the sentence into his notebook. Then he noticed something else, a pattern he hadn't expected. Half the diary was about weather. Too much rain, then none, then too much again. The family's whole year turned on water, when it came and when it didn't.

That reminded him of the argument two girls from his class were having at the next table over a poster for their Egypt project. "Why did they only have three seasons?" one complained. "Everyone has four." Colton leaned over. "I read the plaque in the Egypt room," he said. "It went by the Nile. Akhet was the flood, Peret was the growing season, and Shemu was the harvest." The girls stared at him. "Three seasons of water, then," Colton said slowly, "like this diary. Their year turned on water too, just a different river." He hadn't planned to say that out loud, and it surprised him a little.

He decided to revise his plan for Monday. Instead of one paragraph on soil, he would write about water: the rain the settler waited for, and the flood the Egyptians waited for, and how people built their whole calendars around whatever their land gave them. It felt like a more sophisticated idea than "economic opportunity," and it had come from a brown-inked page and a lucky argument at the next table. On his way out, Colton turned the little valve on the old pump, worked the handle three times, and watched clear water spill over his stained hands.

Grandpa's kitchen smelled like butter and old newspapers. Andrew sat at the table with a chemistry book open to the periodic table, tracing his finger down the squares while the pan hissed on the stove. He was supposed to be learning something for science class, but mostly he was stalling, because Grandpa was making eggs and Andrew was hungry.

"You keep staring at that chart," Grandpa said, cracking an egg into the pan. The white spread out, clear and wobbling, and then the edges went white.

"Number eight," Andrew said. "Oxygen. It says the atomic number is eight, so I think that means eight protons. But I can't see protons. Nobody can. How do I know the chart isn't just making it up?"

Grandpa chuckled and tilted the pan. "I worked at the power plant thirty years, boy. Tended the turbine that spun the generators. I never once saw the steam push it, but I watched the needle climb every time it did. You trust the pattern, not the sight of it."

Andrew turned back to the chart. Carbon was six, so carbon had six protons. Gold was seventy-nine, which seemed like a lot of protons for one atom, but the pattern held all the way down: whatever the atomic number said, that was the protons. It was like the chart was a code, and the number was the key to each square. He tested himself, covering the name and guessing from the number alone, getting helium right and messing up nitrogen, which was seven, not six. He'd have to evaluate his guesses more carefully next time.

The egg was done. Grandpa slid it onto Andrew's plate, and Andrew stared at the solid white part, fork hovering. He remembered being little, maybe seven, and watching Grandpa cook while he waited for the egg to turn clear again when it cooled. He'd actually cried about it once, and Grandpa had said something he hadn't understood back then.

"It's permanent," Grandpa said now, as if reading his mind. "Heat changes the proteins in the egg white for good. It turns solid and white, and it stays that way. It's a chemical change. Frying an egg is a chemical change, because heat permanently changes those proteins."

"So it can never go back." Andrew poked the white with his fork. "Not even a little?"

"Not even a little."

Andrew looked from his plate to the chart. Invisible protons you could count anyway, invisible protein changes you could prove with a fork. Atoms changing their partners, eggs refusing to turn back. He cut a piece of egg white and ate it.

"Okay," he said. "But nitrogen is seven. Say it with me so I don't forget."

The gymnasium was a turbulent mess of folding tables, extension cords, and tri-fold boards, and Adam's spot was between a potato battery and a volcano that kept threatening to erupt sideways. His own display sat in the center of the table: two hammers, one orange with flaking rust, one clean and gray, both labeled. His board read WHY? in letters he had traced twice to emphasize the question.

He had found the rusty hammer in Grandpa's garden bed, half buried in the dirt, and the clean one on a nail inside the dry shed. Same hammers, bought the same summer, now completely different. His board explained what he had tested: he had set a third hammer outside in a jar with water, a fourth outside under a roof where rain couldn't reach it, and a fifth in the shed. After two weeks of a damp towel and misting bottle, only the wet one outside had started turning orange. Something in the air plus water did it, and the something didn't reach the shed one much. But when the judges asked "what is the orange stuff, actually," he froze, because he didn't have a word for it.

"It's not just dirty metal," the first judge had said, tapping the rusty head. "It changed into something else. What would you call that?"

Adam flipped through his notebook so fast the pages tore. He found his sketch of the periodic table, taped into the back cover because he thought it looked official. Iron was number 26. He knew that meant 26 protons, and he had written it on the board like it mattered, but right now it wasn't answering anything. He ran his finger across the row anyway, looking for a second element, one that might pair up with iron in the rust. Oxygen, number 8, eight protons, a gas, everywhere in the air and dissolved in water. He circled it twice.

"It's iron and oxygen together," Adam said. "The iron in the hammer reacted with oxygen, but only where there was water. The one in the dry shed never got wet, so it stayed fine. It's a new substance." He paused, remembering the word from the encyclopedia he'd flipped through at eleven the night before. "It's called iron oxide."

The judge wrote something down. "And the protons?"

"Iron is atomic number 26, so 26 protons. Oxygen is 8, so 8 protons. They're still iron and oxygen even after they combine, just arranged into something new." He lifted the rusty hammer and held it beside the clean one. "This one's iron oxide now. Same iron that started here, plus oxygen it pulled out of the water and the air."

Behind him, the volcano finally erupted sideways, and a girl two tables over grabbed her towel and muttered, "Every year. This is not a democracy, Justin, move your project." Adam grinned and set both hammers down in front of the judge, side by side.

The planetarium smelled like dust and old carpet, and Hailey had exactly forty minutes before her demonstration to the astronomy club. Her problem was simple and terrible: she still could not explain why Earth's tilt caused the seasons, and Mr. Ruiz expected her to stand under the dome and teach it to twelve kids who would ask questions. She had volunteered three weeks ago, confident, and every night since, her notecards had become more confusing instead of less.

In the corner of the exhibit hall stood a giant globe with a lamp on an arm, the kind that could swing around it like a slow planet. She dragged it toward the middle of the floor, and something rattled inside the stand. Two thin dotted lines circled the globe's middle, one above the equator and one below, like rings of plumbing pipe wrapped around a water tank. She traced the top one with her finger and frowned. She had never noticed them before.

"What are those lines for?" said a small voice. A boy, maybe nine, had wandered over, dragging his own backpack like a suitcase. He pointed at the dotted circles. "Are they roads?"

"I don't actually know," Hailey admitted, which felt dangerous to say out loud. She knelt and read the tiny printed label near the base. Tropic of Cancer, the top one said. Tropic of Capricorn, the bottom one. "Those are their names," she told him. She turned the lamp on and swung it toward the globe. The label was no help at all. She spun the globe slowly, and the boy watched the light slide across oceans.

Then she noticed the small calendar dial on the lamp's arm. She clicked it forward, month by month, and stopped. In late June, the lamp's beam hit the globe dead straight, and when she crouched to eye level, her stickpin shadow at the Tropic of Cancer vanished to nothing. The noon Sun was directly overhead there. She clicked the dial on and on, through autumn, and in late December the shadow disappeared again, but at the other line, the Tropic of Capricorn. She sat back on her heels. The lamp hadn't moved up or down much. The globe was tilted, leaning like a tired person, and its lean never changed as it traveled. The beam struck each tropic straight on at those moments, and everywhere else it arrived slanted.

"So the light's more direct there," she whispered. The boy leaned in.

"More direct where?"

"At the top line in June," she said, "and the bottom line in December. Around June twenty-one the noon Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. Around December twenty-one it's directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn." She pushed the stickpin into Missouri, where they lived, and clicked the dial. In June the shadow lay short and stubby. In December it stretched long across the Pacific. Short shadow, steep light, heat. Long shadow, slanted light, cold. Her notecards suddenly seemed like a tranquil lake she could finally see the bottom of. The whole thing could transform from a jumble of facts into one swinging lamp and one leaning globe.

Mr. Ruiz's shoes squeaked in the hallway. Twelve kids were coming, and the boy was already raising his hand with a question, the one about the roads she never answered.

Florence had until Sunday night to build a model of a river canyon for Monday's science fair, and so far all she had was a plastic tub, a bag of sand from Grandpa's shed, and a smooth gray stone she'd found in the creek behind his house. The stone bothered her.
