It was perfectly round, like an egg, with no sharp edges anywhere, and she wanted to know what had polished it, because whatever did that was probably the same thing that had carved the real canyons in her textbook.

"Supper's at six," Grandpa called from the porch. "And I need that tub back by Sunday, I'm mixing concrete Monday morning." That gave her two days.

Florence sat on the back steps and turned the stone over. The creek was barely ankle deep. How could something that small cut through rock? She remembered the textbook's two-page spread, a canyon with striped walls and a caption about millions of years, but the caption never said how. Maybe, she thought, the water itself was just soft and harmless, like a shower. So the water couldn't be doing the work. Something in the water had to be.

She went inside and came back with a mayonnaise jar, a fistful of creek sand, three pebbles, and a scrap of soft chalk from Grandpa's garage. She dropped the chalk and everything else into the jar, filled it with water, and shook it hard for a count of one hundred. When she fished out the chalk, its edges were worn and there was a gritty white smear in the water. She shook it again, longer this time. The corners had gone rounded. She was still holding it when Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade.

"It's called abrasion," he said, peering into the jar. "That's what the old-timers around here always called it, the sand and stones grinding the bed." He tapped her stone. "Little creek did that, one grain at a time."

Florence spent Saturday building her model. She tilted the tub, lined it with a layer of sand and clay, and poured a slow trickle from a watering can at the top. The water picked up sand, dragged it downstream, and dropped it in a fan where the slope flattened out, which her textbook said was deposition. On Sunday morning she cut the trickle and studied the channel. It was deeper. Not much, but deeper, and the deepest part was where the most sand had traveled over the clay. She propped a luminous orange sign beside it, MILLENNIA IN A TUB, and packed her rounded stone in a sock so she could show it at the fair. Grandpa waved from the porch as Dad's car pulled out Monday morning, and Florence held the model steady on her lap all the way to school.

Sara got to the science room early to claim the lamp, because the whole grade would be presenting season models that afternoon and the good equipment went fast. Marcus arrived two minutes later with their globe tucked under one arm, and he stopped in the doorway when he saw her, like he had forgotten they were still partners.

"Your mom signed the form," Sara said, not looking up. His mother worked nights at the hospital and had missed the last two permission deadlines, and Marcus had spent those trips sitting in the office, which everyone pretended not to notice.

"She did." He set the globe on the table. Heat began to radiate from the lamp as it warmed, and Sara angled the shade so the light fell across the tabletop like a small sun. She had taped a red X over their town on the Northern Hemisphere, and Marcus's job was to walk the globe in a circle while she talked. They had rehearsed once, badly, mostly in silence.

The problem showed up immediately. Every time Marcus carried the globe around the lamp, he turned it so the X faced the bulb, the way a person naturally aims the front of something at a light. It looked right, too, which was the annoying part. Bright side, warm side. Sara stopped him on the second lap.

"You're spinning it," she said. "The axis has to point the same way the whole time. Like it's pinned to the wall behind you."

Marcus frowned at the globe. "But then the X ends up tilted away from the lamp over here." He walked it halfway around, holding the top steady toward the back wall, and the red X leaned out into the dark side of the orbit.

"Exactly," Sara said, and then she heard it, the whole thing snapping together in her head. "So for this part the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and over there it leans away. Same tilt, different part of the orbit. It never changes direction."

"That's why you don't turn it," Marcus said slowly, walking it again, slower this time, keeping the top aimed at the back wall like a compass needle. The X tipped toward the light, then away, then toward again as he completed the circle.

They ran it three more times until he could do it without drifting, and by then the room was filling and the hallway outside had gone quiet and almost desolate while everyone crowded in to watch the first presentations. Sara looked down at her peasant blouse, the good one she had saved for today, and realized she had leaned against the chalk tray and streaked the sleeve white. Marcus noticed and offered her the only thing he had, a nub of pencil eraser, which of course made it worse, and they both laughed, quietly, for the first time in weeks.

They went third. Marcus walked the globe around the lamp with his arm locked steady, and Sara said, "The axis points the same direction in space all year, so for part of the orbit the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun, and later it leans away," and pointed to the X tipping into shadow as the room watched the little world turn slowly through its year. Afterward Ms. Okafor wrote something in her binder, and Marcus whispered, "We nailed it," and Sara looked at the chalk mark on her sleeve and said, "Say that louder."

Chase sat cross-legged on the floor of his aunt's guest room with a photocopy of the Havdalah blessing spread in front of him. In three weeks he would stand in front of ninety people at his Bar Mitzvah and recite it by heart, and right now he could not get past the fourth line. He tried again, mouthed the words, lost the thread, and flopped backward onto the rug.

Downstairs, his cousin Priya was arranging a plate of laddus on the kitchen counter. Her family had come to stay for the week after Grandpa Joe's funeral, and the house still smelled like casseroles and incense from two different traditions. Chase wandered in and slid the photocopy onto the counter. "How do you memorize a whole prayer? I keep forgetting the middle."

Priya tilted her head. "When my grandfather died last year, I learned a shloka for him. It took me eleven days." She tapped the paper. "It's gradual, like anything. One line locks in, then the next. My teacher says a neuron fires the same path every time you repeat something, and the path gets stronger."

"Eleven days," Chase groaned. "I have twenty-one." He stared at the page, then looked up. "Can I ask you something weird? Where do you think Grandpa Joe went? Like, actually went."

Priya set down the plate. "In Hinduism, the soul passes through samsara. That means a cycle of birth, death and rebirth, around and around." She traced a circle in the air with one finger. "And karma decides the direction. Karma is the results of a person's actions, and those results shape the next life."

Chase turned that over while he stole a laddu. A hidden rule, like gravity: you could not see it, only the effects. He wondered if it could be tested the way you test anything invisible, by watching what it did. "So if somebody was kind all the time, the kindness would... land somewhere?"

"That's the idea," Priya said. "Grandpa Joe gave my mom his winter coat the day they met. That kind of thing counts."

That night Chase tried something new. He drew the prayer as a circle instead of lines, arrows curving from each phrase to the next, so that the end flowed back to the beginning like Priya's finger in the air. When he forgot the middle, he could travel the loop the other way and arrive from the far side. By bedtime he had the whole thing, and the words no longer felt like a wall but like a path he had walked twice.

At the ceremony, three weeks later, he reached the fourth line and felt his mind go blank. He pictured the circle, traveled backward from the end, and the missing words appeared exactly where the arrows said they would be. He finished strong, and in the front row Priya drew a slow circle in the air.

Penelope slid into her seat in the art room just as the bell rang, pulling her sketchbook out before her backpack even hit the floor. Today was the day. Mr. Ruiz had promised they would finally learn to draw a street that looked real, the kind that seemed to go back and back until it disappeared, and she had been waiting all week.

"Vanishing point," Mr. Ruiz announced, tapping a single dot he had drawn on the whiteboard. "Everything heads there. Now here's your challenge. Draw your orthogonals first."

Around her, pencils hesitated. Marcus leaned over and whispered, "Ortho-what?" A few kids just started drawing buildings and hoped for the best. Penelope stared at the dot. Orthogonal had to be a name for something, and she had one clue: Mr. Ruiz had said "everything heads there." So an orthogonal was probably a line that ran back toward the vanishing point. But which lines? That was the hidden part. You couldn't see the rule sitting on the desk; you had to hunt for it.

She decided to test an idea. In her mind she walked down her own street, the one with the crooked mailbox and the bakery on the corner. What lines seemed to run away from her as she walked? The edges of the road, for sure. She drew those first, two lines slanting in toward her dot. Then she guessed the curbs, and added them. Too timid. She erased and made them bolder, so eager she nearly tore the paper.

"Mine looks like a sandwich that got stepped on," Marcus groaned behind her, holding up a drawing where his buildings floated like parade balloons.

"You're drawing the fronts first," Penelope said. "Try the lines that go back. Roofs count. Watch." She flipped her sketchbook around. Her rooflines, her curbs, her road edges all marched toward the dot like they were in a line for the bakery. Marcus frowned at it, then at his paper, then grabbed his eraser so fast it flew out of his hand and rolled under Devon's chair.

"Road edges, curbs, rooflines," Marcus muttered as he drew, tapping each one. "Orthogonals."

"Exactly," Penelope said, and her chest did a small proud flip. The erosion of her doubt was complete; every line she put down now looked like it belonged. Windows appeared along her walls, each one smaller and closer together as the street ran back. She even added the bakery sign, squashed tiny near the dot, and it worked. The street wasn't flat anymore. It went somewhere.

Mr. Ruiz stopped behind her desk. "Now that," he said, "generates a whole neighborhood. Where's the next street go?"

Penelope grinned and put her pencil back on the paper. "Right there," she said, and added a corner.

The assignment was due on Friday, and Landon had spent three days avoiding it. Now he sat in the school library at four o'clock, a blank page in front of him, and the clock above the biography shelves ticking like it was counting down a siege. He had to write a short story with dialogue, and the dialogue had to be punctuated right, and the whole thing needed a climax. Ms. Ferrante had circled his last attempt in red and written "See me" at the top, which was worse than any grade.

He tried a sentence. "Where are you going," He asked. It looked wrong the moment he wrote it, but he could not say why. His friend Priya slid into the chair across from him with her own paper and a granola bar. She leaned over his shoulder.

"Question mark," she said, tapping the page. Landon frowned. He flipped through the class packet of examples until he found one: "Where are you?" he asked. There it was, the question mark sitting inside the quotation marks, and the tag after it starting with a lowercase h. That seemed backwards to him. He asked was its own kind of sentence, wasn't it?

"Watch," Priya said. She took his pencil and wrote the whole thing out plain, without any marks: Where are you he asked. "Now decide where the question ends. Is He asked part of the question?" Landon stared at it. The question was only the part in the guy's mouth. The tag belonged to the narrator. He tried it both ways on the page, once with a capital H, once without, and read them aloud. The lowercase version sounded right, like one breath instead of two broken pieces. He erased the capital.

His old ideas for the story, a spaceship battle, suddenly felt dormant, like something that had been sitting too long in the dark. He had wanted a siege scene with robots. Instead he started writing about two brothers in a treehouse, one hiding something, and by the third line of dialogue he was writing fast, punctuating the questions without slowing down. Priya had moved on to her own paper, but when he read a line out loud she laughed once, quietly, and the librarian glanced over. Landon felt his ears go hot.

The problem was the climax. He wrote four versions where the brothers argued, and each one fizzled out. Then he tried having the younger brother finally ask the question he had been afraid to ask all story long: "Why didn't you come to Mom's funeral?" he asked. The older brother went silent on the page, and then Landon knew exactly what happened next, because the whole story had been waiting for that one question. He wrote the ending in a single sitting, twenty minutes, his hand cramped around the pencil.

When he read it through, though, the robot siege was gone for good, and he felt a small pang about that, the way you do when you trade something loud and fun for something quieter and harder. Priya packed up her bag and paused at his table. "Read it to me tomorrow before class?" she said. He slid the paper into his folder, smoothed the crease flat with his palm, and said, "Only if you fix my commas first."

Georgia had one job at the polling station: hold her grandmother's place in line while Gran fetched her glasses from the car. But the line was slow, and beside the door somebody had taped up a poster of the town charter, all forty rights printed in tiny columns. Georgia started reading to pass the time.

She was halfway through the list, lips moving, when a man in a green jacket came out of the voting hall. She recognized him. Councillor Ruiz, the one from the newspaper photo. He had voted against the bylaw that banned skateboarding in the library plaza, the bylaw that had emptied the plaza and pushed every skater in Georgia's grade onto the cracked lot behind the gas station.

"You're Councillor Ruiz," she said. "You said the plaza ban was wrong. So when are you changing it?"

He smiled, but not much. "I can't change it alone. A single councillor can't change a bylaw alone. A change needs a majority vote of the whole council."

Georgia stared at him. "But you agree it's a bad rule."

"Agreeing isn't voting power. There are seven of us."

She looked back at the charter poster. Right there, near the top: the right of citizens to gather peacefully and to petition their government. She'd read it twice without really reading it. Now she said it out loud, slowly, testing it. "So we can ask. Together. That's not just a decoration on a wall."

"That's the idea," Ruiz said. "Petitions matter. Voters matter. Today, especially."

Georgia's mind was moving fast. This was polling day, and the whole town was walking past this door. People who cared enough to vote cared enough to sign something. That was the hidden pattern: the ban hadn't been defeated by one enemy, it had passed because nobody had shown up to argue, and now the people who could argue were all standing in one line. She ran to Gran's car, grabbed the notebook from the back seat, and tore out six pages.

"Sign here if you want the plaza bylaw reconsidered," she called, standing where everyone had to pass. A woman with a stroller signed. Two teenagers signed without asking questions. A man in a volatile mood, red-faced about parking tickets, refused, but then a library volunteer signed right after him and told him the plaza used to be full of kids before the ban. He scowled and kept walking, but slower.

By the time Gran came back with her glasses, Georgia had ninety-three signatures. Ninety-three, in one hour, from one line. She counted them twice on the bench by the door.

She had wanted Ruiz to fix it, one important person snapping his fingers. Now she wanted something different: seven votes, and a stack of paper heavy enough to matter. She folded the pages, squared them against her knee, and walked the stack straight back to Councillor Ruiz.

"You said majority," she told him. "So start counting."

Ariana set her trumpet on the music stand and glared at the twelve-bar blues chart like it had insulted her family. "You're going to improvise a solo today," Mr. Ruiz had said, which was easy for him to say, since he wasn't the one who had to invent notes in front of the whole jazz band. She'd practiced the chord progression until she could play it asleep, but the moment she tried to make up a solo, everything came out in a panicked rush, notes tumbling over each other like they were fleeing the scene.

"You're rushing again," said Marcus from the piano bench, grinning. "That solo lasted about nine seconds."

"It did not." Ariana checked the clock. It had, in fact, lasted about nine seconds.

Marcus reached into his bag and pulled out a small wooden box with a sliding weight and a pendulum. He wound it, and the thing began to tick, steady as a dripping faucet. "Try it under this." Ariana assessed the little machine, turning it over, watching the weight slide up and down its scale. "Where did you even get this?"

"My grandpa. He says it's older than jazz itself." Marcus tapped the lid, where a worn brass plate read Maelzel. "Johann Nepomuk Maelzel patented the mechanical metronome in 1815. A ticking device that sets a steady tempo." He said it the way Grandpa must have said it to him, like a magic password.

Ariana had a sudden flashback to fourth grade, when she'd played "Hot Cross Buns" at approximately the speed of a hummingbird's heartbeat, and her teacher had gently suggested the audience might enjoy hearing some of the notes. So rushing was an old habit, a hidden pattern inside her that she couldn't see, only hear from outside, like a voice recording that sounds nothing like you. But the metronome could see it for her. That was her idea, and it was simple: if she played with the ticking, either the tick would slow her down or she would prove the tick wrong.

She lifted her trumpet, set the pendulum swinging, and started the solo again. The first four bars felt like walking a tightrope, her fingers wanting to sprint while the tick kept saying not yet, not yet. By bar eight something clicked, or rather stopped clicking out of turn, and her notes landed square on the beats. On bar twelve she ended on a low note that bent downward, the way she'd heard on old records, and let it hang there.

Marcus played a little ta-da chord. "Nine seconds of glory, no more. Well, more like thirty."

"Consumer of my solos, you are a negligent audience," Ariana said, pointing the trumpet at him. "That one deserved applause."

"Fine." He gave her three slow, sarcastic claps, perfectly in tempo with the ticking box.

Flight 47 to Phoenix was delayed again, and Florence spread her science homework across two plastic seats in the gate area. Her graph for the Sonoran Desert showed rainfall bars so short they looked like a typo, while the rainforest graph she'd copied from the library book had bars like a row of broken teeth, tall and constant. She had to compare them using temperature too, and the assignment sheet called for a paragraph she had not yet managed to formulate.

Her little brother Theo leaned over her shoulder with a topographic map of the mountain near Grandma's house. "You said we'd go sledding when we land," he said. "Pick the hill before Mom changes her mind."

"Mom already changed her mind twice," Florence said. "Once about the window seat."

The map was covered in wiggly brown lines, close together in some places and far apart in others. Checking each line against the height numbers printed on it was tedious, and Florence kept losing her place whenever the gate agent announced something nobody listened to. She traced one slope with her finger where the lines bunched up like angry eyebrows, then another where they were scattered wide, and a third where they marched down the page at regular intervals, like fence posts.

"That one," Theo said, poking the regular one.

"Why that one?"

He shrugged. "It looks calm."

Florence frowned. The lines on that slope were evenly spaced, each one the same distance from the last, all the way from the top of the hill to the creek. On the other slopes the spacing changed, tight then loose then tight again. She thought about what the spacing might be hiding, since the map could not show her the actual ground. Wide spacing had to be one steepness and narrow spacing another, so if the spacing never changed, then the steepness never changed either. "Contour lines spaced evenly apart," she said slowly, "show a slope that has the same steepness all the way along it."

"So no surprise cliffs?"

"No surprise cliffs." She drew a red circle around the slope and wrote GO HERE under it, then held the map up to the window. Beyond the tarmac, a fuel vessel sat parked beside the plane, and a man in orange ear protection was checking its gauge.

She turned back to her graphs, and now the comparison wrote itself almost without her. The desert's temperature line swung up and down with the seasons while rainfall stayed nearly nothing; the rainforest stayed warm and soaked month after month. Two places, two patterns, and you could read the whole climate off the shapes. She finished the paragraph, then looked at the clock and at the map.

"Forty minutes till boarding," she said. "Enough time to check the map for a backup hill, in case the first one is full of kids who also like calm."

Cole lined up five glasses on the kitchen counter like a scientist preparing a difficult experiment, which was exactly what he considered this. In the first glass he poured lemon juice, in the second water with a pinch of baking soda, and in the third a splash of cola. His friend Marcus sat on a stool, spinning a strip of litmus paper between his fingers.

"Bet you the lemon and the cola test almost the same," Marcus said. "It's not like one's a laser and the other's a flashlight. pH three, pH four, what's the difference? One number."

"One number on a scale where each whole step is a tenfold change," Cole said, but he said it quietly, because he was not entirely sure he remembered it right. His science notebook was upstairs, and going to get it would mean admitting he needed to check. Instead he took the strip from Marcus and dipped it into the cola. It came out red. Red meant acid. The lemon juice turned its strip red too, but somehow a deeper, angrier red, and Cole felt something tighten in his chest.

He remembered his grandfather's old garden kit in the drawer under the phone, a box with numbered color cards from pH one to pH fourteen. He dug it out and held the wet strips against the cards, tilting them toward the window light. Cola matched the card for four. Lemon matched the card for three.

"See?" Marcus said, leaning over his shoulder. "One apart. Only a little more acidic."

"No." Cole's mouth was dry. "Each whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change, so pH three is ten times more acidic than pH four. The lemon isn't a little more acidic than the cola. It's ten times more acidic." He watched Marcus's face go through disbelief, then doubt, then the slow widening of eyes that meant the math had landed. Ten times. From one number.

"In vain did Marcus search the counter for some flaw in the cards or the strips," Cole wrote later in his notebook, because his teacher wanted full sentences. But right then he was busy pouring water into the lemon glass, testing again, accommodating every strip the kit had left until the color crept from three toward four. Marcus grabbed the last strip and dipped it into the baking soda glass himself, where it turned blue as a summer sky.

"Wait," Marcus said. "So two steps would be a hundred times?"

The assignment sheet said one thing in bold: you must use a primary source. Lucy stood in the second-floor gallery of the county history museum, where a glass case held a copy of an 1846 settler's diary, its brown ink faded to the color of weak tea. Her friend Devon was supposed to be helping, but he had wandered three cases down to a giant timeline of empires and was now pointing at it.

"Look at this," Devon called. "It says the Roman Empire ended in 476. But this other label says the eastern half kept going. That makes no sense."

Lucy leaned over the timeline with him. The map showed the empire split in two, and the eastern portion, shaded green, stretched forward across the centuries while the western part stopped dead.

"That's the Byzantine Empire," Devon said, reading the small print. He tapped the last green date. "It says the Ottoman Turks captured Constantinople in 1453." He counted on his fingers, twice, because the number seemed wrong. "That's almost a thousand years longer than the western half lasted. How can an empire fall twice?"

"Maybe the whole thing didn't fall at once," Lucy said. "The western half fell, and the eastern half just kept going. Empires aren't one block." She looked back toward the diary case, and something clicked. If an empire could split and one piece survive, then a story people told about the past could also be only half of it. Her textbook said people moved west for "opportunity," but that word covered everything and explained nothing. She needed the diary to tell her which half of the story was true.

She went back to the case and read the transcription card mounted beside it. The settler, a woman named Ruth Ellery, wrote that her husband's mill had failed after two bad harvests, that the land they rented in Ohio had grown "thin and tired," and that a letter from her brother in Iowa described soil "so dark it stains the wagon wheels." Lucy tested a simple idea against the words: if people moved because the East was worn out, the diary would complain about the land before it ever mentioned adventure. It did. Ruth wrote nothing about starting fresh or seeking fortune. She wrote about exhausted fields and a brother's letter. Lucy copied the three best lines onto her notecard, then held them up next to the museum's wall map of migration routes. The routes ran away from the older states and toward the newer ones, like water finding a downhill path, though she reminded herself that was a simile, not evidence.

"Can I see?" Devon said, coming over. He read her notecard. "So the book says opportunity, but she says the ground gave out."

"That's what I'm going to argue," Lucy said. "The source beats the summary."

Devon frowned at her notecard, then back at the timeline. "So maybe I could argue the timeline the same way. One piece of Rome died in 476 and the other piece, the Byzantine Empire, lasted until 1453 when the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople. Almost a thousand years longer."

"Then the sign upstairs isn't wrong, it's just vulnerable," Lucy said. "It only shows the western half."

A museum guard started toward them, and Devon stepped away from the case so fast his elbow knocked the rope stand. Lucy grabbed the stand before it tipped, her notecard still pressed flat against her chest.

Rachel lined up the meter stick along the lab bench while her partner Marcus held the steel ball at the top of the ramp. Their assignment was due at the end of the period: measure the speed of a rolling ball using distance and time, then draw a distance-time graph. The graphs did not intimidate Rachel the way they seemed to intimidate half the class, but today the numbers were refusing to cooperate.

Marcus released the ball and Rachel clicked the stopwatch, calling out the time each time the ball crossed a chalk mark: one meter, two meters, three. They ran it three times, wrote the times in their table, and Rachel plotted the points on graph paper. Most of them climbed in a neat diagonal line. But between two meters and three meters, the points went sideways, the same distance for a whole stretch of seconds.

"Your timing is off," Marcus said, peering over her shoulder.

"My timing was fine." Rachel tapped the flat stretch with her pencil. "Same distance, different times. Something happened to the ball right there."

She looked down the bench. Halfway along, someone had left a lump of dried glue near the two-meter mark. She crouched until her eyes were level with the surface. The glue sat exactly where the graph went flat.

They ran it again with Marcus watching that spot instead of the stopwatch. The ball rolled, hit the glue, wobbled, and sat there for a moment before creeping over the edge. It was stuck, briefly, in the same place while time kept going.

"That's it," Rachel said. She marked the glue spot in her notes, then scraped the lump off with a spatula and wiped the bench down. "Do it again."

The fourth run produced a clean set of points. Rachel plotted them, and this time the line climbed steadily from corner to corner, no flat part anywhere. She calculated the speed by dividing the distance by the time and got nearly the same answer for every stretch of the run. Marcus leaned over to check her arithmetic and frowned at the earlier graph still lying beside it.

"So that flat part," he said, "what does that even tell you?"

"It means the ball wasn't moving," Rachel said. "Stuck on the glue, not going anywhere."

She stapled both graphs to their lab sheet, the flat one and the clean one, and wrote a sentence under the first: ball caught on glue between two and three meters. Then she flipped the glue lump into the trash with the spatula.

"Same time tomorrow?" Marcus asked, packing up his bag.

"Bring your own stopwatch," Rachel said. "And somebody should warn the sixth period class about that bench before their turn."

Justin sat in the back row of Room 12 with his ankle propped on his backpack, the brace stiff against his swollen tendon. He had skipped basketball practice, which was voluntary anyway, but the whole day felt like a list of things taken away from him. Now Mr. Okafor had assigned an essay: explain why people moved west in the 1800s, using one primary source. Justin had picked the fattest book off the cart, a modern textbook with a shiny cover and a chapter called "Westward Expansion."

"You grabbed the wrong thing," said Priya, leaning over from the next desk. "That's not what he means."

"It's got everything. Maps, dates, a whole section on reasons." Justin flipped pages at her. "Land, gold, jobs."

Priya shook her head. "My cousin had this assignment last year. A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, like a settler's diary. A secondary source is written later by someone studying it. Your textbook is the second one."

Justin looked at the shiny cover, then at the cart, where a thin pamphlet with a brown spine sat ignored at the bottom. He pulled it out. It was a copy of a diary kept by a woman named Harriet Lane, who had walked part of the trail in 1852 with her husband and two boys. He started reading, mostly to prove Priya wrong.

The first entry talked about rain and mud. The second mentioned that their wheat had germinated in the wagon after a soaking, and how Harriet's husband laughed because it meant they'd been carrying wet seed for weeks. Then, deeper in, Justin found what the textbook never said. Harriet's husband owed money to a bank in Ohio, and one of the boys had a cough that wouldn't clear in the damp river town. "We do not go for gold," she wrote. "We go because the debt man comes on Fridays and the doctor says drier air. Isaac cries at night and pretends he doesn't."

Justin copied the line into his notebook. The textbook said "economic opportunity," which covered the debt but not the crying, not the doctor, not Fridays. The diary showed the reason from inside a person who was actually there, and he could suddenly see the pattern the textbook flattened out: the big words were made of small ones like these. He raised his hand and asked to change his source, and Mr. Okafor nodded and made a note on his clipboard, which meant someone else would have to fight over the remaining diaries.

At the last bell Priya found him at his locker. "So I was right," she said.

"You were right," Justin admitted. He handed her the pamphlet, since he'd already photographed the pages he needed, and she grinned and hurried off down the hall. He stood there a moment, weight on his good foot, thinking of Harriet's boys coughing in the mud while seeds sprouted in the wagon bed. His essay would be the best thing he'd written all year, and he'd never play in Friday's game. He zipped his backpack, swung it over one shoulder, and limped toward the doors.

The gym smelled like floor wax and old sneakers, and Dominic sat on the bleachers with his laptop balanced on his knee, trying to build his first debate case before Friday's round. The resolution was about building wildlife corridors so animals could move between fragmented forests. He knew what he wanted to argue. He just couldn't figure out how.

"You're staring at a blank page," said Priya, dropping onto the bench beside him with her own notebook. "Claim, evidence, warrant. Remember?"

"That's the problem. I have the claim. Corridors help the ecosystem recover. I have the evidence, the study showing more species survived where corridors were built. I don't have the warrant."

"Then write down why your evidence proves your claim."

He tried. He typed, deleted, typed again. Then he flashed back to Tuesday's practice round, when Marcus from the other team had stood up and told a long story about a single mountain lion that died trying to cross a highway. The room had gone quiet. Everyone felt terrible for that mountain lion. But then Dominic's team had read three statistics about survival rates, and the judge had voted for the numbers anyway. Marcus had slammed his notebook shut and said, "I don't get it. My story was better."

Dominic had gotten it wrong too, at first. He'd thought the judge was being cold. But his sister, home from college, had glanced at his notes and said, "Aristotle figured this out a long time ago. In his Rhetoric he described three ways to persuade: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, reasoning and evidence." She'd tapped his page. "Marcus had pathos and nothing else. You had logos. That's why you won."

Back in the gym, Dominic looked at his blank warrant. He tested an idea. If he wrote, "The study shows survival rates rose when corridors existed, therefore corridors cause survival to rise," that was a warrant, but a weak one. He frowned at it. Maybe the problem was that his evidence only matched his claim if the reader accepted that what happened in the studied forests would happen everywhere. So the warrant had to say that. He typed: places with similar conditions produce similar results, so evidence from comparable forests applies to the plan in the resolution.

"Got it?" Priya asked.

"Test it," he said. "Hit me with an objection."

"The study's from another country. Doesn't apply here."

"That's an attack on my warrant," Dominic said, and grinned. "Last week I wouldn't have even known that's what you were doing. You'd have just sounded stubborn."

"Obstinate," Priya said. "The word is obstinate."

"Fine. You're obstinate, and I answer it." He held up his screen. "Same climate, same species, same road density. It applies."

Priya read the page, then nodded once. "Okay. Now do the mountain lion story."

"For pathos?"

"For the judge who's also a person," she said, and turned her laptop toward him. "We'll put it last."

Dominic dragged the story of the mountain lion to the end of the case file and hit save.

Arthur had forty minutes before the book club's shared folder locked at four o'clock, and his paraphrase of Macbeth's "Tomorrow" speech was still a mess. The five of them met in the corner of the school library every Thursday, and today Ms. Okonkwo had told them their written responses had to follow proper MLA format when they uploaded them. Arthur didn't know what that meant, exactly, but Priya did, and Priya noticed everything.

"You quoted the whole speech inside your sentences," Priya said, leaning over his laptop screen. "It's swimming."

"It's my favorite passage," Arthur said. "I want all of it in there."

"Then you can't keep it inside a sentence." Priya scrolled through her own response until she found an example. "Watch. In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks." She highlighted her block, and Arthur saw the passage sitting alone on its own lines, pushed inward, with no quotation marks anywhere around it. "Long ones get their own room. Short ones live inside your sentence."

Arthur tested it right away. He copied the speech into a draft and counted lines on his screen. It ran past four lines, so he hit Tab once, watched the whole thing slide half an inch from the margin, and deleted the quotation marks. Then he counted again to be sure. Four was the cutoff, and he was over it. "So if I trimmed it to exactly four," he said slowly, "it could go back inside the sentence?"

"If it fits," Priya said. "But why would you cut your favorite part to squeeze it into a sentence?"

She was right, and Arthur knew it before he finished nodding. Instead of trimming the quote, he worked on the paraphrase beneath it. That was the actual assignment: take Macbeth's speech and say it in modern English. "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow" became "one day after another after another, dragging along." He tried to condense the whole speech into a few plain lines, the way Dex had done with his scene from Romeo and Juliet last week. Dex had made the balcony speech sound like two kids texting, which everyone agreed was terrible and also, somehow, completely authentic to the way people actually talked.

Arthur kept circling one part. Macbeth says life is "a walking shadow, a poor player that struts and frets his hour upon the stage and then is heard no more." Arthur wrote and crossed out three versions. It wasn't just about a bad actor. It was about everything ending, the way a species can vanish into extinction and leave nothing behind but a gap where it used to be. Macbeth was saying people were like that too. He wrote, "We're shadows that walk around for a while, make noise, and then nothing."

Dex read it over his shoulder. "That's grim."

"It's the play," Arthur said. "It's already grim. I'm just translating."

The clock on the wall read 3:47. Priya checked the folder, Marcus uploaded his, and then it was Arthur's turn. He looked once more at his block of quotation, indented half an inch from the margin, no quotation marks, four-plus lines on its own. The paraphrase sat under it in his own words. He hit upload, and the progress bar crawled toward done.

"Thirteen seconds to spare," Priya announced.

Arthur closed the laptop. "Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow," he said, "except there's no folder after today."

Nathan spread his poster board across the kitchen table and stared at the empty space where his explanation was supposed to go. His science presentation was in two days, and his topic was the monsoon: how the land of South Asia heats up in summer, how air rises over it, how moisture-laden winds sweep in from the ocean and drop the rains that rice fields drink for months. He understood it, mostly, but every time he tried to say it out loud, it collapsed into a jumble of words.

"Say it to me," said his older brother Ravi, who was sitting at the counter with an ice pack strapped to his head. Ravi had taken a concussion at cricket practice three weeks ago, and the doctor said loud noises and screens were off limits, which left him with nothing to do but listen. "If I can follow it, anyone can."

Nathan went to retrieve the globe from the shelf by the window and set it beside the poster. "Okay. In summer, the land gets hotter than the sea, fast. Hot air rises, and that pulls in wet ocean air from the south and west. When that air hits the mountains and the land, it rains for months. The rice needs it." He paused. "But here's my problem. People say it's all about the sun being directly overhead, near the equator. So I figured, near the equator equals monsoon. Then I checked."

He spun the globe and stopped it with his finger. "I looked up capitals to test it. Quito, the capital of Ecuador, lies less than a quarter of a degree south of the equator, so its latitude is almost zero. Zero! Closer than almost any capital on Earth. But Quito doesn't get monsoon rains the way India and Bangladesh do." He tapped the globe. "So latitude can't be the whole answer. It's the difference between land and sea heating up that matters. That's the hidden part, the thing you can't see. Sun, land, sea, mountains, wind. It's a chain."

"Chain," Ravi repeated slowly. "One link pulls the next."

Nathan grabbed a shallow baking pan, filled it with water, and set it in the sun on the windowsill next to a dry ceramic tile. Every hour he touched both and wrote down what he felt. By late afternoon the tile was hot enough to make him jerk his hand back, while the water had barely changed. He was still scribbling the numbers when the sky outside turned the color of wet slate, and rain hammered the window so hard he could barely hear himself think.

The next morning the power was out and school was delayed, and Nathan paced the kitchen with his flashlight, certain the presentation would be canceled after all that work. Ravi came downstairs, ice pack gone, and pushed the poster board toward him. "You're on in front of Mom and me. Full audience." Nathan took a breath and started at the beginning, pan, tile, globe, Quito and its almost-zero latitude, land heating faster than sea, wet winds rising and dropping their rain on the rice. When he finished, Ravi nodded and said, "Understandable even with a concussion. That's a legitimate test."

From the doorway, Mom cleared her throat. "The school called back. Power's restored, and your teacher moved your slot to first period instead of last." Nathan groaned, then grinned, and Ravi said, "At least now you'll be fresh." Nathan looked out at the flooded garden and said, "Great. Now I have to explain a monsoon before the one outside drains away."

Alex had promised Mr. Delgado he would finish his history project today, which was why he was sitting on the cold steps of the war memorial with a photocopied settler's diary spread across his knees. The assignment seemed fundamental to his grade: use a primary source, an actual person's own words, to explain why families moved west in the 1800s. The diary's handwriting slanted and cramped, and the wind kept lifting the pages like it wanted them to go west too.

"Careful, that paper's older than my knees," said Mr. Okafor, the volunteer who polished the memorial plaques every Saturday. He set a smooth stone on the corner of the pages and settled onto the step beside Alex. His hands were trembling a little today, so Alex held the polish cloth while Mr. Okafor guided the rag in slow circles over the bronze.

Alex read aloud a line where the settler wrote that his brother's farm had failed and prices had fallen so low that staying meant losing everything. "That's it," Alex said. "Hard times pushed them. But how do I prove that's a pattern and not just one grumpy guy?" He flipped to the back of the packet, where a second family wrote almost the same thing, and a third. Same push, different pens. That felt like evidence, not luck.

Then his eye caught the longest plaque, the one Mr. Okafor was polishing. Names from two wars, and at the bottom an inscription about the peace that followed the first. "Mr. Okafor, my great-grandpa's on this wall. After that war, didn't they make Germany shrink its army? How did it get big again so fast for the second one?"

Mr. Okafor tapped the line he'd just cleaned. Alex leaned close and read it aloud. "The Treaty of Versailles limited the German army to 100,000 soldiers and banned Germany from having an air force." He read it twice. An entire air force, gone, by rule. And still, twenty years later, planes everywhere and armies in the millions. "So the rule didn't hold," Alex said slowly. "Somebody broke it, and my great-grandpa ended up on this wall anyway." He copied the sentence into his notebook, word for word, the way he'd copied the diary lines. Two sources, two wars, one habit: go to what people wrote at the time.

"You know what your problem is, Alex?" Mr. Okafor said, and Alex braced himself. "You think you have to finish everything in one day." He nodded at the notebook. "Read it to your grandfather tonight. He knows more about all this than any plaque."

Alex looked down the long list of names, then at the diary pages weighted by the stone, and started folding them into his backpack with the care of someone carrying something borrowed. "Grandpa," he said, testing the plan out loud. "I brought you some homework."

Brooke had forty dollars of birthday money in her pocket and a plan: a new backpack from the mall's sporting goods store. But on the way, she passed the bank kiosk near the fountain, where a poster showed two lines climbing side by side over five years. Simple interest grew in a straight staircase. Compound interest curved upward, because each year's interest earned interest of its own. She stared at the graph until her cousin Dana elbowed her.

"You're doing money homework at the mall? Tragic," Dana said.

"There's a difference," Brooke said. She grabbed a flyer and a pen from the counter. "If I put forty dollars in at simple interest, I get the same flat amount every year. Compounding pays me on the whole balance, so it accelerates." She sketched five quick boxes on the back of the flyer, doubling her totals in her head, and the numbers diverged by year three. The compound line pulled away like the fast lane on the escalator.

Then she spotted a display card beside the poster: a corporate bond paying nearly twice the interest of the savings account. Twice. She turned to Dana. "Why would anyone pick the savings account? This is obviously better."

"Nothing's obviously better," Dana said. "When we got our apartment lease, Mom said the landlord had to accommodate her service dog or we'd walk. Landlords who want something from you have to give something up." Dana tapped the card. "So ask yourself what the borrower wants from you and what they're giving up."

Brooke frowned and pulled up a finance page on her phone, typing in the bond's name. The rating was far below the top grades. She read the entry twice. "These are called junk bonds," she said slowly. "Companies that are more likely to fail to pay have to offer higher interest to get anyone to lend to them. That's why it pays double. It's not free money, it's a warning sticker." The page also called them high-yield, which sounded glamorous until she remembered what the yield was compensating for.

"So what do you do?" Dana asked.

Brooke laid the flyer flat on the counter and made two columns. The savings account had a small, certain rate that compounded every year; the bond had a big rate attached to a borrower who might not pay her back at all. She thought of it like a variable in math class: one thing she could hold constant, and one thing that could swing either way. "The credible choice is the boring one," she said. "For now. Maybe when I have more than forty dollars, I can take one small risk."

She walked to the bank desk and asked the teller to open a savings account with compound interest, then fed her two twenties into the bill reader. The receipt printed with a balance of $40.00 and a date five years in the future, when the account would be worth more.

"Backpack?" Dana asked as they headed for the escalator.

"Next birthday," Brooke said, folding the receipt into her pocket. "This one's climbing the curve."

Harper had decided to paint her grandfather for his birthday, which was ambitious, since she had exactly three weeks and one sheet of printer paper. She laid the first pale wash across the forehead, a colour she called "old lemon," and watched it soak in. So far so good. The second wash, a slightly deeper gold for the cheeks, went on beside it, and the third, a warm shadow under the nose.

Then the paper began to wrinkle. It rose in little waves, like someone had shrunk it in the wash, and her grandfather's face buckled into ridges. His forehead looked like it had grown accordion folds overnight.

"Grandpa's going to think he aged forty years," said Priya, leaning over from the next easel. She was painting a portrait of her cat, which was going about as well as a cat portrait ever goes, which is to say the cat looked like a loaf of bread with ears.

"Very funny. But why is it doing that? I didn't touch the edges." Harper turned the paper over, then back again. It was flat-ish when dry, wavy when wet. She tried an experiment: she painted a small square of wash on a corner of a fresh sheet and watched. Within a minute, that corner alone puckered. So it was the water. But her teacher's demo paper, which had been soaked repeatedly last week, lay flat as a pancake. Same water, different paper. Same washes too. The difference had to be the paper itself.

She carried her ruined grandfather over to Mr. Duffy, the studio volunteer, who was sharpening pencils as though it were a competitive sport.

"My paper's doing a wave impression," she said. "Yours doesn't. What's yours made of, dragon skin?"

Mr. Duffy chuckled and held up his pad, thick as a slice of bread. "It cockles if it's too thin. That's what they call it when it buckles. Watercolour artists usually use the heavy stuff, about 300 grams per square metre." He tapped the cover. "It's also sold as 140-pound paper, if you see that on the label."

Harper traced the number on the pad with her finger, then felt her thin sheet, which was about as substantial as a receipt. "So my paper was doomed from wash one."

"Doomed from wash zero," said Mr. Duffy. "Take a sheet."

Back at her easel, Harper taped the heavy paper down and began again: light lemon first, then the gold, then the shadow, building her grandfather's face in layers from pale to dark. The paper drank the water and stayed stubbornly flat. She was rather vain about her mixing of the perfect grey for his ears, since it took eleven tries, and she made herself sketch the curve of his nose twice, because noses were basically cartilage with ambitions.

Priya drifted over. "Your grandpa doesn't look like an accordion anymore."

"He never did," said Harper, and dipped her brush for the next wash.

Grandpa's porch was the best place in the world to figure things out, and Colton had a big thing to figure out before Monday. His cousin Marcus was visiting too, along with a neighbor kid named Theo, and Grandpa had promised them all lemonade and a chess set older than anyone in the room.

Theo was quiet and wore the same dinosaur shirt two days in a row, which gave Marcus all the material he needed. "Nice shirt," Marcus said, grinning. "Did you dig it out of a museum?"

Theo's comeback was fast and clever. "At least I don't look like a potato with eyebrows."

Colton actually laughed before he could stop himself, and Theo's face went red. Marcus didn't laugh back, though. He leaned forward like a hawk spotting something small and helpless, which was exactly the predatory look the older kids at school got right before things got loud. "A potato with eyebrows?" Marcus said. "Okay, fossil boy. Does your mom still cut your hair with a bowl?"

"Does yours cut yours with a weed whacker?"

By the third round, Theo was shouting, Marcus was shouting, and the chessboard sat forgotten. Colton realized he was watching the exact pattern from school. Last week a kid named Ryan had teased a classmate named Dev, and Dev had fired back a brilliant insult about Ryan's shoes. He'd expected applause. Instead the teasing got ten times worse, and Dev ended up eating lunch alone. Colton had been trying for days to work out why a good comeback made things worse instead of better.

He stared at the chessboard, moving a knight in his head. A clever insult gave the other person something new to attack. That was it. It was like handing your opponent a fresh piece.

"Grandpa," Colton said suddenly, "are you a descendant of any famous chess players?"

"One or two, supposedly," Grandpa said, setting down the lemonade. "Why?"

"Just wondering if it's in the blood." Colton turned to Marcus. "Hey, back off the shirt thing. It's not funny, so stop."

Marcus blinked. His mouth opened, hunting for something to grab onto, and found nothing. "Whatever," he said, and looked at the board instead. "Whose move is it?"

"Yours," said Theo, and for the first time all afternoon he smiled.

They played two full games before the mosquitoes came out. Theo won the second one by sacrificing his queen, which he explained in a whisper while Marcus pretended not to be impressed. On Monday, Colton walked toward Dev's table in the cafeteria with his tray, already deciding exactly what he'd say if Ryan started up again. Short, calm, nothing new to fight about. He sat down across from Dev and said, "Save me a seat tomorrow?"

Riley set her debate packet on the library table so hard that the pages fanned out like a dropped deck of cards. Her assignment sheet said, in Ms. Okafor's looping handwriting, "Thesis and three-point outline before any draft. No exceptions." Riley had a draft already, two pages of it, written last night in one long sprint about why the school should start a recycling program. The problem was that her draft said three different things, and she could not tell which one she actually believed.

Across the table, her friend Devon was marking up an essay with a green pen, circling words one by one. Riley watched him fix "recieve" to "receive" and "there" to "their" and move a comma.

"Is that revising?" she asked.

"Yep," Devon said. "Revised it twice already."

Riley slid her laptop toward him. "Can you look at mine, then? Just tell me what to fix."

He read for a minute, then turned the screen back to her. "There's like one spelling error. Congrats. But your first paragraph says recycling saves money, your second says it saves the planet, and your third says it teaches responsibility, and then they all just kind of wander off."

Riley exhaled slowly and stared at the ceiling tiles. "So if fixing spelling is revising, what's this other thing called, where I have to take my own argument apart?"

Devon shrugged. "My tutor says the word 'revise' comes from the Latin revisere, meaning 'to look at again'." He went back to his green pen. "So real revising is supposed to be seeing the draft again, like a civilian who never met you, not fixing typos like a machine."

A civilian who never met you. Riley sat with that. She opened a new document and typed one sentence at the top: "The school should fund a recycling program because it saves money, builds student responsibility, and sets an example for the district." Then she made three headings and dragged chunks of her draft under each one. Under "saves money," she found she had almost no evidence, just enthusiasm. Under "responsibility," she found her strongest paragraph, the one about the sixth graders who ran the cafeteria compost bins. Interesting, she thought. The outline was like a map of her own brain, and apparently her brain had been marching in three parallel directions at once.

She deleted her entire second point. It hurt a little, like throwing away a drawing she'd spent an hour on, but the map was clearer with two roads instead of three, so she split the responsibility point into two halves and rebuilt.

At 3:45 Devon packed up. "How's the typo situation?" he asked.

"Extremely bad," Riley said. "I just cut two hundred words and moved everything." She turned the screen toward him. "But I looked at it again. First time, actually."

He leaned in, read the new outline top to bottom, and laughed. "Riley. Your thesis says the program saves money."

"It does."

"Your evidence is a compost bin run by sixth graders."

Riley looked at her outline, really looked, and the flaw opened up under her eyes like a pothole. "Okay," she said, cracking her knuckles. "Round two."

Jack had the assignment taped to the fridge: pick one right from the country's charter, put it in your own words, and take one real action about it by Monday. He'd chosen the right to contact your elected representative, because his street lamp on Crescent Road had been dead for three months, and his little sister Maya had to walk home from her friend's house in the dark on Tuesdays. His dad had once called the city about it and gotten nowhere, but the assignment said representatives had to respond to citizens. Jack wanted to test that.

First he tried the city website and found a wall of forty-some councillor names, each with a photo and an email. He couldn't email forty people. He noticed, though, that every name had a small label beside it, a number and a name like "Crescent Heights." He got out a street map his mom kept in the junk drawer and made a meticulous list of nearby street names, matching them against the labels. A pattern emerged: the labels weren't random. Each councillor was attached to one specific area of the city.

"That's a ward," Maya said, reading over his shoulder while eating toast. She'd learned it on a field trip. "Each councillor is elected to represent one ward."

"So I just need ours," Jack said. He typed their address into the site's ward finder, and up came Ward 9, Riverside, with a photo of Councillor Amara Odell. One name instead of forty. That was the hidden rule he'd been looking for, the thing that made the whole task possible, and it had been sitting in plain sight the whole time.

He drafted an email, deleted it, and drafted it again. He wanted it to signify a serious request, not a kid's complaint, so he stated the facts plainly: the lamp had been out since November, the street had no other lighting, and a twelve-year-old walked there every Tuesday. Maya leaned against his chair.

"Say there's a motion sensor on the back porch across the street and it doesn't reach," she offered. "So it's really all dark."

"Good," Jack said, and added it. He hit send at 8:52 on a Thursday night, and then there was nothing to do but wait. He checked his inbox Friday at recess, and again after dinner, and found only a notice that the basketball team pictures had been rescheduled.

On Saturday morning Maya shook him awake, holding the tablet in both hands. "You got mail. Real mail." Councillor Odell had written three paragraphs, thanking him for the detailed report and saying she would ask Public Works to inspect the lamp, and could he confirm the nearest cross street. Jack typed back "Crescent and Fifth" before he was even fully out of the blanket, then read the email aloud a second time while Maya toasted them both an English muffin.

Tuesday night, they stood at the window. A city truck rolled slowly down Crescent Road, its beacon circling, and a worker in an orange vest raised a long pole toward the dead lamp. It flickered, blazed, and steadied, laying a clean square of light across the sidewalk.

"It works," Maya said, and pressed her palm flat against the cold glass.

Laurence knelt on the stone floor of the temple annex with a folded sheet of Sanskrit verses in front of her. In three weeks she would chant the whole prayer from memory in front of the congregation, part of her coming-of-age ceremony, and so far she could get through four lines before the words slipped away from her.

Her cousin Priya found her there after the morning bells. "You look like you're trying to stare a hole in the paper," Priya said.

"It won't stick. I read it over and over and it just slides off." Laurence flattened the page against the floor. "How did you ever memorize anything for your ceremony?"

Priya sat down beside her. "I didn't memorize for that. I danced. Two hours a day for four years, and last spring I finally did my first full solo performance. It's called an arangetram. It means ascending the stage." She straightened the edge of her shawl. "It marks the end of my first formal training."

Laurence looked at her. "Four years. And you're still the one who complains about practice."

"Exactly because of that." Priya laughed.

That night Laurence thought about the difference between Priya's four years and her own three weeks. Priya hadn't learned her dance by reading it. She had learned it with her feet and her hands, the same movements repeated until her body knew them without the mirror. Laurence had been treating the prayer as something on paper, a thing outside her, instead of something she could carry in her mouth and her breath.

The next morning she tested the idea. She stood in the temple courtyard, left the sheet folded in her pocket, and chanted the first line while touching the pillar nearest the door, the way she had done on her first day. Then the second line at the tulsi planter, the third at the low step. She walked the route six times, tying each line to a place she could walk to.

On the sixth round, her aunt tried to intervene, saying she should come in and eat before the priest arrived, but Laurence held up one hand and finished the verse at the bell rope without a single mistake.

At breakfast her uncle asked why she was grinning at her idli. "I thought memorizing meant being biased toward my eyes," she said. "All reading, no doing. I was wrong. It's in my feet now too." Nobody in the family had paid a single rupee for lessons, unlike Priya's parents, whose income had stretched thin over four years of dance fees, and that made the walking method even better.

On the day of the ceremony she stood before the congregation, closed her eyes, and saw the courtyard in her mind, pillar, planter, step, bell rope. Her voice moved from station to station. When she finished, she opened her eyes, and Priya, in the second row, raised her hands in a dancer's salute.

The onion came out of the root cellar still cold, and Oliver peeled a single layer of skin from its curved side with tweezers, the way the science booklet said, laying it flat on a glass slide. His grandfather's microscope sat on the kitchen table between the salt shaker and a jar of bolts. It had been in the barn loft for years, and Oliver had spent half the morning polishing its little mirror before he could see anything at all.

He wanted this to work. He had written to his grandfather three weeks ago, when the science fair project was assigned, asking if he could borrow the microscope, and yesterday a letter had finally come back. The letter was in his pocket now, soft at the folds from being read too many times. His grandfather wrote about the farm and the weather, and then, near the end, about a summer long ago when he had volunteered in the Galápagos Islands counting finches. That part Oliver had read four times.

First, though, he had to see the cells. He dropped a bead of water and a thread of iodine onto the skin, pressed the cover slip down, and bent to the eyepiece. At first there was only a pale blur. He turned the knob a fraction at a time, the way a careful person turns a key in an old lock. Then the blur sharpened into rows of brick-like cells, each one walled off from the next, and there inside each cell, faintly, a dark dot.

He sat back. He found the diagram in his booklet and matched it piece by piece. The thick outer line of every brick was the cell wall. Just inside it, so thin he could barely tell it apart, was the membrane. The dark dot was the nucleus. He labeled them on his own drawing, and where he could not decide whether a line was wall or membrane, he guessed, and the guess felt arbitrary, so he checked it twice.

Then he took out the letter. "You asked once whether bigger is always better," his grandfather had written. "On the island of Daphne Major, the medium ground finches had big beaks, good for big hard seeds. But after the very wet El Niño year of 1983 brought many small, soft seeds, selection reversed, and smaller beaks were favoured." Oliver read it again, thinking of his grandfather the year he sold the big tractor and bought the small one, and how the neighbors had laughed, and how nobody laughed after the dry summer. He looked back into the eyepiece at the little walled city, every cell the same size, nobody bigger than anybody.

The screen door banged and his mother came in with two buckets of feed. "You find them?" she asked.

"Wall, membrane, nucleus," he said, and slid the letter across the table to her, still open to the last page.

Rosalie stood on the auditorium stage with her scene partner, Dex, and tried to hand him an invisible pizza. "Here's the pizza you ordered, sir," she said. "No," said Dex. "I ordered soup." Behind the curtain, the debate team was rehearsing, and the clock on the back wall said the improv showcase started in thirty minutes. Mrs. Okafor had been clear: pairs who couldn't sustain a scene for two minutes would be cut.

"You have to say yes," Rosalie whispered. "That's the whole thing. You accept the offer and add to it." Dex shrugged, and she noticed he was flexing his right hand like a tendon in his wrist had gone tight from gripping his debate notes all day. "I'm a debater," he said. "My instinct is to argue." She tried again with the pizza. He said no again, and this time added, "You're just an actor, you wouldn't understand blocking an offer."

From behind the curtain, a voice drifted out, sharp and bored. It was the debate judge, a tired senior with a clipboard. "Marcus, when you said 'you're just a sixth grader,' I had to mark that down. That's an ad hominem fallacy. You attacked the person instead of the claim." There was a pause, then a younger kid's voice said, "So it doesn't matter if my argument was right?" and the judge said, "The claim stands or falls on its own. Attack the claim, not the kid."

Rosalie chewed on that. Dex had just done the same thing to her. He hadn't said her idea about saying yes was wrong; he'd said she was just an actor, as if that settled it. She couldn't see the rule of improv any more than she could see the rule of debate, but she could test whether the two corresponded. Maybe blocking a scene and attacking a person were the same move: refusing the offer in front of you by pointing at who made it.

She set down the invisible pizza. "Try this," she said. "When I make an offer, don't tell me what I am. Tell me what happens next." Dex frowned, then rolled his shoulders back like he was starting a rebuttal. "Fine. Sir, the pizza arrived, and it's on fire." Rosalie blinked, then grinned and fanned it with her cape, which she decided she was wearing. "Yes, and the fire spell can only be broken by a debate champion." Dex stepped forward, extinguished it with a wave, and looked almost competent doing it. Mrs. Okafor's footsteps were already coming up the aisle.

They had ninety seconds before she reached the stage. "Ready?" Rosalie asked. Dex raised one hand, palm out, as if holding a very small, very important pizza. "Yes," he said, "and this time I ordered it."

Grayson spread his Spanish worksheet across the library table with the confidence of a general deploying troops. On it he had written a whole conversation for his pen pal letter: how to order tacos, ask for water, and find out how much the bill cost. "¿Cuánto cuesta?" he muttered, testing it out. "Cuánto cuesta el taco de pescado." Tomorrow was the exchange video call with Mateo in Oaxaca, and Grayson wanted to sound like someone who could actually survive in a restaurant, not like a lost tourist pointing at a menu.

Priya dropped her backpack on the chair beside him and leaned over the page. "Ready for the big call?"

"Almost. I just have to write the last paragraph where I tell him I'll speak Spanish with the waiter." Grayson wrote "hablé con el camarero" and underlined it twice for emphasis.

Priya squinted. "That says you already spoke with the waiter. Past tense. You chopped hablar down to habl- and stuck the wrong ending on it."

Grayson stared at the word. He had been so sure. He flipped back through his notes and found a list of verbs, hablar, comer, pedir, and then, near the bottom, a line he had skimmed: hablaré. He looked at it, then at his own botched attempt, then back again. The whole infinitive was still sitting right there inside the word, hablar plus é, like a train with a new car hooked on the end instead of the engine getting replaced.

"Hablaré," Priya said, tapping the example. "That means I will speak. It keeps the whole infinitive and adds the ending onto it."

"So I don't chop anything off. I just bolt something on." Grayson tested the pattern out loud, quieter and quieter as the kid at the next table glared at him. "Comeré. Pediré. It's the same trick every time." He felt a little naive for having assumed the future would work like the past, but at least he had caught it before Mateo did, which would have earned him a laughing emoji and probably a screenshot.

He rewrote the paragraph. "Esta semana practicaré pedir la comida en español," he read to Priya. "And then I ask how much everything costs, so when I visit, Mateo's mom can't sneak the expensive flan onto my half of the bill."

"Bold plan," said Priya. "Now paraphrase your whole letter for me in English so I know you're not accidentally promising to buy everyone dinner."

Grayson walked her through it, paragraph by paragraph, and Priya delivered her critique: good ordering, decent questions, one word that sounded like he was asking to adopt the waiter. He fixed it, folded the letter into his binder, and headed for the front desk to check out a Spanish phrasebook for extra backup.

At the circulation desk he paused, turned around, and called back to Priya, "¡Pagaré!" Then he patted his pocket where his lunch money lived.

Katherine sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with Priya's laptop between them, three orange slices deep into an argument about the swim team's points. Priya swore the Dolphins were crushing everyone this season, and she had a spreadsheet to prove it. "Look, I'll show you," Priya said, opening the file. "You type the scores in this column, then in the cell below you put equals, S-U-M, open parenthesis, then drag over the cells you want, close parenthesis, hit enter." Katherine typed it herself, and when the number appeared at the bottom of the column she actually bounced a little. "It added the whole thing. Twelve scores, one click." Then Priya showed her the chart button, and a bar chart sprang up with the Dolphins' bar towering over the Stingrays'.

"That's not right," Katherine said slowly. The Dolphins had 214 points and the Stingrays had 205. She knew that from the paper list on the wall, because she was the one who kept it for the coach. Nine points out of more than two hundred, and on the chart it looked like the Dolphins were double everyone. She leaned in and studied the side of the chart, the little numbers running up the axis. "It starts at two hundred," she said. "Not at zero." Priya squinted. "So?" Katherine clicked the axis, found the scale settings, and changed the minimum to zero. The bars shrank until the Dolphins' lead looked like what it was: a sliver, a margin so thin the season wasn't decided at all.

Priya didn't say anything for a moment. "I made that chart for the team group chat," she admitted. "The vote was unanimous because everyone saw it and figured the season was basically over. We agreed to skip the last meet since we'd already lost." Katherine felt the orange slices turn sour in her stomach. "You didn't lose," she said. "You're nine points back with one meet left. That's nothing. That's catchable."

Priya grabbed her phone and typed fast, sending the fixed chart to everyone with the words "we can still win this, come to practice tomorrow." The replies started coming in within a minute, and Priya's face went from gray to glowing. Katherine was glad, truly glad, but there was a small ache underneath it. She had made the chart honest, and the consequence was that Priya's team would now fight hard in the last meet, the meet Katherine's Dolphins would have to win all over again. She was going to have to swim her best race of the year against her best friend.

"To verify it's really fixed, check the axis on my phone too," Priya said, holding it out. Katherine looked at the little screen, at the honest little bars standing close together, and nodded. "It's fixed," she said, and clicked the button to send it to the coach.

The kitchen smelled like burnt garlic, and Easton was trying to write an essay at the table while his cousin Mira practiced tinikling between the counter and the fridge. She had two wooden spoons and was tapping them on the floor, and her friend Daisy was stepping in and out of them like her ankles were made of glass. "Tap, tap, clap," Mira counted, loud and nervous, because in the real dance two people tapped bamboo poles on the ground twice and then clapped them together on the third beat, and if Daisy miscounted, the spoons would snap shut on her ankles like a cranky turtle.

"Can you count quieter?" Easton asked.

"Can you write quieter?" Mira said. "Your pencil sounds like a rebellious squirrel."

Easton looked down at his paper. The assignment was to compare how two faiths explained what happens after death, and he had exactly two sentences, one of which was his name. His lola believed in heaven and purgatory, which she described as being made clean before you went home. His friend Tomas's family was Buddhist and talked about being reborn, coming around again in a different form. Both ideas were about something nobody could actually see and come back from to report, which struck Easton as the world's worst homework design.

Then Daisy yelped. Mira had gotten excited on a turn and clapped the spoons a beat early, catching Daisy's sock. Daisy hopped on one foot, laughing, and Mira covered her face. "I'll embarrass myself at the recital," she groaned into her hands.

"No, wait," Easton said, standing up. "Count out loud, like you were doing. You kept her ankles clear when you counted. It went wrong when you stopped counting."

Mira gave him a suspicious look but started again. "Tap, tap, clap. Tap, tap, clap." Daisy's feet flicked in and out, safe every time, like the pattern was a law of nature instead of two wooden spoons.

Easton sat back down and looked at his blank page, and something clicked that felt like a spoon clapping shut. Both beliefs were patterns too, ways of counting past something you couldn't see. His lola's way said you went home after being made clean. Tomas's way said you came around again, like the third beat returning to the first. He couldn't test either one, not the way he'd just tested Mira's counting, but he could set them side by side and watch where they matched and where they clashed. His pencil finally started moving.

"Done!" Daisy announced, arms up like a champion.

"Tap, tap, clap," Easton read aloud from his page, then scribbled a new first line: Life, life, and then what?

Kayla stood at Grandma Rosa's counter with an onion the size of a softball and a knife she was slightly afraid of. Her older cousin Marco always chopped the onions at family dinners, and everyone laughed about how he cried through every sauce. This year Kayla had asked to learn, and now here she was, being shown how to curl her fingers into a claw, knuckles forward, so the blade could only find the vegetable and never her fingertips.

"Watch," Grandma said, tucking her own hand into the same claw shape. "The knuckles are the wall. The knife rides along them." Kayla copied it, feeling a little like a crab. Her first cut was crooked, but the second was straighter, and by the fifth she noticed a pattern: the closer the tip of the knife stayed to the board, the less the onion slipped. She wondered if that was true for every vegetable, or just onions with their slick skins.

The sauce came together piece by piece. Onions into the oil, then garlic, then the tomatoes Grandma had crushed by hand. Kayla tasted it and frowned. "It needs something," she said. "I want to revise it. More salt? A pinch of sugar?" Grandma slid the sugar jar across the counter without a word, which Kayla took to mean she'd guessed right.

The problem arrived with the rice. Grandma's timer went off while the bread still had ten minutes in the oven, and there was no free burner, because the sauce was bubbling away on the last one. Grandma reached to lift the pot and hesitated. Kayla called her friend Priya, who cooked dinner at her house every Thursday. "Take it off the heat," Priya said, "lid on. It can rest like that for several minutes and the trapped steam finishes it. That frees the stove for other dishes." Kayla reported it, and Grandma raised an eyebrow, wiped her hands, and moved the pot to a cold burner with the lid pressed down tight.

While the bread finished, Grandpa wandered in still taking his antibiotic for his chest, so Kayla pushed the orange juice away from him and poured him water instead. He watched her stir the sauce and asked what was in it, and she told him: onion, garlic, hand-crushed tomatoes, one secret pinch of sugar. She kept glancing at the rice pot, wondering what was happening under that lid that she couldn't see. Was it really still cooking, or just sitting there? When she finally lifted the lid, the grains stood plump and separate, steam curling up past her face. "It worked," she said. Grandma tasted a forkful, nodded, and pointed at the pasta water, which had just begun to boil.

Easton spread his bar mitzvah study folder across the synagogue library table and felt his stomach drop. Rabbi Stein had handed him two packets instead of one, and the second packet was thick. "Wait," Easton said. "I thought I only had to chant my Torah portion."

Rabbi Stein was already halfway to the door. "You have the haftarah too," she said. "A reading from the books of the Prophets. Most b'nei mitzvah students chant both."

Two readings. Easton's bar mitzvah was in eleven weeks, and he had promised himself he would master every letter of one reading, not fumble through two. Then he remembered the other promise he had made, to his social studies teacher, Mrs. Okafor, who had assigned a project where students had to categorize how two different faiths explain what happens after death. Easton had picked his own and his friend Deshawn's church, and tonight was his chance to ask questions at the youth group Deshawn had invited him to.

At the church basement meeting, the pastor talked about heaven, about being welcomed home. Easton wrote it down, then asked, "So how do you picture it? Like, what does it look like?" A woman beside him smiled and said everyone pictures it differently, which was not much of an answer. Deshawn leaned over and whispered, "You're asking like it's a place you can visit."

That was exactly what Easton had been doing, and he knew it. His grandfather, a descendant of the synagogue's founding families, had taught him chess and had always said you figure out hidden things by what you can see on the board.
