Easton decided to test a simple idea: maybe each faith's answer to death was hidden somewhere you could actually look, in their texts and their rituals, not just in what people said out loud.

Back home, a letter was waiting in his grandmother's careful handwriting. "Your grandfather asked me to give you this when you started studying for your bar mitzvah," she wrote. Easton unfolded it and read his grandfather's words: "When I chant the Prophets, I am listening to voices older than me. They disagreed about everything, including what comes after. Argue with them. That is how you honor them."

Easton grinned. His haftarah portion sat right there in his folder, Isaiah, full of images of consolation. He read it twice, then read the pastor's pamphlet from youth group, then drew two columns in his notebook and filled them with what each one actually said. It was like the chessboard: pieces you could see, patterns underneath.

The next Sunday at the library, Deshawn found him still writing. "You solved your afterlife project?"

"Better," Easton said. "I found out I had two readings to learn, not one, and the second one might be the best source I've got." He tapped the Prophets packet. "Want to hear the tricky part? These guys didn't agree with each other either."

Deshawn pulled up a chair. "Read me the part you underlined."

Adam had until Friday to turn in a bar chart showing how many decomposers he had found in each bag of leaf litter, six bags, six counts, and his science teacher wanted the numbers in a spreadsheet with a formula that added the whole column. Adam did not own a computer, so after school he walked to the public library with his crumpled data sheet in his back pocket. He felt that handing in raw numbers scrawled on paper would look negligent, like he hadn't tried at all, and he had tried. He had counted pill bugs, earthworms, and one moldy beetle.

At the first open terminal, Adam searched for a free spreadsheet tool. The very first result, sitting at the top of the page in its own shaded box, said FREE in capital letters, so he clicked it. The page loaded, invited him to start his project, and then asked for a credit card to "verify his trial." Adam stared at it. He was twelve. He did not have a credit card, and even if he had, his mother would not hand the number to a website that shouted FREE at him. The second link on the page, below the first one and without a box around it, led to a plain tool that opened instantly and asked for nothing.

"Not the top one," Adam murmured, making a note of it. The first link at the top of a search page wasn't necessarily the one to trust. He would remember that.

He typed his counts into a grid, one column for each bag, and hunted through the menus until he found a function that would add them. When he typed it in and pressed enter, the total appeared in the cell at the bottom: forty-three decomposers altogether. He highlighted the column, clicked the chart button, and watched six bars rise out of nothing, tall where he'd found the damp corner bag crawling with sow bugs, short where the dry bag near the fence had held almost nothing. He saved the file and then retrieved it twice more, just to be sure it was really there.

Mrs. Okafor came by with a cart of returns and glanced at his screen. "That's a nice chart," she said. "What program is that?"

"The free one from the second link," Adam said. "The first link wanted a credit card."

She smiled and tapped the edge of the monitor. "You know these computers have spreadsheet software installed already? Has for years. It's right there on the desktop."

Adam looked at the little green icon in the corner of the screen, then at his finished chart, and slid his data sheet deeper into his pocket. "Can I print it anyway?"

Kaylee had exactly one free period before the photography club's web page had to go live, and the computer lab smelled like warm keyboards and somebody's grape soda. Her plan was simple: a title, a few pictures of lichen from the school nature trail, and a heading that sat dead center instead of hugging the left edge like it was afraid of the page.

"You're still on the heading?" said Marcus, sliding into the seat beside her. He was supposed to be finishing the club's Python quiz program, which kept score but refused, so far, to display anything sensible.

"I'm still on the centering," Kaylee said. She typed `text-align: center;` into the style block, saved, and hit refresh. The heading stayed stubbornly on the left, like a cat that had decided that corner was its corner now.

While she stared at it, Marcus ran his program. A question came up, he answered it, and the score line printed `777`. The half of the club still in the lab gathered around and laughed, because a score of seven hundred seventy-seven was, in Marcus's words, "generous."

"That's not the math," Marcus said. "I added seven three times. It should be twenty-one." He scrolled through his code like he was looking for a burglar hiding between the lines.

Kaylee leaned over. The problem, whatever it was, wasn't something she could see by reading; the code looked fine, which meant the cause was somewhere underneath, like the reason her heading wouldn't move. She had an idea. She opened a Python console and typed it small and quick: `'7' * 3`. The screen returned `777`.

"There," she said. "In Python, multiplying text by a whole number repeats the text, so '7' * 3 gives '777' instead of 21."

"So my sevens are strings?"

"You quoted them when you built the question. So it glued three sevens together." Marcus went back and found it, a pair of quotation marks doing quiet damage, and fixed it. His next score printed 21, and the club applauded like he'd landed a plane.

Kaylee turned back to her own hidden cause. If his bug had been invisible, hers probably was too, so she stopped reading the words and started reading the shape of them. The braces, the curly ones that opened the style rule, didn't match. One opened, and the browser, finding no reason to trust anything after it, ignored the whole thing. She added the missing one, saved, refreshed, and the heading drifted to the middle of the page at last, over a row of gray-green lichen thriving on an old stone wall.

"Beautiful," Marcus said, peering at the screen. "Opaque background, too. Very solid."

"Like my debugging," Kaylee said, and clicked refresh one more time just to watch it happen again.

Jonathan had one job at the science fair table: dip the strip, read the color, call it. Mrs. Okonkwo had given him twelve bottles, all labeled with letters instead of names, and a stack of litmus paper, red and blue. His poster explained that acids turn blue litmus red, bases turn red litmus blue, and that the pH scale runs from zero to fourteen, with acids low and bases high. It should have been simple. But bottle H had turned his blue strip red, and his red strip red too, and then, when he tried the second strip from the same bottle, both stayed blue. That could not happen, and yet it had.

He stood very still, holding the wet paper up to the gym lights. Behind him, judges moved down the row of tables. Somewhere a baking-soda volcano burbled. In front of him, his display looked neat and certain, while the evidence in his hand disagreed with everything on it. If the paper was bad, his whole results chart was worthless. If the bottle was bad, then something invisible was going on inside it, something he could not see, only reason about.

"Your table's cool," said Priya from the next booth, where her eccentric model of a chlorine atom hung from a coat hanger, painted balls wobbling on fishing line. Her index card read MASS NUMBER 35, ATOMIC NUMBER 17, and then NEUTRONS, followed by a blank she had covered with a scribbled 20. "I don't get the blank though. My grandma wouldn't just tell me. She had me doing a practice sheet at her kitchen table last night and she said the mass number counts the protons plus the neutrons, so I should be able to figure it out myself."

Jonathan looked at the card, not really meaning to. Then he looked again. If the mass number counted protons plus neutrons, and the atomic number was the protons, then neutrons had to be the part left over. Thirty-five take away seventeen. Eighteen, not twenty. "You wrote twenty," he said slowly. "But the neutrons are the mass number minus the atomic number. That's eighteen."

Priya frowned, checked her card, and erased the twenty with such force the card bent. "Grandma's going to be smug about this."

The movement made her elbow catch her water cup, and water arced across the boundary of their tables and splashed, impossibly, onto the far end of Jonathan's stack of litmus paper. He grabbed the stack. The bottom third was soaked and useless, and there, in the puddle, sat his mystery bottle H, which he had capped badly and left too near the edge. A thin line of liquid had been seeping out along the table all morning, pooling under his paper strips. His first test had been honest. Every test after that had used paper already touched by the leak, and the leak, he realized, was base, because his spare red strip, dipped clean on its dry end into fresh water, turned blue when a drop of the puddle reached it. He had not been testing the bottles. He had been testing his own spilled solution.

A judge stopped at his table, clipboard ready, and asked him to evaluate his results. Jonathan took a fresh dry strip, held it up, and said, "Give me thirty seconds. I have to redo one, and I can tell you exactly why."

Brielle leaned close to the screen so the code seemed to magnify, every line of it jumping out at her. The assignment said her Python program had to ask for a number and print whether it was prime, and she was determined to finish before anyone else in the class. She typed the input line, then a loop that checked each possible divisor, and pressed run.

"Nine," she whispered, typing it in. The screen printed "not prime," and she nearly knocked her chair over. "Yes! It works!"

Then Desmond slid his laptop across the table. His cat sprite walked across a golden coin again and again, and the coin never vanished. "My game is broken," he said. "The cat touches it and nothing happens."

Brielle grabbed the laptop. She clicked the coin's script and stared at the blocks. "Your 'if touching' block is just sitting out there by itself," she said. "It's not in any loop. It only runs once, when the script starts, and then it's done." She pointed at the stack below it. "Put it inside your forever loop. Then it gets checked again and again."

"Forever," Desmond repeated, dragging the block into the loop.

They hit the green flag together. The cat padded across the coin and the coin popped out of existence with a sparkle. Desmond whooped so loudly that their colleague two seats over, a quiet kid named Priya, looked up from her own screen.

"That's the same thing my program does," Brielle said, spinning her chair around. "The loop tries dividing the number over and over. One check wouldn't be enough. You have to keep checking."

Priya frowned at her screen. "Mine says eleven is not prime, but it is prime."

Brielle rolled her chair over. In Priya's loop, the check read the number as text instead of a number, so the comparison came out wrong every time. Brielle showed her the one small fix, and Priya ran it again. "Prime!" it printed, and the three of them grinned like they had won something.

Desmond tested his game one more time. The cat walked over the coin, and this time he collected it. "You want to be my quality tester?" he asked. "Fair warning, my opinion of your testing is subjective. I'll say you're great no matter what."

"Deal," Brielle said, and saved her program with a flourish. Then she leaned toward the screen and typed one more number to test: ninety-seven.

"Prime," the computer answered.

Mr. Okafor's computer lab smelled like warm keyboards and old carpet, and Zachary had one goal before the bell: get his heading to sit in the middle of the page. He had typed the tag for his heading, saved the file, and opened it in the browser. The words "Zachary's Fossil Finder" sat stubbornly against the left edge, like a kid refusing to move over on a bench.

"Try the style part," said Priya from the next computer. "The CSS. That's what it's for." She turned her screen toward him, showing her own page about anime, its title floating dead centre.

Zachary stared at his file. There were two languages on the screen, one building the bones of the page and one decorating it, and he couldn't see either of them doing anything. The heading only existed because of invisible instructions, and something invisible was keeping it crooked. He had a theory. Maybe the decorating language had a rule for centring, the way a game has a rule for jumping. He tried typing a line that said text should be centered, saved, and hit refresh. The heading slid to the middle of the page.

"Whoa," he said. "It moved."

His grandfather, who was visiting for Grandparents' Day and had been watching from the doorway, wandered over. "In my day we thought coding meant typing walls of letters," he said. "My friend's grandson shows me programs he builds by snapping blocks together."

"That's Scratch," Zachary said. "It came out of the MIT Media Lab. It was first released in 2007." He pulled up the Scratch site on his screen so his grandfather could see the colored blocks clicking together like LEGO.

"Blocks," his grandfather repeated, shaking his head slowly. "So the computer doesn't care whether you type or snap?"

"I guess it all turns into the same thing underneath," Zachary said. He wondered whether that was true, whether every language, even the block one, dissolved into the same invisible stuff before the machine understood it. He refreshed his page again just to watch the heading jump to centre a second time.

Mr. Okafor paused behind them. "Nice work, Zachary. Next week we start storing user answers in a database, so your fossil quiz can remember who took it."

"That's like a file cabinet the page can look things up in," Zachary said, mostly to himself. His mind was already racing ahead, ideas fluctuating between a page where visitors typed in their town and one where the site suggested nearby dig sites. This lab felt fertile, like a place where things you built could grow into bigger things.

His grandfather leaned closer to the screen, squinting at the centred title. "So show me," he said. "Where do I snap my first block?"

On Friday afternoon, room 214 was supposed to be silent for free reading, but the table by the window was not silent. Devon had his Monopoly box open, setting up a game for indoor recess, and Marcus was imitating the way Eli had said "actually" during homeroom, drawing out the word until the boys on either side of him laughed. "Actually, that's not in the rules," Marcus said in a pinched voice. "Actually, actually." Eli stared at his book and turned a page he had not read.

Harper watched from two tables over. She wanted to tell Marcus to knock it off, but last month she had done exactly that in the cafeteria, yelling at a sixth grader for teasing her friend, and the teasing had simply moved targets, landing on her friend for needing a bodyguard. Shouting made it worse. That much she had learned. What she had not figured out was what to do instead, so she sat there feeling useless while Eli kept his eyes on his page.

Then she noticed something. Every time Marcus did the voice, he looked around to check whether people were laughing. When Tyson had smirked and gone back to his comic, Marcus repeated the joke louder. When nobody reacted at all, the joke got smaller. That was her inference: the teasing ran on an audience, the way a fire ran on air. She could not take the air away by ordering people to stop laughing, but maybe she could give the audience something else to do. She had an idea, and it was worth a test.

She walked over, sat down at Devon's table, and said, "Can I play? We need at least three." Devon nodded and handed her the dog. Eli glanced up once. Marcus drifted over too, because a game was starting and nobody was watching his performance anymore.

They played, and on Eli's second turn he landed on Marvin Gardens and passed on buying it. Devon reached for the dice, but Eli said, "Actually, that's not right. The official rules say if a player lands on an unowned property and chooses not to buy it, the bank auctions it to the players." Marcus snorted. "Nobody gets auctioned." Harper flipped the rule sheet out from under the box lid, ran her finger down the column, and turned it so Marcus could see. "It's right here." Marcus read it, shrugged, and said, "Fine, but I'm not investing my money in Marvin Gardens." They auctioned it anyway, and Devon won it for cheap, which made him so pleased he forgot to be lethargic about counting his bills, as he had been all afternoon.

They played until the bell, and Marcus never did the voice again, not even when Eli beat him to Park Place. On the way out, Eli caught up with Harper in the hallway. "Thanks for the game," he said. "You were two dollars short on rent, by the way."

Easton had told his mother he would make dinner for once, and now, at Priya's counter with a whole onion in front of him, that promise felt like a decision made by someone else entirely. Priya's parents would be home at six thirty, which gave them fifty minutes to produce a pasta sauce from scratch and no time to go to the hospital.

"Curl your fingers under, like a claw," Priya said, demonstrating. "The knuckles guide the blade. The fingertips stay out of the way."

Easton curled his fingers and lowered the knife, waiting for the onion to fight back. It didn't. The slices came off thin and even, and he felt briefly like a person who knew things. "This is actually working."

"You look shocked," Priya said, stirring the canned tomatoes they were turning into sauce with garlic and a pinch of sugar. "Don't get cocky. The onion gets harder near the root."

She was right, but only slightly, and by six ten the onion was fully chopped and nobody was bleeding. Easton scraped it into the pan, and the kitchen turned warm and humid with steam while everything sizzled. Priya moved the sauce pot to the back burner and put a tray of garlic bread into the oven.

"Timer's set for eight minutes," she said. "Then we pull the tray."

At six twenty-one, Easton washed his hands at the sink while the pasta boiled beside him. A wave of water sloshed over the edge and soaked the oven mitt hanging on the hook, and he thought nothing of it. When the timer beeped, he grabbed that mitt and reached for the oven door.

"Stop." Priya caught his wrist. "It's wet. Wet oven mitts can burn your hands. The water in the cloth carries heat quickly, and it can turn to steam."

Easton looked at the mitt, then at the red mark already creeping across the heel of his palm where the damp had touched it. So the heat hadn't just sat on the surface of the cloth like it did when the mitt was dry. It had traveled through, fast, carried by the water, and somewhere in there it had boiled. He filed that away next to the onion trick: invisible rules, running underneath ordinary things, waiting for someone to grab the wrong one. Priya interpreted his silence correctly and handed him a dry mitt from the drawer.

The garlic bread came out golden. At six twenty-nine, sauce bubbling, they heard the garage door open.

"Dinner," Easton announced, "made by professionals."

Lydia leaned over the lab table in room 214, where the radiator hissed because someone had turned the valve the wrong way and steam kept escaping into the already humid September air. In front of her lay two printed climate graphs, one for Cairo and one for Singapore, and Mr. Ruiz had asked the class to decide which place got more rain. The bars for Cairo looked taller in three different months, and Lydia tapped the paper triumphantly.

"See? Cairo wins in March, April, and May," she told Marcus, who sat across from her with his arms crossed. "The bars are right there. Taller means more."

Marcus frowned. "Singapore is a rainforest. My cousin went there and said it rained every single afternoon. Cairo is a desert. Deserts are dry, that's the whole point." He slid the papers closer to himself as if the graph might confess.

"You can't argue with a graph," Lydia said, but a small doubt hindered her from saying it too loudly. Deserts were dry. She knew that. She pulled both sheets back and looked again, not at the bars this time but at the numbers running up the left side of each page. On Cairo's graph, the rainfall axis climbed to 300 millimeters at the top. On Singapore's, it climbed to 400. She found March on both. Cairo's tall bar stopped at about 40. Singapore's shorter-looking bar, on its much taller axis, stopped at 170.

"Oh no," she said. "Look at the axes. The bars aren't on the same scale." She turned the papers so Marcus could see. "A short bar can stand for more rain if the axis goes higher. You can only compare the bars by height if both graphs use the same scale."

Marcus leaned in, traced the numbers with his finger, and sat back slowly. "So Singapore gets more rain in March. A lot more."

"And every other month too," Lydia said, checking the rest of the year and finding the same thing over and over. She had been so sure, and she had been wrong in front of the whole table group. Priya, two seats down, had heard everything and was already whispering it to someone else.

Mr. Ruiz walked by and set a small stack of fresh worksheets on their table, graphs with matching scales printed on both. "Try these," he said, and moved on.

Lydia took the top sheet, but she kept the old ones too, folded into her binder. She wanted to remember being certain and wrong at the same time, so next time she would look at the numbers before she pointed at the bars. "Fine," she told Marcus. "Your cousin's afternoons were right."

"Want to tell Priya that?" Marcus asked.

Lydia looked over at Priya, still whispering, and shook her head. "I'll tell her myself at lunch."

Louis sat on the porch steps of Grandpa's house with a sketchpad on his knees, staring at the driveway sketch he'd made the night before. Something about it was wrong, and he couldn't say what. The road looked like it was tipping sideways, like the whole street was sliding off the page.

He was drawing the view because of a promise he'd made at summer camp two weeks ago. Flashback: on the last day of art class, Ms. Reyes had pinned everyone's street sketches to the cabin wall, and Louis's had drawn a groan from the kids. "Your road edges are going three different ways," his friend Devon had said, tapping the paper. "Mine too," Louis admitted, though he hadn't even noticed until Devon pointed it out. Ms. Reyes had said only, "Everything going back into the distance shares one point." She never said where, and the bus home came before Louis could ask.

Now he looked up from the porch at Grandpa's actual street, the one that ran straight back toward the far fence line. He held up his pencil at arm's length, level with his own eyes, and squinted along it. The road's edges, the sidewalk lines, even the cracks between the driveway slabs all seemed to lean toward each other the farther back they went. His intuition told him they weren't really leaning at all. They were parallel, side by side, the same distance apart all the way down. The slant was only in the looking.

He drew a light horizontal line straight across his paper, level with where his eyes would be if he were standing in the picture. Then he marked a single dot on it, right where the road seemed to disappear. From each bottom corner of his road he drew lines up to that one dot, and the same for both sidewalk edges. He checked it against the real street again, then added windows and doorways with lines aimed at the same spot. It was strange, like the dot was a magnet pulling everything in.

Grandpa came out with two glasses of lemonade and leaned over his shoulder. "What's that dot for?" "It's called a vanishing point," Louis said. "Every line going straight back runs to it, right on the horizon, at eye level. One point for all of them." Grandpa squinted at the drawing, then at the street, then back. "Huh. I've lived here forty years and never saw that."

Louis texted Devon a photo of the finished sketch that evening, and the reply came back fast: "NOW it looks real. Do my street next." He grinned and flipped to a clean page.

Hailey slid into her seat just as the last bell finished ringing, and the computer lab smelled like warm keyboards and the janitor's lemon spray. Mr. Ruiz had written one sentence on the whiteboard: "Write a program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime." She had sixty minutes, and she wanted the green "CORRECT" on the checker more than she wanted lunch, which was saying something, because today was pizza day.

She typed fast, her fingers still cold from the walk across the courtyard. She knew the concept: a prime number has no divisors except 1 and itself, so she should try dividing by every number in between. She wrote a loop, hit run, and typed in 7. The screen printed "not prime." She tried 11. "Not prime." She tried 5, 3, even 13, which she had known was prime since fourth grade. Every single one came back "not prime."

"Yours broken too?" whispered Deshawn from the next computer. He leaned over, chewing his pencil. Around them, papers with the assignment began to circulate as students printed their attempts and compared answers in low voices.

"Every number," Hailey said. "Even the primes." She stared at her loop, then at the output, then back at the loop. Something invisible was happening between those two lines of code, and she meant to find it. She added one print statement, a temporary spy: every time the loop found a divisor, it would report which one. She ran it again with 7, and the screen filled with a single line: divisor 7.

"There it is," she said. "It's dividing 7 by 7." The checker's complaint suddenly made sense. Her loop went range(2, n), and that stopped one number short, at n minus 1. At least she thought it did. She tested it with another spy, printing everything the loop actually tried for 7, and out came 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. The number 7 itself never even entered the loop, so her earlier line must have grabbed it some other way. She scrolled up and found her mistake sitting there in plain view, dividing n by n before the loop even started. She deleted it, and range(2, n) did exactly what she needed: it tried 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, every possible divisor except 1 and 7 itself.

Deshawn leaned over again. "Is that fix going to work, or is the problem more ambiguous than that?" She grinned, typed 7, and hit enter. The word "prime" appeared, small and green on the dark screen. She reached over and tapped his paper with her pencil. "Try 13," she said.

Elizabeth dragged the garden hose across the backyard and pointed it at the sandbox her little brother Caleb had claimed as his kingdom. He stood on the ladder of the slide with his arms crossed.

"That's my city," he said. "I'm the tenant. I pay rent in candy."

"You're squatting," Elizabeth said. "Move your buildings." She had a science project due Monday: she was supposed to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, using erosion and deposition, and she refused to just read a paragraph off the internet. She wanted to build the thing.

Caleb slid down and started relocating his plastic dinosaurs while she raked the sand into a smooth slope and turned the hose to a trickle. At first nothing happened. The water spread out and vanished. She narrowed the stream with her thumb and persisted, holding it in the same channel for ten minutes, and a small groove began to cut. Sand lifted from the upstream edge and traveled, then dropped where the flow slowed at the bottom, building a fan-shaped delta. She felt a jolt of recognition. Erosion on one end, deposition on the other, the canyon creeping backward between them. If a trickle did this in ten minutes, a river over millions of years made the carving inevitable.

"But it doesn't matter," Caleb said, kneeling to inspect her groove. "My rocks don't change. This gray one has been gray forever. Rocks are rocks."

"That's wrong," Elizabeth said. She held up two sandbox stones, one smooth, one jagged. She rubbed them together and grit fell onto the sand, the same grit the water was already carrying away. The jagged stone was becoming sand, and sand could press into new rock, and rock could melt or get squeezed and heated until it was something else entirely.

"Any rock can become any other rock," she said. "Melting, weathering, heat and pressure. It's called the rock cycle."

"You're making that up."

"Look it up yourself." She turned the hose back on, and the water found her groove again, deepened it, and split around a buried rock, leaving it standing on a little column of sand like a tiny mesa. Caleb watched the delta spread toward his last dinosaur.

"That's going to flood my guy," he said.

"Then move him. That's what the river does. It doesn't knock."

Alicia had run the eight hundred metres four times this season, and four times she had sprinted the first lap like a burglar escaping with the good silverware, then shuffled the second lap like a grandmother looking for her glasses. Coach Ruiz kept saying one word at her: pace. But pace was invisible. She couldn't see it, couldn't hold it, and it refused to explain itself.

At Thursday practice she set out to test an idea. Her plan was to run the first lap at what felt almost insultingly slow, the equivalent of jogging while pretending to be busy, then spend everything she had left on lap two. She asked Marcus, a sprint hurdler who was loitering by the water jug, to stand at the two-hundred mark and yell "SLOW" if she went out too fast. Marcus agreed, mostly because he wanted an audience.

Marcus had his own problem. His hurdle rhythm kept falling apart, and while Alicia circled the track he clattered over the barriers, landing heavy every time, like a chair being dropped. On her third lap she slowed to watch him. He rose up tall over each hurdle, chest proud, practically waving to the crowd, then came down dead, all his speed gone.

"You're landing like a piano," she called. "Lean your chest forward over your lead leg when you clear it. Keep your body going that way instead of up."

"Up is where the hurdle is," Marcus said, reasonably.

"The hurdle is only knee-high. You're jumping to the moon."

He looked at his hurdles the way you look at a dog that has bitten you before, and Alicia jogged on, but the idea stayed with her. Marcus's trouble and hers were the same trouble, she thought, running her cooldown. He wasted his energy going up when the race went forward. She wasted hers in the first lap when the race had two. She just couldn't see her own mistake the way she could see his.

At Saturday's meet she went out slow, so slow that the field streamed past her and a man in the stands audibly reassured his daughter that the girl in last would catch up eventually, probably. Alicia stayed calm. Three hundred metres, four hundred, and the bell rang. Then she began passing people, one by one, like she was collecting them. She crossed the line third, which had never happened, and lay down on the infield grass to enjoy the sensation of legs that had betrayed her only partially.

Marcus came over, sweating and grinning. He had run the hundred hurdles and taken two seconds off his best time. "Leaned the chest forward over the lead leg," he reported. "Didn't go to the moon once."

"Coach Ruiz says next time I go out even slower," Alicia said from the grass.

"There's slower than that?"

She squinted up at him. "Burglar walking pace. Bring the water jug."

The essay was due Monday, and Jayden had exactly zero words written. He sat at his grandpa's kitchen table with his laptop open, the cursor blinking on a blank page, while outside the window the garden baked in the August heat. His thesis sat in his head in a hopeless jumble: somehow he was supposed to argue that the town should fix the old public pool, and he had until Sunday night.

His friend Marcus had sent him a strange text an hour before. "Just read the first sentence of each body paragraph. That's the trick. If your argument doesn't hold up that way, it's broken." Jayden had stared at it, suspicious. How could anyone understand a whole essay from a handful of lines? He decided to test it. He wrote his thesis at the top of the page: The town council should repair the Maple Street pool. Then he tried to build an outline around three points, one for each paragraph, and something felt wrong. He had three points but they overlapped, and when he wrote only the first sentence of each planned paragraph, the argument collapsed into mush.

He tried again with fresh points, and this time he made each opening sentence reach back and grab the thesis, the way a rope ties a boat to a dock. Point one: the pool is cheap to fix compared to building new. Point two: it serves the most families in summer. Point three: repairs could be finished before next season. When he read just those three lines, the whole argument stood there like a skeleton, complete. He typed the first sentences to Marcus, and Marcus texted back a single thumbs up. Something in Jayden's chest unclenched, though he refused to be optimistic yet. He was pessimistic about one thing: the body paragraphs themselves, which could still stretch on forever if he wasn't careful.

His grandpa shuffled in, sweating, a hormone-triggered redness still on his face from mowing the lawn, and set down two glasses of lemonade. "How's the paper?" he asked. Jayden turned the screen toward him. "Watch this," he said, and read only the first sentence of each paragraph aloud. His grandpa listened, nodded slowly, and tapped the table. "I understood the whole thing," he said, "and you skipped everything else."

Jayden grinned and started drafting, but he made a rule for himself: no paragraph would run long just to prolong the page count. Every sentence after the first one had to earn its place. Outside, sprinklers hissed over the brown grass, and his fingers were already moving across the keys.

Lauren's flashcards had deteriorated into a curled stack of coffee-stained index cards, and she still could not get past the fourth line of the prayer she had to recite at her confirmation next Sunday. She spread the cards across the kitchen table and glared at them, as if they were hiding the fifth line somewhere under the smudges.

Simran arrived at four o'clock with her backpack and a bag of samosas, because that was the deal: Simran quizzed Lauren on the prayer, and Lauren helped her with algebra. "Ready?" Simran asked, sliding into the chair opposite her.

"Line five keeps disappearing," Lauren said. "I say it ten times, and then it's just gone."

Grandma shuffled through the kitchen, her bad knee popping where the cartilage had worn thin, and set down a plate of mango slices without a word. Lauren watched Simran's hands. They were shaking a little, and Simran kept smoothing her dupatta flat against her notebook even though it was already flat. That was odd. Simran was the calm one, the one who never erased anything.

They drilled for twenty minutes, and Lauren's concentration deteriorated fast. Then she noticed something. "Wait," she said. "I know every single word of forty songs. All of them, no cards. But one prayer, nothing. Same brain. Why?" She thought about what was different. Songs had tunes. The words were tied to something you could hear, not just see on a card. She had a theory and no proof, so she tested it: she picked a melody from one of her favorite songs and sang the prayer's first four lines to it, then kept going. Line five came out on its own. Line six followed. She sang the whole thing.

Simran's mouth fell open. "That's it. Do you know what Japji Sahib is? My part for the ceremony at the gurdwara. It's actually meant to be sung, it's a prayer with a rhythm, and I keep blanking on it like you did, and I was too embarrassed to say so." She laughed and covered her face. "I came here to quiz you and I needed the quiz myself."

"I guessed," Lauren said. "Your hands were shaking the whole time."

"You noticed that?" Simran pulled out her own worn sheet of paper, folded so many times the creases had gone soft. She took a breath. "The tricky part isn't memorizing, it's understanding it. My dad says we believe in rebirth and karma, and Guru Nanak taught that the body takes birth because of karma, while salvation is attained through God's grace." She traced the last line with her finger. "That's what I have to mean when I say it, not just say it."

"Then you'd better understand mine too," Lauren said, "because you're the one who has to sit through it Sunday. Front row."

"Second row, remember? Front row is Grandma's, and nobody argues with Grandma." Simran stood, then winced, pretending her knee had popped just like Grandma's. "See, I'm basically family already."

Lauren grabbed the piano bench and dragged it to the middle of the kitchen. "New deal. You sing yours, I sing mine, and nobody stops until both of them stick." She set the mango slices between them and held up the first card. "Line one, ready?"

Simran straightened her dupatta one last time, and this time her hands were still. "Ready."

The bus jolted over the railroad tracks just as Norah opened her English book to the scene Ms. Okafor had assigned. Tomorrow each student had to stand up and read a speech from Macbeth, then paraphrase it, which meant saying the same thing in words a normal person would actually use. Norah had inherited her grandmother's old copy of the play, its margins crowded with faded pencil, but so far that hadn't helped her understand a single line.

"To-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow," she read under her breath, hunching so the seventh graders behind her couldn't hear. "Creeps in this petty pace from day to day." She squinted. Creeps was easy. Petty pace, fine, slow. Then the speech turned into candles and walking shadows, and she lost the thread completely.

Dex slid into the seat beside her at the next stop, balancing his trumpet case on his knees. He glanced at her page. "You look like the bus ran over your book."

"Macbeth. I have to paraphrase this speech and I don't even know what's happening. Why is he talking to nobody?"

Dex leaned over and read the stage direction at the top. "It says 'alone.' Huh." He tapped it. "My sister did this play last year. She called that kind of speech a soliloquy. A character, usually alone on stage, speaks their private thoughts out loud so the audience can hear them."

"So it's like thinking out loud?" Norah looked at the page again, and something shifted. If Macbeth was alone and just speaking his private thoughts, then everything he said was a secret. He wasn't performing for anyone in the story. He was telling the audience what he really believed, the stuff he'd never say to his wife or his soldiers.

She tried it as a test, translating line by line in the margin. Tomorrow keeps coming, one day after another, until the end of time. And all our yesterdays have shown fools the way to dusty death. She wrote, our past days just lead stupid people to the grave. Out, out, brief candle became life is short, like a candle you blow out. "He thinks nothing means anything," she said slowly. "That's the secret. He's lost, and only we get to know it."

"That's actually kind of sad," Dex said. He pulled out his own worksheet, which was crumpled at the bottom of his bag. "Can you help me with mine after? Mine's the one where the guy pretends to be a pig farmer."

"It's a disguise, not a soliloquy. You're lucky." She smiled and wrote her last paraphrase at the bottom of the margin, next to a stray pencil note her grandmother had left decades ago: vulnerable when alone on stage. Norah underlined it twice and passed Dex a fresh pencil without his asking.

Sawyer pressed his face close to the display case, where a coil of copper wire sat next to a voltmeter and an ammeter. The sign said YOU MEASURE IT, so he clipped the probes where the arrows pointed and watched the needles jump. Six volts. Half an amp. A third dial showed a symbol he didn't recognize, something like a tiny horseshoe with feet, next to the number twelve.

"Is that a horseshoe?" asked a girl beside him, lanyard swinging. "Like, lucky twelve horseshoes?"

"It's not a horseshoe," Sawyer said slowly, though he wasn't sure what it was. "It's Greek. My math teacher writes something like that on the board." He copied the symbol onto his palm with a finger, wondering what a letter had to do with wire.

The sign above the meters told him only this: divide volts by amps. He tried it in his head. Six divided by half an amp meant twelve, and that matched the number beside the little horseshoe. So the meter had done the same arithmetic he just had. He changed the dial to a thinner wire and the current dropped to a quarter of an amp, and when he divided this time he got twenty-four. The horseshoe number climbed exactly with his answer. It was like guessing there was a rule running quietly behind the glass, invisible until you checked the numbers against it.

He revised his first idea, then. The meter wasn't measuring the wire directly like a ruler measures length; it was figuring the value out from the two things he could see, the volts and the amps, and then displaying the answer with that Greek letter. "Omega," he said out loud, suddenly certain, because he remembered now where he'd seen it, on a worksheet about Greek letters that he'd mostly ignored. "Resistance is measured in ohms," he told the girl, pointing at the symbol. "Ohms, written with omega."

She looked skeptical. "Says who?"

"Says the numbers." He liked that better than any sign. He'd been pessimistic about the whole electricity wing when they'd walked in, expecting walls of paragraphs, but this was more like a detective puzzle where the culprit never shows his face and you catch him anyway. The climax came when he found the display's challenge card: a mystery wire, meters unlabeled, and a blank box for the answer. He measured nine volts and three amps, divided three into nine, and wrote a three in the box, then drew the horseshoe beside it as carefully as he could, feet and all.

When the light above the box blinked green, the girl squinted at his symbol. "Still looks like a horseshoe to me."

Hunter slid his paper menu across the lab table and tried again. "Quisiera el pollo con arroz," he said, and Ms. Reyes nodded, so he pushed his luck. "¿Cuánto cuesta?"

"Ocho dólares," she answered, holding out her hand for the fake money, and Hunter counted out eight paper bills from the envelope. That part was going fine. Ordering the food, asking the price, paying. The part that kept wrecking him was the game at the end, where one student played a waiter giving directions to the restaurant and the other had to walk the route through the classroom.

Last week he had ended up at the pencil sharpener instead of the door twice. His partner, Dana, kept grinning at him, and Hunter was tired of it. His older sister had promised to take him to a real Mexican restaurant on Saturday if he could get through one whole round without a wrong turn, and he wanted that dinner more than he wanted to admit.

He listened while Dana played the traveler for the kid before him. "Sigue derecho hasta la mesa de la maestra," the waiter said, and then, "después gira a la derecha en la silla azul." Hunter watched the kid walk. He went straight past the teacher's desk, then turned right at the blue chair, and ended up exactly at the pretend kitchen door. Interesting. Hunter had heard both those words as the same word before, all one blur of "derecho, derecha, whatever." But the kid had treated them as two different things, and it had worked.

When his turn came, Hunter stood at the back of the room under the paper canopy that the class had hung from the ceiling to make the classroom look like a patio. He gripped his paper menu. "Buenas tardes," said the waiter, a kid named Marco. "El restaurante está cerca. Sigue derecho," and Marco pointed straight ahead, "hasta el escritorio, y luego gira a la izquierda."

Hunter took one step straight toward the desk, then stopped. He wanted to test it. "¿Derecho significa a la derecha?" he asked, tipping his hand toward the right wall, where the supply closet was.

Marco shook his head. "No. Derecho means keep going straight. A la derecha means to the right." He pointed forward, then pointed right, with an obvious difference between the two.

So they really were two words, and the difference mattered. Hunter walked straight to the desk, turned left, and made it all the way to the pretend kitchen door without one wrong turn. Dana clapped once, slowly, like she couldn't believe it. Hunter went back to the counter and ran the whole thing again, this time with the waiter saying "a la derecha" first, and he turned right at the blue chair, then straight, and arrived again.

After class he copied the menu prices into his notebook and converted them in his head, eight dollars to what he'd actually need from his allowance, because Saturday he was ordering for himself, in Spanish, without a script. He wrote the two words at the top of the page in big letters and underlined them both. Ms. Reyes passed his desk on her way out and tapped the page.

"El sábado," Hunter said, and pointed at the underlined words, then at himself.

"Muy bien," she said, and held the door.

Zack sat at the corner table in the school library, a blank page in front of him and twenty minutes until the writing lab closed. His social studies essay was due Monday, and the assignment sheet said he had to state a thesis and outline a three-point argument before drafting a single paragraph. He had picked his topic, that the town should build a bike trail along Miller Creek, but every time he tried to start, his mind went as barren as the empty parking lot outside the window.

He flipped through a folder of sample essays Ms. Okafor had left on the shelf. One was about why the school day should start later, and it moved smoothly from one idea to the next. Another, about school uniforms, was choppy; each paragraph sat alone, like separate islands. Zack read them twice and noticed something. The smooth essay kept using small words at the start of its paragraphs: first, however, furthermore, therefore. The choppy one hardly used any. He set the two essays side by side and traced the words with his pencil. First introduced the opening point. However signaled a turn. Furthermore added something on top. Therefore showed what followed from everything before.

His friend Priya dropped into the chair across from him with a stack of books. "What are you doing, playing connect the dots?"

"Sort of." He slid the choppy essay toward her. "Read this paragraph, then the next one."

She frowned. "They don't go together. It's like the writer teleported."

"Now read it this way." He had copied a paragraph onto scratch paper and added one word at the start, furthermore. Priya read it again and her eyebrows lifted.

"Oh, that's better. Ms. Okafor calls those transition words."

Zack pulled his own paper back and built his outline. Thesis: the town should build the Miller Creek trail. Point one: the census counted four hundred more kids in town than five years ago, so the parks were crowded. Point two: the trail would keep riders off the busy road. Point three: the creek path was already public land, so the cost would be low. Then he added his connectors. First, the town has grown. However, the roads were never widened. Furthermore, the land is free. Therefore, the trail should be built.

He wrote the opening paragraph, and for the first time the sentences came out in order, each one pointing to the next. When the librarian flicked the lights twice, Zack packed his bag slowly, reading the outline one more time on his way to the door.

"Monday, I'm actually ready," he told Priya, and he held up the page so she could see the four little words circled in the margin.

Carson had the sheet of paper taped to the refrigerator, right next to the thermostat, where the whole family would pass it a dozen times a day. The words of the ceremony song ran down the page in two columns, left and right, and for three days he had been muttering the left column at the counter while he scrambled eggs. His little sister Zaria kept bumping the paper with her elbow just to annoy him.

"The left side is easy," Carson said on Saturday morning, tapping his pencil against the mug. "It's the right side that falls apart every time." Zaria leaned over his shoulder, chewing a piece of toast. She wanted the solo in her school chorus more than anything, and she had been eyeing the ceremony program like it was a tryout sheet. "Then let me be the right side," she said. "You do the left, I answer."

He sang the first line, cautious as somebody testing ice. Zaria fired back the answering line, loud enough to rattle the cabinet doors. It worked. He tried the second line, she answered, and the whole thing rolled down the page like two people passing a ball. "It's call-and-response," Carson said, grinning. "The leader sings a line and the group answers." He remembered now: Great-Aunt Ruth's old records in the attic, the choir leader throwing out a line and the whole room catching it. She had told him the pattern ran deep in African musical traditions, and in gospel and work songs, the kind her father had sung laying railroad ties. He'd thought it was boring then. It did not sound boring now, bouncing off the kitchen ceiling.

So he tested an idea. Instead of memorizing the song as one long ribbon of words, he learned only his half and let Zaria's half pull his out of him. When he blanked, she hummed the shape of her answer, and his line rose to meet it, like the words were waiting just behind the sound. By noon he had conserved his voice by whispering his lines and still not once lost his place. "You're not even looking at the paper," Zaria said, impressed despite herself.

That afternoon at the community center, the ceremony director asked who would lead the call for the rehearsal. Zaria's hand shot up so fast it nearly knocked over a music stand. Carson's stomach flipped, and his hand went up anyway, reckless and trembling. He stood, faced the rows of folding chairs, and threw out the first line. Forty voices caught it and threw it back. He grinned and gave them the next one.

Brayden crouched behind the folding table in the gymnasium and rolled a marble down the ramp for the ninth time, muttering, "Two meters, one point four seconds. Come on, be consistent." His graph paper was supposed to show a neat climbing line for the judges, distance on one axis and time on the other, so anyone could read off the speed of his rolling ball. Instead his points scattered like confused ants. He needed this to work because Priya Nair, at the next table, had built a working model of a lock made entirely of popsicle sticks, and he refused to lose to popsicle sticks.

"Your marble hates you," Priya said, leaning over. "That's a scientific conclusion. I can make a graph of it."

"It's not the marble, it's the ramp." He picked up the marble and held it to the light like a suspect. Somewhere behind them, a kid at the physics table was trying to explain why sound traveled, and failing, which gave Brayden a dangerous idea.

He remembered last summer at his grandmother's residence, the old porch with its loose floorboards, when he had stomped his foot at one end and his cousin Marcus, lying at the other end with his ear against the wood, had sworn he felt the thump before he heard it through the air. They had argued about it for an hour. Marcus said the sound was the thump itself sliding down the board, like a hockey puck. Brayden had said that made no sense, because then the board should end up piled at Marcus's ear.

He looked at Priya's table. She had a slinky and a box of dominoes, leftovers from a demo she'd abandoned. He borrowed both. "Watch," he said, and set the dominoes in a line across her table, then flicked the first one. Clack, clack, clack, all the way down. "Sound's like that," he said. "A push goes down the line, but each domino just tips over where it stands. The dominoes don't travel with the sound."

Priya frowned. "So the last domino doesn't slide to my hand?"

"Nope. It only moves back and forth, kind of. Like this." He stretched the slinky between them and nudged his end. A round ripple rolled toward her, and the coils between them just wiggled in place, elastic and shiny, none of them actually arriving anywhere. Priya touched the far end and yelped when the bump reached her fingers.

"So the air between me and Marcus does that," Brayden said, grinning. "Each bit of air wiggles and passes it along. The push travels, the air stays home. Marcus owes me a soda."

"But the push, the wiggle, that's what your graph is missing," Priya said suddenly, jabbing at his paper. "You're measuring total distance at total time, but the speed is the slope. Mark where the marble is at each half second. Little dominoes of data."

He divided his timing into marks, rolled the marble again, and plotted the points. They climbed in a straight, obedient line. A judge stopped, ran a finger along the graph, and said, "Nice slope."

"That's the speed," Brayden said. "One point four meters per second, give or take a marble's opinion." He held up the slinky and gave it one more happy nudge, and the ripple rolled all the way down to Priya's fingers, where it arrived on time.

Alexis had two problems, and both were due on Friday. The first was her health project, a labeled diagram of the brain showing how addictive drugs affect it. The second was Alexis herself: for three nights she had stared at the ceiling until midnight, and by afternoon her jaw ached from clenching it through math class. Her intuition said the two problems were separate. Her intuition, she was starting to suspect, was wrong.

At the library table, she spread out her diagram. She had drawn the pathway with the arrow pointing the wrong way, from the front of the brain backward, and she couldn't figure out why her notes felt off. She traced the labels with her pencil. "It runs from the ventral tegmental area," she muttered, "deep in the brain, to the nucleus accumbens." Her friend Priya leaned over from the next seat.

"That's the brain's main reward pathway," Priya said. "And addictive drugs boost dopamine along it. You've got the arrow backwards, like a dinosaur walking tail-first."

"An extinct dinosaur," Alexis said, and erased the arrow. "Wait. Is that why I can't sleep? My brain's reward thing is all lit up from scrolling?" Priya shrugged, but Alexis decided to test it. She would decompose her evenings into parts, change one part, and see what happened. Like an experiment with herself as the diagram.

That night she plugged her phone in downstairs, an hour before bed, and lay on her floor doing the slow breathing her PE teacher had shown them, four counts in, six counts out. She fell asleep before ten. She woke before her alarm, jaw loose, and the ceiling looked like a ceiling instead of an enemy. The next afternoon in math she noticed her shoulders creeping toward her ears and took three slow breaths, and the tightness loosened. The hidden pattern held: the late scrolling and the clenching and the midnight ceiling-staring were one thing, not three.

On Friday she turned in her diagram, arrow corrected, pathway labeled from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens. Her teacher handed it back with a sticky note: "Come see me." Alexis's stomach dropped. In the hallway, the teacher pointed at the corner of the page, where Alexis had taped a chart of her own week, nights on one axis, phone-down times on the other. "This wasn't required," the teacher said.

"It's my data," Alexis said. "Can I present it too?"

"Present it first," the teacher said, and wrote an A at the top of the page.

Hannah spread the photocopy of the charter of rights across her grandfather's kitchen table, next to the toaster and a jar of marmalade. She had a civics assignment due Monday: explain one of the rights in her own words. Her pencil hovered over section 2, freedom of expression, but her mind kept drifting to the notice taped to the fridge. The town council was meeting Thursday night to vote on closing the outdoor rink, and Hannah had signed the petition to save it. A right on paper was one thing. She wanted to see one used.

Last summer, she remembered, the library board had tried the same trick with the reading room. A dozen parents had shown up to speak, and they had been turned away at the door, told the list was already full. At the time Hannah had assumed the board simply didn't want to hear them. Now she wondered. Her grandfather kept old council agendas in a drawer, and she dug one out. Under the heading "Delegations," it said that anyone wishing to appear as a delegation must register with the city clerk's office before the meeting.

So that was the pattern. It wasn't that the council silenced people; it was that there was a procedure, a small step in the hierarchy of rules that ran the town, and the library group had missed it. The reasoning seemed logical to Hannah: if you wanted to speak, you had to get on the list first. She decided to test it. On Tuesday after school she rode her bike to the clerk's office and filled out a form.

At the Thursday meeting, the chamber smelled like floor wax and burnt coffee. When the rink item came up, the chair called for delegations and read out two names. Hannah's name was one of them. A man in the third row stood up too, holding a folder, and the clerk shook her head. "You didn't register with our office before the meeting," she said quietly. "You can speak at the next one." The man sat down, and Hannah's grandfather, beside her, gave her elbow a squeeze.

She walked to the microphone on legs that felt slightly too long. She had her paragraph ready, the one she'd rewritten three times. "I want to demonstrate what the rink means to this town," she said, and she told them about the Tuesday night skate races, the kids who learned to stop and turn there, the fact that it cost less to maintain than one new parking lot. She kept it to two minutes because the agenda said delegations got two minutes, and Hannah had read the agenda.

The vote was postponed for a month. Afterward the man with the folder stopped her in the aisle. "How'd you get on the list?" he asked.

"City clerk's office," Hannah said. "Before the meeting."

He wrote it on his folder, pressing hard.

Simon stood at the white line on the track, chest still aching from the time trial. Two laps of the track, eight hundred metres, and he had led the first lap by twenty metres, then died. Marcus had passed him on the back straight like Simon was standing still.

"You went out too fast," Marcus said, catching his breath beside the fence.

"I know that," Simon said. "I can feel it. What I can't do is hold back while everyone runs away from me."

That was the real problem. He could not see the energy he was spending, could not see it running out. He only saw it afterward, in the collapse.

He walked past the pool on his way out and stopped. The swim team was doing front crawl lengths, and one swimmer, a tall girl in lane two, kept beating everyone else by half a length. Simon watched her turn her head to breathe, over and over. The others lifted their whole faces toward the ceiling, pausing at every breath, but she barely turned at all. One goggle lens stayed down in the water, and only her mouth swung far enough to clear the surface. Simon counted. Every single breath, the same small turn, one eye still underwater. The others broke their rhythm and lost speed each time they breathed; she never did.

It reminded him of a video he'd seen in fourth grade about lions chasing gazelles. The lion was the consumer, burning huge energy, and it had to cease the chase after a short burst or collapse. The gazelle conserved and lasted. He had thought it was only about animals. Now he thought: the fast girl isn't doing less. She's doing the same work but spending nothing extra on breathing. Nobody watching could see the difference, but the clock could.

The next trial was Thursday. Simon decided to test one small idea: hold a pace he was certain felt almost too easy for the first lap, like keeping one goggle in the water, saving the turn. At the gun he dropped into fourth place. His legs felt affluent with energy, rich and full, and every metre the leaders paid for their speed. At the bell for the second lap he was still whole. He swung past one runner, then two, and with eighty metres left only Marcus remained ahead.

"Where did you come from?" Marcus gasped.

Simon didn't answer. He just kept turning his legs over, smooth and low, one eye on the finish line.

Simon had been sitting in the waiting room of Bright Smiles Dental for eleven minutes, and in that time he had said the word "acetylcholine" wrong in his head about forty times. His science-fair partner, Priya, sat beside him with a stack of notecards, because their project was due Monday and this was the only hour they both had free. Simon's little brother was in the back getting a cavity filled, which meant their mom was busy and the two of them were unsupervised with a topic neither of them fully understood yet.

"Okay," Priya said, shuffling the cards like a magician. "Question one. Why is nicotine so hard to quit? Go."

"It's, um, addictive," Simon said. A man across the room looked up from his magazine, and Simon lowered his voice. "I know that part. I just don't know why addictive. That's like saying water is wet because it's watery."

"That's why we're doing this project, genius." Priya flipped a card. "Here's the piece I found. Tell me if my comparison works. I want to say nicotine is like a fake key."

Simon chewed on that. "A fake key for what?"

"Okay, imagine a lock. The lock is on a brain cell, and it's a protein." She tapped her temple. "The real key is a chemical messenger the brain makes itself, and it's called acetylcholine. That's the brain's own key. The lock normally opens for that one. But the lock is called a nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, and here's the trick: nicotine happens to fit it too. Fake key, real lock. The brain cell responds like the real key showed up."

"So the lock doesn't check ID," Simon said slowly. "It just... turns."

"Exactly. You sounded like you knew that just now."

"I didn't know it. I reasoned it. There's a difference, and it's not subjective, it's measurable." He grinned. Priya threw a notecard at him.

The dental hygienist walked by with a tray of tiny mirrors, and Simon watched her fish a dropped pen out from under the chair with a long hooked picker, like a scavenger hunting a prize. "Could we use her in the demonstration?" he whispered. "No. Focus. Fake key, real lock, brain's own messenger is acetylcholine. I can say it now without dying."

At that moment the inner door swung open and Simon's little brother emerged, cheeks puffy, holding a paper cup. "The dentist says I have to resign from gummy worms," he announced gloomily, "effective immediately."

"You can't resign from gummy worms," Simon said. "You can only be fired from them."

Priya wrote "fake key" at the top of a fresh card and underlined it twice. "Monday, we're getting an A. Monday, you're going to say acetylcholine in front of the whole class without tripping over it. Say it once more, right now."

"Acetylcholine," Simon said, just as the man with the magazine muttered, "Kid, I quit smoking eight years ago, and even I never had to pronounce that."

Simon raised the notecard like a trophy. "Fake key, real lock."

The stopwatch came from a drawer marked obsolete equipment, and it looked the part, with a crack across the face and buttons worn smooth. Emily pressed it anyway, because the class had only five working stopwatches and fourteen students, and Marcus had claimed the good ones for his group within four seconds of the bell.

The plan was simple. Emily would release a marble from the top of the lab ramp, and Josh would stand at the end of the hallway, twenty meters away, and shout "go" the moment it left her hand. Then he would click the stopwatch when the marble crossed the tape line by his shoes. They would divide distance by time, quantify the speed, and draw the distance-time graph Mr. Patel wanted by Friday.

The first run gave them a speed of 0.4 meters per second, which would have been fine for a snail, possibly the only organism slower than their marble. They tried again. 0.38. Again. 0.41.

"That marble is not that slow," Emily said, staring at the numbers. Something was hiding in the setup, something they could not see. She paced off the hallway, counting tiles. Twenty meters, same as before. The ramp angle hadn't changed. The only thing between her and Josh was air.

Then she remembered the lesson from last week, the one about sound. Warm air carried it faster than cold air, gaining about 0.6 meters per second for each degree Celsius. If the hallway was warm, Josh's "go" reached her quickly, but on a cold day it would crawl, and her start would be late, which would make the marble seem slow. She checked the thermometer by the door: 26 degrees. She did the arithmetic on her palm with a pencil. At 20 meters, a small delay in hearing "go" added a real chunk of error to every run.

They tested it. Emily had Josh clap hard against the far wall and timed the echo with the cracked stopwatch, once in the warm hallway by the radiators and once in the cold stairwell, ten trials each. The warm trials came back faster, and when she worked the numbers, the difference matched the rule: about 0.6 meters per second for every degree. She drew the graph with corrected times, and the line came out clean and steep and beautiful.

Mr. Patel walked past and squinted at it. "Nice correction for sound delay. Next time, use the light gate instead of shouting. Light doesn't dawdle."

"Light doesn't dawdle," Josh repeated, nodding, and packed up his stopwatch.

Emily carried the ramp back to the shelf. "One question," she said. "When I released the marble, when exactly did you start timing?"

Josh adjusted his backpack strap. "Right after I heard 'go.' Well. After 'go' and one Mississippi. Mr. Patel said always count one Mississippi."

Emily looked at her beautiful graph, then at Josh, then at the drawer of obsolete equipment, which suddenly seemed like the most honest thing in the room. "Give me the stopwatch," she said.

The folding tables at the festival smelled like cardamom and burnt samosas, which Marcus decided was not the worst combination in the world. He sat behind the temple booth with a paper of Devanagari script in front of him, supposed to be learning the Gayatri Mantra by heart before his sacred thread ceremony next month. His grandmother had told him twice already that the ceremony would come whether or not he was ready, and she had said it in the exact voice she used when his shoelaces were untied.

"You're mouthing it like a fish," said Priya, his cousin, who was stacking laddus into a luminous golden pyramid nearby. "Fish are organisms, Marcus. You are not a fish. Try again."

"I am a fish," Marcus muttered, "a fish with a memory of at least three seconds, which is more than I can say for this line." He squinted at the words. They slid around on the page like ants at a picnic, and every time he got one syllable locked in, another one escaped.

Then his grandmother appeared with a steel plate piled high with rice, and instead of setting it in front of him she set it in front of the aunties at the next table. She poured herself only fruit and water. Marcus had been noticing this for weeks, actually. At home she skipped rice the same way, always on certain days, and he had never caught which days, because the days themselves seemed to wander.

He counted on his fingers, right there among the samosas. New moon, full moon, and then the eleventh day after each one. It landed twice a month, both halves. It fit every skipped plate he could remember, including the birthday dinner she'd turned into a fruit plate while everyone else had biryani.

"Thaathi," he said, tugging her sleeve, "you skip rice on the eleventh day of each half of the lunar month. Both halves. Am I right?"

She raised an eyebrow at him the way she did when he'd finally found the hidden Diwali sweets. "Ekadashi," she said, patting his head. Then she walked off with her fruit plate, leaving him feeling like he'd solved a riddle nobody had told him was a riddle.

Priya leaned over, grinning. "So if I hide your mantra paper on Ekadashi, will you go hungry too?"

"I'll trade you. You get my paper, I get your whole laddu pyramid."

"That pyramid is a sacred organism. It took me twenty minutes." She hesitated anyway, glancing at it. "Fine. But you have to recite the whole first line without the paper, right now, in front of the aunties."

Marcus stood up, took a breath like he was about to dive into deep water, and began, "Om bhur bhuvah svah," and behind him he heard his grandmother set down her fork to listen.

Simon stood at the kitchen counter with an onion, a sharp knife, and a plan: he would make pasta sauce from scratch before Dad got home at six thirty, which gave him exactly fifty minutes. His mom was away for the week, and Dad had promised takeout every single night, which Simon figured he could eliminate if he proved he could cook something real.

First, the onion. The video he'd watched three times said to curl his fingertips under, knuckles forward, so the blade could only nick bone and not skin. "The claw grip," Simon said out loud in a dramatic voice, then actually did it, fingers tucked like a crab. He cut the onion in half through the root, peeled it, and sliced, and the vapor rising off it made his eyes water so badly that he had to walk to the window and blink at the street like a sad owl.

While he sniffled, he got out the scale. The recipe said his sauce needed something called a roux to thicken it, and it said to weigh the butter and flour. He set a knob of butter on the scale. Twenty-five grams. Then he measured out flour. Twenty-five grams. Same number. He frowned at the two little piles, because recipes usually didn't care this much, and this one acted like the amounts matching was a rule.

He called his friend Priya, who had cooked at the community kitchen all summer and acted smug about it. "Why does the butter and flour have to be the same?" he asked. "The recipe just says equal parts by weight and doesn't say why."

"Because it's called a roux," Priya said. "Flour cooked in fat, equal parts by weight. That's just what a roux is. Ours never came out lumpy when we weighed it right." Simon said a rude thing about her smugness, and she laughed and hung up.

So the flour went into the melted butter, and Simon stirred it with a wooden spoon while it bubbled and smelled faintly like toasted bread. It was supposed to thicken things, he knew that much, but he couldn't see how a paste the size of a golf ball was going to turn his pot of watery tomato stuff into actual sauce. He had a test idea: he'd pour in half the tomatoes, watch, then pour in the rest. Science, basically.

The first half of the tomatoes hit the roux and sat there, pale and lumpy, and Simon's stomach dropped. Then he kept stirring, and within a minute the lumps smoothed out and the whole surface went glossy and slow, like lava. He grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. He poured in the rest, stirred, and the sauce thickened right before his eyes, coating the spoon in a way his soup never had. Hidden cause confirmed. He added salt, a pinch of sugar, and the cooked onion, which he'd nearly forgotten on the cutting board.

At six twenty-five, Simon set down two bowls of pasta. Dad walked in at six twenty-nine, sniffed the air, and said, "Who broke into my house and made sauce?" Simon held up his untouched fingers, knuckles still faintly smelling of onion. "Claw grip," he said. "Zero cuts." Dad took a bite, closed his eyes, and pointed his fork at Simon like a judge declaring a verdict. "Takeout is cancelled for the rest of the week. Unanimous."

"There's only two of us," Simon said.

"Unanimous anyway," said Dad, going back for seconds.

Aubrey had been avoiding the periodic table all week, but Friday's quiz left her no way out. She spread her notes on the kitchen table and found the trick her brother had shown her before he left for college: the big number in each box was the atomic number, and that told you the protons. Carbon was six. She checked neon, ten, and gold, seventy-nine, until the pattern felt solid under her fingers.

Then she found the crumpled note Priya had slipped into her locker before moving away. In Priya's looped handwriting it read: "I built a carbon atom for our last project. Six protons, six neutrons. If you build one with eight neutrons instead, is yours still carbon? Text me. I'll wait." Aubrey read it three times. Priya's family had left in October, and this was the first message that felt like they were still lab partners.

Aubrey scavenged through the junk drawer for something to build with. Buttons would work, and dry pasta. She laid out two atoms on the table, using pennies for protons and elbow macaroni for neutrons, keeping the noodles neutral in color so she wouldn't mix them up with anything else. Six pennies in each pile. Six noodles in the first, eight in the second. They sat side by side, clearly not the same.

She stared at them for a long time. If protons made an element what it was, then both piles were carbon, no matter what the noodles said. But she wanted to be sure before she texted Priya, because being wrong in front of Priya had always stung worse than being wrong anywhere else. She decided to invest one evening in finding out: she looked up the two versions in her science book and found them both listed under carbon, side by side.

She grabbed her phone and typed fast. "Mine is still carbon. The protons decide. Yours is carbon-12, mine is carbon-14. They're called isotopes."

The reply came before she finished her water. "I KNEW it was isotopes but I wanted you to figure it out yourself. Show-off." Then, after a pause that stretched long enough for Aubrey to reread the whole exchange: "The new girl here doesn't build atoms with me. It's not the same."

Aubrey picked up the pasta carbon-14 and carried it to her room, where it would sit on the shelf next to the model rocket Priya had left behind. She set the atom down carefully and texted one more line. "Friday night, seven o'clock, my kitchen table. Bring buttons. We'll build the whole second row."

Sofia spread the short story "The Long Dock" across the library table and put her notebook beside it. On Saturday she had to stand up at the book club and explain one example of foreshadowing and one of symbolism, and so far her notebook held only a list of page numbers. Across from her, Marcus was reading the same story for the third time, because he wanted to be the one who found the best example and got his pick of the donated paperbacks on the prize shelf.

"I've got foreshadowing," Marcus said, tapping page four. "The dock boards creak before anyone even drowns. That's the author warning us." He slid the story toward her. "Beat that."

Sofia read his page, then flipped forward, hunting for something better. On page nine she found a line she liked: "The old lantern's light spread thin and did not reach the end of the water." She wrote down that the lantern meant safety that failed, and that the dark water beyond it was standing in for what nobody could control. Then she found a quote that seemed even stronger. "The sea takes whatever it wants," a boy named Dale says on page twelve, after he pushes his brother's boat out too far. Sofia copied it in big letters and underlined it twice. The author's message, she labeled it.

She read her page aloud to Marcus as practice. "The story tells us the sea takes whatever it wants."

"Who says that?" Marcus asked.

"Dale. It's right there."

"Dale's the one who wrecked the boat and blamed the water," Marcus said. "That's his opinion, not the book's. The whole point is that the narrator says the wind was calm that day."

Sofia checked page eleven. The wind was calm. Dale had said the same thing twice before anything went wrong, and both times he was trying to talk his brother into going out. She crossed out the words author's message and wrote Dale's excuse instead. Her first idea, that the quote was the theme, would have sunk her whole talk like a boat with no rudder, drifting wherever the loudest voice pushed it.

She rebuilt her notes around the lantern and the creaking boards, then practiced once more, quieter, while Marcus radiated satisfaction at having caught her mistake and claimed first pick of the paperbacks. He chose a thick survival novel and held it up.

"Saturday, you open with the lantern," he said, "and I'll open with the boards. Deal?"

Clara leaned closer to the library computer, where her spreadsheet filled the screen. She had typed every answer from the school survey into it: one column for grade, one for favorite lunch, and a count for each. Then she taught herself the formula that added the column, and the bar chart sprang up beside it, tall rectangles for sixth grade, seventh, and eighth. The sixth-grade bar won every single question. "Of course they do," said Marcus, looking over her shoulder. "There are way more sixth graders than anybody else."

Clara stared at the chart. It did seem strange that sixth grade swept all five questions, even "Do you like the school mascot?" She clicked through the menu at the top of the screen, hunting for anything that might make the bars mean something fairer. She was not going to resign herself to a chart that just measured crowd size. Under one menu she found an option labeled "Show Values As," and inside it, something about a percentage of the column total.

She clicked it. All three bars shrank, but not by the same amount. The sixth-grade bar dropped the most, because a big class spread its answers over a bigger total. Now the eighth-grade bar was tallest for the mascot question, even though sixth grade still had the biggest raw count. "Wait," Marcus said, pointing. "Eighth grade won that one. But they have the fewest people."

"That's the point," Clara said. "Show Values As turns each count into a percentage, so grades with different numbers of students can be compared fairly." She tested it on the next question, pizza versus tacos, and watched the bars rearrange themselves again. Sixth grade still won that one, but only by a sliver, not by the canyon of the original chart.

Mr. Reyes, who ran the newspaper club, came by to check her results for Friday's issue. "The principal wanted to know which grade likes the new schedule best," he said. Clara turned the screen toward him and showed him both charts, side by side. "The raw numbers say sixth grade," she said. "The percentages say it's almost a three-way tie." He tapped the second chart and said that was the one to print.

Clara saved the file twice, once on the computer and once on her flash drive, because she had an acute memory of losing last month's survey to a crashed laptop and the small fracture it had put in her deadline.
