Then she printed the percentage chart, and Marcus carried it to the newspaper room at a run.

Eve stood in the kitchen with her hands pressed flat against her sides, whispering the words of the blessing she had to know by Sunday. Her grandmother had written it out for her in careful looping ink, and on Sunday, at the ceremony, she would say it alone in front of the whole family. She had to know it by heart.

The problem was her arms. Every time she reached a tricky line, her hands flew up without asking her, as if they could pull the next word out of the air. She'd clamp them down and lose her place. She tried again in the hallway, and her right hand escaped on "bless the road before me." She growled and started over.

Her cousin Fiona came in carrying her dance bag. "You look like you're being electrocuted."

"I'm memorizing."

"Arms down," Fiona said. "In Irish step dancing, that's the rule. Arms still, feet fast." She dropped into position, hands pressed to her sides, and her shoes hammered out a rhythm on the floorboards, heels and toes chasing each other while her shoulders never moved. It looked almost impossible, like two different people sharing one body.

Eve watched her and a question started forming. Her arms flapped when her brain was hunting for a word. Fiona's feet worked fast while her body stayed quiet. What if the flapping wasn't the problem? What if it was just energy with nowhere to go? Maybe it didn't matter which part of her moved, as long as something did.

"Play the reel," she said. "The slow one you practice to."

Fiona raised an eyebrow but found it on her phone. The fiddle started, infectious even at practice speed, and Eve planted her feet and began the simple steps Fiona had taught her last summer, the ones where you never lift your arms. On the third try, the whole blessing came out in order, word after word, her hands glued to her sides the entire time.

She tried it again to be sure. Then once more without music, just her feet marking time on the tiles. It held.

"Percentage of how sure you are?" Fiona asked.

"Ninety. Ninety-five."

"Grandma's going to ask how you did it. You going to disclose your secret method?"

Eve grinned and didn't answer. She started the steps again, hands pressed to her sides, and the first line of the blessing came out steady and strong.

Victoria held her slice of cake and watched Dex back away from the picnic table, his ears going pink while Cole and two other boys laughed at his rumpled jacket. "Nice outfit, Dex. Did you dress in the dark?" It was Mara's birthday party, and nobody wanted a scene, least of all Mara, who was already hurrying over with her hands out like a tiny diplomat negotiating peace.

"Guys, come on," Mara said. "It's my party."

"Chill, we're just joking," Cole said. Victoria knew that tone. Joking meant the teasing would restart the second Mara turned around. She'd seen it happen at the science club meeting last week, when Dex tried to suggest a project idea and Cole talked over him until Dex just shut his mouth and stared at the table.

Victoria stepped between the boys and the dessert table. "We're doing a game," she announced. "Round-robin style." Cole groaned. "A round-robin means each person speaks in turn around the circle," she said. "You don't get to skip, and you don't get to talk over anybody." She pointed at the picnic bench. "Sit. Best birthday memory wins the last cupcake."

Cole shrugged and sat, because it was a game and games had rules, and even he followed rules when cake was involved. They went around. Cole told a loud story about a water park. One boy described a snowstorm blackout. Victoria shared the time her grandmother set her own birthday cake on fire with too many candles, and the smoke smell had saturated the whole kitchen for days.

Then it was Dex's turn. He was quiet for a second, and nobody could interrupt, because that was the rule. "My best birthday," he said, "was when it rained and the power went out, and my dad let us build the whole birthday cake out of marshmallows and cereal because the oven was dead." Everyone laughed, the good kind, and Cole said, "Okay, that's actually exceptional," and pushed the last cupcake across the table to him.

Victoria watched Dex break the cupcake in half and hand part of it to Cole, who took it without a word. She turned to grab her drink and found Mara standing beside her, arms crossed, grinning. "Nice game," Mara said. "Too bad you planned it." Victoria frowned. "What?" Mara pointed at the table, where Cole was now asking Dex, quietly, where he'd found the cereal marshmallows. "You invented a game so nobody could tease him," Mara said. "That's the sneakiest nice thing anyone's done all day."

Victoria picked up her cup. "I have no idea what you're talking about." "Then explain why you're smiling," Mara said, and Victoria hid it behind her cup, badly.

Noemie spread her debate notes across her grandmother's kitchen table, which smelled like lemon polish and old coffee. Her first tournament was Saturday, and her case was dying. Every card was there, every quote copied neatly, but when she read it aloud to the salt shaker, the salt shaker fell asleep.

"It sounds like a robot reading a phone book," she told her grandfather, who was peeling an orange at the counter with the patience of a man who had nowhere to be. He had acted in theaters for forty years, and Noemie sometimes forgot that, since now he mostly acted like a person who owed nothing to anyone.

"Read me one point," he said. She did, in the flat, tedious drone she'd practiced, and he winced like she'd stepped on his foot. "Do you know what a debate case has?" he asked. "Same as a scene. A character wants something in every scene, and the actor plays every line trying to get it. We called that the objective. So. What do you want when you give this point?"

"To win the round," she said, but that felt too big, like wanting to be warm instead of wanting this blanket. She looked at the first point again and formulated it smaller: she wanted the judge to believe the numbers were real. She read the point again, leaning forward a little, pushing the evidence across the table like it was the last piece of bread and the judge was starving. It sounded different. Interesting, even.

She tested the idea on the next component, her second point, wanting the judge to feel a little alarmed. Her voice sharpened; her grandfather raised his eyebrows over his orange slice. When she tried the third point without choosing anything, it went flat again, which proved the pattern wasn't luck. "So the claim is that knowing your objective fixes a flat speech," she said, hunting for a pencil, "the evidence is three points, two alive and one dead, and the warrant is that the voice follows the want."

"That sounded like a debate case," her grandfather said.

"That was a debate case," Noemie said, writing fast. "You just became my evidence. Don't move."

He put up his hands, orange peel still hanging off one thumb. "I've been typecast before. At least this role comes with snacks."

Sydney sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with a laptop balanced on a stack of board games, staring at a spreadsheet full of survey answers. Two hundred and six students had answered the question "What should the new school mascot be?", and Sydney's job, as the newly appointed mascot committee data person, was to figure out which choice each grade liked best. The list just went on and on: name, grade, mascot choice, over and over. "There has to be a faster way than counting these by hand," she said. "My eyes feel like they're revolving in my head."

Priya's grandfather, who was staying with them that month and liked to drift past the door offering snacks, leaned in over Sydney's shoulder. "Ah, a spreadsheet," he said. "You know, I remember the first one. VisiCalc. Dan Bricklin and Bob Frankston wrote it, and it came out in 1979 for the Apple II. First spreadsheet program for personal computers." He tapped the screen gently. "I did our household sums on it. Every rupee of our first mortgage, row by row."

"You had a spreadsheet before I was born," Sydney said, "and I still can't make this one count anything." He laughed and shuffled off to the kitchen, offering no more help than the history lesson. Sydney glared at the toolbar until she spotted a button labeled PivotTable. It sounded plausible, at least, like something that would turn a mess into a summary. She clicked it, dragged "Grade" into the Rows box, dragged "Mascot" into the Columns box, and dragged "Name" into Values. The spreadsheet recalculated itself, and suddenly there it was: a clean little grid of numbers, grades down the side, mascasts across the top.

Then she saw the problem. Sixth grade wanted the Honey Badger by a landslide. Eighth grade, her grade, wanted the Thunder Falcon. But one answer showed up as "thunder falkon", another as "THUNDER FALCON", and one kid had simply written "falcon, but the thunder one", so the table had split them into three different columns and made the Falcon look like a loser. "The data's lying," Sydney groaned. "The eighth graders spelled our own mascot wrong." Priya peeked over and said, "To be fair, Kevin spells everything wrong. He wrote ' library ' as ' libary ' on a poster last month."

Sydney fixed the spellings one by one, refreshed the pivot table, and watched the Thunder Falcon column swell until it beat the Honey Badger by eleven votes overall. She copied the grid into the committee report, feeling briefly like a wizard, and then stopped. Sixth graders were going to be furious. They had more voters in the survey than any other grade, and the one-big-table method she'd just built would flatten them completely. Her pivot table had answered the question, all right, but the question turned out to be a trap. She could report the winner, or she could report winners by grade and start a war.

The cursor blinked on the empty line where her recommendation was supposed to go. Priya's grandfather appeared again with two plates of biscuits and set one beside the laptop. "Thunder Falcon," he read off the screen, and then he saw the grade-by-grade rows and raised his eyebrows. "Ah," he said. "In 1979, that little machine did the arithmetic, but the decisions, those it left to me." Sydney pulled the keyboard closer and began to type.

Naomi sat cross-legged in the window seat with the photocopied scene on her knee and a deadline breathing down her neck: paraphrase every speech into modern English by Monday, or fail the quiz. Her little brother Theo kept leaning over the back of the couch like a gargoyle.

"You're reading it wrong," he said. "That guy sounds like a robot."

"I'm reading it exactly right. That's the problem." She tapped the page. "Every word is a wall. 'Prithee, good mercutio, let's retire.' What is prithee? Some kind of greeting? A curse?"

"It sounds like a sneeze."

Naomi ignored him and read the line again, slower. Retire had to mean leave, because the characters wanted to get out of the heat. Good was just good. But prithee sat there like a locked door, and the character used it three more times down the page, always at the start of a request. "Prithee, tell me." "Prithee, have done." She flipped to the front of her textbook, where a page of word histories was tucked between the introduction and the play itself. The entry was short, and she read it twice to be sure.

"Prithee is a squeezed-together form of 'I pray thee,'" she said. "It means please."

"So he's not a robot," Theo said. "He's just polite."

"He's very polite. That's the whole trick." Naomi felt something click into place, the way a puzzle piece does when you stop forcing it. The character wasn't being strange. He was asking nicely, over and over, for things that mattered. She grabbed her notebook and started writing: "Please, good Mercutio, let's get out of here. Please, tell me. Please, enough." The speeches stopped being walls and became people talking.

She read her paraphrase out loud, giving Mercutio a robust voice, all swagger and noise, and Theo laughed so hard he slid off the couch. "Do the other one," he said. "The angry one." She did, and she illustrated the speech with a jab of her finger at each insult, like she was dealing cards.

"Monday's going to be fine," she said, and meant it.

"It's a treaty, then," Theo said, holding out his hand. "You help me with my book report, I stop calling Shakespeare a sneeze."

Naomi shook it, then turned back to the page and began the next speech.

Eva dragged the basketball, the flashlight, and two lawn chairs into the backyard before her brother even finished his cereal. Tomorrow she had to explain, out loud in front of the whole class, why summer happens, and she refused to say "because Earth gets closer to the sun," which was what Marcus had said last week and which was completely wrong.

"Earth is closest to the sun during winter in the north," she announced, propping the flashlight on one chair and holding the basketball above the other. "So distance can't be the answer. It's the tilt." She stabbed a sticker onto the top of the ball and angled it sideways. Marcus flopped onto the grass with a sandwich, watching with the expression of someone who found all of this voluntary and would rather be anywhere else.

"Shine the light," she ordered. He pointed the flashlight at the tilted ball. Eva traced the bright patch with her finger. "See? When the north end leans toward the light, the beams hit it more directly, straight on, so that half gets more heat. That's summer. When it leans away, the same light spreads out over a bigger area, so it's colder." She spun the ball slowly, keeping the tilt aimed the same direction, and the bright patch slid from the top of the ball to the bottom. "Six months later, the south end gets the direct beams. That's their summer. It's never the distance. It's always the angle."

Marcus squinted, then started picking at the sandwich. "Fine, but you'll still mess up the rock question. Heat always melts stuff. That's just what heat does."

"It does not!" Eva dropped the ball and marched to the rock garden by the fence. She grabbed a flat gray stone crusted with pale green lichen and scraped a clean spot with her thumbnail. "Grandpa said this one's metamorphic." She turned it over. "It got changed way down deep, by heat and pressure, but it never fully melted. That's the whole point. If it had melted, it would be a different kind of rock."

Marcus sat up, which for Marcus was practically applause. "So it can get hot enough to change and still stay solid?"

"Yes! Heat and pressure, deep underground, changed it, no full melting." She held the stone up so the sun caught its banded layers. "And if you contradict me in front of the class tomorrow, I will throw this at you."

"It's a rock, not a frisbee."

"Details." Eva set the stone on the chair beside the flashlight, angled the basketball one more time, and cleared her throat at the empty yard like it was a classroom. "Okay. From the top. Nobody knows why summer happens. Except me, and this basketball."

The cafe smelled like burnt espresso and cinnamon, and Livia spread her papers across the corner table anyway. Two assignments due Friday: a short story with dialogue, and a rewrite of her school lunch report, which her teacher had handed back with one word in red pen at the top. Report. "That's a grade killer," said Dex, sliding into the seat across from her with an empty smoothie cup. He wanted a refill, but the cashier had told him twice that refills ended at noon, and it was 12:04.

"My report had facts," Livia said. "Prices. Menu items. Six paragraphs." She flattened the page against the table. "Everything true."

"Then what's wrong with it?"

She read her own opening line: The cafeteria serves pizza on Tuesdays and chicken nuggets on Thursdays. Dex squinted at it. "Okay. I know that now. So what?"

"So what," Livia repeated. The question sat there like a coin she couldn't spend. She picked up her story draft instead, the one about a girl who finds a sinister note taped inside a library book, and stared at her dialogue. She had written: Maya said "who put this here". No comma, period in the wrong spot, and every character spoke in the same flat voice. She rewrote it slowly, comma before the quotation marks, new paragraph each time the speaker changed, and the page suddenly looked like a real story. The logic of it clicked. Punctuation was telling the reader who was talking, like a map.

Then she stopped. Her story had no climax. The girl just found the note, showed it to her brother, and went home. She'd ended it too early, before anything exploded. She flipped back to the report. Her problem there was the same problem. She'd listed lunch facts and gone home.

"Dex." She pulled the report toward her. "A persuasive essay's goal is to convince the reader to agree with a position or take an action."

"Not just give information about a topic," Dex said, chewing his straw. "Even I know that. You wrote a menu."

She crossed out her first paragraph and wrote: The school should replace Friday's soggy fish sticks with a build-your-own salad bar. Every fact after it now had a job. The prices weren't trivia anymore; they were ammunition. At the end she added a demand: sign the suggestion sheet outside the gym. Then she went back to her story and gave Maya a choice at the climax, follow the note's directions or hand it to the librarian, and let her choose.

Livia calibrated the last paragraph so the ending landed hard and short, then read both pages over once. She slid the story across the table to Dex.

"Read the dialogue out loud," she said. "Tell me if you can hear who's talking."

Dex read, stopped at the note, and looked up. "Okay, but if Maya hands it in, what happens?"

"Turn the page."

He turned it, and his eyes went wide.

Aria sat at the kitchen table with her notebook open to a page that looked like a battlefield. Her English teacher had announced a short story contest, the most prestigious one in the county, and the winning story would be read aloud at the spring assembly. Aria wanted to win, or at least finish, but her draft kept tripping over itself. Every time a character spoke, she lost the thread.

"Who are all these I's and V's?" her little brother Marcus asked, leaning over her outline page. "They look like the numbers on a clock."

"They're Roman numerals," Aria said. "The big points get those. The little details under them get A and B." She pointed at her page. "See? I is the beginning, II is the middle, III is the climax. Under II, there's A, the frog pond, and B, the argument."

Marcus nodded slowly, still squinting at the letters as if they might rearrange themselves. Then he went back to his cereal, and Aria went back to her real problem. Her story was about two sisters who find a dying pond behind their school, an ecosystem slipping away because the water has gone still and sour. The sisters argue about whether to tell anyone. That argument was supposed to be her climax, but on the page it landed flat, like a jump rope with no one turning it.

She decided to test an idea. Maybe the problem was her dialogue. She had been writing, "I think we should tell Ms. Ruiz, said Elena." without punctuation that worked. She tried again, slower this time, saying each line out loud. "I think we should tell Ms. Ruiz," said Elena. "She said the frogs used to sing here." The comma went inside the quotation marks, and the lowercase s on said, because the sentence kept going. She wrote three more exchanges that way, listening to the rhythm. Then she moved a line of dialogue to the very top of section III, so the argument exploded right at the peak instead of drifting there, and she heard the difference immediately, the way a bullfrog can emit one deep note that carries across a whole dark field.

That evening a message popped up on her phone from her friend Dana.

Dana: You still doing that contest? I gave up. My story had no ending, just people talking forever.

Aria: Keep the talking. Move it. Put your loudest argument at the end of your outline, section III, and build everything toward it.

Dana: That's it?

Aria: That's half of it. Fix your commas too. Mine were a disaster until today.

Aria set the phone down, took out a fresh index card, and wrote III at the top, then A and B underneath, the sisters standing at the pond's edge in the last scene. She read her closing line once more, crossed out a comma, and put a new one inside the quotation marks where it belonged.

Emile had exactly one hour before the library computers logged everyone off, and his climate project was due tomorrow. He slid into the seat nearest the window, pulled up the rainfall and temperature graphs the librarian had authorized him to print, and spread them across the desk. One graph belonged to a patch of the Amazon rainforest, thick with green bars for rain every single month. The other, from a desert in Australia, showed rainfall bars so short they looked like someone had tapped the paper with a pen. The desert's temperature line jumped and fell like a rollercoaster while the rainforest's stayed flat and warm. That part he understood. What he did not understand was the coordinate his teacher had written on the handout: a number that started with a minus sign.

His project partner, Priya, dropped into the chair beside him and typed the coordinates into the online map, hunting for their exact spot in the rainforest. "Type it exactly," Emile said, because the minus signs felt crucial, like they were part of the address. Priya waved him off and entered the numbers her way. The map spun, zoomed, and landed on a stretch of dry, cracked land scattered with gray shrubs. It looked exactly like their desert graph. Neither of them said anything for a second.

"That's not the rainforest," Emile said. He leaned over and looked at what she had typed. The first number, the latitude, was missing its minus sign. He retyped it with the minus and hit enter, and the map flew north across the equator and dropped them back into solid green rainforest. Priya tried it again on purpose, dropping the minus from the longitude this time, and the map jumped east, all the way to the other side of the world, into Indonesian jungle instead of Amazon jungle.

"So the minus means something," Emile said slowly. He tried their desert coordinates without the minus on the latitude, and the desert became grassland in the northern hemisphere. He flipped the longitude's sign instead, and the desert landed in Africa rather than Australia. He wrote it in the margin of his handout, testing each one against the map like checking answers in the back of a math book. South of the equator, negative latitude. West of the prime meridian, negative longitude. That was the rule the map kept obeying, every single time.

Then came the twist. When he finally typed their rainforest coordinates perfectly, with both minus signs in place, and compared the site's rainfall chart to the one in his handout, the bars did not match. His teacher had copied the rainfall percentages from the wrong column, and half his carefully labeled graph was wrong. The library lights flickered the five-minute warning, and the printer behind them groaned through somebody else's fifty pages.

They divided the work on the walk to the print desk. Priya redrew the rainfall bars while Emile copied out the corrected temperatures, both of them scribbling on the backs of the old graphs because there was no time for new ones. The printout came out warm and smudged at one corner, but the lines were readable. "Tomorrow she's going to ask where we got the fix," Priya said. Emile folded the pages in half and slid them into his backpack, minus signs still showing in the margin. "Then I'll tell her we got lost first."

Charlotte's mistake happened in the second measure every single time. She was practicing the new piece for Monday's audition, the one her piano teacher had marked up with softs and louds and a big ritardando near the end, and she couldn't get past those opening chords. Her younger sister, Dara, sprawled on the couch behind her with headphones half on, humming along anyway.

"You're singing it wrong," Charlotte said, stopping.

"I am not. I'm singing exactly what you're playing."

"It's not the same note. Not even close." Charlotte played the first melody note, a low G. Dara matched it, and it sounded higher, thinner, like a smaller version of the same sound. Charlotte frowned and played it again. "See? Different."

Dara came and stood by the bench. "It's the same, though. It's like the same note but up high. Sing it with me."

They sang together, and the strange thing was that it worked, the way two gears of different sizes still turn the same machine. Charlotte pressed the G below middle C, then the G above it, one after the other, over and over. Same name, same feeling, different height. She pulled her theory notebook out of the bench, the one Mom had left there with her old sheet music, brittle and frail at the corners, and flipped to the back where she kept questions she couldn't answer yet.

"Here's what I think," she said. "When a note is one octave higher, it's vibrating exactly twice as fast. Twice. That's why they sound like the same note at different heights." She tested it the only way she could, by ear, jumping octaves up and down the keyboard and listening for that same-note feeling, and it held every time, low to high, high to low.

"Okay, but does that fix your measure?" Dara asked.

Charlotte looked at the page. The mistake wasn't a wrong note at all. Her left hand kept jumping an octave on the second beat, hitting the higher G when the piece wanted the low one, and because they matched, her ear never caught it. Now she could hear the shape of it, tall and short, and she played the measure six times clean.

"Better," Dara said. "The loud part's still mushy, though."

"The dynamics. I keep forgetting to get soft before the crescendo, so there's nowhere to grow from." Charlotte set the metronome, its brass alloy case still warm from the lamp, and started from the top. Mom would have to authorize her taking that Tuesday slot at the recital, and that meant auditioning on Monday, ready or not.

She played it through, soft where it begged for soft, swelling where it had to, the final ritardando landing like something set down carefully on a high shelf. When she finished, Dara was quiet for a second, then said, "Play it again."

Charlotte's hands hovered over the keys. Mom's notebook lay open on the bench beside her, its penciled notes in a hand she would never hear explain anything again. She lifted her fingers and began.

The erosion exhibit was the only quiet corner of the museum that afternoon, and Hazel claimed it like territory. A long tank of water trickled over a slope of pale sand, and beside it a painted diagram showed a river canyon sliced down through rock in stair-stepped layers. She was supposed to be filling out a worksheet for science class, but the worksheet's questions felt like a fence around something better. She wanted to actually explain it, out loud, without reading off the placard. She scooped a handful of sand, packed it into a ridge at the top of the tank, and turned the flow up one notch.

The water pooled behind her ridge, then found a low spot and began to cut. Within minutes a thin channel deepened into a gully, and at the bottom of the slope the sand fanned out into a flat, spreading delta. "Deposition," she said to herself, pointing at the fan, and "erosion" at the gully, testing whether the words could carry the whole story. Millions of years compressed into a lunch hour. She was so focused that she didn't notice the boy at first.

He was maybe nine, wrestling with a giant globe on a stand at the next exhibit, where a bright lamp played the sun. He twisted the globe until its metal axis sat perfectly upright, then spun it slowly, frowning. "It's broken," he announced to the room. "The summer patch disappeared."

Hazel drifted over. The globe's surface had small lights, or patches that glowed wherever the lamp's rays struck, and she could see what he meant. Something that had marked a warm season on the little painted continent had gone dark. She knelt to his eye level and looked along the line of the axis. Perfectly vertical. She remembered her uncle's desk globe, the one with the bent rod through the poles, and how the whole thing leaned.

"Try tipping it," she said.

The boy pushed the top of the axis sideways until it slanted like her uncle's. He spun it again, and the glow slid across the continents in slow bands, bright where the light struck straight on, dim near the pole. At one slant, the painted continent glowed warm; at the opposite slant, the far side of the globe did instead. The two of them watched the pattern repeat as the boy circled the lamp's beam around, orbit by orbit.

"If it's straight up, the seasons cease," the boy said, reading his own discovery out of the air.

"If the sunlight hits the same spot at the same angle all year," Hazel said slowly, working it through, "nothing changes. It's like the sun is indifferent. Like it doesn't care about summer or winter at all." She looked back at the globe, then at her sand tank, where the water had kept cutting the whole time she wasn't watching, indifferent too, patient in a way that made canyons out of arguments.

The boy tilted the globe further, nearly to its side, and the glow gathered into one blazing circle at the pole. "What happens now?" he asked.

Hazel opened her mouth, and closed it again. From across the hall, a museum guard was walking toward them, and the globe's base was making a small, uneven clicking sound it hadn't made before.

The departure board flickered to DELAYED just as Asher and his mother reached Gate 14, and his stomach dropped. Four hours in an airport with nothing to do, and his rainforest project due Monday. He pulled the worksheet out of his backpack and flattened it on the seat between them.

"There's a climate graph in my packet," he said, tracing the chart with his finger. Twelve tall bars ran across the bottom, some of them towering halfway up the page, and a jagged line zigzagged above them. His teacher had circled the graph in red and written, "Compare this desert graph to the rainforest graph. Use temperature and rainfall."

His little sister Nadia, eight and bored within ninety seconds of sitting down, leaned over his shoulder. "Why are the bars so tall in summer? Is it, like, two hundred degrees there?"

Asher frowned. He had assumed the same thing at first, that the bars showed heat. But the tallest bar stood over a month where the line hovered low, and the line was the thing that looked like a thermometer, climbing and dipping the way temperature would. He tested the idea against the numbers printed along the left side. The line matched the side marked in degrees. The bars matched a different scale, on the other edge, marked in millimeters. "The bars aren't temperature," he told Nadia. "The line is the temperature, one average for each month. The bars are how much rain falls each month, on the same chart."

"So the desert," Nadia said slowly, "has really tiny bars."

He flipped to the rainforest graph and held the two pages side by side. On the desert page the bars were stubs, barely visible, while the line swung between hot and cooler months. On the rainforest page the bars shot up like a skyline, month after month. Same kind of chart, opposite worlds. He started writing: the desert stays warm all year but gets almost no rain; the rainforest gets heavy rain in every single month.

A man across the aisle, dusty boots and a wide hat, glanced over. "Studying the Sonoran?" he asked. "I survey desert tortoises there. Dry country, but we work to preserve the places they nest."

Nadia pointed at his own wristband, which showed a green frog. "I like rainforest animals better. Our book says a bunch of frog species are headed toward extinction because their forests are getting cut down."

"That's true where I work too," the man said. "When the land gets impoverished, the animals go first."

Asher wrote that word in his notes, then kept writing, filling a whole page with the comparison. Somewhere over the loudspeaker, his flight's zone was finally called. He shoved the pages into his backpack, grabbed Nadia's stuffed elephant before she dropped it, and said, "Come on, graph expert. Let's go."

Isaac leaned over the bathroom sink at school, gripping the edge of the counter. His heart was pounding like he had sprinted up three flights of stairs, even though he had only walked to the bathroom. His breathing came fast and shallow, and he stared at his flushed face in the mirror, trying to figure out what was happening to him. He had a math test in twenty minutes, the second one this week, and his stomach had been aching since breakfast.

He splashed cold water on his face and thought about his friend Devon, who kept going to the nurse every single Tuesday with a stomachache. At first Isaac had assumed Devon was faking to get out of class. Then he noticed the pattern: Tuesdays were the day the math curriculum moved to timed drills, and Devon hated timed drills more than anything. Isaac also noticed that Devon complained of headaches on those days and said he could never sleep on Monday nights. Racing heart, fast breathing, stomachaches, headaches, trouble sleeping. Devon had them all, always on the same day, like a set of symptoms marching together.

"It's anxiety," Devon had said last week, shrugging. "My sister told me that's what it's called. It shows up in your body."

In the mirror, Isaac watched his own chest rise and fall too quickly. If this was the same thing, then yelling at himself wouldn't fix it. He remembered a video he had watched twice, mostly out of curiosity, about slowing your breathing on purpose. He tried it. In for four counts, out for six. His ribs felt tight at first, and he lost count twice and had to start over, which annoyed him. He kept going anyway. After a minute, his breathing slowed, and the pounding in his chest softened from a drumbeat to something more distinct and distant, like rain on a roof.

That night he tried a sleep routine. No phone after nine, lights low, backpack packed so the morning felt less like a trap. He slept through the night for the first time all week. On Wednesday, he sat next to Devon at lunch. "Do the breathing thing before the timed drills today," Isaac said. "In for four, out for six. It worked for me."

Devon looked skeptical, but at 1:15, when the drills started, Isaac glanced over and saw Devon sitting tall, eyes closed, counting silently under his breath.

After class, Devon held up his drill sheet with a grin. "No stomachache. And I actually finished."

Isaac grinned back. Tuesday was still coming, but now he had something to try, and he was starting to cherish that feeling, the one where a problem that used to be invisible had a shape you could work on.

He knocked his fist lightly against Devon's. "Same time tomorrow," he said. "Bathroom sink, four counts in, six counts out."

The bulletin board outside the Black Box Theater held one sparse sign-up sheet with two names on it, and Payton added hers with a pencil so hard it tore the paper a little. Partner improv auditions. Two days away. She'd never improvised anything in her life, and her scene partner would be chosen by drawing names from a hat, which meant she couldn't even pick someone easy to work with.

At lunch she found Marcus already hunched over a stack of index cards in the corner of the mess hall. "What's that?" she asked, sliding her tray down beside his.

"Argument cards," Marcus said. "My dad's making me do debate instead of drama next year. You build a whole case on these." He fanned them out. Three cards, each with one word. Claim. Data. Warrant. "Claim is what you say. Data is your proof. Warrant is why the proof counts."

"That's it? Three boxes?"

"That's what I thought." He flipped a fourth card he'd been hiding under his elbow. Then a fifth. Then a sixth. "Turns out Toulmin's full model has six parts. Claim, data, warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal. I was missing half the case."

Payton stared at the two extra cards, Backing and Qualifier, and then at Rebuttal, the one that answered the other side. Something clicked so hard she actually stood up. "Marcus. That's improv. That's the whole thing."

He blinked at her. "Debate is not improv."

"It is. Watch." She pulled a blank card from his stack and wrote on it in big letters: YES, AND. "When your partner gives you an offer, like 'We're on a pirate ship,' you can't say no, and you can't just say okay. You accept it and you add to it. Your partner gives the claim, you give the data, and together you build the warrant." She tapped Rebuttal. "And when the scene stalls, that's a signal. Something's being blocked somewhere, and you have to find what and turn it around."

They tried it right there over the mashed potatoes. "We're on a pirate ship," Marcus offered flatly.

"Yes, and the captain just fell overboard, so we're the only two left who know the way home."

"Yes, and I can't read maps."

"Yes, and I've been secretly studying the stars every night because I always wanted to be captain." Marcus's eyes went wide, and he leaned forward and grabbed her arm. "Do the stalled one. Block me."

"You're not the captain," she said, deadpan, refusing his offer on purpose. He froze. She counted three silent seconds, then rescued it. "Yes, and that's exactly why you have to take orders from me. Now grab the rope before the storm hits."

Marcus threw a dinner roll at her, laughing, and Payton caught it and held it up like a spyglass toward the window.

Luca stood in the wings of the Marlowe Concert Hall with his uncle's borrowed guitar strapped across his chest, and he could not remember a single scale. For weeks he had practiced at home, looping the same twelve bars over and over, the pattern of chords that rolled around and around like a train on a circular track. But that was his bedroom. This was a real stage, with real lights, and Uncle Ray had whispered, "If the crowd's good, you sit in for one chorus," which meant Luca might have to make something up, right now, in front of hundreds of people.

The opening act was a singer named Dove Holloway, a woman with silver boots and a voice like warm syrup. Halfway through her set, a program note circulated through the wings, printed on thick cream paper, saying that Dove came from a family of quilt makers and had learned to sing while she worked. Some artisan, Luca thought, her grandma must have been, to stitch all those patterns. Then Dove reached for a high note and missed it. Not badly, but enough that her face went tight and her hand flew to her throat like she'd touched a hot stove.

She tried the note again and missed it again, worse. The band behind her kept playing, patient and steady, but Dove's eyes had gone panicky. Luca watched her swallow, stretch her neck, take a huge breath. His friend Priya, who played trumpet in the youth orchestra and had squeezed into the wings with him, whispered, "She's going to blow it a third time."

Something clicked in Luca's head, the same way a chord change clicks when you finally hear it coming. "She's pushing too hard," he said slowly. "It's not about force. There are these two little vocal folds in her throat, and they vibrate when air passes between them. Tightening them is what raises the pitch. She's so scared she's squeezing everything, so the pitch goes weird." Priya squinted at him. "Then what should she do?"

Luca didn't answer, because Dove had spotted them in the wings, guitar and all, and something in her desperate gaze landed right on him. He mimed what he was thinking: he let his shoulders drop, breathed low and slow, and made a loose, easy motion near his own throat, like letting a door swing instead of forcing it. Dove blinked. She turned back to the microphone, and when the high note came around again, she eased into it instead of grabbing for it, and it rang out clean and huge, so bright that a man in the front row stood up and knocked his hat off applauding.

Then Uncle Ray leaned over from the drum riser and pointed his stick straight at Luca. "One chorus, kid. Make it a legitimate blues, not just fast notes." The lights came up hotter, Dove grinned at him and stepped aside, and Luca played the first four bars of the twelve like a train pulling out of the station, waiting to hear where the chords would take him next.

Hazel sat cross-legged on Priya's bedroom floor with a laptop on her knees and a printout of survey answers beside her. The student council had asked every kid in the school which lunch activity they wanted, and Hazel, as the new data person, was supposed to summarize the results by grade before Monday. Priya's older brother had shown them spreadsheets once, but he was at soccer now, and the screen in front of Hazel looked ominous, a gray grid stretching in every direction with hundreds of rows of answers below it.

"Just count them by hand," Priya said, flopping onto her bed with a notebook. Her real ambition this semester was to design the posters for whichever activity won, and she wanted to know the winner early so she could start sketching. "There can't be more than four hundred."

"There are six hundred and twelve," Hazel said. She envied Priya's confidence. Counting by hand would take all weekend, and she would still have to sort it by grade afterward. She scrolled through the columns: A was the grade, B was the activity, C was the student's reason. Somewhere, she remembered, there was a thing called a pivot table that could do the counting for her, but she had never made one.

She tried clicking through the menus. Rows went where columns should go, and the numbers came out as a nonsense total of 612 for every cell. She stared at it. "It's counting everything at once," she said slowly. "I need it to split by grade and then count within each grade." She dragged the grade heading into the rows box and the activity heading into the values box, and suddenly the grid rearranged itself, small counts appearing under each grade like magic.

Priya leaned over her shoulder. "Wait, can it tell us the sixth grade specifically? Text my brother, he's better at this." She sent a message, and when the reply buzzed in, she read it aloud: "He says look at C4. That's the cell in column C, row 4."

Hazel frowned at the screen. She clicked on a cell and the box at the top of the screen showed its address. The one she had picked was C4, and it sat in the third column over and the fourth row down. So that was how it worked: the letter was the column, the number was the row. She moved her cursor to check, and sure enough, C5 was directly beneath C4, same column, next row.

But something was wrong. The value in C4 said 47 sixth graders wanted chess club, and that didn't match what she remembered scrolling past. She looked again at how she had dragged the fields. The grade labels had landed in the values box by mistake, so the table was counting the wrong thing. She fixed it, dragging grade to rows where it belonged, and the numbers shifted, chess club dropping to 31.

"Which one's winning?" Priya asked, pencil already hovering over her notebook.

"Art club, in every grade except eighth," Hazel said. "Eighth grade wants the podcast booth."

Priya gasped and started drawing microphones. Hazel scrolled back to the raw answers to double-check one of the counts, her finger moving down column B, row by row. "Two, three, four, five," she murmured, "all podcast."

Harrison stood in his grandmother's kitchen holding a photocopy of the Havdalah blessings, and for the fourth time that afternoon he got stuck on the same Hebrew phrase. His cousin Eli, who usually led the ceremony, was home with a virus, and Grandpa Morris had pulled Harrison aside after lunch and said, "You're thirteen now. I'm authorizing you to lead in Eli's place. Tonight." The paper trembled slightly in Harrison's hand, which annoyed him, because the words were right there in front of him and he could read them fine. The problem was that the blessing had to come from memory, the way Eli always did it, eyes closed, no paper.

The whole family had gathered at the house for the weekend, aunts and uncles spread across the porch and the living room, and by late afternoon the sky outside the big front window was turning the color of a bruise. Harrison's little cousins, Naomi and Ruthie, had planted themselves at that window with their chins on the sill. "Why are you two camped there?" Harrison asked, and Naomi said, without turning around, "We're counting stars. Three of them."

Three stars, he thought. That was the deadline, then. Not a clock, not a phone alarm, but actual stars. He drifted over to the window and looked out at the deepening blue. Somewhere behind him, Aunt Judith asked whether the soup should be reheated, and someone said his rendition of the blessing had better be credible this time, since he'd been muttering it all day like a boy possessed. Harrison pretended not to hear.

He tried the blessing again under his breath while he watched the sky, and this time he made it past the phrase that had tripped him. The trick, he decided, was rhythm rather than letters. When he stopped trying to picture the printed page and instead let the words fall into their pattern, like the chorus of a song, they held together. He tested the idea by closing his eyes in the middle of the noisy living room, with Uncle Dan's laugh and the clatter of dishes all around him. The words still came. So the paper had been the problem, maybe, not his memory. He folded the photocopy and put it in his back pocket.

"One!" Ruthie shouted at the window. Naomi shoved her. "I saw it first, it's mine." They argued about whether the faint point above the telephone wire counted as a real star or just an airplane, and Grandpa Morris ruled that a dot that moved was not a star, which settled it, barely.

Harrison found the spice box and the braided candle on the sideboard, and he laid them out on the table in the order Eli always used, checking twice. Through the window the second star had appeared, low and steady near the roofline of the house across the street. His grandmother touched his shoulder as she passed with a stack of cups. "You know it," she said quietly. He nodded, though he was not certain he did.

The third star was taking its time. The family began drifting toward the table, chairs scraping, the candle waiting in its holder. Harrison stood at the head of the table with his eyes half closed, running the blessing one more time, and when Ruthie's voice rang out, "Three! I see three!", the room went still and every face turned toward him.

Riley stood in front of the washing machine with three piles of clothes on the kitchen floor and no idea which pile was which. Her mother had left for work an hour ago, and the deal was simple: if Riley could do her own laundry for a month, she got her phone back. Her brother Marcus wanted his soccer jersey washed by four o'clock, and he wanted it now, because the last time Riley had touched laundry she had turned his white socks pale pink, a humiliation he brought up at least twice a week.

"That was two years ago," Riley said.

"Nine months," said Marcus. He was crouched by the back door, squeezing the front tyre of his bike with both hands. "Also, this tyre's gone soft again. I think the pump's broken."

"Maybe you just didn't pump it enough."

"I pumped it forever. It's got to be like fifty." He let the pump handle dwindle back down and tried again.

Riley put the jersey in the cold-water pile and the dark towels in another, and while she carried the first load to the machine she kept thinking about the tyre. Fifty what? Marcus had guessed, that was all. He had no number to aim for, so pumping forever meant nothing. She set the detergent on the counter and knelt down next to the wheel. The rubber sidewall was dirty, so she wiped it with her sleeve. Along the curve of it, in small raised letters, there were numbers, and after the numbers the letters "psi," and in brackets after that, "bar."

"Marcus. It says it right here on the side. Look."

He leaned in. "Seventy psi? Huh. And bar, whatever that is."

"That's the other way they write it, I guess. It's printed right on the tyre." She worked the pump while he held the gauge, and the tyre firmed up long before fifty, and neither of them said anything about the pump being broken.

Back at the machine, Riley stopped before pressing start. The pink sock disaster had happened with hot water and mixed colours, but she had never actually tested whether it was the heat or the mixing. She filled a bowl with cold water, dropped in the one red sock that had sneaked into the wrong pile, and waited. The water stayed clear. She pulled the sock out and started a separate dark load anyway.

When the jersey came out of the dryer at three thirty, clean and grey-free, Marcus held it up to the window. "Okay," he said. "You can do my laundry too."

"Not a chance," said Riley, and folded it her own way.

Lucas tapped his pencil against the rainfall graph for the Thar Desert and frowned. The bar for July shot up like a skyscraper next to the flat little bumps of the winter months, and that did not make sense to him. Deserts were supposed to be dry. The classroom smelled like chalk and the wet rain jackets hanging by the door, and outside the window a steady drizzle streaked the glass.

His teacher had paired the class off to compare a desert climate with a rainforest climate using rainfall and temperature graphs, and Lucas had ended up with Priya, who sat two rows over and always finished her math early. She slid her laptop toward him. "You have to look at this," she said.

On the screen were two satellite images of the same patch of Earth, the Indian Ocean and South Asia. The January picture showed a bright band of clouds sitting in a line south of India, hugging the equator like a belt. The July picture showed the same band, except it had moved north, parked right over India and the surrounding land. Lucas leaned closer until he could smell the laptop's warm plastic fan.

"That's weird," he said. "The clouds moved."

"They're not just any clouds," Priya said. "My cousin in Chennai calls that band the Intertropical Convergence Zone."

Lucas copied the name onto his worksheet, then looked back at his two graphs. The rainforest station in Borneo got soaked every single month, no favorites, steady as a metronome. The desert station got almost nothing all year, except for that one tall tower of rain in summer. He turned his pencil around and held it over the July satellite image, lining it up with the cloud band. Then he slid the pencil north, over the land, and tapped the screen.

"So in January the band hangs down south, over the ocean, and the desert stays dry," he said slowly. "In northern summer the whole thing shifts north over South Asia, and when it does, the rain comes with it." He picked up his graph again. "That's my July tower. That's where all that rain is from."

"That would explain why my aunt says it pours every afternoon in July," Priya said. Her grin was infectious, and even Lucas's frown came undone.

He had a small worry, though. What if he had the direction wrong and the band actually drifted south in summer, the way some kids in his class insisted? That little controversy had started an argument at the back table, and the thought of it started to irritate him. He scrolled back to the January image, then forward to July, checking the coastline of India against the edge of the cloud band. In January the band's southern edge sat below the land. In July the band lay across it. North. It moved north. He wrote it down.

Priya tilted the laptop so the back table could see. "Hey, look at this," she called.

Alice stood in the back of the black box theater, clutching her partner card, and wished she had signed up for stage crew instead of improv. Ms. Ruiz had explained the rule twice: whatever your partner offers, you accept it and add to it. "Yes, and," she kept saying, like it was a magic spell. Alice thought the spell was probably fake.

Her partner was Marcus, who once ate a crayon in sixth grade and had never been allowed to forget it. He bounced on his toes and grinned at her. "We're astronauts," he whispered, before the teacher even called their names. "Stranded on Mars. Go with it."

Alice had a whole refusal ready, something about how Mars was stupid and space had no air. Instead, because Ms. Ruiz was watching, she heard herself say, "Yes, and the ship only has enough oxygen for one of us." Marcus's eyes went wide, and suddenly they were both building the scene, arguing over a hidden air tank, discovering a stowaway mouse, hailing a rescue ship made of recycled lunch trays. The class laughed in the right places. Alice felt something click open in her chest, like a door she hadn't known was stuck.

Afterward, while they filed out, a boy named Dev was still performing his monologue from earlier, Juliet at the window, prowling the stage and peering behind the curtains. "Wherefore art thou Romeo?" he called, squinting into the empty seats as if Romeo might be hiding in row three. His friend Priya smothered a laugh. "You're looking around like she's asking where he is," she said. "'Wherefore' means 'why.' She's asking why he's Romeo." Dev stood very still in the middle of the stage. Then he muttered that nobody had told him that, and Priya said that was kind of the point of four hundred years ago.

Alice turned the words over. Juliet wasn't searching; she was questioning. It was like improv, in a way she couldn't quite close her hand around. You could stand on a stage looking for the wrong thing entirely, and the scene would still go on without you, and nobody would stop it.

On Monday she tried to salvage her old plan of joining stage crew, but the roster was full, and Ms. Ruiz said an amendment to the schedule would not be feasible before the showcase. So Alice walked to the black box theater with her stomach in knots and found Marcus already there, spinning an invisible helmet in his hands.

"Air tank again?" he asked.

Alice took a breath. "Yes, and this time the mouse is captain."

Jaxson sat at his grandfather's kitchen table with a photocopied constitution, three highlighters, and a growing headache. On Monday he had to explain one right in his own words to the whole class, and so far his best effort was "you can, um, say stuff." His grandpa slid a plate of toast toward him and turned on the small TV above the fridge, where a legislative session droned on.

"That's what you're studying?" Grandpa asked, pointing his fork at the paper. "Rights?"

"I have to pick one and explain it," Jaxson said. "Mr. Okafor says if we can't say it in our own words, we don't really understand it." He glared at the list. "Who writes like this? 'Nothing herein shall be construed'... it's like the sentence is hiding from me."

On the screen, a member stood up. "I move that Bill 47 now be read a third time." The camera cut to the Speaker, who droned, "The Bill is now passed and becomes an Act."

Jaxson sat up. "Wait. Wasn't that the same thing? It was a bill a second ago, and now it's an act? Did they rename it? Why does it have two names?"

Grandpa grinned and stole a piece of Jaxson's toast. "You tell me. You're the one holding the rulebook."

Jaxson looked from the TV to his constitution and back. He had an idea, and like all his ideas, it needed testing. He grabbed the remote, rewound the recording, and watched the vote again. Before the vote: bill. After it passed: Act. He checked another clip from the news, a proposal that had failed. It was still called a bill afterward. That confirmed it. "It's like a caterpillar and a butterfly," he said. "It's called a bill until it passes all its stages, and once it passes, it's called an Act. Same thing, different name, depending on whether it made it through."

"So it's a bill while it's still becoming one," Grandpa said, "and an Act when it's arrived."

"Exactly." Jaxson wrote it in his notebook, then frowned. "That's cool, but it doesn't help me with my assignment."

"Doesn't it?" Grandpa tapped the constitution. "Half of the list you're squinting at is Acts. Somebody's bill had to survive all that voting to become a right you can wave around at school."

Jaxson read the rights again with new eyes. He picked the one about not having soldiers quartered in your house, which sounded like a landlord problem from the future, and drafted a summary in plain words. He read it out loud. Grandpa laughed so hard he knocked over the pepper.

"Coherent at last," Grandpa said, wiping his eyes. "Though if soldiers show up here, they get the couch and they're doing dishes."

"Grandpa. You'd charge them rent."

"Ten dollars a soldier," Grandpa said, and raised his coffee mug like a gavel.

The living history museum had given Rose one job for Junior Docent Day: stand by the treaty display in the old courthouse and explain to visitors how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War. Her mother had driven her forty minutes for this, and in twenty minutes the first tour group would arrive. Rose had her note cards, and she had read them eleven times, and the words still slid off her brain like rain off a waxed jacket.

The problem was that she couldn't see it. The war was over there, in the future, and the treaty was over here, in 1919, and the thing that connected them was invisible. "It's like the connection isn't in the room," she told Wendell, the volunteer in the gray docent vest who was straightening the display case. "I can say the words, but I can't make anybody feel how one thing grew out of the other."

Wendell shrugged kindly and went back to his diagonal arrangement of the flags, red and black and tricolor, crossing each other across the back wall of the case. Rose sat down on the bench to despair quietly for a minute, which was when she found the letter tucked into her satchel. She recognized her grandfather's handwriting before she even unfolded it.

Dear Rose, it read. Good luck today. You'll figure it out the way you figured out the garden. Remember the spring you asked me why my tomatoes towered over yours, and we dug into both beds with our hands? My soil was nearly black and yours was pale brown, and the dark soil grew everything better. Same as the old Egyptians. When the Nile flood went down, it left a layer of dark, fertile mud on the fields, which is why they called their land Kemet, the black land. Sometimes the richest thing is the thing somebody leaves behind. Love, Grandpa.

Rose read it twice. Then she stood up, walked to the display case, and looked at it differently. Not at the dates, but at what was left behind. The treaty had gone down, the way a flood goes down, and it had left something on Germany's fields: the debt, the lost land, the blame written into the treaty itself. She couldn't see that layer. Nobody could. But she could see what grew from it, because she had seen it in the garden, where the black bed produced plants twice the size of the pale one. Things that get planted leave layers, and layers grow things, and what grows depends on what got left there.

When the tour group came through, twelve sixth graders and two tired teachers, Rose stepped forward. "Can I show you something invisible?" she asked, and she had their attention immediately, because who can resist that. She held up her two hands. "Imagine my right hand is Germany after the war. The treaty piled stuff on it, money it owed, land it lost, and when the treaty was signed and everyone went home, all that stayed behind, like mud after a flood. You can't see it, but it's there, feeding whatever gets planted next. And what got planted next was a man who promised to dig it all up."

A boy in a green hoodie raised his hand. "So the war started because of dirt?" He wasn't being sarcastic; he was genuinely trying to interpret what she'd said.

"Kind of," Rose said. "Because of what got left in the ground, and who planted what in it."

Wendell, watching from the doorway, gave her a small nod. The sixth graders moved on toward the gift shop, but the boy in the green hoodie lingered a moment, staring at the case. "My grandfather says hatred is a seed," he said slowly, "but I never knew what he meant before."

Rose folded her grandfather's letter and put it back in her satchel, next to the note cards she no longer needed.

The computer lab smelled like warm plastic and the lemon cleaner Mr. Dorsey used on the keyboards, and Abigail had exactly one class period to make her science project page work. The heading needed to be centred, which her notes said meant CSS, and the table of her beetle data needed to appear below it. She had already fixed the heading, typing "text-align: center" and watching the title slide to the middle of the screen like magic she had performed herself.

"Install it on the school site before lunch and you're safe," said Marcus, leaning over from the next computer. He had been hovering all morning, offering help she hadn't asked for, and every time she glanced at him he looked away a little too quickly.

"I haven't even got the table working," Abigail said. She had written a short Python program to print her data, fourteen weeks of observations, each row showing the length of the larva she had measured. When she ran it, only one row appeared on the page: the last one, week fourteen, sitting there alone. She ran it again. Same thing. One row.

"Maybe the loop's broken," Marcus said, but his voice was vague, as if he weren't really guessing.

Abigail stared at the program. The loop looked fine. It said "for week in weeks," and then a line that printed the week and the length. She counted the rows in her data. Fourteen. She counted the rows printed. One. Somewhere, thirteen rows were vanishing, and she couldn't see where they went.

She leaned close to the screen. The print line sat flush against the left margin, while the "for" line above it also sat flush. She had a vague memory of copying an example from the board, but the board was erased now. She tried an experiment, the kind her mother called "change one thing." She pressed the space bar four times in front of the print line, so it slid to the right, tucked under the "for" like a chick under a wing.

She ran the program. Fourteen rows spilled onto the page, week one through week fourteen, every measurement accounted for. So the spaces mattered. The indented line belonged inside the loop, running again and again, once for each week. And before, unindented, it had run only once, after the loop had finished, which was why the last row, and only the last row, had shown up. She tested it once more to be sure, pushing the line back to the margin and watching the table collapse to a single row again.

"Marcus," she said slowly, "did you already know that?"

He pushed his chair back an inch. "Maybe I ran into it yesterday. On my own page."

"You've had a finished page since yesterday and you watched me struggle for an hour?"

"I wanted to see if you'd figure it out," he said, "because I didn't. Mr. Dorsey had to tell me." He pulled up his own screen, and there it was: his heading centred, his table complete, and at the bottom, in small letters, "Thanks to A. for the beetle data."

"That's my data," Abigail said. "That's my whole project on your page."

"I asked Mr. Dorsey if we could present together," Marcus said. "He said to ask you."

Abigail saved her file, installed the page on the school site with two minutes left in the period, and looked at her centred heading shining above fourteen tidy rows. "Then ask me," she said, and turned the screen so the whole class could see it.

The garage smelled like oil and old rain boots, and the only light came from a bare bulb swinging over the workbench where Isabelle had taped a giant printout of the periodic table. Her little brother Theo sat on an overturned bucket, stirring a pot of water on the camping stove they weren't technically supposed to touch.

"I still don't get it," Isabelle said, tapping the printout. "The quiz is Monday, and Mrs. Patel said we have to find the number of protons in any element she points to. There are, like, a hundred of them."

"That's a tsunami of squares," Theo said, watching the pot.

She traced the number in the top corner of gold. "Seventy-nine. That's the atomic number. So gold has seventy-nine protons. Carbon, six. Oxygen, eight." It felt almost too easy, which made her suspicious. Things that seemed easy in her notebook had a way of turning strange on quizzes. She decided to test herself: she would call out a symbol, find the square, and say the protons before Theo could count to five.

"Fe," Theo read, picking letters at random.

She slid her finger down the column. "Iron. Twenty-six." She kept going, helium two, chlorine seventeen, silver forty-seven, and by the time the water was steaming she had missed only one, confusing sodium for sulfur and fixing it herself when she checked the names.

Then the water began to boil, and Theo pointed at the pot. "Bubbles. That's a chemical change, right? Like the baking-soda volcano. Bubbles mean something new got made."

Isabelle leaned over the pot. The bubbles rose and broke at the surface, and the lid was fogged with drops that slid back down when she tilted it. She touched one drop and rubbed it between her fingers. It was just water. "Look," she said, holding the lid out to him. "The bubbles are water vapour. It's the same stuff, only a gas. Nothing new got made." She pulled the printout toward her and pointed at oxygen and hydrogen. "If it were a chemical change, we'd have different substances at the end. We don't. So boiling is a physical change even though it makes bubbles."

Theo frowned at the pot. "So the volcano was chemical because it made a new thing, and this is physical because it didn't."

"Exactly." Isabelle grinned and flipped her flashcards over. "Monday, I'm going to donate one question to you. If Mrs. Patel ever asks about bubbles, you tell her that."

Theo laughed, and behind them the water kept rolling, drop after drop rising and vanishing into steam.

Jaxon crouched at the top of the hallway ramp he had built from a shelf board and a stack of dictionaries. His plan was simple: roll the marble down, time it with the stopwatch, mark the distance every second, and turn the numbers into a distance-time graph for Monday's science homework. He had taped a battery-powered buzzer to the ramp's edge yesterday, so the start signal would be loud and identical every time. He pressed the button. Nothing. The buzzer stayed silent, and the little bulb beside it stayed dark, even though both had worked perfectly the night before.

He checked the wires first. They lay along the floor in a coiled heap, wound tight like an intestine, and he untangled them one loop at a time, but every connection looked solid. Then he unscrewed the bulb and shook it near his ear. It didn't rattle. He sat back on his heels and stared at the battery, turning the problem over. The circuit had worked yesterday and nothing about the wires had changed, so the thing that changed had to be the battery itself. A battery turns stored chemical energy into electrical energy, he remembered, and it goes flat when those chemicals are used up. He had left the buzzer switched on all night. He had drained it himself.

A folded note sat on the kitchen table in his little sister Nia's rounded handwriting: "Can I have your extra battery for my star projector tonight? Mine died. My camping trip story is due Tuesday and I want to practice under the stars on my ceiling. Please please please." Jaxon looked at the note, then at his dead battery, then at the drawer where his last spare sat. His graph mattered, but so did her ceiling of stars.

"Hey, Nia," he called. "Take the spare. I'll figure out my part."

"You sure?" She appeared in the doorway, already hopeful.

"Yeah. Mine went flat overnight. Left the buzzer on."

She hugged him quick and hard, then ran off clutching the battery like treasure.

Without the buzzer, Jaxon improvised. He propped his phone against the wall and filmed the marble rolling past meter marks taped along the floor, then counted frames to get his times. He plotted the points and drew the line, and the graph was impartial, telling him exactly what had happened whether he liked the answer or not: the marble was slowing as friction ate its speed. Not steady. His first guess had been wrong.

He redid the ramps three times, filmed, counted, replotted, until the points fell close to a line he trusted. He slid the finished graph into his folder, then remembered Nia's ceiling and taped a strip of glow stars along her doorway where she wouldn't see it until the projector came on. From her room came a shriek of delight.

"Jaxon, did you do this?"

"Blame the graph," he called back. "It taught me everything runs down, so you'd better enjoy it while it's bright."

Joseph had signed up for the drawing elective at Camp Wren because his mother said it would be calm, and it was, until Friday. Everything they made had to be finished and hung in the dining hall by supper, and the counselor, Theo, refused to extend the deadline even though the whole art shed smelled of panic and pencil shavings.

Joseph's street was going well. He had ruled the edges of the road toward a single vanishing point, which Theo had installed on the chalkboard with a thumbtack and a length of red string so everyone could see where their lines had to meet. The lampposts shrank toward it, the rooflines tilted toward it, and the street looked like it actually ran somewhere.

Then Nadia groaned across the table. Her practice sphere, a simple ball she had to shade before starting her real piece, looked wrong. She had filled the whole dark half with the same even grey, and instead of a ball it sat on her page like a flat grey disc with a rim around it.

"It's a rebellion," she said. "The pencil is staging a rebellion."

Joseph leaned over. He held his own sphere next to hers, the one he had shaded during the demo. His looked round. Hers looked flat. Same size, same light coming from the upper left. Something unseen was different between them, and he wanted to find out what.

He tried an experiment. He copied her method on a scrap, one even grey across the whole dark side, and it went flat too. Then he studied the ball on the table Theo had set under the clip light. He turned it slowly with two fingers. Where the light ended and the shadow began there was a soft border, and just past that border, on the side away from the lamp, the shadow was at its darkest. Farther around, toward the far edge, it actually lightened a little. Joseph took his softest pencil and laid down that one dark band, then let the rest of the dark side go lighter. The ball on the scrap page popped forward, round as an orange.

"Try the darkest part right after the light stops," he told Nadia. "Just past that line."

"The terminator," Nadia said, pointing at the border between light and dark. "Theo's handout calls it that. And the dark band is the core shadow, I found it on the next page."

She shaded the band just past the terminator, keeping the far side of the sphere lighter, and her ball rolled up off the paper. She laughed and immediately began her real piece, an apple on a windowsill, with ten minutes left before supper.

"Is it good?" she asked Joseph, holding up the page.

He looked at the sphere, at the street running to its vanishing point, at the sun going down outside the shed door.

"Hang it," he said.

Sarah stood in the living room holding a spatula like a microphone and waited for her cousin Marcus to stop giggling. They were practicing improv because the community theater held auditions on Saturday, and the director had said the whole audition would be one scene with a partner. The rule, as Sarah understood it, was a principle called "yes, and": whatever your partner offered, you accepted it and added something of your own.

"Okay," Marcus said, still snorting. "You're a tour guide and I'm a tourist. Go."

"Welcome to the museum of famous speeches," Sarah began, sweeping her arm toward the couch. "You've arrived just in time."

Marcus crossed his arms. "This is dumb. Two minutes? You can't say anything important in two minutes."

Sarah almost argued, and then she remembered what had stopped her the same way last week. Their grandmother had been telling the story of a school assembly, how a boy in her class had stood up in 1963 on the anniversary of a famous speech and recited the Gettysburg Address from memory, all of it, while the principal watched the clock. "Abraham Lincoln's Gettysburg Address, given on November 19, 1863, was about 272 words long and took roughly two minutes to deliver," Grandma had said, tapping the arm of her chair. "Longest two minutes of that principal's life, and the most important thing anyone said all day."

Instead of arguing, Sarah said, "Yes, and that's exactly why this museum is special." She pointed the spatula at the bookshelf, holding it perfectly perpendicular to the floor like a real pointer. "Every famous speech here was under three minutes. Two minutes is plenty. Watch." She cleared her throat and began reciting the opening lines she'd memorized from the poster in the hallway. "Four score and seven years ago..."

Marcus blinked. He had expected her to fold, and she hadn't. "Yes, and," he said slowly, catching on, "you're the ghost of Lincoln, and you've been trapped in this museum for a hundred years."

"Sarah accelerated toward the kitchen, her coat tails, which were really just Dad's old jacket, flying behind her. "Yes, and I've been living on the snacks in the gift shop. Follow me, tourist, before the curator catches us."

Marcus chased after her, no longer giggling but actually running lines, his voice deepening into a ghostly boom. They careened around the kitchen table twice, and when Sarah finally collapsed into a chair, breathless, Marcus flopped into the one beside her and slid the cookie jar across the table without being asked, because he knew she'd want one after all that.

"Saturday," he said, "when we audition, do you think they'll give us a scene that good?"

"Better," Sarah said, and broke the cookie in half.

Clara sat on the crinkling paper of the exam table and watched the blood-pressure cuff squeeze her arm until her fingers tingled. "Your heart's racing a bit," Dr. Okafor said, "even though nothing here hurts. Any idea why?" Clara shrugged, but she had noticed things: the tight shoulders in math class, the way she chewed her pencil down to bare wood, the mornings when her stomach felt barren and hollow even though she'd eaten breakfast. She hadn't connected them until the doctor asked.

"That's your body signaling stress," Dr. Okafor said. "We can teach it to settle. Try breathing in for four counts and out for six." Clara did it twice, and the numbers on the monitor above the sink actually dropped. That was the first strange thing: something she couldn't see, changing because of something she did.

At home, Clara made a chart, because a pattern you can't see directly is easier to catch on paper. She wrote down how she felt each morning, and a shape appeared. Mondays were always the worst. The worst Mondays followed Saturdays when she slept until noon, and Sundays when she stayed up past one in the morning watching movies. On weeks when she'd gotten up at her usual time on the weekend, Monday felt almost normal. It didn't seem fair that Saturday could reach all the way into Monday, but the chart said it did.

She brought the chart to her follow-up appointment and spread it on the desk. Dr. Okafor studied it and nodded. "What you've found is the circadian rhythm," she said. "Going to bed and waking up at about the same time every day, including weekends, keeps it steady." Clara frowned at the word rhythm, like her body was a song she'd been scrambling every Saturday. So she set her alarm for the same time all seven days, even though her little brother opposed the plan loudly on Saturday mornings, banging her door at nine while she begged for one more hour.

Three weeks later, her chart showed mostly steady mornings, her pencil had stopped shrinking, and she could breathe four-in, six-out under her desk before a quiz without anyone noticing. She felt almost proud of herself, which was why it threw her when Saturday morning arrived and her eyes snapped open at exactly seven, wide awake, heart pounding, on a day with nothing scheduled and nobody waiting. She lay still and listened. Somewhere outside, a dog was barking, over and over, and her heart would not slow down. Clara sat up, put her feet on the cold floor, and started counting.

The rain hammered the roof of Grandpa's house so hard that Naomi could barely hear herself think, which felt like a joke, since her homework was about rain. On the kitchen table she had spread out two printed climate graphs, one for Cairo, Egypt, and one for Iquitos, Peru, each with twelve bars for rainfall and a jagged line for temperature. Her assignment was due Monday, and it asked her to decide which city belonged to a tropical rainforest climate and to prove it.

The rule from her textbook sat in her notebook, copied in her own handwriting: in the Koppen climate system, a city counts as a tropical rainforest climate only if every single month averages at least 18 degrees Celsius and at least 60 millimeters of rain. Every month. One failure and the whole thing fell apart. That word "every" was starting to feel like a trap.

Cairo was easy. She ran her pencil along the rainfall bars and watched them shrink to almost nothing for months at a time. The temperature line climbed high, but the rain simply ceased to exist for half the year. Desert, no question.

Iquitos should have been easy too. The temperature line never dipped below eighteen degrees, hovering somewhere in the twenties all year. The rain bars stood tall and green, most of them well over a hundred millimeters. Then she reached August, and her stomach dropped. The bar looked small. She held the graph close to the window light. Fifty-eight millimeters. Maybe. Two millimeters short, if she was reading it right, and two millimeters was enough to kick Iquitos out of the rainforest entirely.

"That looks like a graph trying to pick a fight with you," Grandpa said, setting down a mug of cocoa.

"It's picking a fight and winning," Naomi said. "One month might be under sixty."

She refused to guess. The bars were drawn by hand on the printed sheet, thin and slightly smudged, and a shaky bar could fool anyone. So she tested it. She fetched Grandpa's clear ruler from the junk drawer and measured the tallest bar on the page, the one labeled March, which the data box said was exactly 160 millimeters. Then she measured every other bar against that scale, marking each one on scrap paper. March was 32 millimeters tall, so each printed millimeter equaled five real ones. July measured just over twelve printed millimeters. Twelve times five was sixty. She measured August twice, then a third time with the edge of the ruler flat against the paper. Sixty-one.

Every month held. Every single one cleared both hurdles, the temperature and the rain. She wrote her verdict at the top of the page, and it felt like something she had earned with a ruler and a scrap of paper.
