Then she added the sentence the assignment asked for, about the Koppen system and its requirements, and thought it was almost eloquent, for homework anyway.

"Verdict?" Grandpa asked, leaning over her shoulder.

"Rainforest," Naomi said, "by one millimeter of rain, and I measured it three times."

Avery spread the two graphs across the library table and weighted the corners with pencils before the air conditioning could send them fluttering. One showed monthly rainfall in the Sonoran Desert, a flat line that barely lifted off the bottom of the page. The other showed a rainforest in Borneo, where the bars towered so high they looked like a solid wall. The clock above the reference desk read 4:12, and the library closed at five. Her project was due first period tomorrow, and she still didn't have the answer to the question her teacher had posed: why does the same crop fail in one wet place and thrive in another?

She needed a picture of a rainforest farm for her poster. Her younger brother, Marcus, sat across from her with a bandaged thumb he would not stop examining, ever since Mom had warned him that a cut could get an infection if he kept picking at it. He flipped through a book about Asian agriculture while Avery hunted for photographs.

"Wait," Marcus said. "This doesn't make sense. This farmer is planting rice seedlings in a little bed, like a garden. And then these other people are sticking rice plants into a flooded field. Are they planting it twice?"

Avery was hesitant to believe him, because Marcus got things wrong constantly, like the time he insisted fog was smoke from the ocean. But she leaned over and looked. On one page, seedlings crowded together in a small nursery bed, green and stubby as new grass. On the facing page, rows of people bent over a flooded paddy, pushing young plants into the water one by one, by hand. She turned the pages back and forth. Same crop. Two plantings.

"So they start it in a nursery bed," she said slowly, "then transplant it into the flooded field." The pieces began to click against her graphs. The rainforest's enormous rainfall, the flooded fields in the photographs, they belonged to the same story. She grabbed a marker and wrote it out: rice grown first in a nursery bed, then transplanted, often by hand, into flooded paddies. The desert graph, with its stingy slivers of rain, could never flood a field like that. The rainforest could.

"Does that help?" Marcus asked, sounding worried the answer might be no.

"It fixes everything," Avery said. The clock said 4:47. She taped the graphs onto her poster, added the photograph of the farmers bent over the water, and wrote her headline in tall letters: WHERE THE RAIN GOES. A librarian began wheeling a cart toward the shelves, locking the cabinet doors one by one, and Avery slid her poster into her backpack just as the lights over the reference desk blinked twice.

"That's a five-minute warning," the librarian called out.

Avery zipped the bag and held it against her chest. "Race you to the door," she said.

Arthur had lost the same race twice, and both times the same way: a blazing first lap, then legs that felt like wet sand on the second. Today at Riverside Park he set a plan. He would run his first lap slow on purpose, hold something back, and let the second lap decide everything. The track looped past the basketball courts, so his friend Marcus timed him from the fence while a pickup game roared behind them.

On the first try, Arthur panicked. When Marcus shouted the split, Arthur was six seconds behind his usual pace, and he sped up to fix it, burning everything early again. He finished with nothing, gasping by the water fountain.

"That's the opposite of the plan," Marcus said, clicking the stopwatch. "You gotta trust the slow part."

Arthur walked it off, thinking. The problem wasn't his legs. It was something he couldn't see, the shape of the race itself, hiding underneath the numbers. If the second lap was where races were lost, then the first lap's job was only to save fuel. He could infer his pace from the split times without feeling it in his legs, because his legs lied. They always felt great early. That was the trap.

While he rested, the basketball game behind them erupted. "They keep scoring," Arthur said. The taller team ran the same few plays, and every time, one of them bellowed "Screen left!" or "Back door!" loud enough for the whole park. The other team jumped the play every single time, stealing the ball at midcourt.

Marcus waved at his cousin Dev, who played on the losing side. "Why do you guys call it out loud like that?"

"Because how else does everyone know the play?" Dev said, wiping sweat.

Arthur shrugged. "Point guards often call plays with a hand signal, a number, or a code word, so teammates know the play while the defense does not."

Dev looked at him with flat skepticism, like Arthur had suggested they play in dress shoes. But his teammate, a quiet kid in a gray hoodie, said, "He's right. My travel team does it. Two fingers means the double screen." Dev chewed on that, then walked back to the huddle. Within two possessions they ran a silent play, three raised fingers, and the kid in the gray hoodie cut hard along the diagonal from the wing to the basket, caught the pass, and laid it in. The defense never moved. Dev pumped his fist and shot a thumbs-up across the court at Arthur.

Arthur stepped back onto the track. First lap, controlled. Second lap, everything. When Marcus called the split, the number sounded slow, and every muscle begged him to surge, but he remembered that his legs were liars. He held the pace until the far curve, then let it all go. He crossed the line three seconds faster than he'd ever run, bent over, laughing at the grass between his shoes.

"Same time next Saturday," Marcus said. "And Dev wants you at the courts after."

Arthur grinned, still catching his breath. "Tell him I'll bring the signals."

The nature trail behind the school had a wooden bench near the creek, and that was where Isla set up the field kit her science teacher lent her: a pocket microscope, a razor blade, a dropper of iodine, and an onion she had carried in her backpack all morning. Her assignment was due Monday. She had to peel a thin layer of onion skin, stain it, and draw the cells with the wall, the membrane, and the nucleus labeled. She could have done it in the lab after school on Friday, but she had chosen the trail instead, the way she had chosen a solo hike last summer instead of going with her friends. She still wasn't sure that had been the right call, but this one felt like it might be.

Her friend Marisol found her there, as she somehow always did. "You really brought an onion on a nature walk," Marisol said, sitting down on the bench without waiting for an invitation. Isla peeled a translucent strip of skin from the onion's fleshy layer, laid it on the slide, and added a single drop of iodine. Under the pocket microscope, the cells appeared like pale bricks in a wall, each one bordered and neat. She began to draw them in her notebook, labeling the thick outer wall first, then the thin membrane pressed just inside it. The nucleus showed up as a darker dot once the stain soaked in, and she marked that too.

"That's good," Marisol said, looking over her shoulder at the finished drawing. Then she flipped back a page and stopped at Isla's comparison chart from last week's homework. "Wait. You wrote mitochondria as animal-only." Isla's pencil hovered, hesitant, over the chart. She had been proud of that chart. She remembered arguing her logic at the dinner table: animals eat food, so animal cells would need something to release energy from it, and plants make their own food, so they wouldn't need any such thing. At the time the reasoning had seemed airtight.

"Plants have mitochondria too," Marisol said. "Both plant and animal cells have them. They release energy from food." Isla frowned at her drawing of the brick-shaped cells. "But plants make their own food," she said. "Yeah," Marisol said, shrugging. "They still need mitochondria anyway." Isla turned back to the microscope and looked again at the onion cells, imagining the tiny structures she could not see at this magnification, working away inside a layer of skin thinner than paper. She couldn't justify leaving the chart the way it was. She crossed out the animal-only box and rewrote the column.

"It's kind of irony," she said slowly, "that the plant makes its own food and still needs the thing that gets energy out of it." Marisol raised an eyebrow. "That's not really how you use that word." "It's close enough," Isla said, and bent over the slide again, because the light had shifted and a row of nuclei had come into view, each dark dot sitting inside its cell like a seed inside a translucent fruit. She drew them one by one, pressing hard enough that the pencil nearly went through the page.

Peyton had until five o'clock tomorrow to submit a short story to the library's summer contest, and she had promised herself she would not postpone it again. She spread her notebook across the table by the window, where her friend Marcus was already reading comic books.

"Read my opening," she said. "It has dialogue, but I don't know if I did the punctuation right." She read aloud: "'This beach is nice,' said the grandmother. 'It was a good trip,' said Jules." Marcus squinted at the page. "The commas are in the right place," he said. "But I can't see the beach. Or the trip. What was nice about it?"

Peyton frowned. Something about his question tugged at her memory. Last spring, her grandmother had come over with a bag of postcards, and when Peyton said her class trip had been interesting, her grandmother had leaned forward and asked what exactly was interesting about it. Peyton had stammered something about the bus and then, finally, described the moment a hawk had landed on the fence outside the planetarium and stared at them through the glass while everyone was still arguing about lunch. Her grandmother had laughed and said she could see the whole thing, hawk and all. "Nice" had shown her nothing; the hawk had shown her everything.

"So the vague ones," Peyton said slowly, tapping her pencil, "words like nice, good, interesting. They give me my opinion without showing anything." Marcus nodded. "Right. A concrete detail lets me picture it and judge for myself." She crossed out "nice" and wrote, "The grandmother picked up a wet feather and rolled it between her fingers." Then she crossed out "good trip" and wrote that Jules had counted forty-one dead jellyfish on the sand and kept the number in his head like a prize.

Now she needed a climax, the moment everything turned. She had been avoiding it because it felt ambiguous, like she couldn't tell what her story was really about. "Maybe that's the problem," Marcus said. "The climax has to be the moment it turns. Yours is just people talking on a beach forever."

They formed an alliance: Marcus would read every page out loud, and Peyton would not defend anything until he finished. When he read the jellyfish line, he stopped. "The grandmother should find one that's still alive," he said. "Right there. That's your turn." Peyton wrote it: the grandmother kneels, the jellyfish pulses once against her palm, and Jules has to decide whether to leave it for the tide.

At four the next day, she handed the printed pages to the librarian at the front desk, one minute before the deadline. "First entry this year," the librarian said, stamping the corner. Peyton smiled, took back her copy, and on the way out she stopped to look through the window at the parking lot, where a crow was standing on the hood of a silver car, watching the doors like it was waiting for someone.

Theo's problem was the blank index card on his desk. On Friday, Mr. Ruiz would pick three students to explain, out loud and in full sentences, how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War, and Theo had exactly nothing written down.

He flipped back through his notebook to the Oregon Trail unit, where he and Priya had read a settler's diary last month. They had made two columns on the whiteboard, arguing the whole time about which reason went where. "Crops failing, that pushes them out of Missouri," Priya had said. "Free land in Oregon pulls them west." Their teacher had stood back and let them fight it out, which Theo now appreciated, since he remembered every word. Push factors drive people away from home, he thought, and pull factors attract them to a new place. The diary family had both: a failing farm behind them and a promise ahead of them.

So what if a whole country could work like that? He tried it. After the treaty, Germany had crushing reparations, lost territory, and a military shrunk to almost nothing. Those pushed Germans away from their own government, away from the Weimar Republic that had signed the paper. And something pulled them too: Hitler promising jobs, pride, and someone to blame. Theo wrote it out and stared at it. It actually held together.

On Thursday he tested it at lunch, because Priya was the toughest audience he knew. "Pretend I'm clueless," he said, unwrapping his sandwich. "Explain the war."

"Okay. The treaty pushed Germans, the way bad crops push settlers. Then somebody offered them a new home, basically, and they went." He slid the notebook across. "Push factors and pull factors, but for a country instead of one family."

Priya chewed slowly, which was her thinking face. "So the treaty didn't cause the war by itself," she said. "It made people desperate enough to follow anyone pointing at a door." She tapped the page. "You should say the reparations were proportional to what Germany could actually pay. It couldn't. That's your push."

"You just gave a whole speech," Theo said.

"I delegated the thinking to you first. You did the work." She handed the notebook back. "Also your handwriting looks like a spider fell in ink."

Friday came. Mr. Ruiz paced the rows, and when he reached Theo's desk he paused. "Theo. Go."

Theo took a breath and started with the diary family leaving Missouri, then widened the lens until the family was a nation of millions, pushed by the treaty's terms and pulled by a voice offering restoration. When he finished, the room was quiet for a second.

Mr. Ruiz nodded once. "That's the clearest version I've heard today." Then he moved on down the row, and Theo drew a small spider on the corner of his index card.

Claire dragged the cardboard box across the garage floor and set it under the workbench light, where the bulb swung a little every time the wind pushed at the door. Her little brother Marcus followed her in, carrying a printout of the periodic table that he had flattened against his chest like a treasure map.

"I already decided," Claire said. "Carbon. Not gold, not oxygen, carbon."

"Because it's in pencils?" Marcus asked.

"Because Mrs. Ruiz said the model has to be an element we can explain, and I can explain carbon." She pulled a shoebox of Ping-Pong balls from the shelf, then a hot glue gun she wasn't supposed to use without asking, which she had decided was a compromise between asking and not asking, since Dad was in the driveway and could see her through the open door.

Marcus spread the periodic table on the hood of the lawnmower and squinted at it. "This thing has letters and numbers all mixed up. C, and then a little six above it. What's the six?"

"That's the atomic number." Claire said it quickly, then stopped. She had said the words before she had really thought about them, the way you can recite something and still not own it. She took the paper from him and looked at the small six sitting above the C. "Every carbon atom has exactly six protons," she said slowly. "That's what it's counting. Protons, in the nucleus."

"So the number tells you the protons."

"That's the whole point of it." She tested the idea, because reciting wasn't the same as knowing. She moved her finger two boxes to the right, to oxygen, and its little eight. "So oxygen has eight protons. Every single one. In every oxygen atom anywhere." She looked up. "That's actually wild. Nobody can see a proton. Nobody's ever going to hold one. But they counted them anyway, and the number's just sitting there on a chart in a garage."

"You're making six of them," Marcus said, holding up the printout again. "For carbon. Six balls."

She had been planning to use all the Ping-Pong balls and glue a big swirling electron cloud around the outside, something impressive and lopsided. Six protons meant building a nucleus first, a tight little knot in the middle, and that was harder to make look good. "I wanted the cloud to be the big part," she said.

"So make the nucleus the big part."

Claire looked at the six balls he had already counted out and lined up on the workbench, waiting. It was a plausible plan, actually, better than hers, though she wasn't going to say that out loud. She plugged in the glue gun and held the first two balls together until the glue grabbed.

"Hand me number three," she said, and Marcus did.

Marcus's basement smelled like lizard and old carpet, and his gecko, Godzilla, watched from his tank while the two boys hunched over a laptop on the ping-pong table. Tyler had come over to learn HTML, but Marcus had other plans. "I already built the page," Marcus said, spinning the laptop around. "It's about Godzilla. I just need the heading centred and the prime game to actually work. Then I can show it to Ava. She thinks I'm, like, an influential tech genius. I want to keep it that way."

Tyler leaned in. The heading "GODZILLA: REPTILE OF THE BASEMENT" sat stuck in the corner of the page, and below it was a box where you typed a number and the page told you if it was prime. Tyler typed 97 and pressed the button. The page froze. The cursor spun. Godzilla stared, unblinking, a true carnivore waiting for something to move. "It does that on big numbers," Marcus admitted. "Ava's going to think my page is broken. This could demolish my whole reputation."

Tyler added text-align: centre to the heading first, because that part he actually knew, and watched the title glide to the middle. Then he turned to the prime checker. Marcus's code tested every number from 2 up to the one you typed, one at a time, asking each, "Do you divide it evenly?" On a huge number that was millions of questions. Tyler traced the code with his finger, line by line, and noticed something odd: right after the code checked whether the number was divisible by 2, it kept testing 4, then 6, then 8, all the even ones, all the way up.

He had a guess, but he wanted proof before he said anything out loud. In a new file he tried 15 with only the odd tests, 3, 5, 7, 9, and it still said not prime, correctly, because 3 caught it. He tried 21, 35, 49. All found, all by odd divisors. He could not make it fail. "Skip the evens," he said finally, deleting half the checks. "After checking whether a number is divisible by 2, you only need to test odd divisors. An odd number can never be divided evenly by an even one." Marcus squinted at the screen. "That's it? That's the whole trick?" "Run it."

Marcus typed 999,983 and pressed the button, and both boys held their breath, because if the page froze now, everything was over. The answer appeared before Godzilla could even blink. Prime. The heading beamed from the centre of the screen like a trophy. Marcus grabbed his phone to text Ava, then stopped, staring at the instant result. "It's done already? But she loved watching it think." He typed 999,983 again, slower this time, and waited for a freeze that never came.

The clock above the whiteboard read 2:45, and Sadie's rice still needed twelve minutes, the curry eight, and the flatbread, according to her recipe card, exactly four minutes per side. She wrote the numbers in the margin of her notebook and worked backward from 3:15, when Mr. Okafor would ring the bell and expect all three dishes on the table, hot, at the same time. If she started the flatbread last, it would come off the pan just as the curry finished, but the rice would have to go on the burner before anything else. She filled the pot, set it on high, and told herself that timing was just math with consequences.

At the next station, Marcus was draining a pot of pasta over the sink, steam rolling up toward the vent fan. "Stop!" Sadie said, almost knocking over the salt container as she leaned across the aisle. "Save some of that water. A cup."

Marcus stared at her like she had accused him of a crime. "It's pasta water. It's garbage."

"It's not. It's starchy. The pasta lets starch out into the water while it cooks, and if you splash a bit of that into your sauce, the sauce gets thicker and sticks to the noodles instead of pooling at the bottom of the bowl." She wasn't sure where she had read it, some cooking blog at two in the morning, but she was sure of it the way she was sure seven times eight was fifty-six.

Marcus wanted the blue ribbon for Best Sauce at the class showcase on Friday more than he wanted recess, and his sauce was currently thin and watery, sliding off a test noodle like rain off a leaf. He looked at the cloudy cup Sadie had scooped from the pot, then at his saucepan, then back at the cup. "Fine. But if it's gross, that's on you."

He poured a splash in and stirred. The sauce turned glossy and began to cling, coating the spoon the way nectar coats a spoon, slow and heavy. Marcus held the spoon up to the light and actually grinned. "It's clinging," he said. "It's actually clinging."

Sadie turned back to her own station, where the rice was boiling and the curry needed its coconut milk now. The flatbread dough was still a soft ball under a damp towel, waiting its turn. It was probable that something would still go wrong; her last attempt at this had produced gummy rice and cold curry, and the memory of it sat in her stomach like a stone. But she had her timeline written down, and the pot was already bubbling, and Marcus was spooning sauce over noodles at the next table like he'd discovered treasure. She pinched off a round of dough, patted it flat, and dropped it onto the hot pan, where it puffed up in one small, perfect bubble.

Nolan pushed the shopping cart past the cereal, doing math in his head. Two hundred forty dollars. That was what he had in his savings account, and the blue bike in Mr. Herrera's window cost three hundred ninety-nine. "If I add five dollars a week," he muttered, "that's... a lot of weeks."

"Did you say weeks?" his dad asked, tossing in a bag of rice. "Because I was going to tell you about years. The bank pays you interest for keeping money there. Simple interest is a slice of your original amount every year. Compound interest is a slice of your original amount plus all the interest you've already earned. It grows on itself."

"Show me," Nolan said, so at the dairy aisle his dad pulled a receipt from his pocket and flipped it to the blank side. He wrote out five years of simple interest on two hundred forty dollars, then five years of compound, keeping the rate the same. By year five the compound column pulled ahead, and by year ten the gap looked like a small canyon. Nolan stared at the numbers. "So if I just leave it alone, the money does extra work without me?" "That's the idea," his dad said. "Patience pays, and it pays more every year it waits."

In the juice aisle they ran into Priya from Nolan's class, who looked like a plague had swept through her lemonade stand, which in a way it had. "Strawberry lemonade disaster," she groaned. "We charged three dollars a cup because the strawberries cost so much. Everybody wanted the regular lemonade at one dollar. We're stuck with four jugs of strawberry nobody will buy."

Nolan thought about the paper in his dad's pocket, about numbers lined up in columns. High price, lots left over. "So if you charge less," he said slowly, "more people will actually buy it, and you won't be swimming in strawberry." Priya frowned. "But we paid a lot for the strawberries." "But you'll end up with money instead of jugs," Nolan said. "Right now the high price is leaving you with stuff nobody wants." Priya tested it that weekend. At two dollars a cup, the strawberry lemonade sold out by Saturday afternoon. She texted Nolan a photo of an empty cooler with the words "You were right, money boy."

The next Saturday, Nolan stood in the cereal aisle again, this time holding a pencil and the back of a receipt. He wrote his two hundred forty dollars at the top, then added his five dollars a week, then added the little extra the bank would pay on the growing pile, year after year. Somewhere around the third column he grinned. His dad leaned over. "Calculating the bike fund?" "Calculating the bike fund, the second bike fund, and the fund after that," Nolan said, and boxed the final number with a flourish. "Move over, compound interest. You've got company."

Leo knelt on the muddy bank and peeled a papery layer off the onion he had smuggled from his mother's kitchen. "The trick is getting a piece thin enough for light to pass through," he said, mostly to himself, because thin things were the whole point of today.

Maya waded close to the edge and scooped pond water into a jar. She had agreed to accompany him on the condition that they look at pond creatures too, so the jar went into her backpack next to the microscope Leo's uncle had lent him. Back at the picnic table, Leo dropped the onion skin onto a slide, added one drop of iodine, and pressed the cover glass down with his thumb. Then he cranked the microscope's knob with vigorous little turns, too fast, and the image blurred past focus twice before a lattice of brick-like cells swam into view.

"There," Maya said, leaning in. "Draw it before you touch anything."

He drew fast, then slowed down. The cell walls showed as the rigid outer edges of every brick. He remembered the membrane as a thin line just inside the wall, hugging it like a second skin. But the nucleus, the dark blob his worksheet wanted labeled, was nowhere obvious. He tested a simple idea: if the iodine stain made some structures darker, maybe he had not used enough. He made a second slide with two drops instead of one. The consequence was a purplish blob in each cell, plain as a thumbprint. He labeled all three parts and sat back, feeling like he had unlocked something.

"So the worksheet says every food chain starts with the sun," Maya said, squinting at the jar of pond water, where green specks clung to the glass. "The algae in here make food from sunlight, the water fleas eat them, and so on. Sunlight first, always."

"That's what I thought too," Leo said. "Then my sister watched this documentary." He told her what it said: in 1977, scientists in a submersible named Alvin found deep-sea vent communities down in total darkness, and the food chains there start with bacteria that use chemicals from the vents, not sunlight.

Maya frowned at the jar. "So if we sealed this in a dark box, everything would die. But down there, it wouldn't."

"It's like the vents have their own starting point," Leo said. He held the slide up to the light anyway, where the little stained cells glowed faintly purple. "Same rule, different first step."

Maya tilted the jar so the green specks caught the sun. "Draw them next," she said, "before they swim away."

Taylor's motivation for spending her Saturday behind Mr. Alvarez's pasta stand was simple: he had agreed to teach her to cook, and her mother had agreed to stop burning water if someone else took over. The lesson started with onions. "Curl your fingers like a claw," Mr. Alvarez said, tapping her knuckles. "The blade rides against your knuckles, and your fingertips stay out of trouble." Taylor curled, chopped, and produced something closer to onion gravel than onion pieces, but all ten fingers survived, which she counted as a win. She could feel herself begin to perspire under the market canopy, and she blamed the onions entirely.

Two stalls down, Rosa from Rosa's Oven was staring into her display case with the expression of someone whose oven had betrayed her. "Same thing every week," she told a customer. "The tops of my muffins come out golden brown and the insides stay pale. I don't touch the recipe."

Taylor kept chopping, but her mind snagged on it. Golden tops, pale insides. Same batter, same oven, two different results. What was different between the top of a muffin and the middle of one? She turned a cup of Rosa's muffin over in her head while her hands worked the claw grip through a second onion. The top was the part the heat hit first and hardest, the part with no paper wrapper between it and the air. The middle was protected, buried in itself.

She had a theory, and theories needed testing. On her break she bought two of Rosa's muffins, and she borrowed a strip of foil. She wrapped the top of one muffin, set both on a tray in the corner of Mr. Alvarez's little pizza oven, and waited, watching through the glass. After ten minutes she pulled them out. The unwrapped muffin's top had gone golden brown again. The wrapped one's top stayed pale, while the sides that peeked out from under the foil had browned instead. So it was the heat hitting the surface directly, doing something to whatever was in the batter at that surface. She remembered Mr. Alvarez grumbling last week about his bread crust. "Sugars and proteins," he'd said, cutting a distinct line through the crust with his knife. "They react in the heat. That's the Maillard reaction."

Taylor carried the two muffins to Rosa's stall and laid them side by side. "Your recipe's fine," she said. "The tops turn golden brown because the sugars and proteins react in the heat. The insides stay pale because they never get hot enough at the surface." Rosa looked at the pale-topped muffin, then at Taylor, then shouted over three stalls, "Mr. Alvarez! Your apprentice solved my case!"

Mr. Alvarez waved his chef's knife in salute. "Good. Now get back here. You're on onions until you can make them distinct cubes instead of gravel."

Taylor returned to the cutting board, curled her claw, and discovered that onions, at least, had not gotten any easier while she was busy being a detective. She chopped. The pile looked exactly like gravel.

Hannah slid her essay prompt across the library table so Marcus could see it. "Argue for or against a change at our school," she read aloud, "using a thesis and three supporting points. Draft due Friday." The deadline felt imminent, and she had nothing.

"Easy," Marcus said. "Write that we should have a hockey team. Thesis: our school has no hockey team."

Hannah wrote it down. Then she stared at it. "Marcus, everyone knows we don't have one. Nobody's going to argue with that."

"So? It's true."

She flipped to the page their writing club packet had open on the table, the one about thesis statements. She read it twice, then a third time, because something in it kept snagging. A strong thesis makes a claim a reasonable person could disagree with. A statement nobody would dispute, like a plain fact, gives an essay nothing to argue.

"That's the problem," she said slowly. "My thesis is just a fact. There's no argument in it. If nobody could disagree, what am I even defending?"

Marcus shrugged. "So make it something people would fight about."

She tapped her pencil against the table, thinking through the hallway outside the library, the water fountain by the gym that had been shut off since October with a plastic bag taped over the valve. Students had started saying a repair was coming, but it never came. She tested the idea out loud. "Our school should spend its facilities budget fixing the gym water fountain before buying new bleachers."

"Disagree," Marcus said immediately. "Bleachers seat everybody. One fountain is one fountain."

Hannah grinned and started listing points on a fresh page. She abandoned the hockey idea completely, crossing it out so hard the pencil tore a little. Point one: the fountain by the gym is the only water source on that side of the building. Point two: repairs cost less than bleachers. Point three: attendance in PE might drop when students leave class just to get water. She wrote fast, filling the outline before she could lose the thread.

At the next club meeting, their advisor had them read thesis statements aloud. When it was Hannah's turn, she said, "Our school should fix the gym water fountain before buying new bleachers."

Mrs. Okafor raised an eyebrow. "I'd push back on that. The bleachers are a safety issue."

"Good," Hannah said. "That means I have something to argue."

Later, Hannah caught Marcus by the lockers and handed him her outline. "Read point two," she said. "I found the repair estimate from last year's newsletter."

Marcus read it and nodded slowly. "Okay. That's actually pretty convincing."

"Convincing enough that you'd still disagree?"

He zipped his backpack. "Ask me Friday."

Dylan had one weekend to figure out linear equations before Monday's retake, and Grandpa's kitchen table was the only quiet place left. He spread out his homework while Grandpa sorted through a crate of wooden triangle tiles for the birdhouse mosaic he was building.

"You're doing the tiles wrong," Dylan said, watching Grandpa hold two triangles side by side and squint.

"Am I." Grandpa stacked one triangle on top of the other. The edges lined up exactly, corner to corner, no sliver of wood showing anywhere. "These two match. All three pairs of sides, all three pairs of angles, equal all the way around."

"There's a word for that," Dylan said, flipping through his math book. "Congruent. Same shape and same size, so everything matches." He took two more triangles from the crate and stacked them. One corner stuck out past the other like a dog-eared page. "Not these."

"Classify them into piles, then," Grandpa said, sliding the crate across the table. "Matched ones on the left, misfits on the right. I need ten pairs by Sunday."

Dylan got to work, stacking and sorting, and somewhere around the fourth pair he noticed something. When he placed a tile on top of another tile, he couldn't see either one anymore. He could only see the top tile, and whether the bottom one peeked out. The matching was invisible unless it failed. He slid his algebra paper closer and read the problem again: x plus seven equals nineteen. The x was like the hidden bottom triangle. He couldn't see it. But if he did the same thing to both sides, the way stacking treated both tiles the same way, the hidden thing would have to show itself. He subtracted seven from the left side and seven from the right, and wrote x equals twelve. It felt like the corner peeking out.

"Found a use for your homework already?" Grandpa asked.

"It's the same trick," Dylan said. "You do the same thing to both sides and whatever's hiding has to show up. With the tiles I stack them. With the equation I subtract from both sides."

That evening a letter came from Grandpa's brother Leo, who never called because he said phones were an illusion of closeness. Grandpa read it aloud: "Dear Walt. Heard you're tiling again. Still cutting them by hand like a man indifferent to the existence of saws? Your brother, who owns a saw." Grandpa snorted and put the letter under the sugar bowl.

Sunday morning, Grandpa fit the last matched pair into the mosaic's roofline. Dylan checked his homework pile one more time, then folded it into his backpack and tapped the page. "Stay solved," he told it. Grandpa picked up a misfit triangle, the one with the crooked corner, and dropped it into the scrap bucket.

The folded note from Coach Ruiz landed on the bleacher beside Jeremy's gym bag: "You're authorized to call the plays Friday. Point guard means the game runs through you." Practice started in ten minutes, and Jeremy still could not decide how to run the pick and roll against Eastside, whose big men switched every screen.

He dribbled at the foul line, imagining it. Marcus would slide over and set the screen. Jeremy would rub shoulders with him, and either the defender switched and Jeremy passed to a rolling Marcus, or nobody switched and Jeremy drove. The problem was that Eastside always seemed one step ahead, and Jeremy could not see why. There had to be a pattern in their switches, something hidden in how they moved.

Before the scrimmage, Coach had the team run hurdles along the sideline. Jeremy clipped the third hurdle and stumbled through it, landing flat-footed. Marcus sailed over every one, but Derek, the fastest sprinter on the team, kept knocking them down or floating so high in the air that he landed slow, well past the hurdle, his lead leg swinging up stiff and straight like a plank. "You're hanging up there," Jeremy said. Derek tried again and hung there again.

Jeremy watched him closely. Marcus bent his lead knee and drove it over the hurdle first, then straightened the leg on the way down, and he came off each hurdle low and quick. Derek swung his whole leg up rigid, and that lifted his body too high, so he drifted over the top instead of running through it. "Lead knee first," Jeremy called. "Then straighten it." Derek nodded, drove the knee, straightened, and snapped down over the fourth hurdle without touching it. "That's it," Derek shouted, already three hurdles clear.

Jeremy chewed on that through a water break. The thing that ruined Derek's hurdling was not slowness. It was doing a stiff, obvious move that pushed him too high and left him floating where everyone could read him. At the whiteboard he texted his older cousin Rene, who had played point guard at Wilson High: "Eastside reads my drives. What do I do?" Rene's reply buzzed back fast: "If they see the play coming, you've already lost. Make the screen look like one thing, then let it become another. You have until Friday. Figure out the pattern in their switches; every team has one."

So Jeremy made his screen look stiff and obvious, a plank of a move, the same screen every time, for three possessions in the scrimmage. He watched. The switching big man always floated toward the ball, high and slow, sure of himself, reading the obvious move. On the next possession Jeremy called " forty-one," sent Marcus to the wing, and came off a screen that looked like the same plank play, except he bent it, changed direction at the last instant, and hit the approximate gap between two slow-moving defenders. Marcus rolled, Jeremy flicked the pass, and the ball dropped through without touching iron. "That," Derek yelled from the sideline, one hand raised mid-hurdle, "looked nothing like the other ones."

Annabelle got to the microscope station second, right behind Marcus, which meant she had to watch him hog the good scope for five whole minutes while she waited with her onion and her lab sheet. On the sheet, three words waited for arrows: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She had already peeled a paper-thin layer of skin off the onion with tweezers, and it lay on her slide like a ghost of an onion, pale and wrinkled.

Her first slide was a disaster. She dropped the coverslip flat onto the skin, the way you would clap a book shut, and when she looked through the eyepiece she saw dozens of round black-edged circles clustered everywhere. She drew them quickly, three of them, and labeled one "nucleus" before a doubt crept in. They were awfully round. And awfully empty.

"Those aren't cells," said Priya from the next station, leaning over. "Those are air bubbles. You've got a whole sky of them."

Annabelle sat back. Bubbles. She had trapped a pocket of sky between glass and glass, and she had almost turned it in for a grade. She pulled the elastic band off the slide box, snapped it once around her wrist, and thought. The bubbles had to be air that got in when she dropped the coverslip straight down, trapping it under. So maybe the trick was not to drop it flat. Maybe she could let one edge touch first and lower the rest slowly, like closing a door instead of slamming it.

"Try it," Priya said, though Annabelle hadn't said anything out loud. "You look like someone about to advocate for a big idea."

"I am advocating for it," Annabelle said. "Angle. One edge first." She took a fresh piece of onion skin, laid it flat, added the drop of stain, and touched just the edge of a new coverslip to the liquid. Then she lowered it slowly, hinged on that first edge, letting it settle across the skin like a slow shield coming down.

Through the eyepiece, the circles were gone. Instead the field filled with boxes, rows and rows of brick-shaped cells stacked together, their walls outlined clean and dark. Near the center of one cell sat a denser dot, round and small. She found it in the next cell too, and the next. That had to be the nucleus, and the dark border around each box had to be the wall, with the membrane just inside it, thin as a whisper.

She drew it all, arrows and labels, while Marcus complained that his slide looked like a meteor shower. "Bubbles," she told him, turning her drawing around. "Lower it at an angle, one edge first. Want to see mine?" She slid off her stool and waved him toward her scope, and Priya crowded in behind, and above them the ceiling fan spun like a propeller, stirring the smell of onion through the whole lab.

The alarm went off at 3:40 in the morning, and for a moment Cooper forgot where he was. Then he remembered: Uncle Yusuf's house, the spare room with the lumpy futon, and the folded paper on the nightstand with the first three lines of Surah Al-Fatiha written in Arabic letters, the ones he had to have memorized by Friday.

He found the kitchen already lit. Auntie Safa was cracking eggs, and his cousins Hamza and Laila shuffled in behind him, hair flattened on one side, eyes half shut. Nobody looked cheerful, but nobody complained either.

"Sit, sit," Auntie said, sliding plates across the counter. "Suhur time."

"Suhur?" Cooper whispered to Hamza as he took a seat.

"Before the dawn prayer, we eat," Hamza said, yawning. "Then nothing till sunset. No food, no water, nothing."

Cooper stared at his eggs. Nothing until sunset meant his stomach would be growling by math class tomorrow. But that wasn't what worried him. What worried him was the paper upstairs, the verses he'd read forty times without them sticking. He tried reciting them in his head while he chewed, and they slipped away like water through his fingers.

After the dawn prayer, when the sky outside the window had turned from black to thin gray, he had an idea. He watched Laila pull a blanket over her head on the couch and realized the whole house had gone quiet and hungry at the same time, together, on purpose. Maybe that was the trick. His brain wasn't holding the words because he'd been studying alone in a noisy room at home, half watching videos. Here, the words had a reason to matter, a place to fit. So he tested it. He went back to the spare room, set his phone to record, and recited the three lines out loud into it, listening once, reciting again.

By breakfast the next morning, which was 3:40 again, Auntie's eggs again, he had six lines memorized. He recited them for Hamza between bites of toast, and Hamza nodded along like he was checking a receipt. Cooper thought about his grandmother, who had taught these same verses to Uncle Yusuf somewhere across an ocean, and how she probably never transmitted them through a phone recording. He decided that didn't make his way worse. Just different. Though maybe by Friday, when he stood up in front of everyone, he would wish he'd started earlier, alone in his room instead of complaining about it for two weeks.

"Seven lines today," he told Auntie, holding out his plate for more eggs.

"Seven," she said, and cracked two more.

The gym smelled like floor wax and nervous sixth graders, and Alexander was one of them. A theater teacher had come to run a workshop before the debate tournament on Saturday, and she had just written two words on a portable whiteboard: yes, and. "Whatever your partner offers, you accept it and add to it," she said. "No blocking, no denying." Alexander's partner was Priya, who had beat him in the school debate final last month, and he was determined not to embarrass himself in front of her.

They started a scene about explorers discovering a lost city. Priya held up an imaginary shovel and said, "I found a door buried in the sand!" Alexander's whole brain wanted to say "that's just a rock." Instead he said, "Yes, and it opens into a room full of gold microbe samples under glass!" Priya's eyes lit up. "Yes, and one of the slides is still alive!" The scene took off like a rocket, and Alexander felt something click: every time he accepted her offer and built on it, the story got stronger, the same way a good argument did when you backed it up.

Saturday, at the tournament, it all connected. In the final round Alexander argued that school lunches should include more fresh vegetables. When a judge asked how he knew fresh food was healthier, he gave his data, then his reason connecting it, and the judge nodded and said, "Good warrant." Afterward a kid from the other team caught him by the water fountain. "Where does the word warrant even come from?" the kid asked.

Alexander didn't know. But his older sister had a shelf of debate books, and that night he dug through them until he found a battered paperback called The Uses of Argument. He flipped the pages fast, and there it was: a model of argument with claim, data, and warrant, laid out by the British philosopher Stephen Toulmin in 1958. Alexander read the page twice, then raced downstairs to extract a promise from his dad to drive him to Priya's house so he could tell her before he forgot a single detail.

The next Monday in the gym, the theater teacher started a new scene, this one set in a contemporary art museum. "I'm the security guard," Priya announced, "and this painting just moved!"

Alexander stepped forward, grinning. "Yes, and the paint is alive, because the artist mixed in microbes!"

"Yes, and they only eat the color blue!" Priya shouted, and the whole gym burst out laughing.

Hayden pressed his museum badge flat against his chest and walked into the Hall of Earth Science, where a giant globe hung from the ceiling, tilted, with a spotlight fixed at its center. In three hours he would give his first talk as a junior docent, and the topic was the one he had drawn by unlucky chance: why we have seasons. He knew the wrong version, the one half the visitors believed, that summer happens because Earth is closer to the sun. He had even repeated it to his little sister last week. He needed something better than that.

His grandfather had driven him here this morning, same as every Saturday since Hayden started volunteering, but today Grandpa had sat down in the café and said he would wait, because his knees were resigning from long walks, as he put it. That was new. Grandpa used to march through every hall, quizzing Hayden on exhibits until the guards knew them both by name.

Hayden circled the globe. The spotlight stayed still, but the globe spun, and its axis leaned at a steady angle that never changed. He grabbed a floor model of the sun and Earth and carried it to a bench, tilting the little Earth with his thumb and walking it around the lamp. When the north end leaned toward the light, he touched the tabletop and found it warm; when the same end leaned away, the light spread thin and slanted across his hand. It wasn't distance. It was the angle, and the tilt pointing one hemisphere at the sun, then away, all year long. He said it out loud twice, quietly, the way he would have to say it to strangers.

Near the bench hung a photograph of the Grand Canyon, wide and red, with a caption beside it. Hayden read it twice: scientists estimate the Colorado River began carving the Grand Canyon about 5 to 6 million years ago. Five to six million years. He thought of the postcard on Grandpa's fridge, the one from the trip Hayden had been too young for, and how Grandpa used to say rivers were patient workers.

A girl about nine stopped at his bench and poked the model Earth. "Why is it crooked?"

"That's the tilt," Hayden said. "Watch." He orbited it once for her, then twice, and her face changed the way faces do when something clicks.

She ran off to tell her mother, and Hayden began carrying the model back. On his way he passed the café window. Grandpa was sitting alone, turning his coffee cup in slow circles, staring at nothing Hayden could name. They had made a good team once, an alliance of two museum wanderers, and today Grandpa couldn't even come in with him.

Hayden lifted his hand to the glass. Grandpa blinked, then waved, slow and a little unsure, and Hayden mouthed, "Five to six million years," because he was going to tell him everything later, and Grandpa would want to hear it from the start.

Asher had told his lab partner Priya he didn't need the practice session at the community garden, and for three days he had regretted it, because Monday's quiz asked him to label a cell wall, a membrane, and a nucleus, and he had frozen. So on Saturday he brought his worksheet and his grandfather's old microscope to the garden shed, where the garden club kept a crate of onions from the harvest bin.

He pulled a papery skin off an onion layer, laid it flat on a slide, and lowered the lens. The cells showed up like brickwork, pale and neat. He found the wall, the rigid outer edge, easy. The membrane hugged it, thinner, harder to be sure of. The nucleus was a dark dot near the edge of one cell. He drew them on his sheet, then stopped. In the middle of every cell sat a huge pale bubble, taking up most of the space, and it was on no line of his diagram.

A draft slid through the shed and rattled the clipboard, and he shut the window with his elbow, afraid the slide would dry out. His little sister Nadia had followed him, as she always did, and leaned on the table. "What's the giant bubble in the middle?" she asked.

"It's not on my sheet," Asher said, "so it shouldn't matter." But he couldn't let it go, because a bubble that big would crowd everything he was supposed to label. He remembered the science museum trip, the room of giant models. A kid there had asked the guide the same question about the plant cell model, and the answer had drifted past him while he was messing with his phone. He turned to Nadia. "The guide called it a vacuole. She said many plant cells have one large central vacuole, a water-filled sac that can take up most of the cell." He paused, working through it. "Animal cells only have small vacuoles, if any. That's why I never saw one when we did the cheek-cell lab." That was the test, really. Cheek cells had been scattered gray dots with a nucleus and no big bubble. These were swollen with water from the garden's rain barrel.

Priya came in carrying a tomato and stopped at the microscope. "That's a radical slide," she said. "Better than the polymer one Mr. Doyle showed us, that plastic-bag demo." She peered down. "You didn't come to practice."

"I thought I had it," Asher said.

Priya picked up his worksheet and studied the empty middle of his drawing. "You left the biggest thing in the cell off your diagram because it wasn't on the list." She tapped the paper. "Mr. Doyle said the vacuole is the bonus question."

Asher looked from her to the slide, where the pale sac filled each cell like a held breath, and slid the worksheet across the table. "Draw it in for me?"

Sophie had been at city hall for forty minutes, and her petition to keep the community garden open on Sundays already felt heavy in her hands. Nine kids from her block had signed it. She'd counted the signatures three times on the bus.

"You can't hand that to the council tonight," the woman at the front desk said, pointing at the agenda board. "See, item six? A group's petition gets sent to a committee first. The committee studies it and recommends whether the full council should approve it."

"A committee," Sophie repeated, writing it on the back of her hand.

"Room 2B. They meet at seven."

That gave Sophie ninety minutes, and she used them badly at first, pacing the marble lobby and practicing a speech nobody had asked to hear. Then she noticed the table near the council chamber doors, where a man in a gray cardigan was laying out papers with a ruler.

"You're the garden girl," he said. "I'm Arun. I run the mock election demo for the schools." He slid a stack of ballots toward her. "We're teaching the students tomorrow how votes become seats. Want to test it? You look like you need something to do with your hands."

There were thirty paper ballots, and three pretend parties, Red, Blue, and Green. First they counted first-past-the-post: the city was split into five districts, and in each district whichever party got the most votes won the one seat. Sophie scrutinized the tally sheet, frowning. The Greens had nine votes out of thirty, almost a third, but their voters were spread thin, so they lost every district. Zero seats.

"That doesn't seem fair," she said.

"Then do it the other way," Arun said. "Proportional representation. Ignore districts. Count all thirty together."

Sophie did the division. Under the proportional count, the Greens got three seats out of ten. Nine votes had turned into real representation, simply because the rule for counting had changed. She sat back. Nothing on the ballots had moved. Only the system underneath, the thing nobody could see on a single ballot, had made the difference.

"You look like you just found a hidden door," Arun said.

"It's like the committee thing," Sophie said slowly. "Same petition, but where it goes first changes what happens to it."

At seven, she stood up in Room 2B, and her speech about tomatoes and Mrs. Okafor's grandchildren came out too fast and slightly squeaky. Two committee members leaned forward anyway. When the chair asked whether anyone opposed, nobody raised a hand, and then the youngest member said, "I move that we recommend approval."

"Seconded," said a voice behind her, and Sophie turned to find Arun standing in the doorway, holding up one of the Green ballots like a ticket.

"Curved fingers, knuckles forward, and keep the fingertips tucked," Violet told herself, gripping the onion like a claw the way Grandma had shown her that morning. The knife ticked against the cutting board, and the onion fell into neat little cubes instead of the ragged mush of her first attempt. "Grandma, look! No blood!"

Grandma leaned over from the stove, where a pot of water was churning toward a boil. "Beautiful work. Now sweep those into the pan before they dry out." Violet scraped the onion into the hot oil and heard the hiss rise like applause. This dinner was her whole plan: pasta with sauce from scratch, made entirely by her own hands, for her parents arriving at seven.

While the onion softened, Grandma set a bowl of flour on the counter. "While that cooks, we'll do biscuits. Measure me a cup and a half." Violet plunged her measuring cup into the bag and scooped, packing the flour down tight, the way she always did. Grandma stopped her with a raised hand and said only, "Hold on. Do you remember those muffins you told me about, yours and Priya's?"

Violet froze with the cup halfway out of the bag. She had thought about those muffins for weeks. Same recipe, same oven, but Priya's muffins were tall and tender while Violet's sat on the plate like small brown stones. She had blamed her oven, then her mixing bowl, then the universe. Now she stared at the cup in her hand. The flour in it was pressed hard, solid as a brick, and she suddenly remembered watching Priya spoon flour gently into the cup and swipe the top flat with a knife.

"Wait," Violet said slowly. "I dig the cup straight into the bag. That shoves more flour in there, doesn't it? Extra flour the recipe never asked for." She turned the cup over and dumped it out, then tried it her way: she spooned flour into the cup, loose and light, and leveled it off with the back of a knife. Then she weighed both cups on Grandma's little kitchen scale. The scooped cup was heavier by a truly significant amount, enough to wreck a whole batch of muffins.

"Priya's weren't luck," Violet said, laughing. "They were technique!" She measured the rest of the flour the new way, stirred the biscuit dough, and set the biscuits in the oven just as the onions turned golden. She crushed in the canned tomatoes with her hands, seeds squirting between her fingers, and let the sauce bubble while steam fogged the window above the sink. Beyond the glass, the estuary glinted in the evening light, and a heron stalked the mudflats like it was hunting for its own dinner.

At seven o'clock sharp, headlights swept the driveway. Violet drained the pasta, folded it into her sauce, and carried the big bowl to the table with her chin high. Her mother took one bite, then another, then put down her fork. "You made this? All of it?"

"Every single cube of onion," Violet said, and slid the biscuits out of the oven.

Annabelle opened the spreadsheet and typed her aunt's numbers into column A: clicks by day, fourteen days of them. Her aunt Rosa ran a bakery two towns over, and last month the ad bill had jumped to ninety dollars, almost triple the usual. Rosa had told her on the phone, "Every click costs me money. It's called pay-per-click. We bid in an auction for keywords, and we only pay when someone clicks the ad." Annabelle had stared at that sentence afterward, an idea beginning to germinate: if clicks cost money, then somebody could cost her aunt money just by clicking.

In the computer lab, the teacher had shown them how to build a formula. Annabelle selected the cell below her last number and typed =SUM(A2:A15). The total appeared: 612 clicks in two weeks. Way too many for a bakery that usually got sixty a week. She highlighted the column, clicked the bar chart button, and the graph snapped onto the screen, tall gray rectangles towering over the first week's short ones. The pattern was unmistakable. The bars climbed sharply starting on a Tuesday, all fourteen days after that nearly the same height, like a fence.

"Looks weird," said Marcus, leaning over from the next computer. "Like somebody turned a faucet on."

"That's what I think." Annabelle clicked on the tall bars one at a time. Real customers wouldn't click the same amount every single day. But a person trying to drain an ad budget would, the way you'd water a plant on a schedule. She needed proof, not just a hunch. She added column B: days of the week. Then she sorted. The tall clicks fell on every day, including Sunday, when the bakery was closed. Nobody searched for closed bakeries at a steady rate all week long.

She pulled up her aunt's ad account and checked which keyword the clicks came from. One phrase, "heritage sourdough starter," had 400 of the 612 clicks. Her aunt's famous starter, passed down through three generations, was barely searched at all before. Annabelle screenshot everything, pasted the chart into an email, and wrote: "Somebody might be clicking your ad on purpose. Check if the clicks come from one location." She hit send and sat back.

Marcus read over her shoulder. "Could you be wrong?"

"Could be. That's why I sent the chart, not an accusation." She saved the file twice, once to the school drive and once to her flash drive, because a spreadsheet with one good formula deserved protecting.

The reply came before the bell. Rosa had checked the account and found the clicks clustering in one town, the same town as a rival baker. She'd already emailed the ad company. The last line said: "Come Saturday. Free cake. The class voted on your flavor, and it was unanimous: lemon."

Annabelle grinned and closed the laptop. "Marcus," she said, "I'm getting cake."

Elizabeth wanted the drama scholarship more than she had ever wanted anything, and the audition required improvising a scene with a partner, which was the one thing she could not practice alone. Her partner was Marcus, who happened to be the best debater in eighth grade and the worst improviser in the room. Every time Elizabeth offered him something, he knocked it down.

"Welcome to the moon base," she said, stepping onto an imaginary platform.

"There's no air on the moon, so we'd be dead," Marcus said. "Scene over."

They tried again with a pirate ship, then a haunted library, and both scenes died the same fast death. Elizabeth flopped onto the stage steps and tried to infer what was actually going wrong. It wasn't that Marcus was shy. He argued like someone whose job was to find the flaw in every statement, and on stage, that meant he murdered every offer she made.

Then she remembered lunch on Tuesday, when Marcus had been showing off for the debate team. Someone said all kids hate homework, and Priya raised her hand and said she actually liked math homework, and the whole claim collapsed with one counterexample. Marcus had laughed and said, "That's why you need a qualifier, a word like 'usually', 'most' or 'probably', that limits how strongly you say something." He had lost the round anyway, but the words stuck in Elizabeth's head now. A qualifier made a claim harder to knock down. Maybe it could make a scene harder to knock down, too.

She stood up and grabbed his arm. "One more time. You're going to say yes to whatever I say, then add something. Yes, and. That's the only rule."

"There's no way that works," Marcus said.

"Yes, and that's why we're doing it anyway," Elizabeth said, and pulled him to center stage. "We're astronauts, we probably just landed on Mars."

"Yes, and the door is stuck," Marcus said, before he could stop himself. His eyes went wide, like he'd surprised himself.

"Yes, and I have a versatile space hammer in my boot." She knelt and pretended to pry open an airlock, and Marcus reached through an invisible gap and pulled out a flag made from somebody's lost gym sock. They built the scene for two whole minutes, rescue ships and suspicious red dust and a Martian who mostly wanted directions, and when Ms. Okafor called time, the other kids actually clapped.

"That was not terrible," Marcus admitted, still holding the sock.

"Yes, and tomorrow we're rehearsing again," Elizabeth said, and wrote her name at the top of the audition list.

Gavin curled his fingers into a claw, knuckles forward, and set the onion on the cutting board the way Amara had shown him. "The knife rides against your knuckles, never your fingertips," she said, "unless you want to donate blood to the sauce." He laughed, then pressed down carefully, and the onion fell apart into neat little cubes. He was doing this because his mom had worked double shifts all week and he wanted dinner waiting when she got home, something made by him and not microwaved.

Amara's little brother, Amir, sat on a stool stirring the tomatoes with his good arm. He'd had a vaccine that morning, and the soreness in his other arm hindered him so much that he could barely lift the spoon, so Gavin chopped extra slow and let Amir feel like the official stirrer. "Careful with that old pepper in the back of the fridge," Amara warned, holding up a soft, wrinkled one. "Mold can be toxic even after you cut it off. We're using the fresh ones."

Gavin had planned the order himself. He figured the flatbread was the tricky part, the thing most likely to go wrong, so he tackled it first while his hands were steady. He rolled the chapati dough into circles and cooked them on the hot, dry griddle. Each one puffed and browned in only a minute or two, which surprised him. He stacked them on a plate, covered them with a towel, and moved on to the sauce, which had to simmer a long while to get thick.

When everything else was finally ready, he lifted the towel and found the chapatis cold and stiff, more like plates than bread. He frowned at them. The sauce had taken half an hour. The bread had taken two minutes. He turned the fact over in his head: anything that cooks in a minute or two can wait until the very end. "Amara, do you have more dough?" She did, so while she spooned sauce into bowls, he rolled three fresh circles and laid them on the griddle one at a time. Each came off hot, soft, and folded straight onto a plate. Amir grabbed the first one before Gavin could set it down.

At that moment the door opened and Gavin's mom walked in, tired and carrying her coat. "You cooked?" she said, staring at the table.

Amir pointed at the last chapati with tomato sauce on his cheek. "We made the bread last," he announced, "so it wouldn't get cold."

Gavin looked at the empty plate where the warm bread had been. "Then I guess I'm making it last again."

The laundromat smelled like warm cotton and machine oil, and Abigail stood in front of three machines holding a garbage bag that held every piece of clothing she owned. Mom was away at a two-week training in Denver, and before she left she had said, "You can live out of the bag or you can figure it out." Abigail had chosen the bag for nine days. On day ten, the last clean shirt, the one with the diagonal green stripes, had come out of the hamper smelling like gym class, and here she was.

Sorting took longer than she expected. She remembered being six, sitting on the dryer while Mom pulled out reds, whites, and darks like a card dealer. "This one pink sock ruined a whole load once," Mom had said, holding up a faded pink sock like evidence in a trial. Abigail had laughed then. Now she turned a purple hoodie over twice, undecided, and finally dropped it with the darks. She fed quarters into the machine like she was paying a toll, poured in the detergent, and settled onto a folding table to wait, her whole cargo of dirty clothes tumbling behind the round window.

The wash took forever, so she read the safety sticker on the dryer while she waited. She read it twice. Failing to clean the dryer is the leading factor in home clothes dryer fires, it said, according to the U.S. Fire Administration, because built-up lint blocks the airflow and lets heat collect. She looked at the dryer's pull-out filter, which stuck out of its slot at an angle like a forgotten drawer.

When her wet clothes finally landed in the dryer, she yanked the filter out and stared at it. The mesh was covered with a thick grey mat of lint, dense as a blanket, and there was more packed behind it, deeper in the slot, where some earlier customer had clearly just pushed it down and walked away. So that was a job nobody had been doing. She peeled the mat off in one piece, like lifting a pelt, and dropped it in the trash. Then she dug out the packed lint with two fingers until air could pass through clean.

While the dryer ran, she thought about whether she should have called Mom weeks ago and asked how all this worked, instead of wearing the same shirt four times. She hadn't wanted to look helpless. But Mom had left a note on the fridge about the tomato plants needing her to pollinate the cherry tomatoes with a paintbrush, since there were no bees on their balcony, and Abigail had done that part without complaint. Maybe laundry was just another paintbrush.

The buzzer sounded. She folded the striped shirt first, sleeves crossed over, and laid it square on the table.

"One load," she said out loud, to nobody, and started on the socks.

Brooke sat cross-legged on the living room carpet with her laptop on the coffee table, a mug of hot cocoa going cold beside her. Her class had surveyed the whole school about lunch periods, and Ms. Reyes had promised that anyone who summarized the results by grade could present at Friday assembly. Brooke wanted that spot on the microphone more than she wanted to admit out loud.

She built her first pivot table, dragging the grade column into the rows area and dragging the answers into the values area. The counts appeared, and for a moment everything looked perfect: sixth grade, seventh grade, eighth grade, each with its numbers. Then she saw it, a fourth row sitting under the others, labelled "(blank)". She counted the grade rows again, as if counting harder might make the extra one disappear. One hundred and six students had answered, but her table had one hundred and twelve. Six answers had come from nowhere, or from somewhere.

"(blank)," she said out loud, reading the label to the empty room. "What grade is blank?"

Her older brother Dev wandered through on his way to the kitchen, eating cereal straight from the box. "What's blank?" He leaned over the back of the couch, crumbs falling into the cushions, and Brooke pointed at the mystery row. She scrolled back to the raw survey answers in another tab and started scanning the grade column. It took her a minute of scrolling, but there they were: six rows where the grade cell was just empty. She could deduce what had happened. Six students had filled in the whole survey but skipped the grade question, and every empty cell had been gathered into its own group instead of being thrown away.

Dev squinted at the screen. "So the table's wrong?"

"No," Brooke said slowly, "it's right. It's just telling me something I didn't ask for." Last month she had almost deleted a whole column of data because it looked like garbage, and Dev had talked her out of it, which still annoyed her a little. She changed her mind about the "(blank)" row now the same way. Instead of deleting it, she typed a note beneath the table: six respondents skipped this question. At the assembly she could explain that, and it would sound like she had planned it all along.

She counted the rows one last time, then highlighted the mystery group in yellow so she would not forget it. "Hey, Dev," she called toward the kitchen, where he was running water somewhere behind the plumbing under the sink, "guess who's presenting on Friday."

"Wear something without cocoa on it," he called back, and Brooke laughed, an infectious snorting laugh that made him laugh too, all the way from the kitchen.

Riley's family kept the washer and dryer in the garage, next to a shelf of motor oil and a bicycle pump, and every Saturday her mother had done the laundry there. But her mother was in Toronto for two weeks helping Aunt Carol, which left Riley and her father, and her father had already shrunk one of his own sweaters to doll size. "You're thirteen," he said on the phone. "This can be your job." So on Saturday morning Riley stood in the garage with three hampers, sorting clothes into piles: whites, darks, and one pile she wasn't sure about, a pink sock that had turned the whole load last winter, when it snuck in with the whites and dyed Dad's undershirts a pale blush. She put the doubtful sock in with the darks. She read the detergent bottle, measured it, and set the machine for cold. Then she discovered they were almost out of detergent, one load short, and Dad was at work.

She counted her money. The detergent at Halloran's was marked four dollars and ninety-nine cents, and she had exactly five dollars. She rode her bike the eight blocks, found the bottle on the shelf, and carried it to the register. The screen said five dollars and thirty-four cents. Riley counted again, laid out her five dollars, and stood there while the line built up behind her. "That's all I have," she said, feeling her face go hot. It embarrassed her, standing short in front of a cashier and six strangers.

A voice behind her said, "Where I come from, the price on the shelf is the price you pay." It was Mrs. Ferris from two doors down, holding a box of teabags. "In Britain, and in Europe, the tax is already in the price they print. Here in the States, and in Canada too, the shelf price leaves the tax out, and they add it at the till." She put down thirty-five cents. "I moved here from Manchester, and it caught me the first year, every single time." Mrs. Ferris had been wanting an excuse to talk to somebody all week; her daughter never called, and her kettle worked better with company. "Come by for tea after, and tell me if your load came out."

Riley rode home thinking it through. At the garage she pulled the warm clothes from the dryer and shook out her father's synthetic running shirt, which had come out of the dryer crackling with static because she'd forgotten a dryer sheet, and she made a mental note for the next load. She folded the towels in halves, then halves again, so the edges matched, and she liked the symmetry of the stack. When Dad came home she told him about the shelf prices and the thirty-five cents. "Mrs. Ferris wants tea," she said. "Bring the cookies," he said, "and check the sock." Riley pulled the pink sock from the folded darks. Still pink. The navy towels around it, still navy.

The temple hall smelled of camphor and wet stone, and Stella moved to the beat of the mridangam drum, her anklets ticking like a clock. In three weeks she would dance before the deity at the Navaratri festival, her first real performance, and she knew the whole piece by heart except for one moment that kept sliding away from her.

Her grandmother sat against the back wall, watching with her arms crossed. That was the strange part. Last year, when Stella had performed at the school talent show, Ammamma had applauded everything, even the mistakes. Now, every time Stella reached the fourth verse, the old woman's frown deepened. Stella finished the run-through, wiped her neck with the corner of her practice sari, and walked over.

"Ammamma, is it my footwork? The aramandi?"

Her grandmother shook her head slowly. "Your hands," she said. "You are telling the wrong story."

Stella's mind began to orbit the problem the way it did with a hard math proof, circling it, looking for the angle nobody had shown her. She knew the moves. She could feel them in her wrists. But the frown had appeared only in the fourth verse, and only when her hands did a certain thing. In class, her teacher had said that in Bharatanatyam, a classical dance from Tamil Nadu in India, the symbolic hand gestures called mudras work like words to tell a story. Swap one word and the sentence means something else. Stella had nodded that day and filed it away in her head like an entry in a database, something to retrieve for a quiz. It had never occurred to her that a wrong entry could matter.

She stood in the middle of the hall and danced just the fourth verse, slowly, watching her grandmother's face instead of her own hands. At the half-turn, her fingers folded into a beak shape, the gesture for a bird, and the frown came. She stopped. "This one?"

"That is the crow," her grandmother said. "The verse is about the peacock. A crow pecking at the offering, that is what you showed me."

Stella laughed, then felt her face go warm. She had felt so sure, so untouchable up there on the practice floor, and all along one small finger's difference had been turning a holy verse into a joke about a scavenger. It made her feel strangely vulnerable, like discovering that a door she'd been leaning on was never locked.

They stayed after the drummers left, grandmother and granddaughter, shaping peacocks out of their hands under the dim lights while the bells above the sanctum rang for the evening prayer. Ammamma's fingers trembled with age, but the gesture itself was steady, as if it had been waiting in her hands all these years to be passed on.

"Show me the sixth verse too," Stella said, kneeling beside her. "Before I get that one wrong as well."

Levi locked the bathroom door, faced the mirror, and started his presentation for the third time. "The honeybee population would flourish if cities planted more wildflow." His voice snapped in half on the last syllable, sliding from low to squeaky like a cassette tape gone wrong. He gripped the sink. His hands were damp, his heart was drumming, and a hot feeling crawled up his neck. He knew those signs now, because last week his counselor had made him a card with three questions on it: Are your hands sweating? Is your heart fast? Are your shoulders up by your ears? Two out of three, and his shoulders were practically touching his ears.

He set the card on the edge of the sink and counted. In for four, hold, out for six. He did it five times, watching his shoulders sink in the mirror like ice cream softening. Last night he had tested something else too. Instead of staring at his phone until midnight, he had put it in the kitchen at nine thirty, and this morning his head felt clearer, less like a snow globe someone kept shaking.

The crack itself, though, that was a different problem, and he had a theory about it. He flashed back to Tuesday, standing in front of science class, when his voice had broken right on the word "pollination" and Marcus had laughed so hard he knocked over a chair. Afterward Levi had looked it up on the library computer, hunched so nobody could read over his shoulder. He found that during puberty, a part called the larynx, the voice box, grows larger, and the vocal cords get longer and thicker, which makes the voice deeper, especially in boys. So the crack was not him being nervous exactly, or not only. His throat was under construction, doing a gradual rebuild, and the squeaks were construction noise. His theory: if his voice was going to wobble no matter what, then the thing he could actually control was the stress around it. Tonight he would test the idea with a full run of the presentation, breathing and all.

He started over. "The honeybee population would flourish if cities planted more wildflowers." It cracked twice more, once on "flourish" and once on "biodiversity," but his hands stayed mostly dry and he didn't stop talking. That was the twist, he realized, pulling open the door: the presentation could survive a crack. It couldn't survive silence.

His sister Priya was in the hallway with her earbuds in, and she pulled one out. "Was that you rehearsing? It sounded pretty good."

"It cracked, like, four times," Levi said.

"Pfft. Devon's voice cracks every day and nobody cares anymore." She held out the earbud. "Want to hear the song I think would go good with your slides? You're a strong candidate for background music, since your topic is so dramatic."

Levi took the earbud and listened, and by the second chorus his shoulders were all the way down.

The courthouse smelled like dust and old folders, and Sebastian clutched his notes so hard the paper went soft at the corners. His civics class had been assigned to explain one right from the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in front of a real judge, and Sebastian had chosen section 3, the right to vote. He regretted it now. Last year he had frozen during a speech about recycling and had stood there for forty seconds opening and closing his mouth like a fish, and Marcus Tran still did an impression of it in the hallway. He was not going to be a fish twice.

In the front row, waiting for his turn, he spread out his materials on the wooden bench. He had a printout of Canada's 2015 federal election results, because his grandfather had voted in it and never stopped talking about it. Sebastian ran his finger down the numbers. The Liberal Party had won 184 of the 338 seats in Parliament. He did the division on the corner of the page. That was more than half, which meant a majority, even though the page also said they had gotten about 39.5 percent of the popular vote. He frowned and checked it twice, because those two things seemed like they shouldn't fit in the same sentence. Fewer than four in ten voters had picked that party, and it still got more than half the seats. He tested a simple idea: maybe the seats were just counted wrong. He added the other parties' seats up, 338 total, no mistake. So it wasn't an error.
