There was some pattern in how votes turned into seats that he couldn't see directly, only see the shadow of, like a landlord you never meet but whose rules you live under anyway.

"Sebastian Marsh," the clerk called.

He walked to the front. The judge, a small woman with reading glasses on a chain, nodded at him. "Your right, please."

"The right to vote," Sebastian said, and then, before his mouth could seal shut, he kept going. "It means every citizen gets a say, and no government can just take the say away. It's yours like your name is yours."

"Can you give it teeth?" the judge asked. "Make it less ambiguous."

He thought of his printout. "In 2015, the Liberal Party won 184 of 338 seats, a majority, with about 39.5 percent of the popular vote. So votes and seats don't match up neatly. Which is exactly why the vote itself matters. It's the one part no one can rearrange after the fact, no matter how the seats come out. Nobody gets to invade that." He heard Marcus snicker at the word invade, and Sebastian grinned for half a second before going on. "My grandfather waited his whole life to use that right in that election. If it can be stretched or shuffled, people still lined up for it. That has to count for something."

The judge took off her glasses. "So in your own words, one sentence."

"Voting is the door every citizen gets a key to, even if the hallway behind it is weird," Sebastian said.

There was a pause that felt like a year. Then the judge wrote something down and looked up. "The hallway is definitely weird," she said, and beckoned the next student forward. Sebastian walked back to his bench, sat down, and smoothed the crumpled printout flat on his knee, running his thumb over the number 184 one more time.

Maya's basement smelled like dust and old carpet, and the only light came from a desk lamp bent over her laptop. Ella pulled a second chair up close, because their history project, a web page for Monday's mock trial exhibit, had to exist by tonight, and so far it existed only in Maya's head. The defendant in their case, a fictional ferry captain accused of scuttling his own boat, deserved better than a plain typed sheet taped to the wall.

"First the skeleton," Maya said, typing. She wrote out angled brackets, and a heading appeared at the top of the page, sitting stubbornly in the left corner like a cat that refused to move. "Now CSS," she said, and typed a few more lines. When she refreshed the browser, the heading stayed exactly where it was.

Ella leaned in. Something had to be wrong in the part they couldn't see, the code itself, and only the screen showed the evidence. She pointed at one line. "You closed the style tag before you wrote the rule. The browser never even read it." Maya moved the tag, refreshed, and the heading drifted to the centre of the page at last, calm and even, like it had always meant to be there.

Then Maya grinned and opened another file. "Watch this. I'm also checking the raffle numbers for my brother's club, and the program tells whether a number divides evenly." She typed quickly and added, "The percent sign gives the remainder, so n percent d equals zero exactly when d divides n evenly." Ella squinted at the little window. She typed 14 and 7, and the program printed True. She tried 14 and 4, and it printed False. From those two results she could infer the rule was doing its job, because 7 went into 14 without anything left over, while 4 left a remainder behind. "Your brother will think this is magic," she said. "He's gullible that way," Maya said. "He believed me when I told him our basement floods with orange soda."

They kept working until the defendant's name sat centred under the heading in tall blue letters, and below it a short paragraph laid out the charge against him, the missing cargo, the quiet harbor, the night no one could explain. Maya read it out loud once, slowly, the way a lawyer might. Ella saved the file twice, just to be sure, and pushed back from the desk as the clock on the wall ticked toward the hour her mom was coming. "Send it to yourself," she said. "Right now, before the wifi does something weird." Maya hit send, and the little paper airplane icon spun once and flew away.

Nicholas ran his thumb along the laminated periodic table taped to his grandfather's workbench, counting squares until his finger stopped on carbon. Six, the box said, in a small corner number he'd never paid attention to before. He was trying to get ahead of Monday's quiz, and his best shot at passing it was this garage, because at home his little brother interrupted every five minutes.

The garage smelled like oil and cut grass. A toaster sat on a crate near the door, left over from the yard sale, still plugged in. Nicholas had brought bread because his grandfather said a person couldn't think on an empty stomach, and he'd been eating slices while he worked out the pattern in the table.

"So the little number tells you protons," he muttered. "Oxygen, eight. Iron, twenty-six." He tested himself, covering the symbols with his palm and guessing from the number alone. He got sodium right, then mixed up neon and nitrogen, both starting with N, and had to check twice.

His friend Marcus shoved the side door open, holding a blackened slice of bread. "Your brother burned this at your house and blamed me. Give me a dollar, I'm starving."

"Toaster's over there. And it's not my fault Denny can't work a dial." Nicholas slid a fresh slice in.

Marcus leaned over the table. "What are you doing?"

"Learning protons. Sixty for neodymium. It's just a code, kind of. Once you see it." He tapped the boxes.

Marcus dropped the burnt slice on the workbench. "That's toast. It's still bread. It just got dark, like when you draw on paper with pencil. Physical change."

"No." Nicholas pulled his own slice out, golden at the edges. "Watch." He held up the burnt piece next to his. "Heat makes new brown stuff in there, that's why it smells different. You can't turn it back into soft bread. It's a chemical change. Once it's brown, it stays brown."

"That's the toast's business, not science."

"It's both." Nicholas took a bite. "Grandpa said heat from that toaster can't insulate anything, it does the opposite, and that's how I knew something had to be happening to the bread, not just to it."

Marcus picked up the burnt slice and squeezed it. It crackled and stayed flat. He dropped it. "Fine. Chemical. What's the criterion, then? How do you tell them apart?"

"If you can undo it, physical. If you can't, chemical. Ice melts back, toast doesn't." Nicholas found the element for gold, seventy-nine, and circled it in pencil. "Also, that's an approximate answer. Grandpa says nothing's perfect."

Marcus grabbed two more slices of bread. "Then I'm testing the chemical change myself. Butter side up."

Nicholas watched the coils glow orange, then pushed the lever down for him.

The community centre had ice on one side of the building and a pool on the other, and Charlie ran the concrete loop between them, eight laps for eight hundred metres, watching the Zamboni crawl past the boards like a slow white animal. Her problem was simple and stubborn: the first lap always felt so easy that she sprinted it, and the last two laps she died, her legs turning to wet rope while Priya Kowalski sailed past her at every meet. Coach Reyes kept saying "regulate your effort," which Charlie heard as "be someone other than yourself," and she hated it.

Her best friend Marisol swam mornings in the pool, and Charlie watched through the observation window between laps, mostly to avoid looking at the clock. Marisol's head cut through the water and beside her face there was a dip, a little hollow in the surface, and Charlie could see her mouth grabbing air in it. Charlie stopped and pressed her hand to the cold glass. The water elsewhere was flat, level with the tile line, but next to Marisol's cheek it had dropped, and her mouth reached that pocket below the flat surface.

"How do you breathe in that?" Charlie asked afterward, dripping sweat onto the pool deck.

"My head pushes a bow wave," Marisol said, wringing out her cap. "It leaves a dip beside my face. Air comes to me instead of me lifting up for it."

Charlie turned that over all week. Marisol wasn't fighting for air; the dip arrived because she kept moving, because she didn't stop being a swimmer in order to breathe. Running, Charlie figured, might have its own version, some hidden economy she'd been missing. Her simple idea: if she counted her steps on the first lap and held that count on every lap after, the pace would carry her the way the bow wave carried Marisol's mouth. Equivalent effort, lap after lap, instead of a sprint and a funeral.

At the meet she counted. Ninety-two steps the first lap, when her legs begged for seventy. Ninety-two through the second. Priya pulled ahead at the three-hundred mark and Charlie's whole body screamed to chase her, and she didn't, she counted, ninety-two, ninety-two, and on the last lap the counting held her up like a hand under her chin. She passed Priya with sixty metres left and won by half a stride.

She found the note taped inside her locker afterward, in Priya's round handwriting: "You finally stopped going out too fast. Took you long enough. Rematch Thursday?" Charlie smiled, then felt the cost of it, her quads shaking so hard she had to sit on the bench to read it twice. She peeled the note off the metal, folded it into her pocket, and went to find the ice cream money she'd promised Marisol.

Eleanor's problem had a name, and the name was Mr. Okafor's worksheet: "Use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s." She sat in the school library with a photocopied page of a settler's diary in front of her, and the diary refused to cooperate. "The land here is flat as a griddle," the settler had written, "and my wife has planted hollyhocks perpendicular to the fence, which she says will fool the wind." That told Eleanor exactly nothing about why anyone had dragged a wagon across half a continent. She flipped the page over. The library's copy machine had accidentally printed part of the next article on the back, something about President Wilson and a peacekeeping body called the League of Nations.

Marcus slid into the chair across from her and stole her pencil. "Still fighting that worksheet? You look like the diary insulted your family."

"It kind of did. This guy writes three paragraphs about hollyhocks." She tapped the back of the page. "But listen to this part. The Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations. The president helped plan the whole thing, and his own country said no thanks."

Marcus stopped chewing his pencil. "Wait. That's like baking a cake for the whole class and then being the one kid who isn't allowed a slice."

Eleanor laughed, then frowned, then laughed again. "It contradicts everything I assumed. I thought if the president wanted something, it just happened." She copied the sentence onto a sticky note, because it felt like the kind of thing that could sneak up on her later.

Then she went back to the diary with new eyes, hunting for the hidden reason the way she'd hunted for the hidden fact. The settler's grandfather had lost a mill in the East. The land office in Ohio had promised two hundred acres. There it was, buried under the hollyhocks: people moved because of money and land, and the pretty sentences were just decoration. She tested it on the next page. "Sold the clock, kept the rifle, bought seed corn." Money and land again. The pattern held.

"I've got it," she announced. "The diary never says why directly. You have to read past the flowers."

Mr. Okafor wandered by, scanning worksheets like a hawk with a grading pen, and paused at her paragraph. "Evidence?" he asked.

She held up the page. "Lost the mill. Two hundred acres. Sold the clock." Then she added, because she couldn't resist, "Also, the Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles, so the United States never joined the League of Nations. Just so you know I know things."

"That's a different unit," said Mr. Okafor, but he was smiling.

"Consider it a preview," said Eleanor, and handed Marcus his pencil back.

Camille stood in the wings of the community theatre with her hands trembling so hard that her cue sheet flapped like a small bird trying to escape. She was not even performing tonight; this was only the Saturday improv workshop, and still her fingers shook. Beside her, her friend Priya from science class was bouncing on her toes, and Camille noticed that Priya's script, all two lines of it, was trembling too.

"Yours does that too?" Camille asked, pointing.

Priya nodded and managed a grin. "My mom says it even has a name. Glossophobia. Fear of public speaking. She said it's one of the most commonly reported fears, so basically half the planet feels like us right now."

"That many people?" Camille had assumed she was the only one whose body betrayed her this way. Somehow knowing there was a word for it, and a crowd behind it, made the shaking feel less like a personal failure and more like weather. She flattened the cue sheet against her thigh.

Last summer, she remembered, she had auditioned for the youth production of Peter Pan and frozen mid-sentence, standing on that same stage while the director waited and the silence grew until it felt like the whole impoverished theatre, with its cracked seats and one working spotlight, was holding its breath. She had walked out. She had not come back until Priya dragged her to this workshop.

"I don't get the point of making up scenes in front of people," Camille had told her that morning. "I'd rather memorize lines."

"You'll see," Priya had said, and Camille had changed her mind about at least coming, mostly because Priya had promised her mom's brownies would be involved.

Now the mentor of the workshop, a college student named Ruthie with paint-stained overalls, called them out. "Camille and Priya, you're up. Rule is simple. Whatever your partner says, accept it and add to it. Yes, and."

Priya stepped into the empty stage square and announced, "We're astronauts and the ship is out of fuel."

Camille's mind went blank, then she remembered the rule. Accept the offer. Add to it. "Yes, and we can land on that marshmallow planet."

"Yes, and the marshmallows are radioactive."

"Yes, and they make us grow to the size of buildings!" Camille mimicked a giant, looming over an imaginary city, and Priya shrieked with laughter and mimicked one back. Somewhere in the third or fourth exchange, Camille realized her hands had gone still. She was too busy building the scene to fall apart.

Afterward Ruthie high-fived them both. "Nice work. Same time next week?"

Camille looked at Priya, who was already nodding. "Yes," Camille said, "and we're bringing brownies."

Jace slid his ruler across the paper for the fourth time and erased the line again. The assignment was a street in one-point perspective, every building, curb and power line running toward a single vanishing point that existed nowhere on the real street, only in the drawing. He put a dot in the middle of the page and tried to make the lines obey it. His buildings kept leaning like they had given up on gravity halfway down the block.

"You're guessing," said Priya from the next stool, not even looking up from her painting. "Last week you guessed on the portrait too, and I got a nose."

"You got a nose because you asked for a nose," Jace said. "It was a decent nose."

"It was a nose on my paper without permission." She held up her current piece, a girl in a dark shirt with a small pendant necklace. "Now I'm trying to paint around these tiny highlights on the chain, and my brush is too fat. I keep losing the white."

Jace remembered the nose incident, and before that, the time in seventh grade when he had traded his lunch for what he thought was a lucky eraser and it turned out to be a lump of gray rubber that smeared graphite instead of lifting it. He had a habit of grabbing solutions before checking whether they were real. Maybe that was why the perspective assignment bothered him. There was no guessing allowed. The lines either met at the dot or they didn't, and anyone could see it instantly.

He flipped through the supply cabinet, hunting for anything that could save Priya's necklace without saving his pride along with it, and found a small brown bottle with a battered label. It said the stuff was a liquid rubber you painted onto areas to keep them white. Once it dried, you painted over it, then rubbed it off to reveal the paper. "Hey," he said. "Try this."

Priya read the label twice, which was one more time than Jace had. "So I paint it on the little highlights, let it dry, paint the whole shirt dark over it, and then rub it off and the white comes back?" She looked at him sideways. "Is this another lucky eraser situation?"

"That eraser was one time." He watched her dab the milky liquid onto the brightest links of the chain with a toothpick, since no brush was small enough. It went on looking useless, like school glue, and dried to a faint peachy film. Then she swept the dark shirt color straight across it without dodging at all, which felt to Jace like watching someone walk a tightrope on purpose.

While it dried for the second time, Jace turned back to his street and decided to test an idea instead of guessing. If the vanishing point controlled everything, then the curb, the rooflines and the stripes down the middle of the road should all aim at the same dot, no matter how arbitrary the buildings' sizes were. He drew one line at a time, checking each against the point like he was calibrating a scale. When he finished the roofline on the left side, it landed exactly where he'd wanted. Perspective, he decided, was a fair adversary. It beat you only when you made things up.

Priya rubbed at her pendant with a fingertip. The rubbery mask balled up and rolled away, and underneath it the little links gleamed white against the dark shirt, exactly where she had put them. She held the painting out at arm's length, then closer, then out again.

"Okay," she said. "You can trade me useless art supplies anytime."

Harrison typed `if n % 2 == 0:` and sat back, certain he had just written the world's most brilliant prime checker. The computer lab hummed around him, twenty machines all running at once, and Mr. Delgado had promised that anyone who finished both parts of the project could test their program on the big projector screen. Part one was the Python program. Part two was a simple webpage explaining it, which was where Priya leaned over from the next seat and squinted at his screen.

"Why is your title in h3?" she asked.

"Because it looks the right size," Harrison said. He had scrolled through the tags, tried h1, thought it looked like a shout, and settled on h3 like a person compromising between a whisper and a yell.

Priya shook her head. "There are six heading levels, h1 to h6. h1 is the most important one. Your page title is the most important thing on the page, so it should be h1."

"Six of them?" Harrison said. "Who needs six sizes of heading?" But he changed the tag anyway, and the title snapped into place at the top, big and unmissable, like it had been waiting for him to get out of its way.

Then he ran the prime checker, and his confidence collapsed. It said 2 was not prime. It said 9 was prime. He stared at the screen, because the bug was invisible, hiding somewhere in the logic where he could not see it, and he would have to hunt it by testing rather than by looking. He tried 3. It said 3 was prime, which was right. He tried 5. Right again. So the program was not completely broken; something specific was going wrong, some pattern he had not noticed yet.

He grabbed a scrap of paper and wrote out what his code actually did, step by step, like reading an X-ray of a program to find the broken bit. His rule checked whether n was divisible by 2, then looped from 3 upward. But 2 itself was divisible by 2, so the program called it not prime. And 9? His loop jumped by twos, checking 3, then 5, then 7, sailing right past the moment when 9 divided evenly by 3. "It skips the very number that catches it," he muttered. Priya snorted so hard she sounded like a goose.

He fixed both problems, one careful line at a time, then tested every number from 2 to 30. All correct. His program was durable now, built to survive even Marcus typing a million into it just to be annoying. When Mr. Delgado called his name, Harrison walked to the projector computer, plugged in his drive, and entered 97.

"Prime," the screen announced.

"Prime," Harrison said, and pumped his fist, and behind him Priya whispered, "And it only took you six levels of thinking to get there."

Arthur had exactly forty minutes before his museum workshop started, and he meant to use every one of them. The workshop was called "Build Your Own Atom," and each student had to pick an element, then construct it out of foam balls, wire, and glue. Arthur wanted carbon, because carbon was in pencils and in him, which felt important. The trouble was the instruction sheet, which said: "Find your element on the periodic table and give it the right number of protons." Arthur stared at the giant table painted on the wall. It was a colorful plateau of little boxes, numbers, and symbols, and he had no idea how anybody read it.

A girl named Priya was already digging through the box of wire. "The wire's for the electron rings," she said, holding up a loop she'd bent into a neat circle. "You know electrons go around the nucleus in certain fixed orbits? Energy levels, like little racetracks."

"Sure," said Arthur, though he didn't, exactly.

They found the answer together on a plaque near the atom exhibit. Priya read it out loud: "In 1913, Niels Bohr proposed a model in which electrons travel only in certain fixed orbits, or energy levels, around the nucleus." She tapped the name. "So that's why the wire rings. Bohr was the first to draw atoms that way. I'm going to document this in my notebook so I can prove to my brother I learned something on a Saturday."

Arthur wasn't worried about brothers. He was worried about protons, which nobody could see, and which the sheet demanded in the correct amount. He ran his finger along the carbon box on the wall. There was a big 6 at the top, a C in the middle, and a longer number underneath that said 12.011. Two numbers. Two suspects. He tried an idea: maybe one number told you how many protons, and the other was something else entirely. But which?

He tested it on oxygen, because he knew oxygen was number 8 from a poster in his classroom. The big number at the top of oxygen's box was 8, and the smaller decimal was 15.999. So the top number matched the protons. Then he checked helium, which he knew had 2 protons from a book about balloons, and there it was again: big 2 at the top. The pattern held. The big whole number at the top was the atomic number, and the atomic number was the number of protons. That meant carbon had six protons, six little invisible specks he could now count on his fingers.

He grabbed six foam balls for his nucleus, then bent a wire ring and slid three electrons onto it. "It's sort of ironic," he said to Priya, arranging the second ring. "I'm building the part I can see, the electrons, using a guy's idea from 1913. But the part I really had to hunt for was the part nobody has ever seen." Priya held up her notebook, where she had written Bohr's name twice and underlined it once. "Six protons," Arthur announced to the whole table, holding up his carbon nucleus like a trophy. "Carbon, coming through."

The line at Jefferson Elementary School stretched past the bike racks, and Muhammad stood at the very end of it, holding his grandmother's coupon book while she searched her bag for her voter card. A folding table near the double doors held a display he hadn't expected: a large poster titled "Know Your Rights," with articles from the Constitution copied out in careful block letters.

"Read it to me," his grandmother said, squinting at the small print. "My glasses are somewhere in this bag, and we're not losing our place in line."

Muhammad read the First Amendment aloud, then the Fourth, then stopped at one about due process. "It says no state can deprive any person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law," he read slowly. "Baba, what does that mean, really?"

"It means," she said, "you tell me."

He thought while the line shuffled forward. "It means the government can't just take your stuff or lock you up because it feels like it. There has to be a real process. Steps. Like... a foundation under a house. You can't skip it." She nodded but said nothing more, which meant he was on his own.

A man ahead of them was grumbling into his phone. "They passed the water bill, then they didn't pass it. How can both be true in one week? I'm telling you, it's rigged."

Muhammad's ears turned warm. That was the bill his social studies teacher had put on the board Monday. He remembered two different wordings, two headlines, one saying passed and one saying stalled. Something clicked into place, though he couldn't see it yet, like a pattern hiding under a floor.

"Excuse me," Muhammad said to the man. "Was it the House version or the Senate version?"

The man lowered his phone. "House voted Tuesday. Senate voted today on their own copy. Different words in it, the radio said."

"A bill has to pass both the House and the Senate in identical form," Muhammad said, the rule assembling itself out loud, "before it goes to the president. So if the words aren't the same, it's not law yet. Both things you heard can be true."

The man stared at him, then at his phone, then laughed. "Twelve years old and you just untangled the news for me."

The voting machine emitted a low beep as the man stepped up to it, and the line moved again. Muhammad's grandmother had stopped rummaging. She was looking at him with an expression he couldn't read.

"Say the due process one again," she said. "In your own words. My friend Rosa is inside working the table, and she argues with everybody about that one."

"She argues?"

"Every election. You'll see." She took his hand and pulled him toward the doors. "And don't be polite about it."

Michael sat cross-legged on the rug in Dara's basement, laptop balanced on a stack of board games. The plan was simple: a web page called the Prime-o-Matic, with a giant centred heading and a box where you could type a number and find out if it was prime. He had typed the HTML first, then added the CSS, and the heading still sat stubbornly in the top left corner like it had been glued there.

"Did you save the file?" Dara asked from the couch, where she was rolling a tennis ball along the armrest. "The browser can't retrieve the new styles unless you save first."

Michael clicked save, then hit refresh. The heading drifted to the centre of the page, dark blue and enormous, and he sat back with the satisfied feeling of a door finally swinging open on the second try. The page asked a question in plain grey text: Enter a number. He typed 7, pressed the button, and the page said 7 is prime. Correct. He tried 9, and it said 9 is not prime, also correct. Dara came over and typed 97. Prime. They were halfway to a victory snack when she said, "Try zero."

He typed 0 and pressed the button. The page said, in cheerful green letters, 0 is prime.

"That's wrong," Dara said. "Zero isn't prime. It isn't anything." Michael stared at the green line and felt a small, cold drop of despair, the kind you get when something you built confidently turns on you. The checker worked by trying every divisor starting at 2, so for zero the loop found nothing to reject it with, and the code fell through to the prime answer. He couldn't see the loop failing; he could only see its wrong result, like footprints in snow with no animal in sight.

"Okay," he said slowly. "The loop starts at 2. Zero, and 1 too probably, and negative numbers, they never get tested, they just sneak past." He rolled the thought around, then typed an approximate guess at the fix, a single line near the top of the function, and refreshed. Dara typed 0 again. The page said 0 is not prime. Then 1. Not prime. Then -5, and the page held the line: not prime. All the numbers below 2 got sorted out before the loop even began, which was where they belonged.

"So it only checks real candidates now," Dara said, and typed 11, and the heading glowed blue above the words 11 is prime.

"Boom," Michael said, and reached over to change the heading's colour to green.

Blake sat cross-legged on Dara's basement carpet, staring at a laptop screen that stared back with an error message. He had typed nine lines of Python, and the program had refused him nine times.

"It says invalid syntax," he said. "Again."

Dara leaned over from her beanbag, headphones around her neck. "You forgot the colon after the for loop. You always forget the colon."

"I do not always forget the colon." Blake scrolled up, found the missing dot, and added it. The goal was simple: the program would ask for a number, then print whether that number was prime. Dara had bet him a bag of chips he couldn't finish it before dinner. Blake wanted those chips more than he wanted to admit.

He ran the program again. It asked for a number, so he typed 7. "7 is prime," the screen announced. He typed 9. "9 is prime." Blake groaned. "Nine is not prime. Three times three. It's the most not-prime number there is."

"So your checker is broken," Dara said. "It can't see the factors hiding in there."

Blake thought about that. The factors were invisible until you actually divided. That was the whole trick. A number could look prime and secretly be a product of smaller numbers, and the only way to know was to test it. "Okay," he said slowly, "what if I try dividing by every number up to the square root? If any of them divides evenly, it's not prime."

"You're going to replicate the test for each divisor?" Dara asked. "Like, loop it?"

"Exactly like loop it." He rewrote the middle of the program, mumbling to himself, deleted a stray semicolon that had wandered in from somewhere, and ran it again. 9 came back "not prime." So did 15. So did 21, that obstinate little fake. He tried 13, 17, 97. Prime, prime, prime.

"Pay up," Blake said, holding out his hand.

Dara tossed him the chips, then pulled her laptop close and opened Scratch, dragging a sound block into a loop. A record scratch blatted out of her speakers, and she wiggled a sprite back and forth with it.

"You know why it's called Scratch, right?" she said. "DJ scratching. A DJ moves a record back and forth on a turntable to remix sounds."

Blake crunched a chip. "So you're basically a DJ. Except your turntable is code."

"And you're the consumer of my art," Dara said, hitting the green flag again.

The record scratched. Blake typed 2 into his program, and the screen said, "2 is prime."

Jackson stared at the blank page in his notebook and wrote his first line of dialogue: "Give it back," Marcus said. He checked the board twice, making sure the comma sat inside the quotation marks. Ms. Rivera had promised that anyone who punctuated every line correctly and built to a clear climax would get to read their story aloud on Friday, and Jackson wanted that spot more than he had wanted anything since tryouts.

His story was about two friends fighting over a lost dog. The trouble was the fight itself. He had written the shouting match first and the quiet apology after, and when he read it back, the whole thing felt like a balloon losing air. His pencil hovered. Why did it feel wrong when all the pieces were there?

He flipped through his reading binder and found the notes from the debate unit in October. There it was, in his own handwriting: some writers order their points from weakest to strongest, so the argument builds and the reader finishes on the most convincing reason. Jackson sat back. Maybe stories worked the same way. Maybe the quiet apology, the small moment, was the weak point, and the shouting match was the strong one, and he had them backward. It was an inference, not a fact, but it was testable.

He cut the pages apart with Mrs. Chen's scissors from the supply cabinet, taped them in the new order, and read it aloud under his breath in the corner by the window. The small moment came first: Marcus finding the dog's collar on the sidewalk and saying nothing. Then the argument grew, and the shouting cracked open at the end. His skin prickled. It worked.

At lunch he showed the taped pages to Priya, who was still stuck on her own story. "I nominate your ending for best line in the class," she said, pointing at Marcus's last words. She hesitated, then added, "My teacher from last year would say it's too aggressive to end on yelling."

"Yelling isn't the point," Jackson said. "It's the top of the hill. You climb weakest to strongest so the reader finishes on the most convincing part." Priya frowned at her notebook, then grabbed a pen and started numbering her scenes.

On Friday, Jackson stood at the front of the room and read the whole story without tripping once. When he finished the last line of dialogue, "I found his collar the day he ran," Marcus said, and Jackson put the period inside the marks exactly where it belonged, Priya was the first one clapping.

The first night at Camp Windrock, Alyssa lay awake listening to a girl named Priya breathe in the bunk above her. By the second night she noticed the pattern: Priya stopped unpacking whenever the lake test came up, chewed her thumbnail raw, and snapped at anyone who touched her duffel bag. On Wednesday, Priya got aggressive over a borrowed hairbrush and then cried behind the boathouse, and Alyssa sat down next to her in the gravel.

"You get stressed before the swim test," Alyssa said. "I can tell because of your hands."

Priya stared at her. "You noticed that?"

"My mom taught me the signs. Mine is stomachaches. Watch." Alyssa counted Priya's breaths out loud, slow ones, four counts in and six counts out, the way the camp mentor had shown the whole cabin after lights-out. Then she said, "You're not sleeping either. I hear you turning over like the top bunk is orbiting the earth all night."

Priya laughed a wet, hiccuppy laugh. After a minute she whispered, "Sometimes I think about hurting myself. Just to make everything stop. Don't tell anyone. Promise?"

Alyssa's promise rose in her throat and then stuck there. She thought hard. Keeping secrets was a rule she'd always followed, but a promise that could let her friend get hurt wasn't a rule at all, it was a trap. She remembered the counselor saying exactly one thing at orientation: if a friend talks about hurting themselves, you tell a trusted adult right away, even if they asked you to keep it a secret. Alyssa had thought it was strange advice at the time. Now it felt like a flashlight in a dark tent.

"I can't promise that," she said, standing up and dusting gravel off her shorts. "Come with me or I'll drag you. Your choice. I'm very strong, I did the ropes course."

"You're the worst secret keeper alive," Priya said, but she got up too.

They found Counselor Dana by the fire pit, and Alyssa said the whole thing in one breath before her courage escaped. Dana didn't lecture anyone or look disappointed. She put her arm around Priya and said, "I'm really glad Alyssa walked you over. That took guts from both of you." Then she told Priya they'd call her parents together in the morning, and that tonight she'd sleep in the quiet room next to the infirmary, with a fan and no top bunk orbiting above her.

That night Alyssa did her own slow breathing, four in and six out, and made a deal with herself: phone in the duffel at nine, headlamp off at nine-thirty, lights out. In the morning Priya appeared at breakfast with her hair actually brushed and slid a tray of hash browns across the table.

"For the worst secret keeper alive," Priya said. "Extra crispy."

"I'll take it," Alyssa said, and stole her orange juice too.

The library smelled like old paper and lemon cleaner, and Claire had exactly ninety minutes before it closed. She spread the photocopy of Macbeth across the table, scene three, and glared at it. Tomorrow in English she had to stand up and paraphrase every speech into modern English, and right now the lines looked like someone had dropped alphabet soup on the page.

"Double, double toil and trouble," she muttered. Fine, that one she could handle. "Toil means work. Trouble is trouble." She wrote "keep working and keep having problems" in her notebook. But halfway down the page, the script threw a word at her she could not paraphrase at all, because it was not a speech. It sat in brackets, all by itself: exeunt. She flipped back to scene one. There it was again, exeunt, right after the witches finished talking. Then she found exit, once, when a single messenger left the stage. Three different scenes, two different words, and she could not see the difference. It was like a rule someone had hidden inside the script.

Claire got up and pulled the big Riverside Shakespeare off the reference shelf, mostly because it had more scenes in it, more evidence. She laid it beside her photocopy and started counting. Exit appeared when one person left. Exeunt appeared at the ends of crowded scenes where two, three, sometimes a whole mob of characters walked off together. Scene after scene, the pattern held consistent. Exit for one, exeunt for a crowd. She sat back so fast the chair creaked.

Behind her, someone cleared a throat. Marcus from third period stood holding a soda he was definitely not supposed to have indoors. "You've been muttering in Latin for ten minutes," he said. "It's kind of scary."

"It's Latin?" Claire said.

"Obviously. Exit is Latin for he or she goes out," Marcus said, like it was the most normal thing in the world. "And exeunt is Latin for they go out. They use it when two or more characters leave."

Claire stared at him, then at her notebook, then at him again. "How do you know that?"

"My mom makes me read the footnotes." He shrugged and slid into the chair across from her, dragging her Riverside closer without asking. "So what's all this for, anyway?"

She told him: the paraphrasing assignment, tomorrow, out loud, graded. Marcus pulled the photocopy toward himself and read the witches' speech in a dramatic whisper that made a woman at the next table glance over. "Okay, so this part where the witches cook the stuff," he said, "the paraphrase could be, we'll preserve this potion in the cauldron until it's ready." He wrote it down, misspelling preserve twice before getting it right.

They split the speeches between them, trading lines back and forth. When they reached the end of the scene, Claire tapped the bracketed word with her pencil. "Exeunt," she said. "That's them, plural. Both witches, plus Hecate, plus everybody. They go out."

Marcus checked the stage directions against their notes, one scene at a time, and every single one matched. The overhead speaker crackled that the library would close in fifteen minutes. They gathered the papers fast, and Claire copied the two words onto her palm in smudged ink. At the door, Marcus held it open and said, "If Mrs. Pell makes you say the Latin part out loud tomorrow, do the witch voice."

"Fire burn and cauldron bubble," Claire croaked at him across the parking lot.

Penelope unrolled the climate map across the picnic table and weighted its corners with two flashlights and a bag of trail mix. Tomorrow night, back home, she had to stand up in geography class and explain how a monsoon forms and why rice farmers in South Asia depend on it, and right now she could not make the map cooperate. Tiny letter codes, Af and BWh and Am, were printed in the oceans and across the continents, and she had no idea what they meant. Her little brother, Marcus, leaned over her shoulder with a marshmallow stick still in his hand.

"What do the letters say?" he asked, poking at the Bay of Bengal.

"They say I'm going to fail," Penelope said, and he laughed, which was not helpful.

She pulled out her phone, which had one shaky bar of signal at the edge of the campground, and typed the codes in. The screen loaded slowly, like something dragging itself uphill. The letters, she read, were part of the Koppen climate classification, still used on climate maps today. It had been developed by Wladimir Koppen, a climatologist born in Russia who worked in Germany. She said the name out loud twice so it would stick.

"Koppen," Marcus repeated, chewing his marshmallow stick. "Sounds like a kind of cookie."

The code for the monsoon lands of South Asia was Am, and that was the piece she needed. She thought back to a demonstration her teacher had done in the fall, before the teacher announced she would retire at Christmas. She had set a hairdryer over a pan of sand and a pan of water, and the sand had heated fast while the water had stayed cool, and over the water a little wheel of paper had spun because air was rising there and pulling air in from the sand side. Penelope had understood it then, but standing at a picnic table she needed to test it herself, because tomorrow she would have to make thirty kids see a wind they could not see. She filled one pot from the water jug and left the other empty, set both in the sun on the table, and laid a strip of paper between them, pinned with a pebble so it could swing like a compass needle. Then she waited, drawing the monsoon arrows into her notebook, a symmetrical pair of curves, one pointing toward the land in summer and one reversing in winter, when the land cooled faster than the ocean and the flow turned around. Rice needed the summer flood of rain those onshore winds carried; without it, the paddies cracked dry.

After twenty minutes the paper strip trembled and drifted, gently but definitely, toward the empty pot, the hot dry one. Air over the hot pot was rising and air was creeping in to replace it. It was small, but it was real, and it meant her explanation was true at the scale of a kitchen pot and at the scale of a continent.

"Watch," she said to Marcus, and she cupped her hands and breathed warm air over the wet pot while he shaded the dry one with his jacket. The strip shifted again, wobbling back the other way.

"Did we just make a monsoon?" Marcus asked.

Penelope folded the map, careful with the corners, and grinned at the paper needle still swinging between the pots. "We just made a monsoon."

Elliot had recited the New Year prayer forty-one times in the courtyard of the temple, and he still stumbled on the same line. Behind him, in the hall with the red pillars, drums and gongs and cymbals crashed together, then stopped, then crashed again. His cousin Marcus poked his head around the door. "The lion keeps falling over," Marcus said. "Come watch."

Inside the hall, the lion costume lay crumpled on the floorboards like a pile of laundry. Two boys from the temple's youth group climbed out of it, one from the front and one from the back, and stood blaming each other. "You turned too early," said the boy from the head. "You were late," said the boy from the tail, which contradicted him so flatly that Elliot laughed before he could stop himself. The drum master, Mr. Lou, raised one hand and the noise died away. Elliot had never considered that a lion dance was done like this, two dancers inside one costume, one working the head and the other the tail, moving to the drums, gongs and cymbals. He had always assumed it was one very tired person.

He crouched by the fallen costume and had an idea. "Try counting," he said. "The drums give you a pattern. If the head moves on the beat and the tail moves on the same beat, you can't contradict each other, because you're both following the same thing." It was the same trick his grandmother had given him for the prayer: match the words to the rhythm of the bells, and the line you keep forgetting attaches itself to the sound. The two boys looked at each other, shrugged, and climbed back in.

The next run was not perfect. The lion wobbled, knocked over a folding chair, and sat down hard. But on the run after that, when the cymbals flared, the head rose and the tail followed in the same instant, and the lion leapt onto the bench by the incense burner as if it were buoyant, weightless, alive. Mr. Lou actually smiled, which Marcus whispered had never happened before in the history of the temple.

That evening Elliot stood in the courtyard with his grandmother, the paper lanterns glowing above the stone lions at the gate. He recited the prayer all the way through, riding the rhythm the way the tail had ridden the drumbeat, and did not stumble once. His grandmother folded her hands and nodded slowly. "Again," she said, "but this time with the bells."

Madison sat at her grandma's kitchen table with the school's lunch survey open on Grandpa's old laptop, the one that ran hot enough to send up a faint smell like vapor from the vent. The student council meeting was at seven, and she had promised the president she would bring an answer to one question: which grade actually voted for the later lunch? Six hundred students had filled out the survey, and the answers sat in three long columns called Grade, Answer, and Answer again, a wall of rows she could never count by hand.

"Grandpa used to say that spreadsheet could do the counting for you," Grandma said, setting down a mug of cocoa. "He never showed me how, though. He just grinned and clicked."

Madison clicked too. She found something called a pivot table, dragged Grade into the box labeled Rows, and a tidy list appeared: sixth, seventh, eighth. She dragged Answer into Columns, and across the top it read later lunch, earlier lunch, no opinion. The third column of Answer she dropped into Values, and the whole table filled itself in with counts, how many students in each grade gave each answer, row by row.

"There it is," she whispered. She could infer the rest without adding anything up. Eighth grade had picked later lunch by a mile, and sixth grade, her own grade, had mostly wanted it earlier. Her best friend Priya had spent a week telling everyone the sixth graders were the ones pushing for the change, and Priya was wrong. Madison saved the file, then sat back. Winning the argument would cost something, and she could already picture Priya's face.

"You look like your grandpa when he solved something," Grandma said, peering at the screen. "He'd have called that table exceptional."

At the meeting, Madison plugged the laptop into the projector before anyone could stop her. The president leaned forward, reading the rows. "So it's the eighth graders," she said slowly. "Huh. The whole plan was built around the sixth grade."

Madison's hand hovered over the keyboard. Priya was in the third row, arms crossed, waiting. "I can show the numbers," Madison said, "or we can talk about it first."

"Show them," said the president.

Madison looked at Priya one more time, then pressed the key that put the table on the wall.

The basement smelled like dust and orange soda, and one bare bulb swung whenever the furnace kicked on. Asher set his laptop on the ping-pong table beside his friend Dante's, between a shoebox of insulated wires from Dante's uncle's old electronics kit and a poster of a symphony conductor that had come with the house. Dante was already typing.

"Okay," Dante said. "You said you wanted a program that asks for a number and says if it's prime. So start with input."

Asher typed. His first attempt just printed "prime" for everything, including 9. He stared at the screen, then got a piece of scrap paper. "Nine isn't prime," he muttered. "So something in my loop is wrong. Three times three is nine, so my program should catch that." He read each line slowly, tracing with his finger, and found he had written `if number % 2 == 0` and then given up too early. Even numbers got flagged, but odd composites like 9 slipped through.

"So you have to try every divisor, not just two," Dante said, spinning a marker between his fingers.

"Right. From two up to, like, the square root of the number. If none of them divide it evenly, it's prime." Asher rewrote the loop with a flag variable he called `is_prime`, set it to True, and flipped it to False the moment a divisor worked. He ran it. Enter a number: 9. Not prime. He tried 7. Prime. He tried 97, 100, 51, which fooled him for a second until the program said not prime, and he checked: 3 times 17. The program was faster than he was.

While Dante tested more numbers, Asher pulled up their old Scratch project, the one where a cat collected coins and a score went up. Except the score wouldn't go up. The coin sprite had its own copy of the number that never changed. Asher clicked through the menus until he found it. The variable had been made "for this sprite only," so the coin had its own and couldn't touch the cat's.

"Try making it for all sprites," Dante said, leaning over. "Then every sprite can use it."

Asher deleted the old variable and created the score again, choosing "for all sprites" this time. He clicked the green flag, ran the cat into the coin, and watched the score climb from zero to one, then two.

Just then his phone buzzed. A text from his cousin Maya: "Did your prime thing work? Send me the code, I want to try 31." Asher grinned, copied the file, and typed back, "It works. And I fixed Scratch too. Come over Saturday."

Dante was already loading a harder challenge on his screen. "Ready for the next one?"

Asher cracked his knuckles and started typing.

The bus home from Marsh Creek Elementary had eleven minutes of road between the last stop and Edouard's, and he had decided those eleven minutes would be the new meeting room for the Chess Club. He stood at the front, holding his notebook open against a pole, and read from the page he had titled "Agenda."

"Item one," he said. "The problem of Marcus and Devon."

The two boys glared at each other from opposite seats. Marcus had accused Devon of taking the club's good clock, the one Edouard had saved four weeks of allowance to acquire, and Devon swore he had only borrowed it for his cousin's birthday party and brought it back with a cracked corner. Nobody had seen the crack appear. The club had been fighting about it for so long that Ms. Ruiz called it "chronic" and had threatened to shut the club down if they couldn't settle it themselves.

"I just want us to be friends again," Marcus said, arms crossed. "Can we just do that? Be friends again?"

Devon shrugged. "Fine. Friends."

Edouard wrote "friends again" in his notebook and felt uneasy, though he couldn't say why. It seemed too easy. He kept thinking about it while the bus rattled over the railroad tracks, and finally he flipped back a page. At his grandfather's church, when two neighbors quarreled, they didn't just say sorry. There was a meeting, and at the end each person agreed to specific actions they would each take, so each one knew exactly what he had promised. That was the part Edouard had thought was boring. Now it didn't seem boring at all. It seemed like the missing component, the piece that made "friends again" actually stick.

"Wait," Edouard said. "Marcus, what will you do tomorrow? Say the exact thing."

"Be nice to him, I guess."

"That's not a specific action. Say what, exactly."

Marcus blew out a breath. "Fine. I'll stop calling him Clock Thief at lunch. Out loud, anyway."

Devon looked at the floor. "I'll ask before I take anything from the club box. Every time. And I'll bring my dad's screwdriver Thursday to try to fix the corner."

They both said it again, slower, so Edouard could write it down word for word. He tore the page out, split it in half, and handed each of them the piece with his own promise on it. "Now you each know exactly what you promised," Edouard said. "Item two. Tournament snacks." He tapped his pen against the notebook and waited, but both boys were still reading their half-pages.

Marcus folded his and put it in his shirt pocket, patted it once, and said, "Thursday. Screwdriver. I'll hold you to it."

The card table sat under the big oak near the craft cabin, and Addison had claimed it every afternoon since Monday. Today three boys from her cabin had taken it over, and they had dragged Theo's cards away from him because, as Drew said, "slow players ruin everything." Theo had a stutter that came out worst when he was rushed, and everyone at the table knew it, which was exactly why they rushed him.

Addison stood a few feet away with her water bottle, watching. Last summer she had snapped at kids who teased her little cousin, and it had gone badly; the teasing just moved indoors and got quieter. This summer she wanted a different result, and she turned the problem over while she unscrewed the cap. If she made the boys feel accused, they would dig in. She needed a way to stop the game itself, not the players.

"You're dealing wrong," she said, walking over. "That's not how you deal for whist."

Drew looked up. "It's just cards."

"Whist has real rules," Addison said. "My grandpa plays it every Sunday, and he deals it two cards at a time, face down, clockwise. He says it has to be done according to Hoyle." She let the name sit there, and when Drew squinted at it, she went on. "Hoyle wrote the book. Edmond Hoyle. His book from 1742 set down the rules of whist, so when Grandpa says 'according to Hoyle,' he means following the rules exactly." She laid her hand flat on the deck. "So if you want to play here, you play it right, or you're just slapping cards around."

"Who even are you?" Drew said, but the boys at the table were already arguing about whether dealing two at a time was faster, and Theo had slid back onto the bench without anyone noticing him arrive. Somebody asked Addison to demonstrate the deal, and she did, slowly, so that Theo could see where each card landed.

By the time the bugs came out, they had played two full hands. Theo called trump twice, and though his words caught on the first one, nobody said anything, because everyone was busy counting tricks. Drew even asked Theo which suit to lead, which was more than Addison had hoped for. Walking back to the cabins in the fading light, she noticed the lettuce seeds she had planted in the camp garden had begun to germinate, tiny green loops pushing out of the soil. Something about that made her think of Theo at the table, quiet and steady now, no longer looking like he might bolt. The guilt she had carried around all last summer, watching her cousin get picked on, loosened a little and let go. The old oak's frail lower branches swayed as the evening breeze came through, and behind her she heard Theo call out, "Same table tomorrow?"

The book club met in the back corner of the library, where the radiator clanked and Mrs. Okafor's supply cart blocked half the window. Grayson spread his notebook on the table and slid his answer sheet toward Priya. On it, under "Theme of 'The Skylark,'" he had written one word: friendship.

"That's not a theme," Priya said. "That's a topic." She tapped the page with her pencil. "A topic is a subject a novel is about, like friendship. A theme is a full statement of what the novel says about that subject."

Grayson stared at his word. Last week he had skipped the reading and guessed on everything, and Mrs. Okafor had written "See me" in red pen, which he still hadn't done. Maybe if he'd actually read the story, he would know what it said about friendship instead of just slapping the word down like a label on a jar.

"Fine," he said. "So what does it say?"

"That's the part you have to figure out." Priya pushed the paperback across the table. "Try again."

He opened the story to the first page, where the fisherman's wife keeps a chipped blue vessel on the shelf and polishes it every morning even though it's empty. Grayson had skimmed right past that on his first attempt, back when the whole assignment had seemed like a barren stretch of busywork, nothing growing in it for him. Now he read slower. On page three, a bird lands near the window. On page five, the wife says the vessel belonged to her sister, "before she went away." Grayson sat up.

"Wait. The bird shows up three times before the sister is even mentioned. That's foreshadowing. The bird is like... her." He flipped pages to check, and there it was again, the skylark on the windowsill the morning the letter arrives. "And the empty vessel isn't just a jug. It's the space the sister left."

"So what's the theme?" Priya asked. "Make it a whole sentence."

Grayson wrote, erased, wrote again. "Friendship needs to be nurtured, or it becomes an empty space you keep polishing." He read it aloud, and Marcus, who had been drawing a dragon on his folder, actually looked up. Priya nodded slowly, the way she did when she was deciding whether to argue.

Mrs. Okafor came by and picked up the sheet. "Interesting," she said. "The author never says the sister was ever a friend. Read page two again." She set the sheet down and moved on toward the cart.

Grayson turned back to page two, finger on the first line, and Priya leaned over his shoulder.

"You copied that print line ten times?" Priya leaned over Henry's shoulder, laughing so hard she knocked over her can of root beer.

Henry stared at the laptop screen in the glow of Priya's basement string lights. He had come over hoping to build something impressive before Monday's coding club meeting, a program that asked for a number and printed whether it was prime. He had the prime part figured out: check whether the number divided evenly by anything from two up to the number itself. But his screen was a wall of identical print statements, one for each count of divisions he had found, copied and pasted until his eyes hurt.

"It worked, didn't it?" he said, though a flicker of guilt crept in, because it hadn't quite worked. When he tested the number 7, three of his print lines fired instead of one, and he couldn't tell which.

"That's a chronic problem with your code," Priya said, tapping the screen. "You paste the same line over and over, then one of them is wrong and you can't find it. There's a better way. Watch."

She deleted almost everything he had typed. Henry winced, but she was already typing something short: for i in range(1, 11): followed by one indented line.

"Try that first," she said. "Just make it print i. Run it."

He ran it. The screen filled with numbers, 1 through 10, one after another, and Henry felt the way he did when a magic trick got revealed and it turned out to be almost insultingly simple. "Wait. That's it? One line did all ten?"

"One line, ten times," Priya said. "A Python for loop runs its indented block once for each value, so for i in range(1, 11) runs that line ten times."

"Once for each value," Henry repeated, and the whole wall of pasted prints suddenly looked absurd to him. He thought about the mystery of the number 7, the three print lines that had fired. He couldn't see which line had gone wrong, but if the loop ran the same line for each value, then the loop itself could tell him. He could print i right next to the count, and the pattern of the numbers would expose the hidden culprit without him hunting through pasted copies.

"Give me the laptop," he said, already reaching for it.

He rebuilt the program in five minutes, the loop checking each possible divisor, then a single print statement at the end reporting prime or not prime. His hands were shaking a little as he typed 7 and hit enter. NOT PRIME, the screen announced. Henry frowned. He poked through the loop, and there it was: he had written a greater-than sign where an equal sign belonged, and the count was coming out wrong for the number 1. One fix, one run. PRIME.

"Yes!" He threw both fists in the air and nearly knocked the root beer off the table again.

"Now test nine," Priya said, arms crossed, grinning like she was trying to provoke him on purpose.

Henry typed 9 and hit enter. NOT PRIME. He checked it in his head, three times three. The program was right, and it was right every time, and it was short enough to actually read.

"We still have two hours before my mom drives you home," Priya said, sliding the laptop back toward him. "So. What number do we throw at it next?"

The porch boards of the meeting house were warm under Camille's bare feet, and beyond the carved doorway the valley lay green and fertile, stitched with sheep and a single winding river. She had the prayer folded in her back pocket, though she wasn't supposed to need it by Sunday. Her coming-of-age ceremony would be held right here on the marae, in front of everyone, and her part was a karakia she had to carry in her head, word by word, the way her grandmother had carried it before her. She kept forgetting the middle stanza. Every time she reached it, the words scattered like birds.

Hemi found her there after school, sweat-dark shirt sticking to his back. He was practicing the haka his kapa haka group would perform for the school welcome on Friday, and he wanted an audience. "Watch my stance," he said, dropping low, fists against his thighs. "I had to modify it. My knee." He launched into the chest-slapping, foot-stamping chant, and though Camille had heard Ka Mate a hundred times at rugby matches, she realized she had never once wondered what the words actually meant. She only knew they made the hair on her arms stand up.

"What are you saying?" she asked when he finished, breathless. "In the words, I mean."

"Ka mate, ka mate, ka ora, ka ora," Hemi said. "It was composed around 1820 by Te Rauparaha, the Ngāti Toa chief. He was hiding from enemies who were chasing him, and when he came out alive, he made the haka to celebrate surviving." He wiped his face with his shirt hem. "It's about being afraid and then not being dead. That's the whole thing."

Camille sat with that. She had always thought the haka was about power, about being terrifying, but underneath the stomping it was about hiding in the dark and coming out. She remembered, suddenly, being nine and refusing to speak at her grandfather's funeral because she was scared of crying in front of everyone, and how her mother had carried her sorry little note to the front instead. She had never decided whether that had been wisdom or cowardice, and she still couldn't. But Te Rauparaha had been chased and had hidden, and the hiding had not been the end of his story. That felt like something, though she couldn't have said exactly what.

She pulled the prayer from her pocket, looked at the middle stanza once, then folded it away and stood up. "Do it again," she said, "and this time I'll do the words with you." When Hemi shouted the first line, Camille's voice cracked on it, then steadied, and the sound they made together rolled out over the porch and down toward the river, which caught the late light and held it like a blade. Behind them, high on the ceiling of the porch, the old electric fan spun its slow propeller circles, pushing the warm air around and around.

On Sunday she would stand in that doorway with nothing in her pockets at all.

Lillian spread the agenda for the Science Club's first ever proper meeting across her kitchen table, weighting the corners with salt shakers so the paper wouldn't curl. Three members were coming to her house: Marcus, who had a hundred ideas an hour, Priya, who wanted to discuss the fundraiser, and Dexter, who nobody ever wanted in their group because he wore the same dinosaur shirt every single day and talked like a documentary narrator. She'd invited him anyway. Now she just had to keep the meeting from collapsing before it started.

The problem showed up in the first four minutes. Priya was explaining the bake sale budget when Marcus slammed his fist gently on the table, the way he did when an idea landed on him. "Wait. Wait. What if our fundraiser mascot was a capybara? Capybaras are the most chill herbivore on Earth. Everyone loves them. I'm thinking plush toys. I'm thinking a costume." Dexter opened his mouth, and Lillian knew exactly what was coming, because everyone at school did the same imitation of his voice, slow and floaty, like a nature film. She felt her face go hot on his behalf before anyone even spoke.

"Lillian," Priya said, pointing at the clock, "we're supposed to vote on the bake sale in ten minutes."

Instead of snapping at Marcus, which would only provoke him into defending the capybara for the rest of the afternoon, Lillian grabbed a sticky note and a pencil. She wrote capybara mascot? in her neatest letters and slapped it on the refrigerator door. "It's a parking lot," she said. "Off-topic ideas go there so we can discuss them later instead of derailing the current item." She'd found the trick in her mom's book about running meetings, and she'd been dying to try it.

Marcus tilted his head, considering the note like it was a strange artifact. Then, remarkably, he sat back down. Dexter raised his hand, which nobody had asked him to do, and said, "I move that we discuss the capybara after the budget vote." A motion. He knew meeting procedure, it turned out, better than all of them, probably from watching town council videos for fun. Priya seconded it just to be efficient.

They voted on the bake sale, chose lemon bars, and only then did Lillian peel the note off the fridge. "Parking lot time," she announced. Marcus launched into the capybara pitch, and Dexter interrupted, in his documentary voice, "Actually, capybaras are semi-aquatic. They nap in water. Sometimes birds sit on them." For once nobody made a face or whispered. Marcus leaned forward like Dexter was the most interesting person in the room, which, right then, he kind of was.

They voted the mascot down, seven plush toys to none, but made Dexter head of fact-checking for the whole club. Priya drew a little capybara on the corner of the agenda anyway, and when they passed around the plate of crackers, Dexter took two, symmetrical stacks, and said, "The herbivore snacks."

Lillian wrote parking lot on a fresh sticky note and put it in the drawer for next time.

Lydia had forty-three dollars in her savings account and a plan that would take five years, which felt roughly as long as the line outside the phone store she was standing beside. Her mother had offered a deal: if Lydia saved half the cost of the new phone, her mother would pay the other half. Lydia had asked the bank teller that morning which account earned more, and the teller had said the compound one, so Lydia had chosen it, though she couldn't have said why. Simple interest paid on what you deposited. Compound paid on what you deposited plus everything it had already earned, which meant the money made money on its own money, quietly, for years, without her doing anything.

She was working this out on a napkin at a food court table when her friend Dev slid into the seat across from her. He leaned over her scribbled columns and frowned.

"You're doing math at the mall," he said. "Voluntarily."

"Five years," Lydia said. "The simple account would give me the same flat amount every year. The compound one starts slower and then curves upward. By year five it's ahead by enough to matter." She tapped the napkin. "I can't see the curve. That's what bothers me. I have to trust it."

Dev stole one of her fries and pointed at the fruit stand two tables away. "You want to see something you can't trust, look at that. Strawberry smoothies are four dollars more this month."

They walked over. The stand's sign listed strawberry everything, and as they stood there, Lydia noticed the smoothie cart near the escalator, which hadn't sold strawberries a week ago. Beyond it, the yogurt place had a new strawberry banner. She counted three stands in one corridor selling the same fruit that had just gotten expensive.

"Wait," she said. "The price went up, and now there's more of it for sale everywhere?"

"That's supply," Dev said with his mouth full of stolen fry. "Price up, sellers pile in."

Lydia looked down the corridor at the three stands. None of them obstructed her view of the yogurt place, which was a small mercy, since the mall's newest tenant had apparently decided strawberries were worth the rent. She thought about her compound curve, invisible inside her account, doing whatever it did while she slept.

"So if lots of people sell them," she said slowly, "does the price come back down?"

Dev shrugged, being optimistic about nothing in particular. Lydia folded the napkin into her pocket, next to her phone money math, and headed back toward the bank. She wanted to see the teller's face when she asked whether the curve ever curved the other way.

Juliette set her laptop on the cafe table between a cold hot chocolate and her crumpled assignment sheet. The sheet said her history essay needed a thesis statement and a three-point outline before any drafting, and the essay was due tomorrow morning. She had four paragraphs of raw writing already, which was exactly the wrong order, and a little green bar at the bottom of her screen that said "Readability: Difficult."

"What's Difficult mean?" asked Marcus, sliding into the seat across from her with his own homework. He leaned over and squinted at her screen.

"It's rating my draft. Hard to read, I guess." She clicked the tiny question mark next to the bar. A help window opened and she read it silently, then out loud. "It uses the Flesch Reading Ease test, created by Rudolf Flesch. It scores how easy writing is to read using average sentence length and average syllables per word."

"So long sentences and big words drag the score down," Marcus said.

She wasn't sure she believed it, so she tested it. She copied her first paragraph into a new file and rewrote one monster of a sentence, forty-one words with "consequently" and "nevertheless" buried inside, into three short ones. The bar shifted from Difficult toward Average. Then she swapped "utilized" for "used." The bar moved again. It was like an invisible scale, and she was learning to read it by dropping weights on one end.

"Fine, but you still don't have a thesis," Marcus said. He didn't ridicule her draft exactly, but his eyebrows did something skeptical when he scanned it. "You've got four points in there, not three."

She found them herself, circling phrases on a napkin: the canal cut costs, it moved people faster, and it changed the towns along it. Three points. She wrote one sentence at the top of the napkin that held all three, and suddenly the paragraphs didn't seem like a swamp anymore. They were rooms in a house she could actually draw.

The fatigue hit her around paragraph three, that heavy-eyed blur where "economy" starts to look misspelled. She bought a second hot chocolate, cut the last long sentence in half, and watched the readability bar settle at Average, then edge into Fairly Easy. She should have felt only proud. Instead she stared at her original file, still open behind the new one, with its forty-one-word sentences and its stubborn "utilized," and felt a small ache, like she'd sanded something ornate down to pine.

Marcus packed up at closing time. "Read it to me," he said, standing in his jacket.

She read the thesis aloud, the clean one-sentence version. It was so simple it sounded like something a much younger kid might write.

"Wow," Marcus said. "Reads easy."

Juliette looked at the bar, glowing green, and then at the napkin covered in crossed-out complexity. "It's supposed to," she said. "That's the whole trick." She slid the ornate original into the trash folder and closed the lid before she could change her mind.

Samantha stood at the counter of Horizon Travel with two brochures spread in front of her and a graph printout pinned under her elbow. The agent, Ms. Delgado, had given her rainfall and temperature charts for the Sonoran Desert and the Amazon rainforest as homework, and tomorrow her class would debate which place their imaginary trip should go. Samantha wanted to win that debate, and she wanted to win it with numbers, not opinions.

"Look at this," she said, tapping the rainfall bars for the desert. "Almost nothing for ten months, then a short spike. The rainforest gets heavy rain every single month." Ms. Delgado leaned over the counter. "And temperature?"

"Desert swings wild. Boiling days, cold nights. Rainforest stays warm all year, barely changes." Samantha laid the two temperature lines side by side. "So the desert's line looks like a roller coaster and the rainforest's looks flat."

"That wasn't random," Ms. Delgado said, smiling. "I picked those two on purpose. They demonstrate the extremes better than any other pair."

Behind them, Samantha's father was hunched over a topographic map of a road near the rainforest lodge, part of the same trip package. He was a cyclist and he'd been quiet for five minutes, which meant trouble. "Sam, come look. There's a climb between the lodge and the river. The contour lines say we rise about 100 meters, and the map scale shows that happens over 500 meters of road. Is that rideable?"

Samantha pulled out her notebook. "You divide the rise in height by the horizontal distance." She wrote 100 over 500. "That's one fifth." She multiplied by 100. "It's a 20 percent grade."

Her father lowered the map. "Twenty percent. That's brutal. I'd be walking most of it."

"So don't take that road," Samantha said. She traced an alternate route on the map, a longer one that curved around the ridge. Her dad checked the contours, checked the scale, and let out a breath.

At home that evening, Samantha built her whole debate argument on the same foundation: the graphs showed the desert as extreme and the rainforest as steady, and steady meant predictable, and predictable meant a better trip. She practiced twice in front of the mirror, then marked her favorite line with a yellow highlighter.

At school the next morning, Marcus, her debate opponent, slapped his own desert poster on the board. "Desert wins," he announced, "because adventure."

Samantha held up her charts. "Numbers first."

Nevaeh sat down at the lab computer during study hall and typed her password for the eighth time. The snack-stand fundraising page rejected it again, which was a problem, because the whole spreadsheet of October sales lived on that site, and her tech project was due Friday. She wanted a bar chart of which snacks sold best, and she could not build it from memory. She only remembered that chips had done well and that someone had bought eleven granola bars.

She clicked the link that said "Forgot your password." It offered to let her set a new one. It did not offer to tell her the old one, which seemed rude at first. Why not just show it? She walked to the counter where Mr. Ruiz, the repair tech who fixed the school's laptops, was replacing a keyboard.

"They can't email me my old password," she said. "Is that just policy?"

"They store a hash," Mr. Ruiz said, not looking up from his screwdriver. "A scrambled one-way fingerprint, instead of the password itself. That's how the good sites do it."

Nevaeh stood there a second, working it through. One-way, like a fingerprint pressed into clay. You could compare a new print against the dent, but you could not climb back out of the dent to the finger. So the site could check whether what she typed matched, without ever keeping the real word. That meant her password was not hiding somewhere waiting to be found. It was gone, truly gone, and only the scrambled version remained. The irony hit her: she had spent ten minutes trying to recover something the website had never stored. She reset her password, downloaded the sales numbers, and got to work.

In the spreadsheet she typed the snacks down column A and the totals down column B, then clicked the empty cell at the bottom of column B. She tried "=SUM(" and dragged over the numbers from B2 to B7. The total, 214, appeared. To test it, she changed one number from 18 to 19, and the total ticked up to 215. So the formula was live, not a frozen number. She reversed the change, highlighted the whole table, and inserted a bar chart. The chips bar rose above everything else, and the granola bar stuck up like a toothpick next to it. She had assumed chips were the winner, and the chart proved her right, but the second-place result surprised her: fruit strips, not cookies.

Her friend Dev leaned over from the next computer. "Why's the fruit strip one so tall?"

"Beats me," Nevaeh said. "Maybe because Coach bans them at practice and everyone wants what they can't have." She dragged the chart bigger, so the chips bar stretched nearly to the top of the screen.

Lucas had half an hour before his grandmother's restaurant opened, and three things had to reach the table together: rice, curry, and flatbread. She refused to help with the timing. "A cook who cannot finish a meal at once," she said, tapping the big clock above the stove, "serves cold rice." So he stood in the hot kitchen with his notebook, writing numbers. Rice took twenty minutes. Curry took forty. Flatbread cooked in two minutes a piece, but the dough had to rest for fifteen. He worked backward from six o'clock, starting the curry first, then the rice, then the dough, and saving the flatbreads for last.

The curry needed onions, and that was where everything stopped. The cutting board sat on the end of a table with one short leg, so the whole surface tilted whenever he pressed down. He set an onion on it and reached for the knife, and the onion rolled straight off the board and bounced onto the floor. He picked it up, set it down more gently, and turned to grab a bowl. When he looked back, it had rolled again, off the edge and into the bin of potato peelings. The wobbly table wanted everything to slide toward the low corner, and the round onion had no way to stay put.

He thought about his grandfather then, and the camping trip two summers ago. They had chopped vegetables on a folding table by the lake, and Lucas remembered watching him cut an onion in half from top to root before slicing it, then laying each half flat side down. The halves had sat perfectly still on that uneven table while his grandfather's knife worked fast and even. At the time Lucas had thought it was just how old people did things, slow and systematic, one extra step that a kid would skip. His grandfather had even said, "You have to halve it first, top to root, or it runs away from you." Lucas had laughed and gone to look for frogs.

Now he washed the onion, cut it in half from top to root, and laid each half flat side down on the board. Neither one moved. He sliced carefully, and even when the table wobbled under his pressure, the halves stayed where he put them. He finished the onions in half the time the rolling ones had cost him, dropped them into the pot, and got the curry going at ten past five, right on schedule.

While the curry simmered, he started the rice and mixed the flatbread dough, setting it under a cloth to rest. He wiped down the board and thought about his grandfather again. Maybe he should have paid more attention that summer, instead of assuming every lesson was boring until it was needed. Or maybe that was just how learning went, and nobody could hurry it. He glanced at the clock, pressed a flatbread into the hot pan, and watched it bubble.

At six exactly, his grandmother came through the swinging door. She looked at the steaming pot, the fluffy rice, the stack of warm flatbreads, all of them ready together.
