She tore a piece of bread, scooped up curry, and ate it standing. Then she pointed her spoon at the cutting board, where one onion half still sat flat and unmoving, waiting for the next order. "So," she said, "the frogs were not worth it after all?"

Leo had until Sunday night to finish his chart, and the Buddhism column was still blank. His teacher wanted two religions side by side, each with its own answer to one question: what happens after we die? The Christianity side had been easy, because Grandma Ruth talked about heaven the way she talked about her garden, like it was a place she knew the route to. But the Buddhism side had nothing but a half sentence copied from a library book, and the book had to go back Monday morning.

He found Grandma on the porch shelling peas. "Do you know anything about Buddhism?" he asked. "The afterlife part?"

She tipped a handful of pods into her lap. "Mrs. Tran would know better than me. She's been my neighbor thirty years and I've never once asked her that question. Maybe it's time I did."

Mrs. Tran ran the little bakery on the corner, and Sunday afternoon was slow enough that she could sit with Leo at a corner table while her nephew watched the register. The whole shop smelled like sugar and warm dough. "You want to know what happens when we die," she said, "so you want to know about rebirth first. In Buddhism, we are born again and again, life after life, like a wheel going around."

"Forever?" Leo wrote wheel in his notebook.

"Unless it stops." Mrs. Tran folded her hands on the table. "It stops when you reach nirvana."

"Okay, but what makes the wheel keep going? Why doesn't it just stop by itself?"

She smiled like he had asked the right question instead of a dumb one. "Craving. And ignorance. Those are what keep the wheel turning. When you end the craving and the ignorance, you reach nirvana, and the cycle of rebirth ends. That is the whole of it."

Leo wrote fast, afraid the words would evaporate from his memory the way dream details did the moment he woke up. "So in my chart, Christianity says you go somewhere permanent, and Buddhism says you stop going anywhere at all. The wheel just... doesn't turn anymore."

"That's a good chart," Mrs. Tran said. "Better than most grown-ups could do."

By the time Grandma Ruth came to walk him home, the streetlights were on and Leo's hand ached from writing. "Did you get your answer?" she asked.

"I got a better question," Leo said. "I'm going to title the chart that." He held up his notebook so she could see the new heading, written large, underlined twice: How Does It Stop?

The gym smelled like floor wax and cold coffee, and posters of smiling candidates saturated the walls around the folding tables where people lined up to vote. Aria stood beside her grandfather, holding the homework sheet her teacher had assigned: read one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms and explain it in your own words. She had picked the sheet of paper out of a pile an hour ago because it looked short. Now she wished she had picked a longer one, because the short one made no sense.

"Section 3," she read under her breath. "Every citizen of Canada has the right to vote in an election of members of the House of Commons or of a legislative assembly."

"You're muttering," her grandfather said. He was next in line.

"I have to explain it. In my own words. To the whole class." She looked up at the sign above the registration table. It said who could vote: Canadian citizens, eighteen or older, living in the riding. Aria stared at it. The sign didn't mention the Charter at all. So where did the right actually come from? Was it from the sign, or from something behind the sign?

She tested her idea the only way she could think of. She walked to the woman at the registration table, a gray-haired lady with a lanyard, and asked, "If the sign says who can vote, does the sign decide?"

The woman shook her head. "The sign is just a reminder. Section 3 of the Charter gives every Canadian citizen the right to vote in elections for the House of Commons and the provincial legislatures. That's what decides."

Aria wrote fast, then stopped. "Wait. Provincial too? Not just federal?"

"Provincial legislatures too," the woman said, and pointed at a voter heading toward a booth. "You could ask him. He's here for the provincial one, not the federal."

The man grinned. "There's more than one kind of election, kid. Same right covers both."

Back in line, Aria tried the words out loud, quietly, then rewrote them twice. When her grandfather came out of the booth, she read it to him in the parking lot, her breath fogging in the October air. "So the Charter, Section 3, means if you're a citizen, voting is a right you have, not a favor someone hands you, and it counts for the big federal election and for your province's legislature too. Conventional rules, like the sign, just tell you the details of how."

Her grandfather zipped his coat. "Say that Monday. Word for word."

She folded the paper into her pocket, right beside the stub he let her keep, the one with the little pencil smudge on it.

Brayden's geography grade had dipped to a C-minus, and Mr. Okoye had offered one way out: a project comparing the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs. Brayden wanted the extra credit badly, because his father had said no basketball tryouts until the grade came up. So on Saturday he spread two printed graphs on his grandfather's kitchen table, along with a folded topographic map of the hills where Grandpa planned to take him hiking the next morning.

"Sixty millimeters of rain in one month," Brayden said, tapping the rainforest graph. "The desert gets that in a whole year, maybe." The desert's rainfall bars were short stubs, some barely visible, while the rainforest's rose like a wall every single month. He wrote in his notebook that the two places almost seemed to mimic each other in reverse, one drowning and one starving for water.

Grandpa leaned over the topo map instead, running a thick finger along a wiggly brown line. "I want the trail that stays on this one," he said. "It goes all the way around the hill."

"Why that one?" Brayden asked. He had assumed Grandpa just liked the shape.

"Because it's a contour line," Grandpa said. "Every point on it sits at the same height above sea level. Stay on it, and you never climb."

Brayden didn't fully believe that. A line could wander anywhere. So while Grandpa made sandwiches, Brayden tested it, tracing the brown line with his fingertip, following every wiggle across a gully and around a spur. It curled the whole way around the hill and closed back on itself, and next to it the map's legend confirmed the height: 2,400 feet. On the other side of the same hill ran a second brown line, labeled 2,800. He put his finger between them and understood that the whole ring of the lower line stood level, and the trail on it would be flat.

At school on Monday, Brayden stood up with his graphs and a surprise. "I picked stations on purpose," he told the class. "The desert one is in a valley bottom, and the rainforest one is on a mountain slope. But when I checked the maps, rainfall didn't care about height. The valley was still dry and the slope was still soaked. What mattered was the rainfall bars, month after month." He had started the weekend thinking the mountains near the rainforest must be the wettest spot on Earth, just because they were high. Now he had changed his mind: height made the trails, but rain made the climate.

Mr. Okoye asked one question about the temperature curves, and Brayden answered it, pointing out how the desert swung between hot days and cold months while the rainforest barely moved. After class, Mr. Okoye wrote A-minus at the top of the rubric and slid it across the desk.

"Tell your grandfather the contour line trick worked," he said.

Brayden folded the paper into his back pocket and texted his dad: Tryouts on Friday?

Sophie had been staring at the same blinking cursor for twenty minutes. Her assignment was due Monday: a short story with dialogue, punctuated correctly, and a climax the reader could actually feel. She had a girl, a storm, and a lost dog in her head, but every time she tried to write the first line, she rewrote it four times and deleted it five.

"Maybe you're doing it in the wrong order," said her brother Marcus from the doorway, chewing a granola bar. He was ten and annoyingly calm about most things. "When I build Legos, I sort the pieces before I snap anything together."

Sophie frowned. "Stories aren't Legos."

"Suit yourself." He wandered off toward the kitchen.

She looked at the blank page again and wondered if there was something to what he'd said. What if she stopped trying to generate perfect sentences and just wrote down what happened, in ugly little notes? She opened a fresh document and typed: girl hears thunder. dog missing. search in rain. found under porch. She added dashes and bullets, no punctuation rules at all, and it took two minutes. Somehow the whole shape of the story was sitting there on the screen, and she hadn't written one actual sentence yet.

Then something clicked. Planning what happened and wording it were two separate jobs, and she'd been trying to do both at once. Now that the plan existed, she could ask herself which scene was the biggest, and it was obvious: the moment under the porch. That was her climax, so everything before it had to build toward it and everything after had to cool down. One factor in her earlier panic, she realized, was that she hadn't known where the story was going, so every sentence felt like it might be the wrong one.

She wrote the dialogue next, checking her rules. "Biscuit," Meg called, her voice cracking against the thunder. Comma inside the quotes, she thought, and felt a small, satisfying spark. She read the whole story aloud, pretending to be an impartial judge who had never met the writer, and cut two sentences that dragged.

Marcus appeared again, reading over her shoulder without asking. "Hey, the dog's name is Biscuit. Like my granola bar."

Sophie looked at the screen. She hadn't noticed. She saved the file, leaned back, and said, "Then tomorrow I'm naming a character Granola Bar, and you can't stop me."

Grandpa's laptop sat open on the kitchen table next to a mug that said WORLD'S OKAYEST EMPEROR, a joke from his days managing a hardware store. Simon had claimed the laptop all morning to build his Scratch game, where a predatory shark chased a little orange fish across the screen. Every time the fish touched a bubble, Simon wanted the score to go up by one, and when the score reached ten, the shark was supposed to speed up. He had a loop that moved the shark forever, and an if-then block that checked whether the score was greater than nine, but the score stayed stuck at zero.

"Grandpa, the bubbles pop but nothing counts," Simon said. Grandpa was in the hallway stuffing pink foam strips around the window frame to insulate the drafty old house, so he only grunted. Simon dragged the bubble sprite onto the stage and clicked it himself. The fish swam through it, the bubble vanished, and the score did not change.

He tried a test. He deleted the if-then block, then deleted the part that hid the bubble, and made the fish touch the bubble in the simplest script he could build: when fish touches bubble, change score by one. The score jumped to one. So the counting worked. Then he put the bubble script back inside the loop that moved the shark, and the score froze again. The loop, he realized, was restarting the bubble script before the fish ever got there. He moved the score block out of the shark's loop and gave it its own forever loop, watching the stage like a hawk.

The fish touched the bubble. The score read one, then two, then five. At ten, the if-then block kicked the shark into a faster glide and Grandpa's shark-themed screensaver behind them suddenly displayed, of all things, a Roman emperor being chased by a lion. Simon laughed so hard he nearly knocked over the mug, and he saved the project twice.
